titleFa: کتاب The Sound and the Fury
author: William Faulkner
introFa: کتاب «The Sound and the Fury» نوشته William Faulkner یکی از منابع ارزشمند و معتبر برای یادگیری زبان انگلیسی در سطح C2 است. این اثر با ساختاری منسجم و غنی، شما را در تسلط بر واژگان و درک مطلب یاری می‌کند.
readingTipsFa: پیش از مطالعه هر بخش از کتاب «The Sound and the Fury»، نگاهی سریع به تیترها و ساختار آن بیندازید.
واژگان و اصطلاحات جدید را در زمینه و بافت جمله یادداشت کنید تا در حافظه بلندمدت تثبیت شوند.
پس از پایان هر فصل، نکات کلیدی و آموخته‌های خود را مرور کرده و به زبان خود خلاصه کنید.

content: Chapter One The Phenomenon of Death 1. Max Scheler Max Scheler is a philosopher whose thought embraces an incredible variety of subjects (Bershady 8). The main pillars of his thought were the theory of values, phenomenology of emotions, philosophy of religion, and sociology of knowledge. However, as Scheler himself stated, there was always one simple but fundamental question that raised his philosophical awareness, i.e., “what is man?” (qtd. in Meyerhoff xii), or, in other words, “what is the human being?” (TM 6). This seems to be the legacy of Rudolf Eucken, the first moral mentor who influenced the later phenomenologist (Bershady 6; Coser 7). In his “Man and History” Scheler clearly explains why the above-mentioned query is the key to his work: “In the ten thousand years of history, we are the first age in which man has become utterly and unconditionally ‘problematic’ to himself, in which he no longer knows who he is, but at the same time knows that he does not know” (qtd. in Meyerhoff xii). The essay “Ordo Amoris,” inspired by one of Pascal’s Thoughts (1670),2 appears to contain Scheler’s reply to the above-stated question: “Whoever has the ordo amoris of a man has the man himself” (100). Thus, the Schelerian “man, before he is an ens cogitans or an ens volens, is an ens amans” (“Ordo” 110), whose heart, filled with love, shapes the image of the world. What is crucial here is the direction of this affection, for this is “not the love that the Other owes, but rather the love of the Other” (Barber 157) that calls to attention.3 Not to mention the fact that social emotions, like love or sympathy, ought to be kindled in our every glance at the person, in Scheler’s epistemology the very act of perception already involves ardent feelings toward the Other (Ranly 76). Moreover, this particular emphasis laid on the individual being near me is further visible in the words Scheler uses in his writings. He opts for the person and the spirit, instead of the self and the soul, respectively (Kelly 112), 2 Pascal’s thoughts 277 and 282 in section IV (Pascal on-line). 3 To examine Scheler’s notion of love, see Karol Wojtyła Ocena możliwości zbudowania etyki chrześcijańskiej przy założeniach systemu Maksa Schelera (91-97).

18 Chapter One preferring the terms participation and co-performance to union, as well (Vacek 175-176). It is also known that Scheler’s explications may sometimes display different shades of meaning or even vary in different works (Bershady 35; Kuderowicz 333; Meyerhoff xi).4 In fact, the philosopher himself admits that he has a tendency to shift his ideas (Scheler “Postawa” 73), calling his philosophy “the philosophy of the open hand” (qtd. in Coser 5), which seems to reflect this habit. As Coser maintains, when Scheler let new concepts overcome his mind, this sometimes resulted in contradictions (5). However, the thinker was conscious of the disorder in his works, which nota bene he apologized for in the preface to the first publication of Formalism in Ethics and Non-Formal Ethics of Values (1916) (TM 59). Nevertheless, with his mind “tossing and turning,” as his friend Ernst Robert Curtius said (qtd. in TM 73), Scheler does not only try to protect human life. His goal is to protect the non-exchangeable and outstandingly unique value of the person (Langan 127),5 obviously implying the relevance of the Other over the value of oneself (Sweeney 106). For Scheler this is an idea that swims against a current in the Western society, in which “public inertia vis à vis death and afterlife is motivated by the contemporary moral tenor in the human race” (TM 139). As Scheler shows in Ressentiment (1912), people have started rating highly the least significant values of utility and senses, and that has brought about “egoism and fear of death [which] are signs of a declining, sick, and broken life” (90). In the 1927 note “For the Conclusion of the Anthropology,” written one year before his death, the philosopher confirms his stance, stating that “modern angst of death… is a token of an impoverished life” (qtd. in TM 297-298), which may be purified only by letting death squeeze into one’s thoughts and have the same status as life does. 4 See Max Scheler: The Man and His Work by John H. Nota, who shows how Scheler’s philosophical thought shaped throughout his life. To learn more about Scheler’s phenomenology, one may also see Jan Krokos Fenomenologia Edmunda Husserla, Aleksandra Pfändera, Maxa Schelera. 5 Scheler’s “The Structure of Values and Their Historical Variations,” which is the fragment of Formalism in Ethics and Non-Formal Ethics of Values. Also see Ron Perrin Max Scheler’s Concept of the Person, chapter 5 “The Person” (87-108), and Stephen F. Schneck Person and Polis: Max Scheler’s Personalism as Political Theory, where the author presents a table “Parallel Typologies Associated with Origin of the Person,” which, in an appealing way, shows Scheler’s concept of personhood (55).

The Phenomenon of Death 19 With the belief that the West may learn more from the East (Barber 157), Scheler favors the attitude cultivated by Eastern traditions.6 The thinker especially values the wisdom of Buddha, whom he recognizes as “the great teacher of death” (MS 98). According to Scheler, Buddha announced that the end of the eternal journey of the soul is achievable by entering the state of nirvana. This basically meant admitting, against all the traditional thinking at that time,7 that nothing is stable or ever-lasting, but quite the opposite – everything passes away and terminates its existence with death (S 71; “Love” 151).8 And for Scheler this is exactly the fact that Western dwellers must be reminded of again and again. Scheler’s first attempts to frame the concept of death may be discovered in his 1911/12 work (TM 295). Later he delivered a 1912/13 lecture entitled “Die Idee des Todes und das Fortleben,” which, although mentioned in Formalism in Ethics and Non-Formal Ethics of Values, was not published until 1933 when Maria Scheler edited the first volume of his collected works, and altered the original title of the text for “Tod und Fortleben,” i.e., “Death and Afterlife” (Frings E-mail 15 Mar.). In the academic year 1923/1924, Scheler gave a series of lectures on the nature of death entitled “Das Wesen des Todes” (Węgrzecki xi). Afterward, the thinker found the subject of death more and more thought- provoking, which may be traced in some references in Schriften aus dem Nachlass. Philosophische Anthropologie (TM 295; Węgrzecki xi). That he was engrossed in the issue in question is also supported by Maria Scheler, who maintains that in the last year of his life Scheler was intuitively conscious of his dying (Mader qtd. in Węgrzecki xi). However, as Frings claims, the notion of demise in Scheler’s writings has not been researched frequently (Frings E-mail 6 See Scheler “The Meaning of Suffering” (98-106); “Love and Knowledge” (148-151); “Wzory i przywódcy” (225-226). Moreover, while writing about the exemplars of the person (there are five: the saint, the genius, the hero, the leading mind of the civilization, and the artist), Scheler alludes to the models that are recognized as the most proper to follow. In Western culture this is the hero whom Scheler personifies as the hunter, whereas in Eastern culture the right model is represented by the wise man, the embodiment of patience (TM 76-80). 7 Bowker, quoting Digha Nikaja, proves that Buddha, after his awakening, was reluctant to share his revelations with people as he knew it would be too difficult for them to understand the state of nirvana and to accept the final termination of everything (198- 199). 8 To better comprehend why Max Scheler appreciated Buddha so much, see John Bowker’s study concerning the perspective on death in Buddhism (195-236).

20 Chapter One 20 Jan.), and “Death and Afterlife” remains Scheler’s only essay on the phenomenology of death (TM 295).9 Scheler’s most complex ideas concerning death are discussed at length in “Death and Afterlife,” yet the study would not be thorough if one did not commence with the essay “The Meaning of Suffering” (1916). The essay should be treated as a prelude to the critical analysis, because in this work Scheler stresses that pain not only resembles death but is its herald: the presence of pain simply awakens our thinking of quietus. Consequently, if every suffering may be regarded as “a death in miniature, a sign of death,” in Bershady’s translation (MS 89), or as “microdeath” in Schuback’s translation (6), one cannot omit the issues referring to pain itself. The human nervous system sends a great number of various signs, amongst them pain. Thanks to this pain one is aware of oneself, since every emotion has “a meaning” or “a sense.” “This emotion presents objective evaluations of states of affairs, of an activity or certain fate that may befall us, or of an anticipated value of such an event” (MS 82). To illustrate his arguments more clearly, Scheler presents the reader with the picture of a person standing before an abyss. The insight into the precipice arouses the feeling of dread, strong enough to prevent one from stepping any further and to enable one to deal with the situation properly. At the end of life, we will all meet the same death preceded by pain, and therefore the presence of suffering should capacitate us to better attend to the impending fate. “The purely sensational and objective aspect of pain and suffering are equally factual for every living person, and this is the inescapable destiny of all,” the German thinker claims (MS 83-84, emphasis added). It should be stressed here that for Scheler a particular feeling, no matter if positive or negative, may be analyzed on various “deep levels of feeling”10 that form the hierarchy and obviously refer to Scheler’s theory of values. Regardless of the probable kinds of suffering, there is one concept inseparable from all of them, i.e., the notion of sacrifice. In spite of many conceivable connotations the 9 “Death and Afterlife” still has not been translated into English (Frings E-mail 20 Jan.), therefore the work which is scrutinised in the following analysis is a Polish translation of “Tod und Fortleben,” translated from German by Adam Węgrzecki as “Śmierć i dalsze życie.” All English fragments of “Death and Afterlife” appearing in the text are my translations of “Śmierć i dalsze życie.” If I quote a given fragment in italics and I mark it with “emphasis added,” this means that I changed a type of an original text. 10 In the case of pain, the levels of feeling are specified as a sensation (e.g., pain felt in one part of the organism), a vital feeling (sensed in the whole body), a psychic feeling (brought about by one’s imagination), and a purely spiritual, religious-metaphysical feeling (e.g., pain felt as a prick of conscience) (MS 85).

The Phenomenon of Death 21 idea might bring in, the Schelerian sacrifice takes place when one has to destroy the goodness standing lower axiologically in the hierarchy of values in order to gain the goodness that is there in a higher position (MS 86). Therefore, in Ressentiment, in his polemic with Nietzsche,11 Scheler talks about the possible renunciation of “lower forms for higher forms of life,” or even about abandoning “individual life for collective life” (107). Nevertheless, the sacrifice Scheler means has nothing in common with preference, as in the case of choosing the lesser of two evils, or deciding on slighter instead of greater pain, for it would only indicate a mere calculation of the “costs,” i.e., ressentiment. It is neither algophilia, since deriving pleasure from it is simply out of the question. Further, sacrifice is always “for something,” which implies annihilating some good which cannot be regained, in order to make higher values come into being (MS 87-88). Accordingly, finitude for Scheler is the beneficial sacrifice of present life for the new one to come. Viewed as such, death becomes an “innovator” or a “revolutionary power,” because, like in the case of uprisings, its occurrence revitalizes existence (Scheler qtd. in TM 296). Scheler also indicates that one condition must be met to let sacrifice occur. There must exist an “ontological relationship” between part and whole, and what the philosopher understands by this is the situation in which individual parts work and sacrifice for the whole that, conversely, dwells in its parts (MS 88). In this sense, a human being may be regarded both as a whole, i.e., as a unity in which various cells and systems co-operate closely, and as a part of a particular social group, of a given nation and of the world for which each entity performs a provided role (MS 88-89). In addition, the thinker tells the difference between the organic whole and the mechanical one. He clearly opts for the former, as it is similar to a living organism. According to Frings, the organic whole is marked by three features completely distinguishing it from the mechanical one: firstly, it is endowed with the energy that stimulates its growth; secondly, it is able to move on its own without an extra supplied source of energy; and thirdly, it grows old, which results in its dying (TM 157). In Scheler’s opinion one of the crucial roles fulfilled by every human being as an organic part for the whole world is the one performed at the moment of death, which stands in strict opposition to the standpoints held by the philosophers who came after Scheler. For example, in his 1970 article “Death,” Thomas Nagel regards demise as evil (68). He defines the issue in question as nothing but “an abrupt cancellation of indefinitely extensive possible goods” 11 Nietzsche used the term “ressentiment” in the work On the Genealogy of Morals (1887). Ressentiment is Nietzsche’s main concept in his discussion of master morality and slave morality with which it is associated (Coser 21).

22 Chapter One (68). Interestingly, what the American philosopher understands by “goods” is not possessions but senses or thoughts (63). Elias Canetti’s opinion is even stronger, when in The Secret Heart of the Clock (1987) he execrates death, whose acceptance amounts to killing (qtd. in Steiner 17). The cited opinions exemplify what is popularly known as the deprivation theory discussed by Fred Feldman, who summarizes its main point. He states that death is simply destructive in a sense that it strips the entity of “intrinsic value” (139). Every individual would be happier if it never occurred, since one could benefit from more goods in this way (144). Thinking of finitude as misfortune is an approach unacceptable for Scheler. For the German philosopher death ought to be viewed from the point of the whole population, because only then it appears to be the blessed renunciation to preserve the human race, to develop it, and in consequence, to lift it up to the upper level of civilization. As he states in “The Meaning of Suffering:” “Death demands a natural self-sacrifice of the individual for the procreation and advancement of the species. This is the ‘sacrifice’ that surrenders one life for more and automatically higher life” (89). Definitely, the opinion echoes the words of Miguel de Unamuno, whom Scheler recognized as an authority (Kelly 109), and whose thoughts in Tragic Sense of Life (1913) substantially deepen our understanding of Scheler’s sacrifice: “In love and by love we seek to perpetuate ourselves, and we perpetuate ourselves on the earth only on condition that we die, that we yield up our life to others” (159). Additionally, Scheler discusses the case of passing away at an advanced age. He claims that death treated as a sacrifice should remain synonymous with “harvest” (qtd. in TM 295), or as Frings elucidates further, with “a feast of accumulation and the giving away of what individual life had gained” (TM 295). In other words, one is to lead a genuine and meaningful existence, which especially at an elderly age is a gift donated to the future generations.12 In light of the above arguments, Scheler establishes a direct correlation between pain, sacrifice and death. Whenever we feel any kind of distress or soreness, we are supposed to recognize it as the primary sensual manifestation of finitude, since it represents “a death in miniature, a sign of death, a sacrifice of part of the organism for the preservation of the whole” (MS 89). As a matter of fact, there is truly nothing remarkable about the statement, because this 12 As it will be shown later, for Scheler, with every single act, one has fewer years to live, whereas the mind grows crossing boundaries by gaining more and more freedom (Frings Lifetime 104-105), which may also indirectly support the above-mentioned argument for death as a harvest.

The Phenomenon of Death 23 appears to be a natural cause of events. The controversial issue seems to be raised when Scheler declares that both pain and death are derived from love. The act of procreation is acknowledged by Scheler to be “the first origin of death” (MS 93) – when two people give a child a gift of life13 at the same time they condemn the child to death.14 As Unamuno states, “it is death, that lovers perpetuate upon the earth” (160). Scheler’s argument is adequately explained by Schuback, who claims that birth and growth represent death, because they denote “the solitude of a non-transferable destiny” of a given person preserving paradoxically the continuity of life (5). Frings also helps us understand the issue when he clarifies that in every stage of life, either it is birth, growth, maturity, decline, or death, Scheler observes an unceasing wave of “becoming- unbecoming” characteristic of impulsion, which is vital energy discovered in both an individual and in the universe (Scheler qtd. in TM 141, 186-187). Permeated with the ever fluctuating impulsion, the Schelerian existence rises and falls interchangeably, since, as Frings sums up, for Scheler “in growing, life also declines and dies; in declining, it also grows” (TM 141), which mirrors enantios (from Greek “opposite,” “figuratively antagonistic”), signifying two opposite phenomena forming a totality that also for Roland Barthes is not a category with two reflections, but the unified one (Lektury 159). Accordingly, love paradoxically resembles the trigger for pain and death, because “as the motive force of each new unison in space and of all propagation in time, love establishes the necessary conditions of sacrifice, which are pain and death” (MS 90-91). To illustrate this point Scheler draws the picture of Janus, a Roman god of gates and doors, the double-faced head, each looking at the opposite direction and representing two sides of life, the positive and the negative, the beginning and the end. If there is love and unity, analogously there must be pain and death, and what is essential here is that it should be grasped not only by intellect, but first of all by the heart. Equally important is the fact that Janus turns out to bear the symbol of renunciation, because “sacrifice embraces both the joys of love and the pain of giving up life for what one loves” (MS 91). Although it is possible to analyze the associations of pain, suffering and sacrifice far more thoroughly, it is time to proceed to Scheler’s fundamental essay on death: “Death and Afterlife.” The thinker touches upon the notion of the 13 In Istota i formy sympatii, Scheler suggests that conceptio is not purely the result of parents’ will; in the metaphysical sense there also exists a “creative act of omni-life” (“twórczy akt wszechżycia”), which causes a child to appear (180, my translation). 14 In Confrontations with the Reaper Fred Feldman calls the act of conception “a life-or- death decision” in a different sense. When a couple decides to give birth to a child, they give him/her life; if not, a child will not live, which does not amount to demise, but in a way resembles dying (190).

24 Chapter One human end when he attempts to prove that it is not the development of science or philosophy that is responsible for expiring religions and fading faith in afterlife in Western European culture. As supported by Parvis Emad, Scheler claims we should blame it on people’s approach to death itself (68), which involves rooting out the awareness of death from consciousness (S 67, 71). Seeing people that ignore finitude, Scheler strives to divert common thinking toward the right route again, examining, as Frings concludes, three fundamental assumptions that underline the nature of dying: firstly, “death is an intuitive certainty during everyone’s life time,” secondly, it is “an act within the process of life,” and thirdly, “just as consciousness in its form of the person can ‘swing beyond’ the lived body experiences during one’s life time, so the person also can swing beyond the body’s remains (Leichnam) during the act of dying and after death” (TM 295).15 Bearing these things in mind, Scheler regards the reinterpretation of the subject of death as indispensable, since people have lost their identity mainly by discerning expiration merely as a potential future event, which strips them of further experiences (Kelly 111). For the “Catholic Nietzsche,” as Troeltsch called Scheler16 (qtd. in Bershady 12; Coser 9), this deprivation theory, as it is called today, is nothing else but an erroneous hypothesis. As for the first assumption, Scheler is conscious of the fact that nowadays our general knowledge of dying stems exclusively from our observations of the external world and from other people’s experience. And although the philosopher endorses the possibility, he clarifies that epistemologically there are two ways of examining the phenomenon of death: from the inside, in one’s consciousness, and from the outside, watching people, animals and plants (S 71, 74). Assessing the former way as more apposite, Scheler asserts that one would be aware of the aging process and death even though the one was the only person who inhabited the world (S 74).17 Therefore, by studying just the appearance, a person would be able to infer the approach of finitude, only observing the changes of one’s body, such as the worsening state of health, wrinkles and gray hair (Emad 71). It would even be possible to derive the essence of death from the moment when one, exhausted, feels the need to lie down and fall asleep. 15 Frings mentions “an intuitive certainty” of death as the second point, and death as “an act within the process of life” as the first one (TM 295). The order has been changed, because this is the sequence Scheler follows in the essay. 16 Vacek claims that Scheler was called this way, because he modified the wide scope of values proposed by Nietzsche, tinging it with the Christian point of view (163). 17 This resembles Scheler’s “an absolute Robinson Crusoe,” who, according to the philosopher, can feel a bond with a community, although he would never meet other people (Frings Max 139; E-mail 6 Oct.).

The Phenomenon of Death 25 Whether we agree or not, Scheler, nevertheless, maintains that one could totally ignore this empirical knowledge. The thinker believes one could still discern that something like aging and death take place, making only the phenomenological analysis in one’s consciousness. In other words, in every phase of life, hypothetically as the only being alive, every person would be cognizant of the impending end of existence a priori, which Langan, explaining Scheler’s idea, decodes in this way: “A signification is termed ‘a priori’ when it offers itself to intuition as evident, without its having to be predicated of a particular object. It cannot be known ‘better’ or ‘less well,’ but rather is either seen, or not seen” (125). Thus, long before the actual expiration, it is possible to “spot” death by focusing only on one’s life perceived as the process that one carries out phenomenologically in one’s consciousness exclusively (S 75, 78). To prove the first above made assumption that underlines the nature of dying, Scheler observes each living “supra-temporal” creature (TM 189) in the objective measurable time18 (S 79). As a result, the person’s existence is synonymous with the process divided into three “phases” (Erstreckungen), translated by Frings as “horizons” in The Mind of Max Scheler (189), or “elongations” in Lifetime (105). The phases are as follows: the immediate past, the immediate present and the immediate future (Emad 70).19 Further, the 18 There are two kinds of time for Scheler: objective and absolute. In objective time a person, as a part of an enormous, quantifiable world, can do very little, being just “a thinking dot,” whereas in absolute time, which Scheler pays much more attention to, a person actively participates in the creation of the world, influencing its evolution (Frings Lifetime xvii-xviii). 19 As Sweeney suggests, there may be a confluence between Husserl and Scheler in terms of the notion of “horizon” (103), although, with reference to The Crisis of European Sciences and Transcendental Phenomenology, Husserl ascribes to it a wider sense, using the term in various contexts, e.g., “the horizon of the life-world” (138), “the world-horizon,” “a horizon for existing objects” (143), “internal horizon” and “external horizon” of perception (162). Also see Husserl Wykłady z fenomenologii wewnętrznej świadomości czasu (65, 79, 172). Nevertheless, one of the fragments in Husserl’s work displays a strong affinity with Scheler’s understanding of the word: “the particular object of our active consciousness, and correlatively the active, conscious having of it, being directed toward it, and dealing with it -- all this is forever surrounded by an atmosphere of mute, concealed, but cofunctioning validities, a vital horizon into which the active ego can also direct itself voluntarily, reactivating old acquisitions, consciously grasping new apperceptive ideas, transforming them into intuitions. Because of this constantly flowing horizonal character, then, every straightforwardly performed validity in natural world-life always presupposes validities extending back, immediately or mediately, into a necessary subsoil of obscure but occasionally available reactivatable validities, all of which together, including the present acts, make up a single indivisible, interrelated complex of life” (The Crisis 149).

26 Chapter One horizons are respectively linked with corresponding acts such as immediate remembering, immediate perceiving and immediate expecting, which are in fact the terms pointed out by Saint Augustine in his division of time into three domains presented in The Confessions.20 All these horizons and the acts assigned to them constitute “the essential structure of human temporality” (Emad 72), and embrace the whole, complete range of experiences and events, which Scheler calls life. Consequently, one comes down to the equation in objective time: life “(the complete range),” at any moment of existence, equals “(the past horizon) + (the present horizon) + (the future horizon)” (S 78-79). When one is born, the comprehensive range on the graph of life commences growing unremittingly, and it extends constantly as one gains new experiences. The same applies to the past horizon, because what one has experienced becomes immediately part of the past, enriching a store of our memories. The situation is reversed in the case of the future horizon. At the moment of birth, it begins diminishing steadily, as a number of events one is to undergo reduces with every minute when the following episode is behind us. It continues till the future horizon reaches the zero point. Meanwhile, as Scheler puts it, the present horizon gets more and more “squeezed” between the past and the future, since, as life goes on and there is less time left, one has fewer and fewer possibilities of experiencing something new at a particular moment, which clearly shows Bergson’s influence21 (S 78-81). All this happens in absolute time. As Frings explicates emphatically: “The shifting dynamics of the three horizons is a fact of time-consciousness and imply Husserl’s ‘leaning toward death’ (der Hang zum Tode).22 The shifting dynamics are also at work in the process of aging. Aging itself is a manifestation of absolute time. Dying is the self-ending of absolute time” (TM 189), which plainly hints here at an individual life. It is interesting to notice that scrutinizing the phenomenon of diminution Scheler seems to allude 20 In Book XI of The Confessions, Saint Augustine holds: “It might be correct to say that there are three times, a present of past things, a present of present things, and a present of future things… The present of past things is the memory; the present of present things is direct perception; and the present of future things is expectation” (120). Analyzing the horizons in the essay though, Scheler says nothing about Saint Augustine’s influence. For Saint Augustine’s impact on Scheler compare, e.g., Sweeney (100) and Vacek (163). 21 Scheler openly admits Bergson’s impact on him in “Death and Afterlife” (S 81); “Duration is the continuous progress of the past which gnaws into the future and which swells as it advances” (Bergson Creative Evolution 5). 22 Frings is obviously aware of Heidegger’s influence, too (Lifetime 103).

The Phenomenon of Death 27 only to time, omitting the concept of space (Drogoś 138).23 As people grow older, the distance they are able to cover is also minimized day by day, and the area within which they move narrows gradually from the whole world to their city, then to a local shop nearby, to their own room and, in the end, to the deathbed. Finally, when one realizes in one’s consciousness the frame of the horizons and the alternations between them, it is easily noticeable that the temporal structure of the process is ceaselessly in motion with the past horizon swelling in one specific direction, which is known from the start. According to Scheler, this “direction towards death” is life-consuming, so each experience in life is death- oriented (Erlebnis der Todesrichtung) (qtd. in Emad 72; S 81). Frings holds that this direction toward death exists autonomously from five aspects of life: a) the direction is independent of what sort of person is getting old, b) of meanings and contents of our experiences and of diversities among races, c) of periods of life and their measurements in different groups, d) of fear of death, e) of the life drive and the death drive (Lifetime 107). Referring to “Death and Afterlife,” the direction seems to be independent of all aspects of life, for it is omnipresent from the very moment of procreation, and it is built into the structure of life permanently, so there is no moment when it disappears or dwindles. As a consequence, if one applies the knowledge of the moving horizons to life, there is a possibility of sensing the process of aging. It is also possible to feel the intuitive certainty of death at every moment of life (S 84), which, as hinted before, accompanies persistently one’s existence from the instant of procreation. As Frings supports in Lifetime, “the inter-contained essence of dying and death is manifest in any phase of the process of living” (104). Undeniably, death realizes itself when the future horizon narrows to the zero point. Nonetheless, as Emad validates, the very certainty of death should be deeply embedded in life from the instant we are able to comprehend the structure of human temporality so that we will not confuse the truth about demise with fear or desire for it (68, 72). The actual passing away is barely, in this case, a kind of final confirmation that death, intuitively extant in every episode, constitutes omnipresent inner life experience. Its discovery depends purely on our perception (S 89-90), i.e., how acutely we can analyze phenomenologically our personhood, which “is not a substance from which acts emerge, but is an intuitable reality given in each of our acts” (Kelly 112, first emphasis added). 23 The concept of space apparently appears missing here; however, it would be misleading to maintain that Scheler omitted it in his writings. On the contrary, as Frings assures us, Scheler did examine space, but it represented for him a lower rank than time itself (Lifetime xvi).

28 Chapter One As stated above, death for Scheler is something more than the experience gained at the end of one’s life. This is the phenomenon, or, in other words, the frame that gives the picture of existence its “totality” (geschlossene Totalität) (S 85). In his essay “Repentance and Rebirth,”24 Scheler presents this issue very vividly in the graph by drawing a line “P(past)-F(future)” that consists of the consecutive experiences a, b, c, d, e, and f in the row named R, and the last experience denoted as g that is outside of R (95). In this way, the philosopher proceeds to present that every experience, although already classified as a past event, “remains indeterminate in significance and incomplete in value until it has yielded all its potential effects” (“Repentance” 95). It means that g is not only determined by the previous f, but by the whole R, and vice versa, the experiences from a to f need g to gain their “full significance and final value,” so we may conclude that the tie-in between all the experiences is the relation of interdependency (“Repentance” 95). In light of this interdependency, Scheler’s arguments sound more convincing when he holds that if it was not for finitude, life would be endless, devoid of unity, and its face could not be the face of Janus. Accordingly, our acts would be enclosed in a completely different dimension; one episode would have neither beginning nor end, as it could continue infinitely; our behavior would not have any far-reaching consequences either (S 84-85). And if a man is regarded as “a story-telling animal,” to relate to Alasdair MacIntyre (qtd. in Higgins 41), each life perceived as a story with the structure “beginning-middle-end” must come to the end one day, so we must accept death as its closure (Higgins 41), and the sooner we do it, the more meaningful existence we will lead. Evidently, in everyday life, the chances to become cognizant of impending death increase when the past horizon gains the advantage over the future horizon, which in short means when one gets older. Nevertheless, for Scheler, there is a difference between being old and feeling old. As a result of this rumination, the thinker introduces the differentiation between “natural age” (how we feel, behave) and “actual age” (how old we really are), which is paradoxically called “artificial age,” too (S 83). Thus, for Scheler, people may look or feel much younger than their actual age would suggest. And vice versa, someone really young could be “burnt out,” which would also imply that inside they naturally died, even though their actual death has not come yet (S 81-84). 24 In the essay Scheler touches upon the phenomenon of repentance as indispensable in true being, because it protects the soul from moral death, bringing each time the rebirth of genuine inner self. He states that the feeling of repentance appears before physical death with redoubled strength, but it is too late for the people who have not incorporated it into their existence before, as there is neither time nor chance for moral improvement that remains an imperative to rediscover the ordo amoris again (87-124).

The Phenomenon of Death 29 Except for disclosing quietus from the inside, in one’s consciousness, there is the other way of ascertaining the intuitive certainty of death. Its disclosure is also possible from the outside, through the analysis of other people’s experiences, since for Scheler “death is secondarily an occurrence in objective time when observed by another” (TM 189). And here it is worth mentioning that death for this phenomenologist never happens by accident (S 85). If one passes away due to external factors, this death is classified as a “catastrophe” (S 86, 97- 98). However, either it is a natural death or a catastrophe, people observing it are capable of realizing what death is,25 and this way they are forced to stand up to the fact that finitude does not signify transformation from one stage into another one. This is the last event in one’s life, which results in total annihilation, out of which nothing physical will arise again. Additionally, through someone’s death people may also uncover that everyone must die on their own (S 87), which later will be reinforced by Heidegger. In conclusion, dying, regarded by Scheler as the last act during one’s existence, which results from the equation drawn above, still belongs to the very structure of life that is observable from the outside (S 87). This simultaneously provides the evidence to prove the second assumption summarized by Frings in the words: “death is one side of a vital process whose other side is procreation” (TM 297), and also in Lifetime: “Both death and birth belong to the phenomenon of life itself. Life, like impulsion, is a process; it is a process of the becoming and unbecoming of all its phases in absolute time” (103). Therefore, we may deduce that for Scheler there is no life-and-death division bringing to light the juxtaposition of two categories. There is rather only life, unified as enantios, beginning with birth and ending in finitude. Although Scheler himself does not draw a clear-cut distinction between death and dying, his line of reasoning seems to concur with the elucidation proposed by Ninian Smart. In his essay “Philosophical Concepts of Death,” Smart perceives death as an event (for Scheler the last act in the structure of life), and dying as a process (for Scheler it starts at the moment of procreation) (27-29). Feldman, too, tells these two issues apart, although his terminology is a bit different. Deriving his idea from Gilbert Ryle, who ponders over two senses of the word “winning,” i.e., one in the success sense (the crossing of the finishing line), and the other in the progress sense (leading during the race), Feldman regards death as “dying1” in the success sense, which clearly shows 25 In Istota i formy sympatii, Scheler comes to the conclusion that we can have a fellow feeling of the experiences which the Other has gone through, but which we ourselves have never undergone (83). In “The Planes of Feeling,” a fragment of The Nature of Sympathy, published in On Feeling, Knowing, and Valuing, Scheler mentions that “one who ‘understands’ the mortal terror of a drowning man has no need at all to undergo such terror, in a real, if weakened form” (52).

30 Chapter One the perfective aspect of the activity, and “dying2” that indicates the progress sense, representing the imperfective aspect of the activity (71-72). With reference to dying, Smart also suggests that the cause why a person is passing away may be found inside him/her, in contrast to murder, which is an example of the Schelerian catastrophe. Smart also adds that there could be a situation where someone is dying, but this may not lead to death, which evokes the argument developed by Roy Perrett, as well. In Death and Immortality (1987), Perrett describes dying as “a process that if uninterrupted by external forces will normally end in death; but dying does not necessarily eventuate in death” (17). The same is later accentuated in Confrontations with the Reaper, where Feldman draws the graph “the history of Adam,” marking eight major facts connected with Adam’s life: conception, birth, dying2, rediscovery, dying2, coma, death, cremation (108), which stresses there is a possibility of dying and later living again. We can see now that even though all the cited philosophers agree on the division into dying as a process and death as an event, there exists one significant point that differentiates Scheler from the rest. The author of “Death and Afterlife” does not interpret dying as a process that could be stopped or suspended for some time, but something inborn, omnipresent, and near us all the time, not only at the moment when we die in a literal sense. As the historical outline illustrates, in such monumental works as those by Philippe Ariès and Michel Vovelle, death has been painted with various colors and in diverse forms by different social classes. However, no matter how many roles demise has played in society so far, which constitutes material for more than one thesis, Scheler distinguishes two major types of social comportment toward the end that people usually display: they darken the picture of death or brighten it in a given epoch. If a particular period is characteristic of the former one, that evidently means the absence of death in people’s existence, which is the immediate effect of quietening the thought of quietus and the inability to be reconciled with expiration (S 91). For Scheler there are two ways of muffling the sound of death in people’s minds (Emad 69). The first one is the natural stifling of the thought of death while completing everyday errands. Considering this point, Scheler notices that on one hand it would be unbearable for human beings to live according to the rule sub specie aeternitatis, consciously feeling the presence of demise every single minute of their lives.26 If that was the case, their existence would be in danger, as they would not pay heed to professional duties or to household 26 There are convents and monasteries living in accordance with the rule sub specie aeternitatis (Wańczowski 328), but it is hard to imagine that monks or nuns remember about it every single minute.

The Phenomenon of Death 31 chores, doing more harm than good in this way. Thus, a certain kind of forgetfulness is acceptable for the German philosopher. On the other hand, it is unbelievable that people, in view of the absolute certainty of death, non- comparable to any other certainty of anything else, are not paralyzed by the thought about death. It is surprising for the philosopher that they have a capability to stay calm and function normally despite this certainty – the phenomenon Scheler names “metaphysical recklessness” (metaphysischer Leichtsinn) (S 93), defined by Frings as “a matter of metaphysical indifference and carefree giddiness” (Max 207). The second mode of uprooting finitude out of life is the deliberate avoidance of death. Interpreted by Emad as “flight away from oneself” (69), it prevails among contemporary dwellers of Western Europe but cannot be approved of by the German thinker. For this “Critic of Modern Man,” as Scheler was nicknamed after the publications of “On Self-Delusions” and Ressentiment (Ranly 5), “contemporary” signifies the second decade of the twentieth century, precisely the time when he wrote and lectured “Die Idee des Todes und das Fortleben.” Nevertheless, his ideas contained later in “Death and Afterlife,” though nearly a hundred years old, are still remarkably authentic. According to Scheler, the overwhelming progress has sculptured a new kind of man, i.e., homo capitalisticus, whose thinking has been replaced with pure calculation (Scheler qtd. in TM 172). One’s Leib, translated by Frings as the “lived body,” with its heart and soul, has been transformed into “the object body,” Körper (TM 86), a complex organism with chemical reactions representing a person only in a physical sense. Such a person, becoming an indistinguishable member of the mass, gradually starts losing the identity, freedom and self-responsibility typical of an active and nonconformist individual (Scheler “Z fenomenologii” 81, 100; “Wzory” 213). And what is worse, with the passage of time, one resembles more an animal than a man (Scheler Istota 64). Lastly, homo capitalisticus represses quietus as its natural consequence and at the end is “trampled to death without rhyme or reason, without sympathy or care” (Frings Lifetime 34). As a result, one dies an anonymous death, which is the immediate effect of replacing the proper hierarchy of values with the principle of utility, which converts a man into a device useful for society to make further advances.27 27 Kuderowicz asserts that Scheler’s philosophy is a sign of the protest against utilitarianism and the ethics whose main value is the interest of the public. Instead, according to Kuderowicz, Scheler opts for ethical personalism, as he himself names it, stressing a moral code of behavior as the most vital issue for the individual (351). A similar point of view is held by Kelly, who in his analysis of personhood in Scheler also speaks of his “ethics of personalism” (113).

32 Chapter One Paradoxically, human achievements have not made communities more buoyant, but frustrated. Development equaling both progress and decadence has not increased people’s well-being. Instead, with its constant drive to work and to control nature, civilization has brought about suffering, not happiness28 (Scheler Istota 59; MS 94), which is also the conclusion drawn in Civilization and its Discontents by Freud (37-39), who influenced the author of “Death and Afterlife.” Yet, such an outcome does not surprise Scheler, since this ethos of work is only a surrogate for disappearing God, faith, afterlife, and valor to come up to death.29 As he elaborates in his essay on “Cognition and Work,” “the pathos modern man associates with the term ‘work’ has become the more intensive the more he has struggled free of the spiritual traditions of antiquity and Christianity and sought to create for himself a view of the world and an ethos out of the conditions of his own existence and life” (qtd. in Wolff 113). At present people live mainly in order to work so as to improve the world and to make it more pleasant for themselves. Yet, the ludicrousness of the situation shows that they do not have enough time to make use of the facilities they have striven for so hard (Ressentiment 152-154), not to mention the inability to feel and enjoy pure spirituality (Frings Lifetime 186). The real now is what you can count, so there is no investment in uncountable, subjective feelings or values, not covered by a warranty, to say nothing of death (S 93-95, 98-99). What follows from all this reasoning is the commonly accepted “mechanical conception of life,” exclusively grounded on counting30 devoid of contemplation or any metaphysical pondering (S 99). This type of calculation repudiates death as an inherent part of life, allowing demise to perform on stage only when there is a corpse. As a consequence, death is not present in the world vision of the people of Western civilization, because, as Scheler claims, they simply do not believe in their own dying. Denuding themselves of symbols that remind them of the end, people do not live in view of finitude. What is even more alarming 28 To confront advanced societies with backward ones, Scheler gives an example of primitive tribes and people from the Eastern parts of the world who, in his opinion, suffer less as they are better prepared to adjust to nature, even though they are more exposed to its hazards. The point is they do not want to gain control over nature but live with it. Here, Scheler shows, once again, that the East gains the advantage over the West (MS 93-94). 29 Supporting this argument, Scheler makes reference to primitive tribes again. There is hardly any fear of death among such groups, because their belief in afterlife is widespread (MS 93). 30 As Frings points out, since Scheler believes that philosophy should be applicable to life in a practical way, calculative reasoning cannot be omitted entirely, but it ought to be controlled (TM 159).

The Phenomenon of Death 33 for Scheler is the fact that the majority feel no fear of finitude, treating it not as a real possibility but as a kind of illusion. It is true though that people try to protect themselves from demise – as we see now, more and more mortals keep paying for life insurances. However, in Scheler’s critique, even if people take dying into account, they see it as “an external, destructive factor” (Emad 69), which, like fire, flood, and earthquake, disturbs their peaceful lives from time to time. Hence, death cannot come to people as something natural, as it is in Eastern cultures, but only as an unbearable catastrophe31 obscure to be spoken about. Then, when it does come, people discern it as callous, barbarous, and violent (Emad 69). And the sad thing is that life without death is the picture people, on their own, have brushed for themselves while denying death, which should make up a truly integral part of existence (S 95-98). Max Scheler reaches the conclusion that progress, not science, through which he also understands philosophy, should mainly be blamed for the ignorance of death in society. Nevertheless, he concedes that science, which patently stimulates progress, has partly made its contribution to diminishing the presence of quietus. To illustrate this point more vividly, he refers to Descartes, who asserts that death parallels the loss of consciousness caused by external stimuli destroying a bodily mechanism (S 98-101). Scheler surely denies this thinking for a few reasons. Firstly, he disapproves of treating an organism as the mechanical whole; secondly, he regards death as a metaphysical issue born in the act of procreation, not as the last event or process taking place in an organism; thirdly, the assumption that death is caused by external stimuli, for example, a shot from a gun, does not constitute what Scheler understands by death, but what he calls “catastrophe.” Further, even if we did perceive an organism as a mechanism, Scheler accentuates, we would still have problems with expounding what demise is. Already, at the beginning of the twentieth century, it was well known that after expiration some body parts still work, so the loss of consciousness cannot be treated as an exact moment of expiration, even from the mechanical point of view, not to mention the possibility of clinical death. Summing up the discussion, Scheler in “Death and Afterlife” takes upon himself to make people conscious again that the phenomenon of death does exist. He strives to prove that death ought not to be accepted as a kind of “truth” – “they died, so I will die too;” instead, each person should unearth the very idea of finitude inductively and get to know death a priori by grasping its essence phenomenologically (S 97). Moreover, he summarizes the occurrence of the end 31 In his work Camera Lucida Roland Barthes perceives each picture as a catastrophe, for it carries the death of a person shown in a photo (96).

34 Chapter One as the gradual ceasing of a certain process (S 105), and as the slow expiration of vitality (S 102), which actually constitutes the conclusion built upon the reasoning of Elie Metchnikoff. According to Scheler, Metchnikoff is the first one that touches upon the notion of “death drive,” which is worthwhile to mention in order to complement this analysis (MS 101, 115, footnote 18). Elie Metchnikoff, the younger brother of Ivan Ilyich – the main protagonist of Tolstoy’s “The Death of Ivan Ilyich,” was a Russian zoologist interested in the phenomenon of death. He examined it not only from the view of biology but also from the perspective of philosophy and literature. In The Prolongation of Life (1907), while scrutinizing reasons for the expiration of plants and of animals, he puts forward the analogy between sleep and death among human population. He holds that if one intuitively feels the need to fall asleep and rest, a person should also feel natural necessity of eternal sleep,32 which appears at the old age and must not be interpreted as a wish to take one’s own life (The Prolongation 125-126). In other words, the instinct of life we are born with, after the years full of purposefulness, ought to be replaced with the harmless instinct of natural death as the most fortunate end for every entity (The Nature 283; The Prolongation 129, 318-319). This is for Metchnikoff the ideal of human nature, called “orthobiosis,” which he also apprehends as the development of a being whose aim is a long and vigorous life, ended with satisfaction and desire to die (The Prolongation 320), which straight away resembles Scheler’s view on death as “harvest.” Consequently, if the instinct of life was accepted with the instinct of natural death, one could die with dignity, even with “pleasure,”33 in the sense of fulfillment, as it was proved not only in literature in Faust by Goethe, but also in real life by John Paul II, whose existence symbolically closed with the book on his coffin on the day of his funeral. Both life and death drives direct us instantly to the late works by Freud, in which the psychoanalyst brings to light two basic inborn urges standing in opposition to each other, i.e., the Eros/life instinct and the destructive/death instinct (An Outline 5), which are also called sexual instinct and ego instinct (“Beyond” 620). The former aims to protect human life, “to establish even 32 In The Prolongation of Life, Metchnikoff extended the theory of the instinct of natural death, which he developed three years earlier, in his 1904 publication The Nature of Man: Studies in Optimistic Philosophy (262-284). In this work he put forward that, already in the Bible, one might detect certain references to the instinct of death (280). 33 Metchnikoff postulates that if in pathological cases people feel such pain that they wish to pass away, death seems to represent the feeling of pleasure. After judging the facial expressions of the people who died, he supposes that the same may happen when death comes naturally (The Prolongation 130).

The Phenomenon of Death 35 greater unities and to preserve them thus – in short, to bind together” (An Outline 5), which makes the germ cells gain the status of being immortal.34 The latter instinct, which Freud, at the very beginning, did not want to believe in (Civilization 73-74; Strachey 8), is “to undo connections and to destroy things” in order “to lead what is living into an inorganic state” (An Outline 5). According to Freud, this state is “an old state of things,” or “an initial state,” out of which the living substance came and which every human being strives to return to (“Beyond” 613). Therefore, if one is to become inorganic again, for Freud “the aim of all life is death” (“Beyond” 613), which is likely to be the view formed under the influence of Schopenhauer.35 In light of the above arguments, it is easily noticeable that Metchnikoff’s theory differs significantly from Freud’s deduction. For Metchnikoff, the life instinct we are born with is successively substituted by the instinct of natural death, treated as a need for eternal rest after purposeful existence. As both instincts emerge in an established order, they seem to complement each other. Moreover, the knowledge of the death instinct is in a sense the fruit of one’s thinking, which shows that people may have an impact on its presence or absence. As for the Freudian outlook, since both instincts are innate, they appear to be created at the same time at the moment of birth; as the author of An Outline of Psychoanalysis (1940) states, they “operate against each other or combine with each other” (6). Additionally, the instincts are termed as “the tensions caused by the needs of the id” (An Outline 5), and if the id represents the deeply repressed and the hidden, the death instinct belongs to the unconscious, and therefore “we have much greater difficulty in grasping that instinct; we can only suspect it” (Freud Civilization 76). Consequently, it is unlikely to put an equal sign between the theories, although they show some similarities, and the names used by Metchnikoff and Freud are close in meaning. 34 To support his view, Freud quotes August Weismann’s theory, which says that living substance may be of two kinds: it may be the mortal body, also called soma, which is subject to death. At the same time living substance may be immortal thanks to germ cells that pass down life to next generations, clothed in a new soma (“Beyond” 617). 35 In his essay “On the Indestructibility of Our Essential Being by Death,” Schopenhauer, in opposition to Metchnikoff, considers life to be a kind of “dream.” He regards finitude as “the awakening” which is the moment of the return to “our original state,… the being’s intrinsic state,… the state of the thing in itself” (42-43). Nota bene, in Świat jako wola i przedstawienie (1819), he may be thought to contradict himself, asserting that death and sleep are the same (1: 425-426); nevertheless, death here is understood as the sleep during which one forgets about one’s own individuality that is the end of a particular phenomenon, but not the Will, i.e., the thing in itself (1: 432).

36 Chapter One Finally, we have to mark that Scheler does not speak at length about immortality, which he does not consider to be within the scope of the phenomenological analysis.36 Rather, he prefers to deliberate phenomenologically over “the question of the possibility of a continuation of life beyond death” (Emad 73-74). There is one condition, though, that determines the faith in existence after death in Scheler’s philosophy: to believe in afterlife, one has to reconcile spiritually with the fact of death by stopping to suppress the very thought of it (S 105-106). Only then, when the individual concurs with one’s own finitude, does s/he begin living in view of death and subsequently is capable of believing in the hereafter (S 123). Plainly, it is logically impossible to prove empirically that one exists after death, for the very moment precludes the possibility of gaining such experience. Nevertheless, for Scheler the difficulty with evidence for or against afterlife should not be an obstacle to carry out a phenomenological analysis, in which the key point ought to be the sense and the essence standing behind all human actions. Scheler reckons that all human acts, like thinking, feeling, loving or hating, are “supra-temporal” (Emad 62). By that he means that acts are independent of organic life and keep prevailing, even if a person, who thinks, feels, loves or detests, passes away. Hence, if one is a friend of someone, the sense of their companionship does not die with one of the friends, but “swings beyond” (Fort- und Hinaus-schwingen) the limits of the decomposing body by transgressing the border between life and death (Scheler qtd. in TM 295; S 122). And the swinging beyond may take place, for all voluntary and emotional acts, together with thinking, constitute timeless and non-spatial spirit (Geist) (Scheler Man’s Place 36-37, 47; Pastuszek 38). As Emad comments, this spirit in turn “is essentially capable to suspend reality, i.e., to existentially detach and liberate man from organic reality” (63). Thus, the body of the individual, as “the finite manifestation of Spirit” (Emad 63), extinguishes with death, yet the spirit, embracing the eternally valid act and value of the friendship in this case, endures endlessly (Scheler S 113; “The Spheres” 223).37 There is clearly no possibility of communicating with the dead any longer, because one is by no means able to hear exact words, statements or opinions. However, the fact that one cannot see 36 In “Love and Knowledge” Scheler does use the phrase “earthly immortality” and relates it to artists, whose works, after their passing away, speak for themselves, making their authors alive again (154). 37 Scheler’s line of reasoning that concerns Ewigkeitssinn, the sense behind all acts, is the continuation of his theory of values, according to which every value exists objectively. Thus, the immense value of friendship is still present, even though two people stop being friends (Kuderowicz 339), which we may also relate to the value of someone’s life after one’s death.

The Phenomenon of Death 37 or hear the person does not mean her/his non-existence (S 107-108), since the “person goes on to exist, i.e., to execute acts,” to put it in Emad’s words (75). As Ladislaus Boros later claims in The Moment of Truth: Mysterium Mortis (1962), “in the moment of death there occurs an inner annihilation of the soul, but this is not capable of annihilating the soul’s spiritual reality” (74). The swinging beyond, with the notion of spirit, overlaps with the phenomenon of the person in Scheler’s rumination. As Schopenhauer, who discerns death as “démenti” pulling apart the individual “essentia” to give life to “existentia” (Świat 2: 716), Scheler, his follower, also perceives the person in two different aspects: the individual person and “the collective person” (Gesamtperson) (“The Experience” 237-239), also translated by Frings as “the totality-person” (Max 139), and later as “the encompassing person” (TM 114).38 The former signifies the personality embodied in one single entity, whereas the latter, exemplified by church or nation, is the counterpart of a collective, united personality (Gesamtperson) consisting of endurable social acts performed by individuals (Scheler “The Experience” 237-238; TM 115). As Scheler states and Frings interprets, the individual personality terminates with the instant of death, but the collective person survives the moment and continues living infinitely, carrying with itself the permanently growing experience of togetherness. That is why the one “who loves, dies comfortably” (Scheler qtd. in TM 297), because “the bodily death of the individual is only a false appearance of death; this is actually only a wandering of the individual into the house of a new body, therefore only the beginning of a new ‘life’ in which love and knowledge must constantly be overcome” (Scheler “Love and Knowledge” 151). 38 Literally Gesamt signifies “all-inclusive” (TM 115). On the further critique of the forms of togetherness, see Ron Perrin Max Scheler’s Concept of the Person (101-104).

38 Chapter One 2. Martin Heidegger The line of Martin Heidegger’s thinking was indubitably stimulated to a certain extent by Scheler, although the former is known for his ambivalent attitude toward his predecessor. Heidegger’s tremendous admiration included in “In memoriam Max Scheler,”39 written after Scheler’s death in 1928, was superseded by solicitous criticism observable in his later writings (Schalow “The Anomaly” 85-86). Still, despite marked discrepancies, Heidegger’s phenomenology would not be the same without Scheler’s thought-provoking reasoning (Schalow “A Pre-Theological” 393-394). While referring to Theodore Kisiel’s “The Missing Link in the Early Heidegger,” Schalow stresses it was Scheler who first rejected the Husserlian emphasis on intellect and then reinforced human nature as an indispensable element of the phenomenological inquiry, which was the direction followed by Heidegger after him (“The Anomaly” 75, 86). As far as the subject of death is concerned, there appears to be a close resemblance between these two thinkers. At first sight, it may even seem startling why Heidegger, in his well-known analysis of Being-towards-death, did not allude to “Death and Afterlife.” Although formed between 1911 and 1913, Scheler’s composition was not published until 1933, so there cannot have been any references to Scheler’s work precisely40 if Being and Time came out in 1927. Let us then proceed with the analysis of Heidegger’s viewpoint on death. Similarly to his predecessor, Heidegger collates two opposing approaches to death: inauthentic and authentic. According to the inauthentic one, death is admittedly perceived “as a well-known event occurring within-the-world” (BT 297), but even if noticeable as reality, this is something exterior and absent in the world of a given entity, William Barrett elucidates (qtd. in Edwards Heidegger 16). As such, finitude truly represents nothing more than “a mishap” without any serious consequences, for “one of these days one will die too, in the end; but right now it has nothing to do with us” (BT 296-297), which immediately reminds us of the Epicurean interpretation of demise, called by Schrag “the external view of death” (100). In the case of Heidegger, such a vague attitude toward demise is, to quote Wood, “our everyday way of thinking of death” (182), imposed by predominant the “they” (das Man), whose aim is to 39 The memorial address by Heidegger, translated for me by my colleague Agata Maziakowska, a teacher of German, is quoted by Wolfhart Henckmann in his book Max Scheler (9-10). 40 In Being and Time Heidegger shows the knowledge of Scheler’s writings, yet in most cases, he mentions Scheler’s theory of values and intentional acts (72-73, 178-179).

The Phenomenon of Death 39 melt away any individuality or distinctiveness. Acting as “publicness,” for the purpose of gaining absolute control over the world, the “they” enslave a person and inflict “averageness” - their way of being – on an individual (BT 164-165). To give an entity a chance of being free, Heidegger adopts the authentic approach to death, built upon phenomenological ontology, which is the philosophy of Being and Time.41 In accordance with this approach, finitude, defined “as the end of Dasein” (BT 303), has to be “‘interiorized’ as a mode of existence itself,” becoming a part of one’s everyday life (Schrag 95). Hence, to grasp what death is, one must first inquire what Dasein stands for, especially if “Dasein is an entity which, in its very Being, comports itself understandingly towards that Being” (BT 78). Therefore, the analysis of Being indissolubly connected with Dasein should be taken now as the point of discussion. Inspired by Carl Braig’ s On Being. Outline of Ontology (1896),42 Heidegger enters into the discussion by restating Plato’s question about the sense of being mentioned in The Sophist (BT 19). The reconsideration of the query is vital to rediscover the fundamentals of existence, for the notion of being, introduced in many philosophical contexts, became too “universal,” and the genuine meaning of the term was lost (BT 21).43 In order to regain its sense, one has to commence with distinguishing Being (Sein) from an entity (Seiende),44 although Heidegger 41 Although Being and Time is dedicated to Husserl, Heidegger’s line of pondering differs from that of his mentor. For Husserl phenomenology, as “the science of consciousness” applied to the whole philosophy, aims at discovering how a given phenomenon of the world is created in our consciousness (Korab-Karpowicz on-line). Heidegger, however, tries to narrow his philosophy to the most fundamental question, i.e., “What is the mode of being of that being in which the world constitutes itself?” (qtd. in Korab-Karpowicz). 42 Heidegger admits Braig’s influence in “My Way to Phenomenology” (74-75). Moreover, as Baran substantiates, in Being and Time, Heidegger, following his predecessor, rejects all definitions of Being, formed so far in the tradition of philosophy. Also, he poses the question concerning the essence of Seiende, “the entity,” pointing out the differentiation between Sein and Seiende, mentioned by Braig (Baran “Przedmowa” xiii-xiv). 43 Heidegger also draws the same conclusions while examining the word “being” from a grammatical and etymological point of view in Wprowadzenie do metafizyki (53-72). 44 Macquarrie and Robinson, who translated Being and Time, state that Heidegger uses two words: sein and Sein. The former simply means “to be,” whereas the latter, which is always capitalized, becomes a substantive rendered into English as “Being.” Das Seiende, a derivative form of the present participle seined, denotes “that which is,” and “ein Seiendes” literally signifies “something which is.” (BT 19, footnote 1, and BT 22, footnote 1). Ralph Manheim, however, translating Heidegger’s An Introduction to Metaphysics, decided to render Seiendes as “essent” or “essents” (qtd. in Wolny The Ruinous 14-15). I capitalize “Being,” following the translators of Being and Time.

40 Chapter One does not focus on the differentiation itself (Baran “Sein” 184). Avoiding the examples of other beings from the history of philosophy, Heidegger tries to show how we ought to understand Being itself (BT 26). William Barrett states directly that Heidegger’s Being is “the unutterable” (210), but let us see if it is so unreachable for us. As hinted above, Being is not an entity, but modus operandi of this entity (BT 29). That implies an entity conditions Being, which is a way of behavior this entity displays. To grasp the essence of existence, one must ask oneself the question about one’s own Being, which leads to the moment when the entity becomes Dasein (BT 27). Asking equals deep thinking (Wprowadzenie 8), which in turn contributes to understanding, “a dimension of Dasein” (Eagleton 54-55). That is to say, “Dasein is an entity which, in its very Being, comports itself understandingly towards that Being” (BT 78); it does so by “looking at something, understanding and conceiving it, choosing access to it,” because “all these ways of behaving are constitutive for our inquiry, and therefore are modes of Being for those particular entities which we, the inquirers, are ourselves” (BT 26-27). Furthermore, we must stress that for Heidegger, following Kant’s Critique of Pure Reason, this knowledge of Being, gained by asking, comes a priori, so it is independent of any experience (BT 31). Also, as Heidegger underlines, Being is the transcendens pure and simple. And the transcendence of Dasein’s Being is distinctive in that it implies the possibility and the necessity of the most radical individuation. Every disclosure of Being as the transcendens is transcendental knowledge. Phenomenological truth (the disclosedness of Being) is veritas transcendentalis. (BT 62) As such, Baran claims, the transcendence is not seen as “going beyond” Being, but as “stepping forward,” further and further into the essence of Being itself (“Przedmowa” xix). Hence, by focusing on its own Being exclusively, Dasein – through the very question – differentiates itself from other entities (BT 32), and eventually becomes “disclosed to itself in its Being” (BT 226). That results in reaching the unique truth about one’s own existence revealed by no one else but Dasein. Yet, what is veritas belonging to Dasein denoted initially as an inquiring entity? According to Heidegger, there are two main characteristics that essentially constitute the structure of Dasein, namely “existence” and “mineness” (BT 67-68). The first notion seems to overlap with the concept of Being, for in the chapter devoted to Dasein, we read: “the ‘essence’ [Wesen] of this entity lies in its ‘to be’ [Zu-sein]. Its Being-what-it-is [Was-sein] (essentia) must, so far as we can speak of it at all, be conceived in terms of its Being (existentia)” (BT 67). Coming straight to the point, existence is Dasein’s focus on its Being, or, as Stephen Mulhall defines, it decodes that “Dasein’s Being is

The Phenomenon of Death 41 an issue for it” (36). Clearly, there arises the superimposition of one term on another, with the difference that Being as a phenomenon may function separately from an entity, whereas existence is ascribed to a given Dasein. Mineness denotes the realization that Dasein relates to the I, and that Being, which should be scrutinized, is mine (BT 67-68). “That entity which in its Being has this very Being as an issue, comports itself towards its Being as its ownmost possibility” (BT 68). To put it another way, the possibility life presents me with is my possibility that helps me disclose myself to myself by myself, which will result in understanding myself. And only when I declare who I am through my existence, I can call myself a person, whose task is also to be part of the earth, as we read in Heidegger’s later essay “Hölderlin and the Essence of Poetry” (314). And how may this possibility, attributed exclusively to me, be realized? That is for each Dasein to decide, for there is no absolute truth for Heidegger, yet only aletheia, which is not simply truthfulness, but “disclosure” grasped by Palmer as “the process of emergence from concealment” (81). Thus, only those that seek for the answer to the question about their existence may become Dasein. As Heidegger confirms, “this entity which each of us is himself and which includes inquiring as one of the possibilities of its Being, we shall denote by the term ‘Dasein’” (BT 27). There are a considerable number of various possibilities Dasein may be confronted with on its “road to Being” (Baran “Sein” 185). For example, Dasein may fall, but it may stand up; it may get lost, but it may later find itself again; it may choose wisely or make a mistake – the list of probable accidents and occurrences is quite long. Yet, despite innumerable events that may happen to it, Heidegger’s Dasein may always grasp oneself “in terms of a possibility of itself: to be itself or not itself” (BT 33). That is to say, in each life situation, the entity has to make one radical choice: to be authentic or inauthentic (BT 68). Let us take authenticity first. For Heidegger it is simply choosing life and choosing oneself. It means putting aside the ideas originated by the “they,” and instead discovering the world in one’s own way, struggling for the real sense of life, destroying the masks behind which one could vegetate. On condition that Dasein “discloses to itself its own authentic Being, then this discovery of the ‘world’ and this disclosure of Dasein are always accomplished as a clearing- away of concealments and obscurities, as a breaking up of the disguises with which Dasein bars its own way” (BT 167). What is relevant is that authenticity is not just given to Dasein as “a formal notion,” to quote David Wood (190). More truly, it stands for “an existential notion” regarded as “a certain way of Being, a certain ontological self-relatedness” (Wood 190), which implies the entity has to work out its own authenticity on the road to its own Being. “The question of existence never gets straightened out except through existing itself”

42 Chapter One (BT 33), which also suggests that authenticity is rather a never-ending process, not a state we find ourselves in. Nevertheless, there may be a situation in which Dasein falls and supports the perspective of the “they,” leading its life according to the inauthentic mode of Being (BT 223). And here some ambiguity arises. On one hand, Dasein is advised to avoid the “they” so as not to fall under their control, because in the event of their dominance it directly loses its own Being (BT 164). As a result, if the “they” do manage to impose their own ideas on the individual, Dasein commences to display a sense of “alienation,” which in reality “closes off from Dasein its authenticity and possibility” (BT 222). On the other hand, Heidegger points out that to be truly oneself one cannot cut oneself off completely from the “they” regarded as well as part of “Dasein’s positive constitution” (BT 167). Also, to reach the level of authenticity, one should modify the Being exemplified by the “they” (BT 168, 224). That implies Dasein might make use of what the world has to offer, as it may also enrich the entity. However, Dasein must first of all apply itself to preserving its authenticity, for the “they” are likely to burden Dasein with falling “everydayness,” and then “everyone is the other, and no one is himself” (BT 165). Authenticity is not the only purpose of Dasein’s life. Another objective on Dasein’s path to Being is the point of reaching its totality, which constitutes “Dasein’s possibility of Being-a-whole” and provides us with a complete comprehension of Being (BT 279).45 And this is the moment when death takes the stage in Being and Time to play two main roles. Firstly, death is to help Heidegger elaborate on how Dasein may be circumscribed as a whole, and secondly, it is an issue that will enable him to advance from the existential analysis in Division One to the ontological description in Division Two (Wood 180). With reference to the first function, paradoxically, “as long as Dasein is as an entity, it has never reached its ‘wholeness’” (BT 280). That is to say, to make up a whole, Dasein needs to lose its characteristic of “Being-in-the-world” and become what Heidegger calls “no-longer-Dasein” (BT 280). In short, Dasein must die to be the whole. That line of thinking instantly evokes a question: how are we able to grasp what this totality is, and following on from this – the knowledge of death, if it is beyond the realm of reason to consciously realize what this wholeness stands for? What opens the discussion to answer the above question is “the death of Others” (BT 281). Initially, it comes out as seemingly “objective,” for it is not 45 David Wood finds this concept unconvincing, since for him it is plausible to study an archaeological edifice as a whole even if there are only some parts of the building left (181).

The Phenomenon of Death 43 our expiration, but theirs. However, considering the death of Others as a foundation for our consciousness of finitude would be an erroneous assumption. Firstly, what we undergo at that point is “a loss,” denoted as “the loss sustained by survivors” (Edwards Heidegger 38), not as “the loss of being sustained by the deceased himself,” which is the emotion one is overwhelmed only while dying (Macquarrie Studies 52). The sensation felt by those who, although grief- stricken, are still alive is totally different, as we are “just ‘there alongside’” – only walking by the dead (BT 282). Secondly, there is no real possibility of representability, which Heidegger renders as the impossibility of substituting for somebody as far as death is concerned: “No one can take the Other’s dying away from him” (BT 284). Still, by experiencing the death of the Other, one does pay heed to their demise, and gain a kind of “preliminary understanding” of death, as Macquarrie calls it (An Existentialist 112), which makes a person at least aware of the transformation “from Dasein’s kind of Being (or life) to no-longer- Dasein” (BT 281). With reference to both the double meaning of the loss and the mentioned lack of representability, it would be illogical not to concur with Heidegger. Nevertheless, as David Wood notes, Heidegger exaggerates when he claims that by the death of Others we can barely spot demise as a fact. Wood opposes the idea, with the example of the death of supposed strangers whose autobiographies and biographies help us touch upon the sphere of mortality (187). Unreservedly, while experiencing the disappearance of our beloved ones, with the stress put on accompanying in person rather than in the pages of history, we cannot omit the emotional bond of love between the deceased and the bereaved that Heidegger excludes, which eo ipso signifies the rejection of the Other “as Sign, as Representation” (Wood 188). Therefore, contrary to Heidegger, Wood regards the death of Others as a valuable lesson, which can help us develop the authentic attitude to demise through love Heidegger seems to avoid (185-187).
