Still, it is worth stressing that only the attitude is at stake, because there is no possibility of “sharing” someone’s death in any of those cases (Mora 179). What we share with the one passing away is feelings, but just to a certain extent, as Edwards says, and therefore there can be no mention of any knowledge of quietus, as ontologists would wish to envisage (“Existentialism” 45-46).46 Unable to fully encompass the concept of finitude through the death of Others, Heidegger gives the analysis of “dying,” also called “ending” (BT 284). 46 In his essay “Existentialism and Death,” Paul Edwards tries to prove that the ontological quest carried out by existentialists in reference to death is absolutely senseless, as their analysis comes down to the query “What does death feel like to the dead?,” which itself is self-contradictory in his opinion (passim 32-61).

44 Chapter One He perceives the issue from two different aspects, distinguishing the expiration of all creatures with limited consciousness from Dasein’s finitude (Wolny “An Ontological” 113). The former is called “perishing” (BT 284), whereas the latter is termed as “demise” (BT 291). Obviously, both types of death are of a biological kind, as demise physiologically resembles perishing. Nevertheless, by the differentiation, the thinker suggests Dasein’s death ought to be treated first of all ontologically, which highlights human mental abilities, whereas perishing purely covers the biological aspect. Leaving behind perishing, let us focus on demise. Recognized as a phenomenon constituting Dasein’s totality, it depicts the “way of Being in which Dasein is towards its death” (BT 291). And since it is the way of Being, exclusively attached to Dasein, the sense of demise must be derived from Dasein itself: “the existential meaning of Dasein’s coming-to-an-end must be taken from Dasein itself, and we must show how such ‘ending’ can constitute Being-a- whole for the entity which exists” (BT 286). Thus, “death, in the widest sense, is a phenomenon of life” (BT 290), or to refer to what Heidegger says in another work: death is at the same time life (Wprowadzenie 123-124). With Eckhart’s influence on Heidegger (Caputo The Mystical 203), this rumination strikingly resembles the philosophy practiced by Zen masters, e.g., Kigen Dōgen and Suzuki Shōsan (Parkes 85), for whom “there is life in death, and there is death in life” (Dōgen qtd. in Parkes 85). This also shows the influence of Buddhism on Heidegger, the result of his dialogue with Japanese philosophers during the 1920s, when he was working on Being and Time (Parkes 90, 187). Further, we must mention the impact of Simmel’s idea on Heidegger (BT 293, 494), especially bearing in mind Simmel’s essay “Death and Immortality,” where the author speaks of feeling death at every moment of life (qtd. in Parkes 90). All in all, the above discourse reminds us of Scheler’s flirtation with Buddhism as well as his second assumption, which, as we recall, places death within the process of life. Dasein’s earthly existence initially seems to be marked by alleged non- totality, because as long as Dasein is alive, there always appears to be “something still outstanding” or “something still to be settled” (BT 279). Nevertheless, if these phrases were to depict finitude, this would imply that death was something Dasein lacked: a sort of supplement attached to life to make it a whole, or as Heidegger clarifies, a kind of debt that would have to be paid off (BT 286). Apparently, this point exemplifies the inauthentic approach, as it burdens Dasein with the feature of being “ready-to-hand” (BT 287), a “category” representing usefulness, reserved for Being of different kind than

The Phenomenon of Death 45 Dasein47 (BT 121). What constructs Dasein authentically then is the concept of the “not-yet” (BT 287). Defined as death already present in our life, the concept should not be regarded as something that literally realizes itself, but as a phenomenon which comprises a part of our existence, builds up successively Dasein’s totality, and complements the entity when the actual end comes. To show us how to comprehend the not-yet, Heidegger, in Being and Time, illustrates this point with the image of the moon, which was actually mentioned much earlier by Rainer Maria Rilke (qtd. in Parkes 87).48 As it is widely known, the moon reveals its totality in the shape of a circle, but until the satellite gets full, only its quarters are visible. It does not mean though that the crescent is not a part of a whole, when the remaining part has been shadowed, and the moon is not the whole yet. Indeed, the given example helps to visualize how “Being of the ‘not yet’” reveals Dasein’s character (BT 287), and explains from what perspective we should consider death in Heidegger. Heidegger also elucidates the not-yet concept with the illustration of a ripening fruit. While still hanging on a tree, a fruit seems to have the characteristic of not being ready yet. However, for Heidegger, the fruit imagery differs from Dasein’s situation. “With ripeness, the fruit fulfils itself” (BT 288), and if fulfilling means “finishedness,” as Edwards translates it (Heidegger 18), we may grasp it as the exhaustion of all possibilities. With particular reference to Dasein, one cannot always speak of death in this context. First of all, Dasein may achieve its fulfillment long before the moment of death, for instance, when we point out motherhood as a woman’s fulfillment in life. Secondly, in death 47 Heidegger differentiates the ways of Being ascribed to Dasein from the modes of Being of other creatures, objects or phenomena: “Because Dasein’s characters of Being are defined in terms of existentiality, we call them ‘existentialia’. These are to be sharply distinguished from what we call ‘categories’ – characteristics of Being for entities whose character is not that of Dasein” (BT 70). Additionally, “the kind of Being which equipment possesses – in which it manifests itself in its own right – we call ‘readiness- to-hand’” (BT 98). Edwards notices that the division is analogous to Sartre’s differentiation between people and objects, i.e., the pour-soi and the en-soi (Heidegger 18). 48 Parkes mentions that in his later essay “Wozu Dichter?,” which was actually his 1946 lecture to commemorate Rilke’s death, Heidegger quotes part of Rilke’s letter of 6 January 1923, where the image of the moon and the notion of death overlap: “Like the moon, so life surely has a side that is constantly turned away from us, and which is not life’s opposite, but its completion to perfection, to plenitude, to the truly whole and full sphere and globe of Being. I shall not say that one should love death; but one should love life with such magnanimity, and without calculating exceptions, that one involuntarily always includes death (as the averted half of life) and loves it along with life” (Rilke qtd. in Parkes 87).

46 Chapter One Dasein is cut off from the possibilities which one still could explore, if one was alive. Thirdly, in most cases, the entity passes away not only “unfulfilled,” for there is always something left to be done, but “disintegrated” and “used up,” so its state at the end of life is far from the ripeness of a fruit (BT 287-288). Summing up the above issue, one concludes that demise as the end marked by the not-yet phenomenon cannot be treated as ripeness or fulfillment. As the following examples show, neither could it be “stopping,” when the rain stops falling, or when working on a canal has to be put to a stop, because the ground turned out to be too marshy (Schrag 112). What is it then? How should the entity grow into Being of the not-yet, which is appropriate to Dasein? After the convoluted argumentation, Heidegger deduces: “The ‘ending’ which we have in view when we speak of death, does not signify Dasein’s Being-at-an-end [Zu- Ende-sein], but a Being-towards-the-end [Sein zum Ende] of this entity. Death is a way to be, which Dasein takes over as soon as it is. ‘As soon as man comes to life, he is at once old enough to die’” (BT 289). In another essay Heidegger also claims, “only man dies – and indeed continually, so long as he stays on this earth, so long as he dwells” (Poetry 221-222), which actually echoes Scheler’s point, which refers to the same issue. In conclusion, if death is a way to be, it also represents Being. “In being towards its death, Dasein is dying factically and indeed constantly, as long as it has not yet come to its demise” (BT 303). For some it may appear to be a contradiction in terms. However, as Wood admits, death does not exist independently, yet as linked to the entity (183).49 As such, demise should be accepted as “a phenomenon of life” (BT 290), which is the point similarly raised by Scheler. Thus, to cite Karl Rahner, we may say “we die throughout life, and what we call death is really the end of death, the death of death” (qtd. in Demske 200, footnote 15). And what is more significant, the act of acceptance, reached through understanding, must not take place at the end of our earthy journey, but during our trip while traveling toward “the death of death,” for it guarantees our wholeness. Additionally, it is worthwhile to accentuate that the act of understanding may be perceived as complete, if we are aware that “the horizon within which the totalization can take place is time itself” (Paul de Man qtd. in Spanos 141). 49 In The Question of Being, Heidegger speaks of an irrevocable relation binding together the subject and Being – a human is attached to Being as Being to a human (77). Nevertheless, in “The Age of the World View,” Heidegger stresses that man, as subjectum, “becomes the center to which the existent as such is related” (10), and because death exists, according to Heidegger, it is grounded in man.

The Phenomenon of Death 47 The next point to discuss is the examination of Being-towards-the-end. Dasein’s Being is founded on the phenomenon of “care,” which is a primary tripartite element constituting the ontological structure of Dasein. As long as Being-towards-the-end belongs to Dasein’s Being, it must also be created by “care,” defined puzzlingly as “ahead-of-itself-Being-already-in (the world) as Being-alongside entities which we encounter (within-the-world)” (BT 293). Fortunately, the author of Being and Time illuminates what it stands for in the following way: “In this are expressed the fundamental characteristics of Dasein’s Being: existence, in the ‘ahead-of-itself’; facticity, in the ‘Being- already-in’; falling, in the ‘Being-alongside’” (BT 293). And if demise is truly considered to be the element supporting the Being of Dasein, the thinker adds, we should describe it with regard to these three qualities. Heidegger appears to multiply various terms, which leave the reader in doubt about their meaning due to their similarity. Such a case is with “ahead-of- itself” and “existence,” because if juxtaposed, there seems to be not much differentiation between them.50 However, in the following fragment, we can infer Heidegger speaks of the ahead-of-itself as the phenomenon that comprises non-totality in Dasein (BT 288). Apparently, he needs the term to explain a foundation for the above-mentioned not-yet concept. “The phenomenon of the ‘not-yet’ has been taken over from the ‘ahead-of-itself’; no more than the care- structure in general, can it serve as a higher court which would rule against the possibility of an existent Being-a-whole; indeed this ‘ahead-of-itself’ is what first of all makes such a Being-towards-the-end possible” (BT 303). That is to say, the act of grasping the end should stem from understanding of Being, that is, from comprehending what existence is for each of us first. Afterward, to make our vision all-round and full, we should add to it death. As a consequence, if we try to apprehend Being-towards-the-end through the ahead-of-itself, we have a capacity to see death as something “impending” (BT 294). Still, this impendence must not be taken in the same sense as waiting for a storm, house, friend, or journey. It should make us understand that death is, first of all, “a possibility-of-Being,” secondly, that this is “the possibility of no-longer-being- able-to-be-there,” and thirdly, that this is the possibility which in fact is my last one (BT 294), which puts us in “the horizon of death” (Sahaj 116). 50 Compare the notion of existence, analyzed before as an equivalent of Being, and as one of two predominant features of Dasein. The definition of the “ahead-of-itself” goes as follows: “the primary item in care is the ‘ahead-of-itself,’ and this means that in every case Dasein exists for the sake of itself. ‘As long as it is,’ right to its end, it comports itself towards its potentiality-for-Being” (BT 279).

48 Chapter One The second useful point in the analysis of care is facticity.51 In the context of Being-towards-the-end, it signifies that Dasein does not find, look for, or obtain its possibility of death once in a while, but apparently it is “thrown into” it, without any knowledge of this occurrence (BT 295). As Heidegger supports, “Dasein does not… have any explicit or even any theoretical knowledge of the fact that it has been delivered over to its death” (BT 295). Nevertheless, the thrownness,52 although hidden and unnoticed, does expose itself to Dasein through the state of mind named “anxiety” (BT 295). Never should we fret that we will not find anxiety, for it will find us, and then, it will direct us to the thought of death (Sahaj 115). Also, as Heidegger claims, anxiety represents the positive state of mind. In fact, it is contrasted with “fear,” a feature of the “they,” which makes one feel at a loss and befuddled (BT 181). Anxiety, quite the reverse, as the ahead-of-itself, has two roles to perform. According to Edwards, firstly, it strives to aid Dasein in grasping that demise is exclusively Dasein’s possibility, and that nobody can stand for the entity when finitude decides to complement it. Secondly, in the mood of anxiety, the entity may experience “openness” to the threat that one may die anytime and anywhere (Heidegger 46-47). The third characteristic of care is falling. In contradiction to the first two, it denotes an inauthentic mode of Being proclaimed by the “they” (Macquarrie An Existentialist 113). As a result, Heidegger discerns falling as fleeing from the chance to develop the right attitude to demise, and mentions three points which characterize the escape. They are “temptation, tranquillization, and alienation” (BT 298). As far as temptation is concerned, Heidegger deciphers it as the already mentioned avoidance of accepting death as my own possibility, which results in treating the end as a “mishap” happening to someone else. In brief, for the majority, this is not the I myself that passes away, but he, she, it, or the “they” – no one concrete, indeed. In relation to tranquillization, Heidegger describes the feature as a sort of persuasion from the side of the “they,” who lead a dying person to believe that s/he will be able to escape finitude, and that, at last will, come back to a normal life again. Such conduct is supposedly intended to console the moribund, but in reality it serves to tranquillize the fear of those who try to comfort the Other. And what Heidegger calls tranquillization, Philippe Ariès names a lie. According to Ariès, this lie made 51 Heidegger denotes facticity in the following way: “Whenever Dasein is, it is as a Fact; and the factuality of such a Fact is what we shall call Dasein’s ‘facticity’” (BT 82). 52 Thrownness, which seems to fall into the category of facticity, in general means that “in each case Dasein, as my Dasein and this Dasein, is already in a definite world and alongside a definite range of definite entities within-the-world” (BT 264, emphasis added). Thus, we know that this thrownness is a bond with the world and other entities.

The Phenomenon of Death 49 people start changing their way of thinking about death, which in the long run turned out to be a process whose beginning dates back to the middle of the nineteenth century (551-552). What is left to explain is alienation, the last feature of falling and a consequence of its first two characteristics. As a matter of fact, alienation has already been cited with reference to the inauthentic Being. In the context of death, the concept conveys a similar meaning, for it describes the situation in which the “they” try to persuade Dasein that it will not die, transforming anxiety into fear (BT 298). In other words, by the ambiguously ideal talk again, the “they” instill in Dasein a conviction that both talking and thinking of quietus are a kind of attenuation. In reality, it induces Dasein to repudiate death and forget that it is one’s own possibility of Being, which assures authentic life. In Heidegger’s view, inauthenticity is also founded on authenticity,53 so it is possible to shift from the former state to the latter (Harries 162). And what is relevant, the realization of inauthentic existence, burdened by Being-towards- the-end imposed by the “they,” may turn out to be constructive. Through the interpretation of falling, Dasein may proceed to a complete existential- ontological definition of death, which enables the entity to mature into a whole (BT 299). The definition goes as follows: “death, as the end of Dasein, is Dasein’s ownmost possibility – non-relational, certain and as such indefinite, not to be outstripped. Death is, as Dasein’s end, in the Being of this entity towards its end” (BT 303). And again to understand we have to deconstruct. Cognizant of what Dasein represents, we may focus on the notion of possibility. In An Existentialist Theology, Macquarrie explains the term as one’s individual choice the entity consciously opts for (112). In a glossary attached to his other book, Martin Heidegger, Macquarrie adds that “possibility, in Heidegger’s thought, does not mean just any contingency that may happen, but refers to the open future for which the Dasein can decide” (qtd. in Edwards Heidegger 27). Quite the reverse, Wood discerns that “to say that death is possible ‘at any time’ is not simply to say that one never knows when one will die, but that human life itself in its every instance derives its fullest significance from its contingency; I need not be at all” (182). What does it mean then? Heidegger explains that Being-towards-death is “Being towards a possibility,” which in turn signifies “‘Being out for’ something possible” (BT 305). Therefore, it would seem that we might think of possibility as actualization, but Heidegger strongly disapproves of it. Firstly, the term 53 Also see Heidegger’s Wprowadzenie do metafizyki, especially the chapter “Bycie i pozór,” where the author designates a path to distorting appearances as one of the ways to come closer to Being.

50 Chapter One “actualization” denotes the features of being ready-to-hand or present-at-hand, which, as we remember, are not characteristic of Dasein. Secondly, the concept of actualization conveys the meaning of “dwelling upon the end in its possibility,” which Heidegger rejects (BT 305). Actualizing, also called “brooding over death” (BT 305), implies that the entity deliberates over when and how it will die. Arguably, such comportment does make Dasein mentally closer to its quietus, for it at least arouses rumination over the subject. Nevertheless, by thinking this way, the entity envisages dying as an event, which is the thought Heidegger repudiates. The author of Being and Time points out “expecting” as another association the term “possibility” might demonstrate (306). In the context of death, expecting, as similar to waiting, would involve watching out for the moment when our expiration realized itself. Thus, demise would be perceived as “a future event” again (Wood 182). Undoubtedly, Heidegger wants life and death to mean more than that. Therefore, he introduces another phrase in his terminology, which this time denotes an authentic approach to the end. He draws the conclusion that Being-towards-death as a possibility ought to be characteristic of “‘anticipation’ of this possibility” (BT 306), which in German is “vorlaufen in die Möglichkeit.” Edwards believes it could be better rendered as “running ahead into the possibility” (Heidegger 32), which also helps us grasp its sense. We may argue, of course, that anticipation, or running ahead, also carries the meaning of actualization, but Heidegger disagrees. Anticipation for him exemplifies the process of understanding death to make us “receptive” to it (Wood 182). This involves the deepest insight into the issue, before the end comes literally. Consequently, as Schrag asserts in Existence and Freedom, death may be “existentially pre-enacted” (113), raising a “courageous awareness” of one’s end (Gelven 157). Furthermore, through such a thorough study, one is able to deduce that death is “the possibility of the impossibility of any existence at all” (BT 307), elaborated on as “the possibility of the impossibility of every way of comporting oneself towards anything, of every way of existing” (BT 307). That is to say, we are to scrutinize our existence with death in mind, for the understanding of finitude achieved by anticipation sheds light on the authentic Being of Dasein. The next point to consider is Heidegger’s argument that the possibility of the impossibility is “the utter nullity of Dasein” (BT 354). As Macquarrie and Robinson amplify in the footnote, the word “Nichtigkeit,” translated as “nullity,” could also be rendered as “notness,” and may cross-refer to anything that is “vacuous, trifling, ephemeral, or ‘nil’” (BT 329, footnote 1). Edwards, on the other hand, prefers to translate the term more literally as “nothingness”

The Phenomenon of Death 51 (Heidegger 49). Regardless of the linguistic nuances, nullity, in the first place, as the possibility of the impossibility, relates to death as something non-existent in a physical sense, because “nil” is tantamount to total annihilation. Furthermore, at a deeper level, both nullity and the possibility of the impossibility are indirectly revealed to us by anxiety (BT 310, 356). In one fragment we read: “In this state-of-mind [i.e., in anxiety], Dasein finds itself face to face with the ‘nothing’ of the possible impossibility of its existence” (BT 310), and in another fragment: “The ‘nothing’ with which anxiety brings us face to face, unveils the nullity by which Dasein, in its very basis, is defined; and this basis itself is as thrownness into death” (BT 356). In addition to that, in the above quoted passages, there is one more feature both phenomena share, namely this Nothing, which Edwards capitalizes, in opposition to the translators of Being and Time. As the issue is controversial, let us take the nothing as the point of departure to clarify it. The concept of the nothing seems to be inaccessible, because it arouses similar associations to non-being. Yet, in his 1929 essay “What Is Metaphysics?,” Heidegger underlines that when we pose a question about the nothing “we posit the nothing in advance as something that ‘is’ such and such” (on-line). Moreover, in a lecture in 1938, reprinted in Holzwege, Heidegger asserts that “the Nothing is never nothing” (qtd. in Edwards Heidegger 57). And in another text, entitled The Question of Being, the philosopher states that the nothing is “nothing negative. It belongs to being present” (“Es gehört zum An- wesen”) (96-97). Hence, we may say that the nothing Heidegger touches upon “presences.”54 In addition, “to let presence means: to unconceal, to bring to openness” (Heidegger “Time” 5), which Hofstadter decodes as “deconcealment,” as well (20). If displayed this way, it is not surprising that 54 In German there is a word “Anwesen,” which means “ground, allotment,” yet this is not the meaning Heidegger bears in mind. Rather, he derives this “An-wesen,” as he writes it, from the noun “Anwesenheit” signifying “presence.” However, there is another explanation. Not mentioning “An-wesen,” Edwards explains that Heidegger forms a verb “wesen,” and therefore in his later writings, we may come across such utterances like “das Sein west” or “das Nichts west.” Although there is a noun “Wesen” in German that signifies “essence,” Edwards supports that the philosopher originates his new verb from the word “Anwesenheit” – presence (Heidegger 70-71). Edwards adds that a great number of American critics followed Heidegger and started using the noun in the form of the verb “to presence,” like, for example, Albert Hofstadter in his essay “Enownment,” where he says that “Being presences” (25). Riddel in turn names poetry as “the presencing of presence” (240). Also see the translation of Heidegger’s “Time and Being” by Joan Stambaugh, in which “Being means the same as presencing” (2), or Heidegger’s “The End of Philosophy,” also rendered by Stambaugh, where “presence presences” (68).

52 Chapter One Arne Naess describes the nothing as a “phenomenon” (225), Macquarrie as “something like an empirical anchor” (qtd. in Edwards Heidegger 50), and Joseph Riddel as “a productive principle” (240). Hence, to quote Edwards, we can come to the conclusion that “Heidegger’s Nothing is not identical with the total absence” (Heidegger 57), especially when in The Question of Being the issue coexists in a way with Being: “Being and nothingness are not side by side,” however, “one intercedes on behalf of the other in a relationship… Being ‘is’ just as little as nothingness, but both are” (97). For Heidegger the nothing surprisingly exists, albeit it does not amount to Being. Instead, “the nothing itself nihilates,” which stands for a sort of act regarded neither as annihilation nor as negation (Heidegger “What” on-line). How to understand it? Confronting the problem in “Death and Metaphysics,” Peter Kraus maintains that this nothingness has two roles to play (102). Firstly, it nihilates our everydayness, habitual behavior, and run-off-the-mill existence, revealing the essence of being again. Secondly, it refers to something that transcends Dasein and other beings, leading to “a more primordial reality,” which subsequently enables the entity to see itself and Others in totality (Kraus 100-102). To conclude, as God creating the world out of the void, we in a way may originate Being out of the nothing, as well (Heidegger qtd. in Kraus 110). As Heidegger writes: The old proposition ex nihilo nihil fit [from nothing nothing comes] is therefore found to contain another sense, one appropriate to the problem of Being itself, that runs: ex nihilo omne qua ens fit (From the nothing all beings as beings come to be). Only in the nothing [death] of Dasein do beings as a whole, in accord with their most proper possibility – that is, in a finite way – come to themselves. (qtd. in Kraus 111) It truly appears to be puzzling and contradictory how from the phenomenon of the nothing as such we can come closer to the nullity, or the possibility of impossibility, perceived as total annihilation. Yet, if Heidegger remarks that the overcoming of nihilism demands to get into its essence by “the oblivion of Being” (The Question 103), for him one has to breathe life into death phenomenologically, before virtually crossing the line of nihilism, called by Jünger the “zero meridian” (qtd. in Heidegger The Question 35).55 By an analogous operation, a phenomenological attitude prevails, when one is ready for “a reorientation of perception,” to put it in Spanos’s words (138). Nil admirandum then. 55 The Question of Being is dedicated to Ernst Jünger. Here, among other issues, Heidegger touches upon the concept of the line as the sphere where nihilism realizes itself, which relates to Jünger’s “Across the Line” (“Über die Linie”).

The Phenomenon of Death 53 Having discussed the concept of possibility, let us now turn to other issues in the existential-ontological definition of death. First of all, Heidegger assumes that demise is Dasein’s ownmost possibility, which for Demske represents “the most intimate and most individual possibility of one’s own existence” (37), and for Glen Gray, “this most private… possibility” (qtd. in Edwards Heidegger 10). In a dictionary there is no entry to clarify what “ownmost” means. Nevertheless, if we follow Edwards’s suggestion and relate it to the Heideggerian “eigenst,” literally translated as “most my own,” the sense of the term sharpens (Heidegger 10). In The Gift of Death, Derrida also deconstructs Heidegger’s issue: “No one can die for me if ‘for me’ means instead of me, in my place” (41). In other words, the irreplaceable I is exclusively the only one responsible for its own passing away, since the end “can never be taken, borrowed, transferred, delivered, promised, or transmitted” (Derrida The Gift 44). Accordingly, Dasein’s ownmost possibility stresses mineness, the main feature of Dasein, and coalescences with the lack of representability, mentioned in regard to death of Others. There are, however, voices of dissent against the above argumentation. Paul Edwards, referring to what he calls the “untransferability of death,” is extremely critical of Heidegger. He draws the conclusion that the author of Being and Time repeats the trivial, tedious, “‘grammatical’ truth” (Heidegger 13), because, for instance, if someone suffers from gout, or feels a cramp in one’s leg, it is obvious this is this person’s own gout or cramp. The same point, albeit with lesser criticism, is also pointed out by David Wood (184-185). Unreservedly, he denies the exceptionality of expiration, and explains there is no representation in death, since no one can substitute for us in any biological functions of our organism: we ourselves have to digest, go to the bathroom, feel love, or comprehend what Heidegger says. While reading this elucidation, it is hard to believe though that the author of Being and Time would disagree with it, because his point was not to explore the issue as something new. As Riddel assures, interpretation for Heidegger is based on something “what is before us,” yet to uncover the issue in question we have to challenge its story using “displacement” as a technique (236-237). Alongside the idea of death as an ownmost possibility, Heidegger claims that quietus is the possibility that is “non-relational.” As Macquarrie and Robinson put forward in the footnote, this term may be rendered as “devoid of relationships,” which in the context of death indicates that “Dasein is cut off from relations with others” (BT 294, footnote 4). Heidegger himself states that while being toward this possibility there is no need to bother oneself with “Being-alongside the things” or “Being-with Others” (BT 308). Hence, the philosopher does not believe in any bonds between the dying and the alive,

54 Chapter One because, as Macquarrie supports in An Existentialist Theology, the Heideggerian demise “isolates the individual” from the Others (111). In his book Heidegger and Death, Paul Edwards strongly objects that a person always passes away by oneself, and accuses Heidegger and his followers of misusing the phrase “dying alone” (9). First of all, in the scholar’s opinion, the statement is veracious when one dies with no people around them in a physical sense, but expiration in the presence of the Other does not mean “dying alone.” Secondly, quoting Elisabeth Kübler-Ross, the critic also maintains that one does die alone, if they have undergone a wave of coldness from the side of their relatives, or medical personnel, but this does not happen when patients have constantly been comforted and reassured by the ones looking after them. However, Edwards does not mention acceptance, the last fifth stage of dying, pointed out by the author of On Death and Dying.56 At that point, as Kübler- Ross asserts, people arrive at “final decathexis,” which is the time when any disturbance from the outside world is regarded as unnecessary and daunting (266). In quest for separation from the surrounding reality, which is discerned by the dying ones as something natural, but stays incomprehensible for the family that sees such conduct as rejection, patients are ready to die in peace and dignity, not hindered either by doctors or their friends, who are obviously expected to be around, but silently (170). Thirdly, Edwards affirms that “dying alone” may be contrasted with “dying together” (Heidegger 8). With reference to Alvarez’s The Savage God, Edwards retells the history of the poet, Jacques Vaché, who, in a letter sent from the First World War front, strongly protested against both being shot in a battle and dying alone: “I shall die when I want to die, and then I shall die with somebody else. To die alone is boring, I should prefer to die with one of my best friends” (qtd. in Alvarez 190). And this is what he did. In 1919, at the age of twenty-three, Vaché prepared a lethal dose of opium for himself and his two friends, both unaware of what awaited them (Alvarez 191). Edwards regards this act as the third counterargument to abolish the alleged loneliness of death, but the scholar does not seem to notice the fact stressed by Alvarez, namely that it was “suicide and double murder” (191), so each of them did die alone, close to one another, but not “together,” as Edwards would wish. Coming back to Heidegger’s definition, death, as the ownmost and non- relational possibility, cannot be outstripped, i.e., won over, outdistanced, outrun, overtaken, or left behind. Here, Heidegger stresses again that the entity, who 56 In On Death and Dying, Elizabeth Kübler-Ross points out five stages of passing away, which outline how patients suffering from fatal diseases shape their attitude toward incoming death. They are as follows: denial, anger, bargaining, depression, and acceptance (passim).

The Phenomenon of Death 55 considers death as the not-to-be-outstripped possibility, is able to single out those opportunities that liberate us and guarantee authentic, individualized existence, long before the end (BT 308). In addition to this, Dasein also becomes conscious of the fact that the Others, having undertaken similar efforts of their individualization, discover their own paths in life. Accordingly, the realization of this fact closes Dasein to other people, since it begins to comprehend the Others’ ways of being, too: “As the non-relational possibility, death individualizes – but only in such a manner that, as the possibility which is not to be outstripped, it makes Dasein, as Being-with, have some understanding of the potentiality-for-Being of Others” (BT 309). The next two concepts Heidegger touches upon in his existential-ontological definition of quietus concern the affirmation that death is a certain and indefinite possibility. Although Heidegger’s disquisition on the issues, in large measure, reviews what has been stated before, there are a few points we should add. Despite their seemingly clear obviousness, conveyed by the Latin expression mors certa, hora incerta, Heidegger “displaces,” using Riddel’s terminology, their meanings. For the philosopher, to believe in the certainty of death, the individual has to maintain it is true, and behave accordingly. In other words, Dasein must accept a priori the knowledge of quietus as its ownmost and non- relational possibility, and reflect the gained wisdom in its behavior on a regular basis (BT 300-301). While analyzing death as the indefinite possibility, which echoes the concept of thrownness, the author of Being and Time considers this ignorance to be a blessing for us. Unaware when we will die, we continually experience a feeling of “threat,” which does not allow us to forget about the end (BT 310). Further, this threat is positive as derived from anxiety, which, as we recall, signifies a frame of mind that keeps us constantly cognizant of the fact that quietus stands for the possibility of the impossibility, which, in fact, is nothingness. Finally, bearing all that in mind, we can give a synopsis of the existentially authentic Being-towards-death as expounded by Heidegger: anticipation reveals to Dasein its lostness in the they-self, and brings it face to face with the possibility of being itself, primarily unsupported by concernful solicitude, but of being itself, rather, in an impassioned freedom towards death – a freedom which has been released from the Illusions of the ‘they’, and which is factical, certain of itself, and anxious. (BT 311) That is to say, it is only thanks to Being-towards-the-end that Dasein can see itself in truth, which paradoxically leads to “freedom towards death.” Further, anticipation guarantees Dasein’s freedom from the corrupted visions of the world promoted by the “they,” which results in living authentically as well as gaining the totality. Here, we must underline that for the German thinker this

56 Chapter One evolution into a whole occurs only ontologically, not physically – it happens only by reaching a particular level of consciousness, when we adopt the phenomenon of death a priori. And, subsequently, the ontological acceptance of demise, as Heidegger assures again, occurs only on condition that it stems from Dasein itself (BT 311). “Only by affirming himself in his being unto death can man exist as a whole” (Harries 163). It is visible now that Scheler and Heidegger understand totality differently, and what provides the contrast is the phenomenon of death. For Frank Schalow, the bone of contention is hidden in the quandary over whether to set limits to our earthly existence or not (“The Anomaly” 76). According to Scheler, our personality passes away irretrievably, but our voluntary and emotional acts, like friendship or love, swing beyond and enrich the non-spatial spirit (Geist) embodied in “the collective person” (Gesamtperson) (Scheler “The Experience” 237-239). In the case of Heidegger, finitude clearly marks the border where our existence terminates, and we are to gain totality phenomenologically before we die. These two contrasting attitudes to totality result from the philosophers’ different visions of the human being and one’s universe. In the religion-oriented world, where Scheler extols human nature over reason, each person forms a microcosm that reflects God’s macrocosm (Scheler qtd. in Schalow “The Anomaly” 82). This is achievable by the individual through one’s intentional acts directed unreservedly toward the Other: “It is ultimately through ‘person’ that Scheler reaches the entire realm of beings as well as the being of the divine” (Emad 61). That by all means creates a bond of sympathy on the grounds of which arises human “co-dependency” constituting “a larger whole,” which in turn makes a man be a reflection of God’s order (Schalow “The Anomaly” 79). Thus Scheler, for whom “no man is an island, entire of itself,”57 calls for emotional ties with the Other to create one’s inner world holistically. Distinguishing theology from philosophy (Heidegger “Fenomenologia” 121), Heidegger talks about the totality achievable exclusively by the mortal through self-awareness. In Dasein’s world there seems to be little room for the otherness, even if Heidegger interprets “the Others” as “those among whom one is” (BT 154), and “the world is always the one that I share with Others” (BT 155). Yet, in the connection the relationship ends, for “to say that it [the entity] is ‘illuminated’ [erleuchtet] means that as Being-in-the-world it is cleared [gelichtet] in itself, not through any other entity, but in such a way that it is itself the clearing” (BT 171), so what counts solely in the end is just Dasein. 57 John Donne “Meditation 17” in Devotions Upon Emergent Occasions (1107), which is also a motto in Hemingway’s For Whom the Bell Tolls.

The Phenomenon of Death 57 According to John D. Caputo, in the early Freiburg lectures on the philosophy of Kampf, while commenting upon life as a battle in which we should fight for our existence, Heidegger does not talk about the Other who we should go to war for. He leaves behind the cripple, the blind, the leper, the widow, the harlot, and all the Others cast out of society, forgetting that cura also means healing, lending a hand, and showing mercy (Caputo Demythologizing 58-59). In short, there are no victims in the history of Being, which Caputo calls emphatically “Heidegger’s scandal” (Demythologizing 131). Secondly, Heidegger disregards biology, a man of flesh and blood, taking advantage of the overwhelming reason, of phronesis, as Caputo further notes (Demythologizing 64). Additionally, there appears to be no room for “emotive insight” in Heidegger’s philosophy (Frings “Insight” 113), which severely neglects the sphere of emotion. Furthermore, even though Heidegger does touch upon feelings, like love or liking, he paradoxically grounds them in reasoning. In What Is Called Thinking?, Heidegger quotes Hölderlin’s poem “Socrates and Alcibiades,” where Socrates answers Alcibiades: “who the deepest has thought, loves what is most alive” (20). To add to the conclusions mentioned above, the focus on the authentic Being-towards-death makes Dasein free and independent. However, there is no physicality, there is no emotion pulsating through the veins, there is no Other by one’s side. And if no one is near us, neither is there a group leading to a state, where Dasein could find a place to dwell. As Kluback and Wilde remind us, echoing Plato, to truly possess a place in the world, man has to perceive oneself in two dimensions: vertical, i.e., ontological by focusing on oneself, and horizontal, i.e., political by concentrating on one’s relation to a state (19). With Heidegger’s above arguments, we are certainly able to see ourselves in the vertical dimension: we develop consciousness and individualism, we expand our inner worlds phenomenologically, not only with reference to death. There appears to be a problem with this horizontal dimension, because in our efforts to reach the authentic Being-towards-death, we rarely come into the world of the Other to form a group and to build a state.

58 Chapter One 3. Emmanuel Levinas Traditionally death has always been perceived either as a transition to a kind of existence after our earthly life, like in Plato’s Phaedo (285), or as nothingness, like in Heidegger’s Being and Time. Rejecting this alternative, in Of God Who Comes to Mind (1982), Emmanuel Levinas does not want to look at the human end as a choice between “to be or not to be” (OG 129), which would rank death as the first or the last issue to consider (Derrida Adieu 6). Instead of giving one answer, Levinas regards finitude as “a tertium quid” (“The Philosopher” 154), or as “an excluded third” (GDT 33). Thus he joins both traditional perspectives on finitude, and he thinks of death as existence as well as nothingness (TI 232-233). In God, Death, and Time, the French philosopher explains how such thinking is possible: demise can be seen as this “excluded third,” because the thought of death is “the end of what makes the thinkable thinkable” (GDT 90). In other words, while meandering through the mind, the thought of death goes beyond any possible rationalization, therefore it cannot enter any consciousness with any unequivocal statements. Moreover, Levinas is surprisingly unsure whether finitude as such is certain, and if the fact of expiration signifies annihilation (GDT 10). Similarly to Heidegger in Being and Time, Levinas starts his course “Death and Time”58 with a deliberation on the death of the Other. While watching how people pass away, finitude appears to be, among other things, “an immobilization,” “a departure,” “a decease” (GDT 9), “decomposition” (GDT 11), “a scandal, a crisis” (GDT 14). Additionally, on the face of any human being, the French philosopher perceives death which presents itself as “a question without givens, a pure interrogation mark” (GDT 14). Regardless of the names used to call it, Michael Purcell states that what accompanies the death of the Other is always emotion, which, nevertheless, has no possible imaginable representation (530-531).59 Levinas himself stresses ambiguity brought by death: “Death is at once healing and impotence; an ambiguity that perhaps indicates another dimension of meaning than that in which death is thought within the alternative to be / not-to-be. The ambiguity: an enigma,” the philosopher asserts (GDT 14). 58 “Death and Time” is one of the lecture courses Levinas gave in the academic year 1975/76. Together with another course entitled “God and Onto-theo-logy,” it constitutes the contents of God, Death, and Time. 59 Purcell writes: “The affectivity which one experiences in the face of death lies beyond intentionality and thematisation, refractory to all phenomenal appearance” (530).

The Phenomenon of Death 59 If death is an ambiguous notion, which is even unthinkable, the query remains why it occupies such an important place in Levinas’s philosophy. First of all, the word “nothing” cannot stop the thinker from discussions. Secondly, his philosophy is not a lecture full of fixed phrases, but rather a flow of various thoughts compared to waves60 which take us further, showing uncharted territory. In fact, the philosopher’s deliberations on every subject matter have no end. According to Richard A. Cohen, “the end in Levinas is neither an end, a finality, nor a truth, a comprehension” (“Translator’s Introduction” 2), which also shows why Levinas’s line of reasoning is so difficult, being replete with ambiguities left to decode (Greisch 68). Moreover, in opposition to Heidegger, the death of the Other in Levinas is a key issue, for even if the relationship with finitude remains exterior, it touches upon interiority (GDT 14).61 Yet, before we analyze quietus in Levinas, a few words concerning his stance on existence are necessary. The philosophy of Emmanuel Levinas is, in large measure, a polemic with Heidegger. In Existence and Existents, a work published in 1947, but which originated before the Second World War and was written to a great extent in captivity (xxvii), Levinas speaks of Heidegger as a source of his inspiration (EE 4). In a book published in the same year, Time and the Other, which was actually a series of four lectures delivered in 1946/47 in Paris, the French philosopher employs the same Heideggerian distinction between Sein and Seiendes, although he labels Being as existing or existence and being as existent (TO 44). No matter though how grateful he is to Heidegger for re-channeling the main thought of philosophy toward the fundamental issue of Being, Levinas conceives of the meaning of Being in a different way than the author of Being and Time, the idea that was initially drafted as early as in 1935 in Levinas’s article “De l’evasion” (Manning 36). Asking how we should see Being and beings (EE 2), Levinas’s final answer is that “in Being there are beings” (EE 106), which shows that beings are preceded by the pre-existence of Being. This 60 In his “Translator’s Introduction” to Time and the Other by Levinas, Richard A. Cohen refers to Derrida, who was the first to compare Levinas’s thought to the movement of waves (3). 61 With the Levinasian interiority one must be careful, since, apart from a reference to the entity’s inner state, the notion is also understood in terms of temporality. Levinas clarifies: “each being has its own time, that is, its interiority” (TI 57). Given that, one may reach the conclusion pointed out by Tina Chanter, who in Time, Death, and the Feminine points to the interweaving of the Levinasian issues of time and the Other, stating that “the ethical relation to the other introduces time” (178), and in another fragment, “time comes to me from the other, in the midst of my concrete and egoistic enjoyment of life” (179).

60 Chapter One viewpoint diametrically opposes Heidegger’s assumption that Being, as modus operandi of a particular being, always abodes this being, which actually conditions the very Being. Paradoxically enough, Time and the Other proves doubtless that Levinas’s idea about Being’s pre-existence is derived from Heidegger’s Geworfenheit (Manning 54), i.e., “thrownness” – the moment when a being becomes Dasein, when it is “thrown into existence” (BT 321). Furthermore, there is one difference that must come to the fore here. Manning stresses Heidegger intends to interpret the meaning of Being through Dasein, to which this Being gives itself in a way, whereas Levinas puts an emphasis on Being in general, Being itself that stands alone, one may say (40). In Existence and Existents, the philosopher plainly explains: “Being cannot be specified, and does not specify anything” (EE 2). A very important phenomenon in Levinas’s philosophy is “il y a,” or “there is,” as translated by Alphonso Lingis. The author of Existence and Existents defines it in a following way: “This impersonal, anonymous, yet inextinguishable ‘consummation’ of being, which murmurs in the depths of nothingness itself we shall designate by the term there is. The there is, inasmuch as it resists a personal form, is ‘being in general’” (EE 52). To bring the reader closer to his vision of the il y a, Levinas, like Scheler, wants us to imagine a situation in which all people, creatures, and objects do not exist. Yet, once we have envisioned this desolation, we cannot conceive of pure emptiness, as “the absence of everything returns as a presence, as the place where the bottom has dropped out of everything, an atmospheric density, a plenitude of the void, or the murmur of silence” (TO 46). In Very Little… Almost Nothing, Simon Critchley juxtaposes the il y a with the Heideggerian Being, even though, according to Critchley, Levinas underlined that there should be no mutual bond between his notion and Heidegger’s es gibt (57).62 For John Llewelyn in turn, 62 And what is the es gibt? Translated by Joan Stambaugh as “it gives,” or “there is,” the es gibt for Heidegger “names Being more clearly in simple language usage than the mere ‘being’ which ‘is’,” as Heidegger explicates in On Time and Being (38). Despite the vagueness found in the cited definition, Heidegger adds that the position of this mere existence, expressed by the simple “is,” may easily be seen in poetry, which he exemplifies by quoting short fragments of poems “Psalm” and “De Profundis” by Georg Trakl, and “Childhood” by Arthur Rimbaud. The last verse composition, taken from the collection Illuminations (1886), is here of great importance, since Rimbaud’s il y a, working nota bene as an anaphora in the poem, should be rendered as es gibt (Heidegger On Time 40). Regardless of this linguistic overlap, Manning mentions Levinas’s autobiographical essay “Signature” to prove the distinction between the il y a and the Heideggerian es gibt, referring to impersonality of the former and generosity of the latter (217).

The Phenomenon of Death 61 the there is constitutes a redefinition of Heidegger’s thrownness (Emmanuel 45), yet what it rather brings to mind is the notion of nothingness defined by Heidegger in The Question of Being as something being present (96-97).63 The phenomenon of the il y a has its immediate origins in one of the earliest memories that have haunted us since childhood. To refer to Ethics and Infinity, in one of the conversations with Philippe Nemo, Levinas answers that the il y a takes shape at night, when a child, lying alone in bed, hears “the silence of his bedroom as ‘rumbling’” that is similar to the murmur of the shell put close to the ear (48). The silence that paradoxically makes a noise is “the rustling of the there is” (EE 55), which amounts to horror throwing one in the state of vigilance (TO 48).64 Suffering from insomnia, one directly experiences the there is. Since it comes in the hours of darkness, it always looms up as something indistinguishable (EE 52), which like Moby Dick’s indefinite whiteness, may stand for various things (Melville 196).65 Moreover, every time it may be something different, because the experience of the il y a is like stepping into Cratylus’ river, which one cannot even enter once, as in the case of Heraclitus (TO 49). Devoid of any specification, what the il y a brings along is inhuman neutrality, already evident in the choice of the words Levinas finds for the phrase. This il, as the third person pronoun used in such expressions like “il pleut” (it is raining), or “il fait chaud” (it is warm), with an impersonal verb form, clearly highlights the lack of personalization (EE 53). The il y a is then something that cannot find its expression in a subject or a noun (TO 46-47), something unclear and vague, shrouded with ambiguity and anonymity (EE 93). “This existing is not an in-itself [en-soi],… it is precisely the absence of all self, a without-self [sans-soi]” (TO 49). The horror of the il y a causes “depersonalization,” which deprives an existent of any subjectivity (EE 56). However, it does not lead to a situation where the mind would confront exteriority or interiority of any kind. On the contrary, nothing has been created; nothing has been gained, because what 63 When one imagines the il y a as described by Levinas, i.e., as the presence that appears in the face of negation of reality, it is possible to think of Moby Dick’s whiteness, which “is not so much a color as the visible absence of color, and at the same time the concrete of all colors” (Melville 196). 64 This veille, translated by Richard A. Cohen as “vigilance,” is not easy to render as it may mean “wakefulness, watchfulness, a vigil, staying up in the night or watching over the night, the state of being on the brink or verge, as well as meaning ‘eve’ or ‘preceding day’” (Critchley Very 57). 65 “Is it that by its indefiniteness it shadows forth the heartless voids and immensities of the universe, and thus stabs us from behind with the thought of annihilation, when beholding the white depths of the milky way?” (Melville 196).

62 Chapter One constitutes the I has been absorbed by the night. It has gone, been drown, swallowed up, there is no noun form that could be used here. What is left is the very fact of being, which the anonymous I is forced to take part in, if the I wants it or not (EE 53). There is nowhere to go, or nowhere to hide, we can no longer withdraw into our private sphere, we are exposed to existence, which becomes our burden. In the context of depersonalization and anonymity, it may be surprising why, in an article “Il y a du quotidian,” Michael Fagenblat insists on the connection of the il y a and the self. However, according to the scholar, what is preserved in the state of the il y a is not psychological or social identification, but the corporality of the self (585). In the presence of nothingness that strips us of our private selves, when we speak of the horror of the il y a, we could associate it with the dread of annihilation. Yet, the fact remains that in Levinas this horror, throwing one into the anonymous vigilance, does not equate with Heidegger’s anxiety about death (EE 56). By surprise, and in opposition to Heidegger’s Being-towards-death, what one should feel apprehensive about is first of all life, i.e., one should feel “fear of being and not fear for being” (EE 58). Engulfed in existence then, one has no choice but to exist – one is condemned to exist, and what one experiences is apparently “the impossibility of death,” or in other words, the possibility of existence even after one’s annihilation (EE 56). In brief, for Levinas one cannot simply die: “The fatality of the tragedy of antiquity becomes the fatality of irremissible being” (EE 57). Earlier death was tragic, now the tragedy seems to be endless existence.66 To exemplify this fatality, Levinas quotes selected fragments of the works by Shakespeare, Racine and Blanchot. Here, we will focus only on Macbeth, who, after receiving the news about Banquo’s murder, sees the ghost of Banquo in his chair. Macbeth comments in act III, scene IV, which Levinas also quotes: The time has been, That, when the brains were out, the man would die, And there an end; but now they rise again, With twenty mortal murders on their crowns, And push us from our stools. This is more strange Than such a murder is. (Shakespeare 677) 66 And here we have a striking difference between Heidegger and Levinas, since anxiety is contrasted with horror - the fear for nothingness with the fear for existence (EE 58), which may additionally serve as an argument for Levinas’s insistence on the separation of the il y a from the es gibt.

The Phenomenon of Death 63 What is noticeable at once is a distinction Macbeth draws between the past in which people “just” died and the present in which they come back to life. This is the moment when Macbeth becomes cognizant of the impossibility of death, or of what Levinas also calls “a decisive experience of the ‘no exit’ from existence” that negates death (EE 57). However, this is not resurrection of any kind, this is just the fact of the there is, which is existence without an existent, as in the case of Banquo, who after going out of the earthly sphere, returns as a spectra that arouses a pervasive sense of horror in Macbeth, making him an insomniac. The subject, nevertheless, may break free from the state of the anonymous il y a thanks to a phenomenon called “hypostasis” (EE 82). As Levinas explains, in the history of philosophy it exemplified an occurrence when a particular action, expressed at first in the form of a verb, later found its expression in the form of a noun (EE 83). However, the grammatical aspect does not play a significant role here (Thomas 45). It rather signifies a transformation from impersonality to subjectivity, because through hypostasis unnamed existing leaves behind the il y a. And out of the il y a, an individual appears with his/her own existence which starts taking shape: “Someone exists who assumes Being, which henceforth is his being” (EE 83). Thus, in the words of Richard A. Cohen, incorporating additional footnotes while translating Time and the Other, hypostasis is first and foremost “the individuation of existence” (TO 44, footnote 6). Additionally, hypostasis should be ascribed both to an instant when it takes place and to a mode of its happening, but we should not treat it as an end product (Thomas 44-45). As “a situation where an existent is put in touch with its existing,” hypostasis also reveals Levinas’s dialectic (TO 51). In this event, the existent masters existence, but, at the same time, becomes burdened with it (TO 55-56). Explaining it, Levinas is far away from tautology. He considers hypostasis rather as a paradox, because the existent, previously locked in the fetters of the il y a, while gaining its freedom, at the same moment loses it. In other words, the subject has “to bear” this freedom (Thomas 47), not only by becoming liable for its irremissible existence, but also by starting to work on a clear direction of his/her life (TO 55). Probably that is why this occurrence comes into view as “a contract with oneself” that demands a tremendous amount of effort (Manning 45). Manning also underlines that it results in the appearance of an individual who is “a solitary, separate entity” (64), thereby suggesting no bond with the neighbor yet. In the long run, as a consequence of hypostasis, there emerges a person who, according to Levinas, is “resistant to the erosion of time and history, that is, struck by a death always violent and premature” (OT 106).

64 Chapter One The impossibility of avoiding existence is especially visible in suffering, which makes one conscious of death (R. Cohen “Levinas” 27). It is not so much the matter of moral pain though, which by arousing some scruples purifies, or sets free our conscience. What counts here is “the impossibility of nothingness” (TO 69), that is, physical pain which cannot be rationalized in any way, which we cannot retreat from, sensing its presence constantly. Its strength, Cohen adds, lies in its “doubling up,” i.e., the pain one feels seems to be inescapable, therefore one has a feeling that it has been doubled (“Levinas” 27-28). “Suffering, as suffering, is but a concrete and quasi-sensible manifestation of the nonintegratable, or the unjustifiable” (OG 128). And exactly in the feeling of physical pain that is unavoidable, irreducible, and non-understandable comes the herald of death (TO 69). As Tina Chanter notices, by contrast to Heidegger’s philosophy, in Levinas “suffering, and not anxiety, is the experience that provides privileged access to death” (“The Question” 100). Heralded by pain, death constitutes “an experience of the passivity” (TO 70). It is obviously a different kind of experience, because one cannot talk about an experience of death in the same context as one speaks of other occurrences which happen to us in life (TO 72). With regard to passivity, Richard A. Cohen vividly pictures the notion with a fragment from Conrad’s Heart of Darkness that shows Marlow’s inner struggle with death (“Levinas” 30): “I have wrestled with death. It is the most unexciting contest you can imagine. It takes place in an impalpable greyness, with nothing underfoot, with nothing around…, without the great desire of victory, without the great fear of defeat, in a sickly atmosphere of tepid scepticism” (Conrad 100-101). Thus, the active subject is involved in life until one feels immobilizing pain. In suffering, the proximity of death comes, bringing along “the limit of the possible” (TO 70). And this is the situation that cannot be elucidated for Levinas, the situation in which death presents itself as “absolutely unknowable,” which excludes every assumption one could make about finitude (TO 70-71). When asked by Christian Chabanis what we may understand by death, Levinas replies that it is “initially the nothingness of knowledge” (“The Philosopher” 153, emphasis added), which may even be seen as absurd (Diamantides 181). It is a thought that denies any kind of comprehension (Berezdivin 197); hence either nothing can be said about death (TI 233), or the only answer that may be given is simply “one does not know” (Levinas “The Philosopher” 153). As a result, in the early phase of man’s attempts to reason over the matter, finitude in Levinas constitutes the least unknown phenomenon out of all other incomprehensible issues (“The Philosopher” 153). When the existent finds oneself in relation to death, one discovers that, first of all, it cannot occur “in the light” (TO 70), with the light referring both to the darkness

The Phenomenon of Death 65 of the anonymous il y a, and to comprehension (EE 9). Secondly, unlike existence, finitude “does not come from itself,” i.e., it does not reveal itself to the existent. When it is here, man is not near it, ergo death for Levinas is “mystery” (TO 70), a never ending dilemma between existence and nothingness. As Purcell concludes, finitude in Levinas, contrasted with Dasein’s Being- towards-death, “cannot be possessed” with Heidegger’s characteristic of mineness, because death “has its own reality” never revealed to us (529). What is more, the scholar maintains, the consciousness of dying does not bestow power on us, as in the case of Heidegger, but rather vulnerability, infirmity, and despair. With death seen as mystery, Levinas, like Heidegger, rejects the possibility of deducing anything about expiration while observing how people pass away. Admittedly, the French philosopher first perceives death of family members as “disappearance or departure” (TI 232). However, when one thinks of one’s own death, there comes “an instinctive knowledge of death” that concerns sensing finitude in the fear about his/her own existence, and receding the finitude of the Other into the background (TI 233). For example, when Hamlet considers whether to be or not to be, he prefers existence, because we always choose what is known to us, not what we are unaware of (TO 73). Afraid and in fear, what one discovers by this instinctive knowledge is not death itself, which for Levinas is impossible to comprehend in contrast to Heidegger, but its nearness, and with it, “menace,” “violence,” even “murder in the night,” which the thought of death brings along, threatening my existence. Together with menace, violence is understandable, so why is there any talk of murder? Richard A. Cohen asserts that the organic life through reproduction is infinite, so when death appears as exterior from the outside, it comes as if it were murder (“Levinas” 34-35). This violence of death that is always premature is then like tyranny. It is something imposed from beyond and “against me” (TI 234), which is explicitly visible to Levinas, a philosopher of Judaism, when he ponders over the Shoah. Nevertheless, the situation is worse than war, because in a struggle one can see and hold its opponent, whereas death “is not open to grasp” (TI 233), either mentally, as non-being of knowledge, or physically, because when it hits with its tools, which are paradoxically graspable, it is not felt or experienced in any way, keeping its secret to itself (TI 234). However, we should not infer that Levinas gives up life so quickly. With the mention of Shakespeare again, the French philosopher draws our attention to the fact that “prior to death there will be battle” which is “a last chance” to act (TO 72-73). Hearing that Birnam Wood approaches the castle, Macbeth does not want to be passive and give up all hope. On the contrary, he wants to fight with incoming fate: “Arm, arm, and out!… / Ring the alarum-bell! Blow, wind!

66 Chapter One Come, wrack! / At least we'll die with harness on our back” (Shakespeare 690). Thus, due to passivity death brings along, there is no hope, but till we stop to act “[dum] spiro/spero” (TO 73), i.e., “while I breathe, I hope.” But how should one approach death in concentration camps, or a situation when death is the cost paid for survival – when death already happened and was an act of dehumanization? Analyzing Outside the Subject (1987), where there is Levinas’s discourse with Rosenzweig’s The Star of Redemption, Chanter answers the query, revealing two features, recognized by Levinas as typically Jewish: “One is that love is manifested as commandment; the other is that the individual mediates Redemption” (Time 206). The mystery of death is ungraspable for the reason that “death is never a present” (TO 71). Here, this present is not a synonym for a gift, as in The Gift of Death by Derrida. It constitutes a reference to temporality, because death in Levinas is always inextricably linked with the indefinite future (TO 71, 76; TI 233). As Lingis confirms, “in dying one finds oneself not grasping a future but drifting, aimless, toward an ungraspable futurity approaching, but not across the horizons of the articulated world, to take one” (xxv). Hence, while other circumstances can be partly visualized, finitude may be based on no correct assumptions. It is nothing that is a priori, nothing that we may draw up as a “project” (TO 74), nothing that lies “within any horizon” (TI 233), it is just “a deferred threat” (Bernet 95). While discussing Levinas’s temporality of death, Bernet, however, seems to be mistaken. He states that “the time of my own life, then, is indeed a temporality ‘in suspense’, engendered by death’s deferral” (95), which rather sounds as the reading of Heidegger, not of Levinas. To correct the view, between me and my death, there is a temporal break whose length scrupulously shortens, and my time and the time of my death, as opposite forces, flow in opposite directions. When I meet my finitude, death will come as an unexpected jump, and the end will take place without my consciousness of it (TI 235). In brief, in Levinas, where Epicurus’ teaching reverberates,67 death as a future event always remains in the sphere the subject will never be able to enter.68 67 “If you are, it is not; if it is, you are not” (Epicurus qtd. in R. A. Cohen “Levinas” 31). 68 There seems to be one exception to the rule when the presence of finitude, together with the determination of its date, may occur, and that is in a work of art. In his essay “Reality and Its Shadow,” giving an example of Edgar Allan Poe’s stories, in which the characters are apprehensive about being buried alive, Levinas recognizes that finitude can occur in existence: “one need only give oneself a constituted duration to remove from death the power to interrupt. Death is then sublated. To situate it in time is precisely to go beyond it, to already find oneself on the other side of the abyss, to have it behind oneself” (11).

The Phenomenon of Death 67 In the present, the existent, whose heroism is born with the above-mentioned hypostasis, has “mastery,” “power,” and “force” (TO 74, footnote 51). This mastery means that the existent is “able to be able” (TO 74), which denotes strength to carry on, to live, and to have opportunities. It obviously brings to mind Hawthorne’s Hester Prynne, whose scarlet letter, with the flow of time, started to mean “able,” which was read, among other things, as “power to do” (121). Death, the other way round, is never linked with physical capability for Levinas, and when it is here, the subject stops to be a being able to master it in any way, for finitude “completes the last leg of the journey by itself” (“The Philosopher” 155). This indicates that, by contrast to Heidegger, the existent cannot subjugate death even phenomenologically, and any acceptance of death is beyond Levinas’s scope. If that is the case, there can be no talk about the freedom that Dasein is able to experience after the phenomenological recognition of death, which finally liberates the entity and opens the gates to other possibilities. Rejecting Heidegger’s stance on death as the possibility of impossibility then, Levinas rather speaks of finitude as “the impossibility of every possibility,” heralded in suffering, which brings fear, violence, and at the end “a total passivity” (TI 235). This impossibility does not lead to other possibilities, but simply cuts them off. In Levinas’s words, it is “an extreme instant, torn from all assumption;… beyond all seizure or all dispossession, and beyond all welcome, pure abduction” (OG 47), which is the reason why Levinas would rather define demise as an “ever-open possibility,” carrying the conviction that its occurrence is ever possible (GDT 28). The author of God, Death, and Time stresses that for Heidegger nothingness brought by death is “thinkable” (GDT 69-70), whereas he himself conceives of finitude as something “unassumable,” “resistant to knowledge” (Levinas “The Philosopher” 155-156). Supporting his assumption with Bergson’s philosophy, 69 Levinas believes that “nothingness is a false idea, and death is not identical to nothingness” (GDT 55). Nevertheless, in the article “The Question of Death,” Chanter claims that the philosopher does not thoroughly repudiate death in terms of nothingness, insomuch as it comes from the Other, not from the I glorified by Heidegger (107). For example, as Chanter notices, a wish to murder Levinas describes aims at nothingness, at annihilation (107; TI 232). We also have to remember that death for Levinas is something completely different from what one has known before, i.e., something “absolutely other” (TO 74). That is to say, 69 “The idea of absolute nothingness, in the sense of an annihilation of everything, is a self-destructive idea, a pseudo-idea, a mere word… in short, annihilation signifies before anything else substitution, the idea of an ‘annihilation of everything’ is as absurd as that of a square circle” (Bergson qtd. in Levinas GDT 68).

68 Chapter One finitude as the possibility of impossibility analyzed by Heidegger in the context of mineness makes a reference only to the mortality of the I. This approach excludes the death of the other person, which for Levinas seems to be a considerable limitation (GDT 47).70 Furthermore, Levinas notes that the death of Dasein as such is just regarded as an abstract possibility with no realization in reality (GDT 52).71 In the instant when this “other” appears, one should realize that there is also the “Other,” which are two key terms in Levinas’s philosophy. Referring in French to autre (other, another) and autrui (fellow, neighbor) respectively, Richard A. Cohen in his “Translator’s Note” informs us that the former is associated with the concept of otherness, that is, “alterity,” whereas the latter is linked with the other person (viii). Nevertheless, Cohen warns the reader that Levinas is not consistent in this clear-cut distinction, using the terms interchangeably, therefore their meaning depends on the context. In the context of death, Cohen implies, Levinas appears to juxtapose both these phenomena, since he talks about death as the other, i.e., alterity, but he also expresses his idea in relation to the Other, i.e., the person.72 In Levinas’s words, which are actually contradictory to Scheler’s reasoning about death: “The relationship with the other is not an idyllic and harmonious relationship of communion, or a sympathy through which we put ourselves in the other’s place;… the relationship with the other is a relationship with a Mystery” (TO 75), which additionally supports the above stated argument for death as alienation. Admittedly, Levinas presents death as the exterior forming no alliance with anything else, but later he states that death as the other shows us an exit from solitude to social life (TO 77). Before we examine how such a transformation in 70 In Time, Death, and the Feminine, Tina Chanter gives the information that in a 1987 essay “Mourir pour…” (“Dying for…”), Levinas points out that mineness “implies an I and a you” (Levinas qtd. in Chanter 186). However, Chanter makes clear that such an opinion is marginal in his philosophy, because, by contrast with other works of Levinas, firstly, it appears to be “a concession” that could never have been written if Heidegger had not been dead, secondly the title is ambiguous, and thirdly, in the words of Chanter, this is “an essay that pays homage to Heidegger, and where in fact Levinas is at pains to be as fair as he can be to Heidegger’s phenomenology,” for he never forgave the author of Being and Time his affiliation with Nazism (185-186). 71 To support his argumentation, Levinas quotes a fragment of Being and Time. “Death, as possibility, gives Dasein nothing to be ‘actualized,’ nothing which Dasein, as actual, could itself be” (BT 307). 72 Footnote 52 in Time and the Other (75). For the sake of clearness, I preserve this distinction, capitalizing the Other while referring to the person, obviously except for certain quotations where I follow the idea of an author.

The Phenomenon of Death 69 his thinking is feasible, a few words about the Other should be mentioned to hold the discussion in a logical way. The situation when the existent starts to build a personal relationship with the Other is perceived by Levinas to be “the encounter with a face” (TO 78). In “The Trace of the Other,” written in 1963, the thinker asserts that the face comes from an alien world totally undiscovered by the existent who confronts it (352). What is more, Levinas mentions “the nudity of the face” (“The Trace” 352), which reveals complete poverty, bareness, and defenselessness. The face also speaks to me in its own language, imposing its existence on me with no possibility of my desertion. According to Jill Robbins, this communication is characteristic of droiture – a term used by Levinas, which Robbins translates as “straightforwardness,” “uprightness,” “rectitude,” or “justice” (56), but which may signify “loyalty” as well as “honesty.” What is equally important is that the face speaks, but it does not use rhetoric as its way of expression. Rhetoric replaces a dialogue (Gibson 59), so when it is used, there is no exchange of thought, no reflection; nobody listens to what the Other wants to say; there is no space for straightforwardness or honesty. With regard to the notion of the face, Levinas also puts forward an idea that appears to be difficult to comprehend. In “The Trace of the Other,” he claims that the trace of the face is not simply a representation, and that its meaning lies in its abstraction (352). It is hard to accept this abstraction, or lack of representation, if a few pages later Levinas states: “A trace is not a sign like any other. But every trace also plays the role of a sign; it can be taken for a sign” (356). To exemplify the point, Levinas tells stories of a detective, a hunter and a historian, who, to find an answer, follow traces left by a criminal, an animal, and an ancient civilization. This explanation grants us clear consent to seek for clues in the face of the Other, helping us to see “the epiphany of the absolutely other” (Levinas “The Trace” 353). Having introduced the issue of the Other, we may start scrutinizing what combines death and the person who lives next to me. The juxtaposition of the other with the Other is possible, because a meeting with another person resembles in Levinas the confrontation with the thought of death. As Levinas explains in Entre nous: “in the Face of the Other always the death of the Other and thus, in some way, an incitement to murder, the temptation to go to the extreme, to completely neglect the other – and at the same time… the Face is also the ‘Thou Shalt not Kill’” (104). That is why, apart from seeing demise as the unassumable other, Tina Chanter observes that Levinas’s impossibility of possibility may be explained in another sense. Drawing nearer to the Other, the existent perceives that the “impossibility of murder already dwells in the face of ethical resistance, in the face of the other,” which simply announces a ban on

70 Chapter One annihilation (“The Question” 107). According to Chanter, in such a situation, the fear inseparably connected with dying is also transformed into the fear of killing the neighbor, which, except for resistance to murder, may be connected with defenselessness that his/her face exposes. The encounter with the Other, defined as “the face-to-face with the Other,” is also the moment that the same as death cannot be assumed, or projected in any way (TO 78-79). What is experienced is silent confrontation with something that is intriguing, but impossible for us to take hold of (Visker 92). As a translator of Time and the Other, Richard A. Cohen adds that alterity is a characteristic attributable to both death and the Other,73 although in his own work on Levinas, Ethics, Exegesis and Philosophy, Cohen speaks of the alterity of the Other as the most radical one, and of death as “not sufficiently other” (97). In addition, both death and the Other come from the same region which is the future (TI 233), and what joins the issues in question is also the will. In Totality and Infinity (1961), Levinas claims: “the violence of death threatens as a tyranny, as though proceeding from a foreign will” (TI 234). Talking about “Cain’s murderous will,” Llewelyn helps us to understand what the will is: “Death is interpersonal. Terrifyingly. For it is personified in the threat of an alien will” (104). Still, Levinas speaks of the will of the I, too, which may be transformed in goodness toward the Other. “The enemy or the God,” says Levinas, “over whom I can have no power… permits me to will, but with a will that is not egoist, a will that flows into the essence of desire…, the desire that is for the Other” (TI 236).
