In other words, although exposed to the threatening will, the entity may wish the opposite for the Other: one may exist for other human beings, one may devote one’s time to them, which is nothing else but the act of making existence meaningful in spite of death (TI 236): This existence for the Other, this Desire of the other, this goodness liberated from the egoist gravitation, nonetheless retains a personal character. The being thus defined has its time at its disposal precisely because it postpones violence, that is, because a meaningful order subsists beyond death, and thus all the possibilities of discourse are not reduced to desperate blows of a head struck against the wall. (TI 236) Yet, the question remains how it is probable that death presented before as passivity, exteriority, and alienation may show us now a gate to socialization. Moreover, how is it possible to postpone the violence of death in the relationship with the Other who is impossible to get to know? There appear to be two roads to the core of Levinas’s deliberation over the phenomenon of finitude – through fecundity and responsibility. Let us now turn to the erotic relationship first. 73 R. A. Cohen notes in footnote 52 in Time and the Other: “What is common to death and social life is an encounter with radical alterity” (75).

The Phenomenon of Death 71 Similarly to death, Eros creates a relation with alterity. In her article “The Alterity and Immodesty of Time: Death as Future and Eros as Feminine in Levinas,” Tina Chanter writes that Levinas treats the sphere of Eros differently from Heidegger (143). The German philosopher does not see the Other with regard to Eros, whereas for the French one this otherness is found in the feminine, who is the Other that builds a one-to-one “society” in an intimate relationship (TI 264-265). With the feminine comes “voluptuousness” or “voluptuosity,”74 or “love of love” (TI 265), which may reshape a world from the one of consumption and already-made products to the one of evanescence, as Irigaray claims in “The Fecundity of the Caress” (231). Also, voluptuousness should be treated neither as a feeling of a lower grade (TI 265), nor as a substitute for Freud’s libido searching for pure sexual pleasure (TO 88-89). Surprisingly, voluptuousness helps the person to discover the self (TI 270), but what is accomplished thanks to voluptuousness is “the common action of the sentient and the sensed” (TI 265). That is to say, the subject feels the Other, feeling exactly what the Other feels. The love of love obviously manifests itself through caress, which, strictly speaking, is “a mode of the subject’s being” (TO 89), a mode that in Irigaray’s words realizes itself in the form of a touch “which weds without consuming” (232). In Totality and Infinity, the caress is explained as something that does not try to catch a person or an object, but “loses itself in a being,” hovering “in the no man’s land between being and not-yet-being” (TI 259). Compared to an unplanned game with something impossible to catch (TO 89), the caress expresses love (TI 258). Paradoxically, the feeling of love neither gives knowledge (TI 231) nor leads to a particular person I am with (TI 264). For Claire E. Katz, in “For Love is as Strong as Death,” Levinas’s caress expressing love looks for something that does not exist yet (125), something that in the thinker’s linguistic game is expected to come (à venir) from the future (avenir) (TO 89), something that in the future will be a child coveted and engendered in voluptuousness through caress (TI 266). In this way, in a sexual intercourse, the future appearing on the horizon brings with itself alterity, which cannot be reduced (Chanter “The Alterity” 138). As a result, the conception of a child in Levinas moves love to the level of fecundity (TI 253), which is not just the plane of biology but of infinity. As Peperzak in To the Other elucidates, procreation constitutes a moment at which a subject survives as a subject, becoming infinite (196). Eros’s “movement consists in going beyond the possible” (TI 261). “Eros hence goes beyond the face” (TI 264). 74 In Time and the Other, translated by R. A. Cohen, it is “voluptuousness,” in Totality and Infinity, translated by Lingis, it is “voluptuosity.”

72 Chapter One What happens is “the reiteration” of the person who is reborn in a child, yet despite being parents’ reflection, the child remains for Levinas “a stranger” (TI 267-268).75 This means that this child, although a faithful copy of its father or mother, retains its “ipseity” understood as its own selfhood (TI 268). As an absolutely different Other, with its own unrepeatable personality, building its own world, which parents can hold no power over, the child is a new beginning; and “in the beginning, there is already being. This beginning is the unity of being and nothingness” (GDT 73), which resembles Scheler’s wave of “becoming-unbecoming,” observable in procreation.76 To return to Levinas, the conception of a child represents this tertium datur, which is the answer to the question of death. This answer may be given, because thanks to fecundity the infinite being, which is “ever recommencing being,” realizes itself again and again in a newly born child, going at the same time beyond death (TI 267-268), ergo the “victory over death” is complete in one way (TO 90). It is relevant to stress here that Levinas is far away from concealing the erotic in a relationship of two people. Having in mind his Jewish origin, we should remember that although Levinas favors intercourse in which a child is conceived, he does not discount sexuality as pleasure achievable now, not in the future (Katz 131).77 Moreover, fecundity defined by Levinas as “the goodness of goodness” (TI 269) is a step further from a one-to-one society to brotherhood, because a couple gives birth to a fecund being, who will conceive another fertile being in the future, prolonging the existence of a given nation (Katz 128-129). Thus fecundity is the end of fear of death as annihilation, marking with a new being a new beginning. Nevertheless, every child born to this world does not herald the constitution of a new totality in every individual. For Levinas one 75 The reference here is made to the Book of Isaiah. The fragment Levinas has in mind is later partly quoted at the end of the chapter “Transcendence and Fecundity” (TI 277). I quote here the whole verse from the Old Testament: “Then shalt thou say in thine heart, Who hath begotten me these, seeing I have lost my children, and am desolate, a captive, and removing to and fro? And who hath brought up these?” (Isa. 49.21). 76 Levinas interprets here the notion of the beginning that Hegel scrutinises in Science of Logic, which involves the discussion of pure being and pure nothing (GDT 72-75). The unity Levinas speaks about is possible thanks to the motion of pure being and pure nothing in which one dissolves in the other. That movement Hegel calls “becoming” (qtd. in Levinas GDT 75), which, like Scheler’s vision of life as the process of “becoming-unbecoming,” or Barthes’s enantios, constitutes a unity of two opposites, that is, being and nothingness. 77 Referring to Levinas’s Difficult Freedom, Katz mentions that in a ketubah, which is a Jewish marriage contract, there are three things that a husband commits himself to providing his wife with: food, clothes, and sexual satisfaction. Moreover, if after ten years a couple is still childless, they may receive an annulment of their marriage (131).

The Phenomenon of Death 73 rather enriches the already existing totality with the element of infinity that abides in it (TI 270). “To be infinitely – infinition – means to exist without limits, and thus in the form of an origin, a commencement, that is, again, as an existent” (TI 281). Infinity is obviously connected with time, which in Levinas is neither the flow of loosely connected instants nor a permanent duration as it is in Bergson. The author of Totality and Infinity compares time to spring, which always brings along something new, but in a way it is burdened with the events that have happened before. Also, time that happens brings alterity. However, to enable this alterity to come, there has to be a break between events, which is produced by death (TI 283-284). “Infinite being is produced as times, that is, in several times across the dead time that separates the father from the son. It is not the finitude of being that constitutes the essence of time, as Heidegger thinks, but its infinity” (TI 284). In her analysis of fecundity, Edith Wyschogrod also states that during “a dead time when the old moment dies and the new moment is not yet born, the individual is freed from his egoity” (138).78 Illustratively, the author of God, Death, and Time prefers to consider the concept of death on the grounds of time (which for him derives, among others, from Ernst Bloch’s philosophy)79 instead of making time conditional on death, as it is in the case of Heidegger’s Being-towards-death. In Levinas’s reasoning, influenced also by Kant, this kind of approach does not deprive finitude of significance, but it does not make death decide exclusively how we should understand other phenomena (GDT 104).80 As a result, Levinas’s existent is able to understand time thanks to the meeting with the Other – not by confronting the thought of death (Manning 74). To join the notions of time, infinity, fecundity, death and the Other, 78 Wyschogrod clearly describes how Levinas understands the notion of time: “lived time is for Levinas time that dies and is born again. Time is noncontinuous; it is full of breaks. In the production of the interval, a dead time when the old moment dies and the new moment is not yet born, the individual is freed from his egoity” (138). 79 Also see the chapter “On Death in the Thought of Ernst Bloch” in Of God Who Comes to Mind (33-42). Bloch’s philosophy perceives Marxism as “humanity in act” (qtd. in Levinas OG 42), whereas death is seen as a failure to complete a particular task whose completion is interrupted by expiration. However, in the subject there is an utopian idea that one will manage to achieve it, which constitutes hope, but in Levinas words: “The nothingness of the utopia is not the nothingness of death” (OG 38). 80 Levinas does not want to see a being from the angle of death exclusively, and he shows his opposition, among other things, through the discussion of hope in Kant’s philosophy (GDT 57-65). He concludes: “The practical philosophy of Kant shows that the Heideggerian reduction [to ontology] is not obligatory. It shows that there might be, in the history of philosophy, a signification other than that of finitude” (GDT 61).

74 Chapter One Peperzak’s accurate summary is worth mentioning here, as it will additionally help to elucidate the above quoted fragment from Levinas more clearly: The ‘infinition’ of fecundity surpasses all possibilities of past and present by its openness to other destinies. Beyond his own death, a ‘father’ receives new chances in the existence of his ‘sons.’ They give him – in the strongest sense of the word – a new beginning, thanks to an interval of time separating his and their life. Beyond death there is a continuity on the basis of discontinuity. (200) Time imposes no restriction on the existent, but enables one, if one wants, to build one’s relation with the infinite in another way than through fecundity. This other way is responsibility. In the heart of the being who knows s/he is finite, there arouses “a rational hope” (GDT 63, emphasis added). Derived from Kantian philosophy, this hope is neither a kind of hope for immortality nor for prolonging time (GDT 63).81 For Levinas it is a hope that death, although ungraspable, may be meaningful rather than nothingness (GDT 64). It is a hope that there is “infinity in the finite” (GDT 110). This “in” denotes nothing else but “the putting in question of me [moi] by the other [l’autre] that takes the form of an appeal to my responsibility” (GDT 110). In “Beyond Intentionality” Levinas also states: “the idea of the Infinite is to be found in my responsibility for the Other” (qtd. in Hand 5), the responsibility of which Derrida says that it stands “before death, before the dead, beyond death” (Adieu 83). Thus this “in- of the infinite” should make me aware that my neighbor is near me (OG 70), because “infinition is the infinition of Desire for the Other, and the infinition of Desire for the Other consists in the increase in responsibility that comes with my response” (Llewelyn 101). In Levinas infinite time starts to realize itself with the proximity of the Other, who does not have to be one of the closest relatives to me. It happens when the I turns toward any person whose face “summons me, asks for me, lays claim to me” (OG 162). Since on the face there is a ban on indifference, when asked, one cannot drop the claim, therefore the only choice one can make is to express the word “I,” which signifies “here I am, answering for everything and for everyone” (OT 114). The phrase “here I am,” or “me voici,” is a biblical expression uttered by Abraham when God asked him to sacrifice his son (R. Cohen Ethics 204; Gen. 22.1). It constitutes the first word for Levinas, and signifies a link between death and language, adopted nota bene from Heidegger (Chanter Time 204). However, through the phrase, the I masters neither death nor speech, because “the other dictates the sense of my words,” the presence of the Other shapes my answer (Chanter Time 204). Thus the infinite dwells in me, 81 Comparing Kant with Levinas, Catherine Chalier states that Kant speaks about the entity’s hope for timeless movement toward holiness (147).

The Phenomenon of Death 75 and I wake it up by taking responsibility for the Other and his/her death, which never signifies “a simple altruism” (Purcell 532), but an act through which finitude is overcome (OG 44). “The relationship with the Infinite is the responsibility of a mortal being for a mortal being” (GDT 117), and it is the liability that makes death meaningful (OG 163). The significance of the unknown enigma is then discovered by Levinas in the death of the Other, which is neither secondary experience nor handed-down wisdom (GDT 10-12). As he writes in Otherwise than Being (1974), my own death is meaningless (3), but when the Other passes away there is “an exception – which confers upon death its depth” (GDT 16). And only when the existent meets something that is other – never understood by the existent, may the meaning of death, ungraspable so far, be uncovered (Purcell 529). With the focus on the person, by seeing finitude in the face of the human being who is totally exposed to me, this initially ambiguous question with no response becomes the question “in which the turning toward the other is effected,” and “every question is a request or a prayer” (GDT 42). This request, or even “a demand,” as it is later called in Of God Who Comes to Mind (175), which is addressed to me, arouses a particular emotion of “disquietude” that causes the response to appear. Again, this is nothing else but my responsibility for the Other (GDT 42), explained by Visker as “an engagement, a self-engaging answer to a need” (92). And the subject acts as responsible when one is afraid to abandon another human being while s/he is dying, to leave one alone with the ungraspable, which is simply an act of goodness the I can give to one, because “death’s meaning begins in the interhuman” (OG 163). That causes responsibility to be more powerful than demise,82 which is the point summarized by Dennis King Keenan in the following words: only the aporia of death – that moment when death as possibility turns into death as impossibility – is adequate to the aporia of responsibility, insofar as death as possibility gives irreplaceable singularity and death as impossibility give the ex- propriation, the anonymity, that is a forgetting or effacement of oneself. The aporia of responsibility calls for being read alongside the aporia of death. (103) Here, we must stress that Levinas’s responsibility is not used to fill in the sphere of the unthinkable, which is left after much deliberation devoted to finitude, but it should be a top priority in the ethical code of behavior (OG 165). The call, which sometimes the Other lets out, even against the Other’s own will (Visker 91), is to make one listen to with no possibility of escaping – be close to, be with, watch over the Other. Additionally, even if the territory of this 82 Levinas makes a cross-reference to Phaedo, where Plato denounces suicide (OT 195; footnote 10).

76 Chapter One accountability is limitless, in the proximity of the Other, the guardian is never near enough (OG 70). Likewise, responsibility allows no substitution to occur: the I was called, and only the I can respond as irreplaceable, for the act of abdication is even more unthinkable for the philosopher in Humanism of the Other than “jumping out of one’s skin” (7). In Outside the Subject, while contrasting his reasoning with Martin Buber’s equality of the I and the Thou, Levinas even conceives of this responsibility as “ethical inequality” (44). He explains the entity’s inalienable subordination to the neighbor in terms of the sense of guilt with the support of the quotation from Dostoevsky’s Brothers Karamazov: “We are all guilty of everything and everyone, towards everyone, and I more so than all the others” (Dostoevsky qtd. in Levinas Outside 44). Nevertheless, the Other the existent answers for has no debts to pay off. On the contrary, this is the existent who is indebted to the Other, because this liability grants one a sense of identity: “I am ‘in myself’ through the others” (OT 112), that is, thanks to other people my existence I am burdened with gains a proper meaning. As Hand confirms, the impossibility of being absolved from answerability leads to the individualization of the responsible (4-5). By turning toward the Other, the existent’s subjectivity changes into “hospitality,” but the entity becomes simultaneously a host – giving, and a guest – receiving (C. Davis 83). This inversion of being leads to the rousing of the subject from “a deathlike passivity” that before aimed at the self (OT 124; OG 164). To quote Mouzakitis: “the death of the Other forces the ‘subject’ out of its solipsistic shell” (68). In consequence, it gives rise to the individualized I, who after fighting with inner egoism has reached its own identity, becoming authentic and unique (GDT 111), which leads to the absolute, too (OT 124). The undelegatable and untransferable responsibility guarantees authenticity. This is not, however, the authenticity defined by Heidegger as the acceptance of my own death. Levinas, who believes that we must go beyond Heidegger, understands authenticity as the acceptance of the responsibility for the finitude of another being, which he calls “the first death” (GDT 43). Although the Others’ deaths do serve as “substitutes” that allow the subject to imagine possible alienation linked with decease, something else is here at stake (Berezdivin 197). In the face of the Other, “death ‘regarded me’,” that is, looks at me and concerns me,83 “before its confrontation with me, before being the death that stares at me, myself” (OG 162). To a certain extent, this is dying for the Other, although it does not happen apparently, for in Levinas’s words, this is 83 Bettina Bergo, a translator of the work Of God Who Comes to Mind, stresses in a footnote a double meaning of the French word regarder, which may signify “to look at” and “to concern” (OG 209, footnote 13)

The Phenomenon of Death 77 “the taking upon oneself [susception] of the ultimate gift of dying for another” (OG 163, second emphasis added). To leave no scope for misunderstanding, we should also underline that authenticity must be marked by the responsibility for the Other’s existence, since “we are answerable not only for the death of the other but for his life as well. And it is in being answerable for his life that we are already with him in his death” (Levinas “The Philosopher” 167-168). In other words, Levinas is attached to being rather than to Heidegger’s Being-towards-death (Thomas 22), insofar as the weight of being is shifted to human relations (Diamantides 182). The first death surely counts, but what counts more is “the first body” (R. Cohen “Introduction” xxxiv), which obviously signifies the neighbor, as well as all his/her needs that are to be satisfied by the responsible. Cohen grasps the point precisely: “To suffer for others is to serve them: to provide for their concrete material needs for nourishment, clothing, health, shelter, and employment; to assuage their pains, anxieties, and fears; to respect their freedom and dignity; to care for the other’s requirements before protecting or catering to one’s own various social identities” (“Introduction” xxxiv). In addition, suffering, as a herald of the unjustifiable death, as passivity, may also acquire significance like finitude on condition that it assumes the form of serving the Other (O’Connor 232). Thus, through the act of giving oneself to the neighbor who dwells next to me, the I forms the definition of authenticity, which, in Levinas’s words, realizes itself as “pure gratuity toward alterity” (OG 165). To go beyond Heidegger then one has to go beyond oneself - one has to choose the responsibility for the Other first, and with them their demise. However, it turns out that it is not actually one’s own choice. Paradoxically, the responsibility is not one’s decision. It was the Good, often capitalized by Levinas, which elected me – the good that is “other than being” (OT 18). Thus for Heidegger everything starts with Being and the acceptance of death, whereas for Levinas with goodness and the acceptance of the Other, because “the Good is before being” (OT 122). Yet, what here awaits us is another of Levinas’s paradoxes. To be oneself, one has to become “a hostage” to the neighbor, one has to sacrifice oneself for the Other whenever it is necessary, which is, strictly speaking, a message sent to us by God through the Love Commandment. As Levinas states in a 1965 article “Enigma and Phenomenon,” “to go beyond one’s death is to sacrifice oneself” (76). “For love is strong as death” (Song 8.6), love is the final answer given by Levinas to the initially unanswerable question of death, which ought not to have the last word (Derrida Adieu 3). The most important thing is clearly the Other, in whose face, which is “the word of God” (Levinas qtd. in Visker 93), one should see the commandment of God, who is infinity coming back to humanity (OG

78 Chapter One 166). Hence, the Other’s countenance expresses à-Dieu (OG 168), which is the term rendered as “the unto-God” by Bettina Bergo, as “the to-God” by Jane Marie Todd, and as the “God bless” by Richard A. Cohen.84 Bearing its French meaning in mind, Derrida explicates what the very adieu may signify: firstly, a salutation or even a benediction, surprisingly sometimes expressed in French at the beginning of a conversation, not at its end; secondly, the word given at the moment of departure, including death; thirdly, “for God or before God,” denoting “any relation to the other” (The Gift 47). However, the à-Dieu “is not a finality,” Levinas writes (OG 177). Thanks to love more powerful than death, thanks to our being near the dying, ethic goes beyond ontology – the subject goes beyond Heidegger’s Being-towards-death, opting for being-toward-God, one may say. Thus the concrete realization of being-toward-God takes place due to love devoid of lust, through love toward a stranger who is not left alone with the mystery of the ungraspable (OG 176). Moreover, contrary to Heidegger, the subject feels apprehensive about this stranger, not about oneself. For these reasons, love, despite being the logos whose meaning, for the French philosopher, is in most cases distorted, “is par excellence the fact that the death of the other affects me more than my own” (GDT 105). This affection uncovered in the face simultaneously becomes a step toward the public at large, since as Keenan asserts, “the à-Dieu also marks the opening of the space of community” (104). The responsibility does not end with the moment when the Other departs this life, because we should be responsible for these whose time is now, and for those who passed away (Spargo 36). Under the influence of Hegel’s Phenomenology of Spirit, in which there is a reference to the deed for the dead, Levinas, echoing Scheler, speaks of the duty to inter the deceased (GDT 83-85). The duty is almost always performed by the family, who never regards the dead one as the flesh, but as a person with a separate consciousness. In fact, owing to funerary rituals, relatives who think of the dead and death (which is now possible to be thought!) make the buried ones come back. “In this way, they transform the deceased into a living memory,” which makes the dead alive in their thoughts again (GDT 86). As a result, the ties of blood devoid finitude of the power of annihilation, and at a funeral a new unusual bond is created between the living and the deceased (GDT 86). Finally, according to Levinas, memory is obligatory, although the thinker warns us against its exaggerated 84 Bettina Bergo translated Of God Who Comes to Mind by Levinas (OG 168), Jane Marie Todd What Ought I to Do? Morality in Kant and Levinas by Catherine Chalier (128), and Richard A. Cohen “Bad Conscience and the Inexorable” by Levinas (40), which later was included in Of God Who Comes to Mind.

The Phenomenon of Death 79 conceptualization. Skeptical of the accounts related by survivors, who may distort the truth about the dead, Levinas’s responsibility for those who passed away should not come down to a commemorative act. Rather, from the very beginning, our memory ought to take form of “an affective response to absence” (Spargo 59). While trying to sum up Levinas’s philosophy, we can turn to Otherwise than Being, which begins with a few epigraphs. One of them is derived from Pascal’s Thoughts, and it reads as follows: “‘That is my place in the sun.’ That is how the usurpation of the whole world began” (OT vii). Despite the risk of oversimplification, the second sentence may be taken as the summary of Levinas’s philosophy, which in turn should be explained as the inversion of philo-sophia (Greisch 77). It is no longer “the love of wisdom, it is only the ‘wisdom of love’” (Greisch 77).85 Thus, according to the French thinker, this kind of knowledge is not a path chosen by Ulysses, who comes back to his native land, which Levinas understands as the direction of contemporary philosophy leading to the land of the I – not the land of the Other (Humanism 26). In Levinas’s case, choosing the Others from their birth to their death is the road taken, and “that has made all the difference” (Frost 1187). 85 “Philosophy is the wisdom of love at the service of love” (OT 162).

Chapter Two The Benjy and Jason Narratives and Scheler’s Phenomenon of Death Seeing the impoverished existence led by people who repudiated dying, Max Scheler regarded the reinterpretation of death as indispensable in order to correct the line of public thinking. William Faulkner’s reasons for writing about quietus seemed to be quite diverse and more personal, with no didactic overtones. In Faulkner: A Biography, Joseph Blotner mentions William Spratling’s conversations with Faulkner, in which the future Nobel Prize winner revealed, somewhere between July and October of 1925, that for him only love and death were “two basic compulsions on earth” (157). This philosophy of life found its reflection in Faulkner’s first novel, Soldiers’ Pay. Published in 1926, with its predominant theme of dying, it tells a story of Lieutenant Donald Mahon, who, wounded severely in the First World War, comes back to his hometown only to collect his soldier’s pay – to see Cecily, his fiancée, married to another man, to wed Margaret, who becomes his wife probably out of pity, and finally to die shortly after that. Later, in 1941, in a letter to Professor Warren Beck, Faulkner in a way affirmed that the thought of demise was one of his underlying motivations for work, and stated that all his life he had been writing about noble values and human ability to stand predicaments with a purpose to live and die at peace (Selected 142). In William Faulkner: The Yoknapatawpha Country, Brooks points out the main themes exposed by the writer in his fiction, that is, “violence, isolation, and agony” (367). The similar view is held by Noel Polk, who maintains that Faulkner is well-known for “violence and destruction,” although there are not many visions in his writing that may be called apocalyptic in the strict sense of the word (“Faulkner’s” 117). In Re-Appraisals, Martin Green speaks more forcibly, criticizing Faulkner for creating in his novels “engines of mental torture, crucifixions of literary sensibility” (qtd. in Sundquist 6). Mentioning Faulkner among the writers of “a literature of darkness,” Leslie A. Fiedler talks about “the Faulknerian syndrome of disease, death, defeat, mutilation, idiocy, and lust,” observable later in the stories of the artists who followed the father of Yoknapatawpha (29, 475).

82 Chapter Two With particular reference to The Sound and the Fury, the very title of the novel calls upon the section of Shakespeare’s Macbeth just after the death of Lady Macbeth (34). In “A Brief Analysis of The Sound and the Fury’s Namesake,” Joel Deshaye notes that in the fragment the title is derived from there is a direct hint at a passing human existence that leads to “dusty death,” being a reminder of the biblical “from dust to dust” (on-line). Deshaye also regards another verse in the fragment, namely “the last syllable of recorded time” (Shakespeare 34), as a clear reference to finitude. Additionally, in “William Faulkner: The Sound and the Fury,” while mentioning Eliot’s “mythical method,” Collins sees in the sections of the novel an inverted correlation between the Compsons’ history and Christ’s Passion (225-226): Jason’s narrative as Good Friday, Benjy’s as Holy Saturday, Dilsey’s as Easter Sunday, and Quentin’s as a day within the Octave of Corpus Christy (a Thursday in 1910), which is the continuation of the observance on Maundy Thursday. Due to this biblical allegory, making The Sound and the Fury an extended version of Christ’s Passion, the novel may be classified as one of “Faulkner’s fatal narratives,” to employ Lisa K. Nelson’s terms, because the story presented there is not only “fated,” with the Compson family doomed to decay, but also “fatal” obviously for Quentin (57).86 Scrutinizing further the contents of the work in question, in his article “Benjy, the Reader, and Death,” Arthur A. Brown infers emphatically that “death is writing this novel” (on-line). With the sound and the fury becoming more and more audible every time one reads the book again, we may conclude, together with Coindreau, that “Faulkner is content to open the gates of Hell” (30-31). Nevertheless, no matter how far the world of death, agony, violence extends, in the essay on “Primitivism in The Sound and the Fury,” Brooks claims with great certainty that the novel itself represents “no statement of nihilistic despair” (9). It is necessary to mention how the story revealed in The Sound and the Fury began for the author himself. In a 1956 interview with Jean Stein vanden Heuvel carried out in New York, Faulkner said: “It began with a mental picture. I didn’t realize at the time it was symbolical. The picture was of the muddy seat of a little girl’s drawers in a pear tree where she could see through a window where her grandmother’s funeral was taking place and report what was happening to 86 Lisa K. Nelson uses the phrase “fatal narratives” specifically with reference to Absalom, Absalom! and Light in August. She explains: “The story of Christ, and by extension any story allegorically structured on it, would of necessity be both fated and fatal: how it ends would and could not change, and the protagonist would die. It is this doubled sense of fatality that structures Faulkner’s fatal narratives under consideration here” (57).

The Benjy and Jason Narratives and Scheler’s Phenomenon of Death 83 her brothers on the ground below” (LG 245). For the sake of comparison, it is also advantageous to quote what Faulkner once shared with Coindreau, the French translator of The Sound and the Fury: “It struck me that it would be interesting to imagine the thoughts of a group of children who were sent away from the house the day of their grandmother’s funeral, their curiosity about the activity in the house, their efforts to find out what was going on, and the notions that would come into their minds” (Faulkner qtd. in Coindreau “Preface” 30). What may be noticed easily in both citations is not only the leitmotif of death in the novel, but the growing consciousness of its presence in the human mind. William Faulkner was “a writer defending universal values” (Maszewski William 31), whereas Max Scheler was a philosopher for whom the value of the person was non-exchangeable and unique (Langan 127). From the first pages the Benjy section echoes Scheler’s philosophy of death connected with the theory of values. When we start reading The Sound and the Fury, we enter the topsy-turvy world, resembling the one described by Scheler in “Death and Afterlife,” where the appropriate system of values has been turned upside down. The non- exchangeable value of Benjy as a person, which Scheler regards as the most relevant, is rejected by the self-centered Luster, who is overwhelmed by the lowest values of utility and senses. Trying to find the quarter he lost, Luster would like to satisfy his need to see a show, which he ranks over Benjy’s existence. The transposition of the values, visible not only in the opening scene in the Benjy section, but in other tableaux of his narrative, results from impoverished life. This kind of life is in turn the outcome of the chaos that appears in every human reasoning when, among other things, there happens to be this “public inertia vis à vis death and afterlife,” as Frings writes in The Mind of Max Scheler (139), or, as in the case of The Sound and the Fury, when we can hear the repercussions of the resistance of Benjy’s parents to share with their children the knowledge of death. The well-known fate of Caddy, Quentin, Jason, and Benjy would not be different, though if they are doomed to lead an impoverished (as Scheler said) and inauthentic (as Heidegger later put it) existence from the very beginning, which carries the traces of Faulkner’s autobiography (Taylor 37). When their grandmother nicknamed Damuddy passes away, the children “are not allowed to be part of the family at a time of death” (Bassett “Family” 412).87 Damuddy’s 87 In Faulkner’s Search for a South, Walter Taylor mentions that Miss Maud, the author’s mother, intended to prevent her offspring from participating in their grandmother’s funeral, but J. W. T. Falkner, their grandfather, insisted on their participation (37). In Faulkner’s Questioning Narratives, David Minter states that after the burial Faulkner and his siblings were sent away to a different place on account of disinfection of the house (41).

84 Chapter Two body is concealed from them, and the four offspring are not taught about dying, which simultaneously deprives them of the possibility of its understanding, and consequently, its acceptance. After playing in the branch, they are denied entering the house through the main door, and the alleged reason for it is guests, not death. Strongly disagreeing with the idea, Caddy declares that she will not only walk into the parlor, but also take Damuddy’s chair (SF 27). By her insistence on taking the chair, which may illustrate the circle of life and death, too, Caddy demands in a way to be informed about the situation. However, she is denied that right, since their father, awaiting them by the kitchen stairs, wants them to be quiet and have their supper in the kitchen, not in the dining room. Additionally, when he is asked by Caddy, who seizes the initiative again, if they have to make no noise because of the company, Mr. Compson just says the meaningless “yes” (SF 28), and this is the only explanation from him that the children receive. The responsibility of explaining to them what happened and what the idea of human death is has been shifted onto Dilsey. Although she talked to her own children about the ensuing situation, surprisingly she leaves the white offspring in the dark. When asked the same question by Caddy, she answers that they will know “in the Lawd’s own time” (SF 29). Caddy does not give up asking what that means, yet the question is left unanswered again. Only Quentin replies that this is Sunday, which is not such a bad answer anyway, since Sunday was the day of Jesus’s resurrection. Nevertheless, the confusion arises in their minds when they hear their mother crying, which Quentin identifies perfectly, but Caddy misinterprets, preferring to believe that it is singing (SF 30). This also shows that, similarly to their father, their mother, acting ambiguously for them, is not a responsible parent either, hiding not only the fact of death from them, but also what attitude people should adopt toward it. In addition, she has not explained to Jason, her favorite child, why since the moment when Damuddy got sick, he has not been allowed to sleep with her. The successive attempts to discover what death stands for end with Dilsey closing “both the doors,” which prevents the children from hearing anything (SF 30). The fact that white and black children were raised together finds its reflection in The Sound and the Fury (Blake 100), so both races should have been informed about death. However, under the Compsons’ roof, there is no story about dying that would be audible for the white who ask. What is heard is a wrong assumption made by Caddy, who concludes they must be enjoying the party instead of mourning for Damuddy’s death (SF 30). This actually makes the novel an excellent exemplification of Scheler’s thanatological philosophy, with the difference that in Faulkner these are white adults who let their children lead a life with no consideration for finitude. If there is such a confusion caused by

The Benjy and Jason Narratives and Scheler’s Phenomenon of Death 85 the parents who befuddle “sense and sensibility” in their children, it is not surprising that life that grows under such a roof cannot be meaningful or authentic much later, neither for Scheler nor for Faulkner, as it is exemplified in the course of The Sound and the Fury. The situation is diametrically opposite in the house belonging to the representatives of the black race, for Dilsey’s children are not only informed about the end, but they give the whites their first lesson about dying. The lesson takes place nowhere else but by the door of Dilsey’s cabin, and the teacher of death is Frony, Dilsey’s daughter, who shares her knowledge with the Compson offspring. Although forbidden to tell about the funeral, as we learn from Versh’s words: “Didn’t mammy tell you not to tell them” (SF 39), Frony is the first one that openly fights against the complete ignorance of death the Compson offspring betray in this scene. First of all, she answers Jason’s question “what’s a funeral” (SF 39), which is certainly not the answer that would be given by an adult, but it is vividly the best illustrating reply that a child could make. Frony describes what people do during a funeral: “they moans,” and how long it may last: “They moaned two days on Sis Beulah Clay” (SF 39). Furthermore, Frony denies Caddy’s incredibly false belief that, firstly, a funeral is something attached exclusively to the black: “That’s niggers. White folks don’t have funerals” (SF 39), secondly, that mortality is attributed to animals, more specifically to the Compsons’ mare, Nancy, which was shot by Roskus and left in the ditch (SF 40). Eaten by buzzards, Nancy represents the only image of death that the Compson children, with the most experienced Caddy, so far have seemed to be familiar with. The picture obviously taught them nothing, or if anything, this was rather indifference toward a corpse. What also strongly testifies to Caddy’s ignorance of finitude is the vague language she speaks, as the word “dead” is not associated with her grandmother, who is depicted by Caddy as “sick” (SF 45), but with dogs: “Dogs are dead” (SF 40). Moreover, she employs the word “undress” while talking about the carnivorous buzzards that simply ate Nancy (SF 40). The symbolic proof that the black children are enlightened about finitude is also a bottle of lightning bugs that T.P., the youngest of Dilsey’s, holds in his hands (SF 38). Moreover, when Caddy, Jason, and Benjy approach their house, Frony and T.P. play in the dirt, which also symbolically shows they have been allowed to get to know what could be unpleasant or repulsive but unavoidable in life. As it is revealed in the Appendix,88 treated by Faulkner as “an obituary” of 88 Hereafter as A. Written by Faulkner in 1945 for the publication of The Portable Faulkner edited by Malcolm Cowley, the Appendix contains a certain number of discrepancies if compared with The Sound and the Fury. 86 Chapter Two the Compson family (Selected 237), that kind of upbringing helps them to be successful in life. What is meant here by success is the fact that at least some of Dilsey’s children do not lead an impoverished life, e.g., they stay in touch with their parents and make a sacrifice for them, as it is in the case of Faulkner’s teacher of death, Frony, who, after starting a family, moves back to Memphis from St. Louis to look after her mother, who did not want to travel (A 426). Yet, even if Faulkner’s African-Americans are generally less disillusioned about life and death, it is important to stress that the writer had no intention of idealizing them. Luster, although informed about death before, is intimidated by it. In the passage relating his grandfather’s death, he is shown as unwilling to go to the barn, because he is afraid of his grandpa’s ghost, who he allegedly saw the previous night (SF 40). Let us now apply to the Benjy section Scheler’s three assumptions, which, according to the philosopher, help people regain the consciousness of death. To begin with outer observation, one of the Schelerian ways of feeling the certainty of death, there are a few images of dead animals in The Sound and the Fury. There is the carcass of Nancy, the Compsons’ mare, that after injury was shot by Roskus, which in fact is the story recalled within Benjy’s recollection 1945 and addressed to Cowley, who had asked Faulkner to correct the differences, Faulkner admitted that there was never a chronological chart to refer to (Selected 207). In another letter to Cowley, dated 18 February 1946, Faulkner once again gave his opinions about the existing differences: “I dont care much for facts,” and further, “the inconsistencies in the appendix prove that to me the book is still alive after 15 years, and being still alive is still growing, changing; the appendix was done at same heat as the book, even though 15 years later, and so it is the book itself which is inconsistent: not the appendix” (Selected 222). In the letter to Robert N. Linscott, written in late May or early June in 1946, Faulkner insisted on printing The Sound and the Fury with the Appendix as first. He also stood it firmly that it should be named “Appendix Compson 1699-1945,” as for him “it’s really an obituary” (Selected 237). Remembering all these facts, in his article “The Textual History of The Sound and the Fury,” James Meriwether warns of drawing too close a relationship between the novel and the Appendix (2). In addition, the reader of Faulkner should bear in mind Stacy Burton’s advice to be sceptical of all the texts printed after the 1929 publication of the novel, in which Faulkner shared his opinions about The Sound and the Fury. In “Rereading Faulkner: Authority, Criticism, and The Sound and the Fury,” Burton shows that Faulkner’s authorial comments revealed in these texts distort the interpretation of the novel, in which no evidence to support his views is found (passim). Following the advice given by both critics, which, in fact, had been given by the very author by saying “the book is still alive after 15 years, and being still alive is still growing, changing” (Selected 222), it is true that caution should be exercised. However, every statement given by Faulkner cannot be treated as contradictory to the novel in question, so in this thesis references to the later texts will be employed.

The Benjy and Jason Narratives and Scheler’s Phenomenon of Death 87 concerning Damuddy’s death (SF 40). In the next fragment, which, interestingly enough, concerns Benjy’s father’s death, we find Benjy throwing a glance at Nancy’s bones again. The picture helps him recollect the moment when he was watching the hovering buzzard over the carcass, which makes Benjy a witness to the gradual process of decomposition (SF 42). While delivering a letter to Mrs. Patterson, Caddy shows Benjy a place where the traces of pig slaughtering are visible. One more time this is a fragment that appears after the passage where there is a direct hint at death, namely Christ’s crucifixion, for the thirty-three- year-old Benjy snags his garment on the nail (SF 3). In the opinion of Michael Millgate, in The Sound and the Fury “evocations of place, of climate, of seasonal change are among the many elements which anchor action and meaning firmly to the human level” (88). While considering the picture of flora and other external factors, we may detect the certainty of death in the Benjy section, too. In the same recollection referring to the delivery of the letter, what does not escape Benjy’s notice is the images of lifelessness: the soil they step on is “hard, churned, knotted” (SF 3), and withered flowers, devoid of color, are just “brown” (SF 14). The climbing vine they pass by is “dry” (SF 14), which is evidently the symbol of dead life. This dry vine in The Sound and the Fury potently contrasts with a mention of the vine in “That Evening Sun,” where it is referred to the moment of conception of Nancy’s child (292).89 The picture of the frozen creek mentioned in the novel may also arouse thanatological connotations (SF 14), especially if one remembers Pierrot from Faulkner’s poem “The World and Pierrot: A Nocturne”90 (Samway 230-231). With a soul compared to a paper lamp “in a garden of dead trees,” Pierrot, who must die, withdraws to frosty peak (Faulkner qtd. in Samway 230-231). All in all, alluding mainly to water and flowers, Michael H. Cowan, in his “Introduction” to Twentieth Century Interpretations of The Sound and the Fury, supports that these images “take on overtones of impurity, narcissism, pain, and death” (12), but obviously such an opinion may be expressed about other elements of nature. Moreover, except for the telling images of the dead animals and plants, the reader together with Benjy may discover death intuitively, observing the change of seasons indicative of the passage of time. He and his sister are to deliver the message in winter, whereas the fragment that precedes and the one that comes after the delivery are set in spring or in summer (SF 13-14). In “‘Each in Its 89 “It [child] never come off of your vine, though,” says Nancy to her husband (292). 90 The poem comes from Vision in Spring, a booklet of poetry presented to his future wife in 1921. Also see Faulkner’s poem “Nocturne” in William Faulkner: Early Prose and Poetry (82-83).

88 Chapter Two Ordered Place’: Structure and Narrative in ‘Benjy’s Section’ of The Sound and the Fury,” George R. Stewart and Joseph M. Backus ascribe the preceding fragment to April 7, 1928, whereas the action in the fragment that follows the winter letter delivery takes place either in spring or in summer, the critics presume (443-444). With such an arrangement of the passages, there is even more to discover than the intuitive certainty of death, since the April 7 fragment refers more specifically to the Easter Saturday, when Christ went down to the kingdom of the dead, while the day when they are to deliver the love message to Mrs. Patterson is exactly December 23, just before Christmas, when Christians celebrate the anniversary of Christ’s birth. Thus, what the reader may additionally observe is the exemplification of the Schelerian wave of “becoming-unbecoming” noticeable in the universe and in human life (Scheler qtd. in Frings TM 141). The support for the conclusion is provided by Kinney, when he discusses how Benjy changes the meanings of loss, which makes the character combine “joy and grief, love and death” (139). This fusion pictures for us the faces of Janus, the figure whom Scheler employs to illustrate the characteristic wave.91 Bearing in mind the observation of people, Scheler claims that a human body would indicate that bodily functions must stop one day (S 74-75). It is true that in The Sound and the Fury Benjy does not spot a human corpse, for his grandmother’s body has been hidden from him. Nevertheless, the eyeing of the aging and weakening Dilsey, always present in his life, gives him a hint that people gradually advance in age, fail in health, lose their strength, walk more slowly, or, like Benjy’s mother, lie in bed with sickness suggestive of the coming end. Moreover, Benjy can discover death not only through the sense of perception, but also through the sense of smell, identified by Faulkner as “one of my sharper senses” (qtd. in Gwynn and Blotner 253). Although the door is closed, he is capable of scenting his father’s death (SF 41). Further, according to one of the black protagonists, Benjy is even able to predict death, as Roskus confirms in the black vernacular: “He know lot more than folks thinks…. He knowed they time was coming, like that pointer done. He could tell you when hisn coming, if he could talk. Or yours. Or mine” (SF 37-38). Nonetheless, as Max Scheler remarks, this empirical knowledge may be put aside, and one should detect death a priori through the phenomenological 91 Upon close examination of Faulkner’s style of writing, Walter J. Slatoff notices that in the author’s descriptions it is possible to find a great number of phrases with contradictory words. For example, in Light in August, the face of Doc Hines’s wife is “peaceful and terrible,” “the town was sorry with being glad;” in The Hamlet, one of the characters is “at once active and lazy” (176). This tendency to present the opposites resembles Scheler’s idea illustrated by the wave of becoming-unbecoming.

The Benjy and Jason Narratives and Scheler’s Phenomenon of Death 89 analysis of death and time, performed in one’s consciousness (S 75, 77). According to Scheler, one would be intuitively cognizant of the approaching end by focusing exclusively on one’s life perceived as a process. In every stage of one’s existence, the process can be seen as the structure of three horizons of the past, present, and future altering constantly in the death-oriented direction. Faulkner thought of the correlation between death and time before he published The Sound and the Fury. In an essay dedicated to the composition of Sartoris, which appeared in January of 1929, whereas The Sound and the Fury was published in October (Blotner 749), Faulkner openly admits that he “speculated on time and death” (qtd. in Sundquist 8).92 What is more, Faulkner’s center of attention is “not outwards but inwards, not centrifugal but centripetal,” as Millgate supports (286), so we should focus on Benjy’s consciousness now, searching for further thanatological traces there. After reading part one of The Sound and the Fury, the word that comes across the reader’s mind is definitely not “process” or “structure,” but “chaos.” However, Donald M. Kartiganer, inferring that what Benjy “tells us is life, not text,” devotes his critical work, The Fragile Thread, to the relevance of the structure in Faulkner’s novels (9). Believing that the “fragmentary structure is the core of Faulkner’s novelistic vision,” the scholar underlines the importance of perceiving “the way in which the different units relate to each other, the way in which they become part – or fail to – of a coherent whole” (xiii). In Faulkner, Warren Beck also speaks of “integrity of composition, in self-contained, consistently keyed fictional form” being Faulkner’s norm (280). With specific reference to The Sound and the Fury, one of its first reviewers, Abbott Martin, in his article in The Tennessean, dated from 17 November, 1929, maintains that “the story does not sprawl. It possesses an organic unity” (83). And in his letter to Ben Wasson, Faulkner himself made the division of the Benjy section into different events. As he remembered “off-hand,” the number of the events was seven, and they all together were to compose “a continuous whole” (Selected 44). Thus, by curious paradox, Faulkner did plan the allegedly chaotic arrangement in the Benjy section (Selected 44), because, as Vickery sustains, the author of The Sound and the Fury always had the order in view (32). In addition to helping his future readers find their way in this maze, Faulkner meant to introduce varied colors of ink in order to mark transgressions from one event to another. He knew, however, that the printing was both very expensive and poorly developed at that time, so he just insisted on italics and 92 The essay was edited by Joseph Blotner under the title “William Faulkner’s Essay on the Composition of Sartoris,” in Yale University Library Gazette 47 (January 1973) (Sundquist 161).

90 Chapter Two refrained stubbornly from any editorial changes proposed by Wasson (Selected 44). Interestingly enough, much later, in correspondence with Malcolm Cowley about editing of The Portable Faulkner, Faulkner wrote that about ten years before he had sent a copy of The Sound and the Fury to Random House, with lines underlined in various colors to distinguish chronologically one episode from another, but Blotner, who edited Faulkner’s letters, claims that such a book has never been discovered (Selected 207). Apart from the facts mentioned above, the order is indubitably palpable in a 2003 hypertext edition of The Sound and the Fury published by Peter Stoicheff, Allison Muri, and Joel Deshaye, scholars of the University of Saskatchewan in Canada, which partly fulfills Faulkner’s dream about the ink publication with at least the Quentin section in color. While analyzing the scene shifts of Benjy’s recollections, the scholars deduced that a given event, even though fragmented, did appear sequentially in the whole section (Stoicheff “A Guide” on-line). On the other hand, in his article “‘Where you want to go now’: Recharting the Scene Shifts in the First Section of The Sound and the Fury,” Robert Dale Parker concludes that “Benjy’s scene shifts keep promising a consistent system, but they never reach the system that they repeatedly promise” (15-16). Parker shows explicitly that although most shifts do emerge chronologically, there are isolated subscenes that get out of order in the following recollections: the name alternation, the letter delivery to Mrs. Patterson, Quentin’s death, Mr. Compson’s death and funeral, Caddy’s wedding, and Benjy’s attack on the Burgess girl. Another thing is that the critics argue about the number of particular events involved in the section. Stewart and Backus mention thirteen “levels,” as they name particular scenes, including a few unidentified lines, as well (444). In the hypertext edition of the novel, Stoicheff, Muri, and Deshaye point out twenty all together; and Edmond L. Volpe, in “Appendix: Chronology and Scene Shifts in Benjy’s and Quentin’s Sections,” enumerates sixteen various scenes (104). To give an example of the inconsistencies, let us scrutinize three passages connected with the episode of Quentin’s death, directly linked with the issue in question. While Stewart, Backus, and Parker see the passage starting with the words “there was a fire” as a fragment about Quentin’s death, which comes second in chronological order (SF 33; Stewart and Backus 443-444; Parker 8-9), Stoicheff, Muri, and Deshaye perceive it as the first in this episode. The passage “what you know about it” is classified the other way round (SF 34): for Stewart, Backus, and Parker it constitutes part of the first fragment relating to Quentin’s death, whereas for Stoicheff, Muri, and Deshaye it is the second chronologically. In addition, it happens that the scholars ascribe particular, cut- out passages to different recollections, for instance, the passage starting with the

Even if the scholars did their best, there is no consensus on the matter of order either in the case of Quentin’s death, or his father’s expiration. Notwithstanding the differences in those episodes, Parker himself admits that “even for scenes that proceed out of chronological sequence, most of the subscenes still fit chronological sequence” (6). When the fragments that build up the recollection of Damuddy’s quietus are carefully examined, they do come chronologically, except for the introductory subscenes that the researchers differ slightly about. With certainty, the order may also be applied to Roskus’s death – the episode whose shortness must have helped in the process of classification, since all the quoted scholars assign it to the identical two fragments appearing in sequence. The same we may say about the passages depicting the April 7 episode set in the present time, for even if the critics’ opinions diverge a little about their number, from 31 (Stoicheff, Muri and Deshaye 2003) to 32 (Stewart and Backus 444; Volpe “Appendix” 105; Parker 8), they are of the same mind that the subscenes building the episode come in order of time. All things considered, the time shifts appear chronological in most cases, and even if there exist some exceptions to the rule, they stand in direct contradiction to Brooks’s conclusion concerning “timelessness” in this part of the novel (William 330). The issue in question now is whether Benjy has any intellectual capabilities to notice any kind of order. Certainly, the results of the above displayed research clash with Benjy’s widely spread and accepted idiocy, recognized, for example, by Collins (“The Interior” 38), or by Kirk and Klotz (29). Also, in William Faulkner: The Yoknapatawpha Country, Brooks states that Benjy “has not much more sense of time than an animal has” (329), but a bit further, referring to the last scene in The Sound and the Fury, he claims that “meaning for Benjy is succession in due order” (348). Moreover, in the same critical work, Brooks later concludes that in Faulkner “disorders are eloquent of the possibilities of

The Benjy and Jason Narratives and Scheler’s Phenomenon of Death 93 order” (368). In addition, Arnold Weinstein believes that when we dip into the first pages of the book, “Benjy already knows all the things the novel is going to teach us” (39). The scholar also observes “a constant to-and-fro between past and present” in this narrative (41), which further challenges the alleged stupidity of Benjy and the lack of order in his section. Aware of Shakespeare’s Macbeth as the source for the novel, with its introductory part being “a tale / Told by an idiot” (Shakespeare 34), most scholars would prefer to label Benjy with the epithet “idiotic.” In “A Note on ‘The Idiot Boy’ as a Probable Source for The Sound and the Fury,” Michael A. Fredrickson infers that Faulkner is infatuated with the figure of the fool, since the character of this kind appears in his other works, e.g., in Absalom, Absalom!, The Hamlet, The Mansion (on-line). According to the critic, Wordsworth’s ballad entitled “The Idiot Boy” also provided Faulkner with inspiration for The Sound and the Fury. Besides this, Faulkner himself harbored no illusions about his protagonist’s mental retardation. In the interview with Jean Stein vanden Heuvel, he openly stated that “Benjy wasn’t rational enough even to be selfish. He was an animal” (LG 246). Nevertheless, at the very beginning of the same conversation, the author of The Sound and the Fury admitted that if he was questioned about a given issue one more time, his reply might differ significantly (LG 237), so one should be vigilant not to treat Faulkner’s comments as his final statements (Absalom 141). To give an example of his inconsistencies, in one of the introductions to The Sound and the Fury, edited by David Minter under the title “Mississippi Quarterly Version,” there is a passage in which Faulkner attributes reasoning to Benjy, and then there follow a few fragments that deny his comprehension (222-223).93 The scholars, like Faulkner, seem to be indecisive. Brooks first speaks of “Benjy’s near-mindlessness” (William Faulkner: The Yoknapatawpha 325), and of “the mind of an idiot” (326), exposing his animal-like features, but later he considers Benjy’s affection for Caddy as “recognizably human” (337). In the article entitled “Primitivism in The Sound and the Fury,” Brooks turns the reader’s attention to “the doubleness of Benjy’s limitations,” which evinces itself in the fact that “Benjy can apprehend the presence of death” (11, emphasis added). Collins adopts the same attitude. Although he identifies Benjy with Freud’s non-rational but instinctive id, he observes that the so-called idiot has “special logic and perception” (“The Interior” 43). As early as 1955, in American Journal of Mental Deficiency, Winthrop Tilley was strongly against 93 “I just began to write about a brother and a sister splashing one another in the brook and the sister fell and wet her clothing and the smallest brother cried, thinking that the sister was conquered or perhaps hurt” (Faulkner “Mississippi” 222-223).

94 Chapter Two treating Benjy as mentally retarded: “Benjy seems to turn out a fabricated literary idiot whose correspondence to any idiot, living or dead, would be not only coincidental, but miraculous” (qtd. in McLaughlin on-line, emphasis added). The same verdict was sustained by Merritt Moseley in 1986, for whom Benjy’s state is just “a literary convention” (qtd. in Truchan-Tataryn 162), to say nothing of Faulkner, who regarded his characters and places as fictional (Cowley The Faulkner 109).94 To add other arguments, Arthur Geffen calls Benjy “a holy idiot” demonstrating “knowledge denied to far more ‘intelligent’ people” (234). Sara McLaughlin, by citing medical sources, indeed fights against Benjy’s idiocy, but still she diagnoses him as suffering from autism (on-line). At the same time, Maria Truchan-Tataryn sees Benjy to be Faulkner’s “tool” rather than a realistic character (162), pointing out that a protagonist who is to be mute for all people around, but whose speech is comprehensible, cannot be classified as mentally retarded (166). She concludes: “The problem is not so much the nature of Benjy as an imaginary figure but that he is perceived to be a mimetic rendition of a person with some kind of cognitive or developmental disability, despite interpretive conflicts regarding the diagnosis” (170), which makes scholars contribute to fossilizing the stereotypical picture of impairment in society.95 To cut off what seems to be an endless discussion, let Faulkner express his opinion: Benjy is an idiot “trying to find the answer.” Further, “to complicate the picture, I had the idea of someone who would be more than just a child, who, in trying to find the answer [what was happening in the Compsons’ house], would not even have a normal brain to use – that is, an idiot. So Benjy was born” (qtd. in Coindreau 30). Moreover, James B. Meriwether claims that Faulkner, by missing out the question marks, wished to express a specific aspect of Benjy’s perception (16), which again backs up the phenomenon of Benjy as a literary idiot with his own unique consciousness. In conclusion, we can ask the question of who is really of unsound mind, and whose madness is more hazardous to society, if, according to Perrin Lowrey, Quentin is regarded as the one with “insane obsession with the relationship of time” (76), Jason’s conduct is characteristic of “frantic dashing about” (77), whereas Benjy’s repetitive cry exemplifies “a lament for the dead past” (66). And even if Lowrey supports Benjy’s stupidity, he claims that to a 94 What also helps to see Benjy as a literary idiot is Evelyn Scott’s comment on his retardation: Benjy “is a better idiot than Dostoevsky’s” (14). 95 Truchan-Tataryn’s final conclusion is as follows: “Disability continues to be the scapegoat that is devalued, rejected and destroyed symbolically to purify society from its fear of sickness, pain, deviancy and death” (172).

The Benjy and Jason Narratives and Scheler’s Phenomenon of Death 95 certain degree, Faulkner’s character “manages to keep the time sequence of an incident straight in his memory” (69). The aim here though is not to totally deny Benjy’s mental condition; one would rather present him in the same way as Lawrance Thompson does in “Mirror Analogues in The Sound and the Fury,” i.e., as Faulkner’s “moral mirror” (88), whose role is to reflect “the antithesis between the human power to create chaos and the human power to create order” (102). His idiocy is rather dubious, which is visible in the final sentences in the Benjy section, where the so-called idiot is able “to convert even darkness into a pattern of meaningful and soothing symmetry, serenity, order” (Thompson 93). With the implied order in the Benjy section and the repudiation of his idiocy, we may start applying to Faulkner Scheler’s temporal structure of life as divided into the three horizons. The horizons concern the first assumption, but it is impossible to analyze them without mentioning the second assumption, which touches upon finitude as an act noticeable in the process of life. Exemplified by an alternation between death and life that interchange in various episodes of existence from the moment of procreation, the second assumption seems to be almost omnipresent in the first part of The Sound and the Fury. Referring to the Benjy section, in The Ink of Melancholy, Bleikasten speaks of the “interweaving of images of life and death,” and infers that “death is a haunting presence” there (67). In the article “Benjy, the Reader, and Death: at the Fence in The Sound and the Fury,” not only does Arthur Brown mention finitude as a main theme of the novel, but he also singles out two kinds of death: actual deaths and symbolic or figurative deaths like, for example, the moment when Caddy leaves home (on- line). Brown’s division will be presented in this paper, as well, but let us first apply the horizons of the past, present, and future to Benjy’s narrative. The considerable part of the section related by Benjy is composed of his memories. The past horizon predominates here with no doubt. As its inseparable component, the act of remembering is observable as well, since, as Stoicheff states in his guide to this section, “it is the remembering that comprises the bulk of the narrative” (on-line). And in the majority of the recollections, the subject matter of dying is interwoven, for Benjy mentions the death of his brother Quentin, of his father and of Roskus, their servant, remembering the funeral of his grandmother, as well. What additionally seems to be etched in Benjy’s memory is a once-a-week trip to the cemetery, which is the scene depicted on the final pages of the novel, too. Apart from that, the events that allegedly have nothing in common with decease are recalled to explain it, because the representatives of the black society, acting in Faulkner as a sort of oracle, perceive Quentin’s suicide as a consequence of the alternation of Benjy’s name. The best illustration of the Schelerian philosophy of dying seems to be Benjy’s recollection of Damuddy’s finitude. The reminiscence has been selected

96 Chapter Two not because it comes into view chronologically as first, but because this particular event is the cornerstone of the structure of the whole novel (Vickery 28). Besides, in the Southern Review version of the introduction to The Sound and the Fury, Faulkner held that “perhaps the only thing in literature which would ever move me very much [was]: Caddy climbing the pear tree to look in the window at her grandmother’s funeral while Quentin and Jason and Benjy and the negroes looked up at the muddy seat of her drawers” (219-220). Walter Brylowski interprets the picture as an act of courage from Caddy’s side to look at death face to face, and as the moment of discovering the forbidden knowledge about finitude (39). Also, with the obvious juxtaposition of sex and death, Bleikasten notices “the phonic kinship of muddy and Damuddy” (The Ink 367), yet the pronunciation is not all. Life, which young Caddy stands for, is in a way enclosed by death, as the word “muddy” in the word “Damuddy,” with the muddy drawers being a peculiar memento mori, “all are of the dust, and all turn to dust again” (Eccles. 3.20), which constitutes a clear alternation between life and death mentioned by Scheler. Another reminder of people’s mortality in Benjy’s recollection of Damuddy is by contrast the grown-up Roskus. It is interesting to notice that he is the protagonist that appears first in the subscene of the recollection, bringing back the grandma’s quietus.96 At the same time he is sequentially the last one that factually dies in the novel. Moreover, his expiration is the theme of the last memory in Benjy’s part, which all together could serve as another example of what Maurice Bassan called “rounding” (on-line).97 Besides, what is meaningful is how Faulkner opens up the subscene, commencing it with the words “and Roskus came” (SF 19). First of all, there is no capital letter that would signify that a new story began, which makes it rather a continuation of another story that was told before; secondly, there is the conjunction “and” that highlights this continuity, as well. For Walter K. Everett, this style of writing seems to be typical of Faulkner, because one of the aspects of his art is the technique of “in medias res” (x). Claude-Edmonde Magny goes even further, claiming that the father of Yoknapatawpha usually starts his story at its end (66). Ergo, we can say that in Faulkner death does not only overlap with life, but it initiates the stories of his characters’ existences, as it is in Scheler at the moment of 96 The subscene “and Roskus came” is the passage classified by all the critics as the one that relates Damuddy’s death. Chronologically speaking, Stoicheff, Muri, Deshaye classify it as first, Parker, Stewart, and Backus as second. 97 Maurice Bassan, in his article “Benjy at the Monument,” speaks of “‘rounding’ the novel” while comparing the opening and closing scenes in The Sound and the Fury, between which he sees a striking similarity with Benjy and Luster as their main actors (on-line).

In addition, Roskus’s presence at the very beginning of the reminiscence of Damuddy’s demise shows how one death in Faulkner may foreshadow other events of passing away in the novel. Another relevant factor showing that death is present in life from the very beginning is the time of action in the Damuddy recollection. When Roskus arrives to call the children home, the day comes to the end, which is the point in time Faulkner certainly did not choose at hoc, because the early version of The Sound and the Fury was a short story entitled “Twilight” (available in the hypertext edition of the novel) (Ferguson 121). According to Mortimer, among possible meanings attributable to “twilight” in Faulkner is “the passing of something into a lesser state, ultimately toward death or absence” (71).98 Also, another story entitled “That Evening Sun” should be mentioned here. Although it came out two years after the publication of The Sound and the Fury, it still relates the story of the Compson family. Its title was probably derived from “St. Louis Blues,” a very popular song by William Christopher Handy, with death as its leitmotif (Johnston 98). Yet, the titles of the tales are not the only source that testifies that the time when the event happens is not a sheer coincidence. The comment that the night is approaching is repeated three times in the whole recollection. Interesting is the fact that the first one who informs us about it is Quentin, who is the next person who dies in the book (SF 23). The following character that speaks about the semidarkness is Caddy (SF 44), whose figure, as it will be later shown, arouses in Quentin thanatological connotations. What reinforces the presence of death is also the fact that Roskus comes to call children for supper, which we may obviously cross-refer to the Last Supper in the Gospel of St. John, during which “Jesus knew that his hour was come that he should depart out of this world” (13.1). Let us now discuss the place of action. When Roskus approaches the group, he finds the children playing in the tributary of a river, which, together with other water images, Grant discerns as a primary recurring symbol in Benjy’s tale. In relation to the theme of Easter, the scholar speaks of water imagery symbolizing “ritual cleansing and resurrection,” which, however, may imply other sources than Christianity (706). 98 Chapter Two reference is to the mythological Styx, across which Charon carried the souls of the dead for an obol either under the tongues or on the eyes of the dead. And here the dead who are ferried to the underground are all the children of the Compsons: Caddy, Quentin, Benjy, and Jason, because, as Irving Howe states, “in the water-splashing incident to which Benjy so persistently returns, the behavior of the Compson children is an innocent anticipation of their destinies” (160). The splashing then may be perceived as the marking of death, being at the same time a prediction that the family in the future will become extinct, with Quentin - Caddy’s daughter, being “the last,” as it is pointed out in the Appendix (A 424). The extinction of the Compsons obviously reveals the death of the family as an institution. With the careless mother and the passive father, the Compson house becomes hell, which Brooks, by means of Milton’s words, describes as a place “where all life dies, death lives” (qtd. in Brooks “Primitivism” 24). In the context of space in the Damuddy recollection, there is one more incident that foreshadows Quentin’s suicide twelve years later, revealing once again the Schelerian assumption pertaining to death as an act in life. When the children have reached the hill on their way home, Quentin is not with them; he stays “down at the branch” (SF 23), which is a clear prediction of his suicide. In fact, when he stands by the branch, death is already there, we may say, for Quentin is described as “chunking into the shadows” (SF 26). In addition, when he finally crawls uphill, he seems to be a walking death as half a ghost, because “his shirt was a white blur” (SF 27), which shows that the line between life and death has faded away again. The fragments in which Benjy narrates his thirty-third birthday on April 7, 1928, are obviously tantamount to the present horizon. As for its primary act of perception, one may bear in mind the already quoted observation of Collins about Benjy’s perception. According to Arnold Weinstein, it is enclosed in the first sentence of the novel (38): “Through the fence, between the curling flower spaces, I could see them hitting” (SF 1, emphasis added), which is derived from the first subscene of the episode set in the present time in “April Seventh 1928.” In principle, the act of perception, recognized by Scheler as the aspect of the present, may equally well be applied to the past horizon in Faulkner’s case, since in both horizons Benjy’s eye, “with a camera-like fidelity” (Millgate 91), records reality so meticulously that Kartiganer regards it as the parody of imagism (“‘Now’” 80). the comparison between Scott and Faulkner see Peggy Bach “A Serious Damn: William Faulkner and Evelyn Scott,” where the essay by Scott is also included.

The Benjy and Jason Narratives and Scheler’s Phenomenon of Death 99 After scrutinizing the passages that take place on April 7, 1928, what is striking is the coherence between the thanatological motifs and themes in the recollection of Damuddy’s death and in the fragments that constitute the present horizon. The part of the day is actually the same, as Benjy relates what happens before, during and after supper, mentioning darkness, as well. The same may be said about the place, as Benjy is put in the branch to play with Luster, Versh’s nephew this time, where after thirty years, he can again watch how other children amuse themselves in the river (SF 15). Apart from this, the Compsons’ ignorance of death, heralded in the Damuddy recollection, takes a heavy toll on the family now. Defined by Jason as “a mad house” (SF 80), the family completely disintegrates with the neurotic mother and detestation between Jason and Caddy’s daughter, who, after expressing her abhorrence toward the house, flees from home for good the same evening. Obviously, the decay of the family has been felt since the very beginning. However, Quentin’s escape may be treated as the final nail in the coffin, if one realizes that she is the only descendant in the family, who decides to disappear (A 426). Also, to stress the degradation of the family, Faulkner pictures the barn as being in a deplorable state with its filthy floor and its falling roof full of holes (SF 13). Bearing in mind their antebellum past, the fall of the household may now be seen as a vivid illustration of the Schelerian wave of becoming-unbecoming, since their breakdown, Cowan claims, “is part of a universal cyclical rhythm of rising and falling, birth and death, from which no natural object can escape” (6, emphasis added). The next clear alternation of life and death is the time of action. The events within the span of the present horizon take place on April 7, 1928, which was an Easter Saturday then (Collins “William” 226). In Christian tradition, as the critic notes, this day is celebrated as a memento of Christ’s descension to the world of the dead. In The Sound and the Fury, it is Benjy’s thirty-third birthday, which, in addition, plainly clashes with the age when Jesus died on the Cross, making Faulkner’s protagonist a Christ-like figure. What is also clearly evident is that the experiences on his birthday resemble more Via Dolorosa than an occasion to celebrate. Similarly to Christ on his Way of the Cross, not only does Benjy become an object of vilification, being insulted by Luster and Caddy’s daughter, who hurl at him scornful words like “old looney” (SF 19), “mulehead” (SF 61), or “a pig” (SF 86), but he is even lashed with a piece of wire by Luster (SF 70). Further, in this part, Benjy, like Christ, is sentenced to annihilation, for Quentin pronounces a verdict that Benjy should be sent to the State Asylum in Jackson (SF 85), which occurs in 1933 (A 423-424). Except for the above pointed out exemplifications, there are other clear references to the Crucifixion. When Benjy comes through a hole in the fence, he
