100 Chapter Two rips his item of clothing on the nail (SF 3). There is also a mention of the tomb, since Benjy has “his graveyard,” as Dilsey expresses (SF 67), which needs further explanation. By curious paradox, his graveyard is a place where Benjy enjoys spending his time, playing with a bottle in which he puts stems of the jimson weed. For Edmond Volpe, the pastime ironically symbolizes the losses Benjy experiences: firstly, the loss of Caddy, who smelled like trees, but unfortunately cannot be replaced with the foul-smelling jimson weed, and secondly, the loss of his manhood, for the reason that the plant in folk belief was considered to represent the phallus, not to mention the fact that it was used by Southern African-Americans as a contraceptive (A Reader’s 103-104). Noticing the sexual symbolism of the weed in Sanctuary, as well,100 Charles D. Peavy finds it disconcerting that Benjy is allowed to amuse himself with the jimson weed. It is a highly toxic plant, by which children have been poisoned, consuming its seeds or flowers (437-438). Furthermore, among the rituals performed on Holy Saturday, there is the burning of a paschal candle, which, according to Collins, may symbolically be linked with Benjy’s birthday candles and his fascination with fire (“Christian” 72). Nevertheless, with reference to another Collins’s article, when we consider the events of Holy Saturday, we can only speak of Christ’s triumph over death, whereas the bellowing Benjy wins nothing on that day, not achieving any mastery over Luster, who emerges the victor in fact (“William” 226). There are other inclinations to remind us that finitude is present within the process of life. Even though it is April, there is no passage in which the color of green would be mentioned. Instead there is plenty of red. Of this hue, Quentin’s mouth is described, as she speaks aggressively either to Luster, ordering him to shut up, or to Jason, who forbids her to date with a show fellow (SF 82, 87). What is interesting is the fact that the color of red is not only attached to Quentin’s aggression and fierceness, but also to the fellow she goes out with, for his tie is also of that tint (SF 59). In a way, the shade of red could stand for their relationship, yet it is not definitely the color of love, because, as it is stated in the Appendix, the pitchman, paradoxically doing the same job as Jason, has already been sentenced for bigamy (A 426), whereas Quentin has climbed down the tree thousands of times to meet her sweethearts. What is also red is the setting sun that reflects itself in the show fellow’s tie (SF 59), which does not paint a rosy picture of their relationship, either. That the color and the sunset reflect rather misfortune and impending end in Faulkner’s imagination one may notice in his already mentioned short story “That Evening Sun” (Johnston 98), 100 Peavy notices that before she is raped, Temple Drake runs in a field where the jimson weed grows (438).

The Benjy and Jason Narratives and Scheler’s Phenomenon of Death 101 and in Faulkner’s Nobel Prize address, where the author refers to the last moment of life as “the last ding-dong of doom… in the last red and dying evening” (ESPL 120), stressing again the motif of twilight. Seen in the Freudian context (Zeitlin 61), Benjy’s castration is the last and the most relevant illustration in the present horizon, showing concurrently Scheler’s first and second assumptions. Regarded by Brylowski as “the dead end of Benjy” (51), or by Bleikasten as “sexual death,” it is the punishment for Benjy’s “sexual aggression” toward the Burgess girl (The Ink 67). Although what is presented in the fragment is not the very moment of castration but its reminiscence, the act of remembering, characteristic of the past horizon, takes place after the act of perceiving, the main act of the present horizon, as Benjy expresses “I got undressed and I looked at myself, and I began to cry” (SF 90). By the glance at his genitals, Benjy may not perfectly fathom what the castration technically signifies. However, the fact that he did cry shows that the act of sparagmos tearing apart Benjy’s body did not escape his notice (Mellard 246). With his sharpened senses and capability to suffer, which Faulkner touches upon in the Mississippi Quarterly version of the introduction to The Sound and the Fury (223), Benjy recalls that the surgery was painful. And pain for Scheler denotes nothing but “a death in miniature, a sign of death” (MS 89). Additionally, the loss is considerably reinforced by the recurrent motif of the jimson weed with its shape evocative of the male sex organ, which ironically pacifies the emasculated Benjy, for Luster gives him the plant whenever he wishes Benjy would stop hollering (SF 5, 15, 61, 65).101 In Faulkner’s structure of Benjy’s life, there exists the Schelerian future horizon. Nevertheless, critics are divided as to what extent this future may be observable in this narrative. On the one hand, for Bleikasten Benjy is just “granted a minimal sense of the future” (The Ink 62). On the other hand, while analyzing Faulkner’s structurally complex, or even “overelaborate” sentences, Aiken claims that the writer wishes “to tell us everything,… every possible future or permutation as well, in one terrifically concentrated effort: each sentence to be, as it were, a microcosm” (137). In this permutated microcosm presented by Benjy, one may say, it is possible to find the act of expectation as connected with the future horizon. The person Benjy always expects to see is obviously Caddy. Whenever he lingers on at the gate in 1911, or plays in the 101 It is interesting to notice that Faulkner treated castration as an act of “being desouled,” which obviously denotes spiritual death. In a speech delivered to the English Club of the University of Virginia, April 24, 1958, he spoke of the task that should be completed by all, i.e., “to save mankind from being desouled as the stallion or boar or bull is gelded” (ESPL 164).

102 Chapter Two pasture in 1928, he weeps at the mention of a caddie, a golf ball. In the opinion of Arnold Weinstein, this phrase “here, caddie” (SF 1) expresses “a tragic destiny for Benjy, since the story of his life is that Caddy is not here but that he is here, waiting for her” (39, emphasis added). In fact, the feeling of longing permeates the whole section narrated by Benjy (Dobbs 37), because even if he is unable to voice Caddy’s absence aloud, he has acutely felt the lack of her presence (Taylor 41). Scheler’s future horizon exists in Faulkner’s first section with all implications that will befall Benjy in the time ahead. From the words of various protagonists, we find out that Benjy will be sent to the State Asylum in Jackson, which takes place in 1933, as confirmed in the Appendix (A 423-424). Obviously, the act is plainly indicative of social death, or death in the process of life, as Scheler would put it. Besides, the fleeting of Caddy’s daughter is revealed for the first time in the Benjy section. The escape clearly heralds the biological extinction of the family, which in the Appendix remarkably contrasts with the only statement left about Dilsey, namely “they endured” (A 427). As we know, this is the last comment in the Appendix, so its significance is rather plain. We also have to remember that Faulkner treated his art as “a longing for a coherent whole, an imaginative product of the process of filling in the gaps between words, sentences, books” (Maszewski William 9). Moreover, all the dwellers of Yoknapatawpha County, who appeared in different Faulkner’s novels, “have played their parts in one connected story” (Cowley “Introduction” xii). If Benjy’s narrative constitutes one part of The Sound and the Fury, and the very novel is incorporated in the Yoknapatawpha saga, there is a possibility of spreading Benjy’s microcosm to his macrocosm, and visualizing the future horizon in Benjy’s process of life in another way. As his mother, Benjy dies in The Mansion published in 1959 (Longley 150). Additionally, when we have a look at the Compson family tree, prepared by John B. Padgett on the academic William Faulkner website, we learn that his life has its end approximately about 1936 (on-line), which closes the complete span of experiences and events in the future horizon. Hence, Scheler’s equation in objective, measurable time may be presented as follows: Benjy’s life in any fragments in The Sound and the Fury equals (the past horizon: his recollections) + (the present horizon: April 7, 1928) + (the future horizon: the State Asylum). Thus, Benjy’s allegedly non-controlled, fragmentary stream of consciousness is a puzzle whose pieces fall into place. What emerges out of the supposedly claimed chaos constitutes Scheler’s structure of the three horizons, giving Benjy’s existence the sense of totality. Between the events creating this totality, there is Scheler’s relation of interdependency. To grasp the whole story,

The Benjy and Jason Narratives and Scheler’s Phenomenon of Death 103 the reader scrutinizing a particular part in the section is forced to always pay heed to the previous and following subscenes, of which each “remains indeterminate in significance” for some time (Scheler “Repentance” 95). Yet, later, as Jean-Paul Sartre confirms, apparently referring to the whole novel, “each episode, once it has been grasped, invokes others – in fact, all the other episodes connected with it” (226). That is why one has to finish reading the Benjy section, then the whole work The Sound and the Fury, and afterward even other novels written by the author, to discover the “full significance” of each fragment (Scheler “Repentance” 95). What also enables us to read Faulkner through Scheler is the part arrangement of the section. While perusing the following subscenes of Benjy’s monologue, the time shifts are experienced concurrently. Moreover, in the discussion of the author’s style, Conrad Aiken mentions Faulkner’s bizarre sentences, which, however, contribute to the whole. When left alone, they are “monsters of grammar and awkwardness” (Aiken 137), yet their role is perceivable when they are read in relation to the whole work. The abrupt movement from one idea to another is also an inherent part of Faulkner’s form, described to be “in motion” (Aiken 138), as Scheler’s structure of the horizons presented in the first chapter. Finally, correspondingly to Scheler’s observations, while putting the scattered passages in order, it is possible to decipher that, among other things, the recurrent phenomenon in Benjy’s text is death. With specific reference to Benjy’s memories, in “Order and Disorder in The Sound and the Fury,” Absalom clearly confirms that “closer and more extensive examination disclose[s] that the majority of these recollections are organized around a few thematic centres which dominate the contents of Benjy’s mind. These nodal centres can be recognized as (a) affection for Caddy, (b) awareness of death, (c) experience of sex” (143). Similarly, Mellard speaks about “structural mnemonics” that binds the scattered fragments in the Benjy section with different narrative knots: “agon, pathos and sparagmos” (246), which definitely help the readers to get their bearings in the text. Referring to Anatomy of Criticism, Mellard, in Frye’s manner, reads agon as conflict, pathos as death or catastrophe, and sparagmos as tearing apart. While bearing in mind Dionysian rituals of the sacrificial victim, we must stress that Mellard, however, highlights sparagmos mainly in meaning of “separation,” straying a bit from Frye’s interpretation (Frye 192).102 Above all, one more thing that concerns the changes in Scheler’s structure is discernible in Faulkner, too. As John V. Hagopian states, Benjy’s section, with Quentin’s and Jason’s included, give readers a 102 For Frye sparagmos also denotes the suspension of effective action and heroism to the advantage of disorganization, doom, and defeat (192).

104 Chapter Two possibility of “experiencing of all present events in an irreversible, one- directional flow. Each of the first three chapters moves inexorably from morning to night, however much that movement is broken by flash-forwards, flash-backs, or memories” (204, emphasis added). Scheler’s last assumption about death is based on his belief that, although the person passes away, the spirit that abides in human flesh can “swing beyond the body’s remains” (Frings TM 295). The spirit encompasses all voluntary acts toward other human beings, and the value of those acts never extinguishes. That is why we may say that for the German philosopher people live after expiration, which is the case observable in The Sound and the Fury in the way Benjy behaves toward his sister. Caddy does not die physically in the novel, but represents, for Dawn Trouard, “a kind of death in life” (27). She is mentally annihilated not only by her mother, who forbids the uttering of her name in the household, but also by Faulkner, who even locates her grave in Benjy: “Ben is the transition: the mausoleum or rather the inviolable alcohol in which the dead sister and brother could be held” (qtd. in P. Cohen and Fowler 277).103 Although buried for the critics and the author himself, Caddy does not perish in Benjy’s mind, because “he remembers Caddy’s acts” showing her selfless love and concern for the brother (Watkins 218). On his thirty-third birthday he hears the golf players shouting “caddie,” which in the context signifies “a golf ball,” yet for Benjy the sound of the word brings back the memory of his beloved sister, who stays literally inviolable for him (SF 1). What Benjy feels then is the spirit of Caddy swinging beyond her body, with the charitable and benevolent gestures the weeping brother recalls so well. Among the reminiscences that make Caddy alive in his mind, there are assuredly all moments when she acted as his mum, dedicating her time to him, e.g., when she soothed him emotionally, carried him despite his weight, protected him from Jason, took him out, and rubbed his cold hands. In the opinion of Ineke Bockting, Caddy is the only person that seems to comprehend what Benjy clumsily tries to express (“A Small” 148), therefore it is not surprising that her figure etched deeply in Benjy’s memory. Adhering to the Schelerian ordo amoris (“Ordo” 100), Caddy answers Scheler’s question what it means to be a 103 Till 1990 it had been believed that the two versions of Faulkner’s introduction to The Sound and the Fury, which were first published by James B. Meriwether in The Southern Review in 1972, and in the Mississippi Quarterly in 1973, were similar to other drafts of the introduction found in the Rowan Oak Papers. In 1990 Philip Cohen and Doreen Fowler published other drafts, discussing the differences between them in “Faulkner’s Introduction to The Sound and the Fury.” What is quoted here is a part from “MS E,” which is one of the holograph manuscript pages published by Cohen and Fowler.

The Benjy and Jason Narratives and Scheler’s Phenomenon of Death 105 human being. As a result, this kind of behavior makes her alive, because even if she is not visible or audible, it does not betoken her non-existence (S 108). In addition, to a certain extent, it may be claimed that Caddy becomes the member of Scheler’s Gesamtperson. It does not escape any readers of The Sound and the Fury that through all her presence in the novel she contributes to the bond of togetherness carried out by Scheler’s collective person that endures. The above analysis has been an attempt to show that Scheler’s attitude to death may provide a useful illustration to the Benjy narrative. However, remembering Arthur Brown’s conclusion that “death is writing this novel” (on- line), it is possible to find other fragments in which the presence of death may be felt, and which enrich the interpretation. Employing Arthur Brown’s division that also exemplifies Scheler’s second assumption, there are also other events of actual death, namely the death of Quentin, of Mr. Compson and of Roskus. What is immediately conspicuous about them is that they do not occupy much of Faulkner’s mind in this first narrative, when juxtaposed with Damuddy’s quietus, which is definitely given priority there. Nevertheless, we should mention a few words about two of the occurrences, omitting for the time being Quentin’s suicide, as it is scrutinized thoroughly in the following chapter. The last actual death in the Compson family concerns the demise of Mr. Compson. What strikes the reader as characteristic of this memory is its similarity to the recollection of Damuddy’s death. Although the event takes place fourteen years later, the same thanatological tokens are mentioned again: the time of supper, the surrounding darkness, and the ditch with Nancy’s remains (SF 35, 40). Instead of Frony and T.P., Luster plays in the dirt in front of the blacks’ cabin, but this time he is with Quentin, the girl, so at least one of the Compsons has symbolically been allowed to touch the biblical dirt (SF 36). Again, Benjy smells death, and his mother wails over another demise in the family (SF 41). In addition, history repeats itself, when the black reveal the recesses of the underworld to the white. T.P. shows Benjy his father’s funeral procession, pointing to the hearse where the coffin lies behind the glass (SF 38), which reminds us of Caddy peeping into the house through the window after Damuddy’s death. Then, the grandma was “sick” for the Compsons’ offspring, which in fact meant “dead.” Now Benjy repeats the same euphemistic word with reference to their father’s demise (SF 41). To Roskus’s death, being chronologically the last one in the novel (Volpe “Appendix” 104), Faulkner pays even less attention. When the reader discovers, with Parker’s help, that the recollection consists of two subscenes (9-10), thanatological motifs, although plain, are scarcely present there. In the two short passages, Benjy remembers Dilsey’s moaning, Luster’s fear of seeing the grandpa’s ghost, and the howling of a dog (SF 39). The howling seems to be

106 Chapter Two Faulkner’s recurrent motif. It reappears in the reminiscence of Mr. Compson’s finitude (SF 41), but also in a short story “Red Leaves,” where Issetibbeha’s old hound wails after his master’s death (331). The last thing noticeable in both these memories of actual death is, in fact, their arrangement in the Benjy section. Being in close proximity, their subscenes alternate, as if Faulkner wishes to mislead his reader, complicating the process of understanding on purpose. Bearing in mind Scheler’s second assumption about death as an act perceivable in the process of life, it is possible to notice the examples of what Brown defines as symbolic/figurative deaths (on-line). The figurative death that the reader encounters in The Sound and the Fury is the day when Caroline Compson alters Maury’s name at the age of five, which constitutes, apart from Damuddy’s death, the memory of paramount importance (Mellard 245). For Van O’Connor, a very name has a significant aspect of Faulkner’s characterization (24), and when Faulkner changes his character’s name, the action always signifies deprivation of selfhood (Bleikasten The Ink 61), as illustrated in literature by Fitzgerald’s Gatsby. Nevertheless, it is very difficult to talk about Benjy’s lost identity or individuality because of his status of the literary idiot. What may rather happen here is not the loss of selfhood, but the symbolic death of Benjy in his mother’s life, and of the mother in Benjy’s, which is the fatality each of them feels. Let us first discuss how Benjy becomes figuratively dead to the world in which Caroline Compson tries to subsist. The change of the name is dictated by the fact that for Benjy’s mother a new name is better, because it is derived from the Bible, which seems to be a vague reason. Benjy was first christened “Maury,” being a variant of Maurice, which is a name of holy beings or martyrs who sacrificed themselves for faith (Fros and Sowa 410). That stands in clear contrast to the uncle whom Benjy was named after, and whose life definitely does not resemble a saint’s path. The uncle’s behavior appears to be one of the real reasons for the name change, being at the same time Caroline’s attempt to erase the fact that in her noble family tree there was a place for a ladies’ man who borrowed money from black servants. Another reason is the meaning and origin of Benjy’s new name. There exists a biblical passage from the Book of Genesis that Faulkner made a clear reference to (Gwynn and Blotner 18). It is the story of Joseph, Jacob’s son, sold by his brothers to Ishmaelites, who later became a main administrator of a pharaoh in Egypt (Gen. 37-45). In the days of famine, while putting his brothers to the test, Joseph only intended to hold their youngest brother, Benjamin, in captivity. When asked during the session at the University of Virginia, why Mrs. Compson speaks of Benjy as the hostage in Egypt, Faulkner answered that he had employed Joseph and Benjamin “interchangeably” (Gwynn and Blotner 18;

The Benjy and Jason Narratives and Scheler’s Phenomenon of Death 107 SF 211). Interestingly enough, Bleikasten footnotes that “Benjamin” in Hebrew signifies a “child of the right hand,” or a “favorite child” - whom the biblical Benjamin is, but Compson is not, which in the context of the novel brings to mind “abandonment and exile” (The Ink 369). And this abandonment is what Benjy experiences indeed, for the day when the mother tries to teach him his new name constitutes a confirmation that she wishes to push him onto the margins by pure elimination. Valuing a position on the social ladder, Mrs. Compson regards “the birth of an idiot son as a kind of personal affront” (Brooks William Faulkner: The Yoknapatawpha 334). As a result, naming Benjy differently is the act of repudiating her son, which denotes his figurative death for her. And again, the black people, who play a function of a lie-detector in the book, have no doubts about it. Versh, who is Dilsey’s son and Benjy’s guardian, while talking to his charge, simply articulates what Dilsey thinks of it: “You know how come your name Benjamin now… Your mamma too proud for you. What mammy say” (SF 85-86), which does not escape Quentin, either (SF 211). In fact, not only does the mother reject Benjy, but other children as well, because at the end of the novel she says: “I’m a lady. You might not believe that from my offspring, but I am” (SF 374). There is one more thing that needs considering in relation to the Bible. If Faulkner made a reference to the above cited passage in Genesis, he must have known the one about Jacob’s wife, Rachel, who died after giving birth in great pain (Gen. 35.17-19). Due to hard labor, she intended to call her child “Ben-o- ni,” that is, the “son of my sorrow” (Wright on-line). Nevertheless, Jacob finally called their offspring “Benjamin.” In the novel in question, the hypochondriac and careless mother seems to identify with the biblical Rachel, but is not she the person who is figuratively dead herself? By contrast to the Bible, which, together with Shakespeare, Faulkner treated as required reading (Cowley The Faulkner 153), in The Sound and the Fury, there is no son that causes a mother’s death. Instead, there is the mother herself who metaphorically brings death to Benjy’s life. Resembling George Willard’s mother in Winesburg, Ohio (1919), which Faulkner praised (Millgate 88),104 Caroline Compson presents herself as a debilitated, bedridden figure. She keeps saying she will soon die, which Bowling recognizes as “her self-inflicted illness,” i.e., “self-pity and selfishness [developed] into a disease” (113). Suffering from no real sickness, not found in her body, but literally outside, as it 104 In “Interview of August 5. With the Press,” one of the interviews recorded in Japan in 1955, Faulkner said of Sherwood Anderson: “he was the father of all my works, of Hemingway, Fitzgerald, etc., all of them – we were influenced by him” (LG 101).

108 Chapter Two is perceived by Benjy “on a cloth on her head” (SF 49), she is “the cancer” in the Compson house (Brooks “Primitivism” 14). What appears then through Benjy’s eyes is the character being “a nonentity or worse” (Brooks “Primitivism” 24), who, similarly to the one in Winesburg, Ohio, stands for death in life. This kind of demise results from her impoverished existence replete with complaints, which again the black people detect as nothing but a continuous series of sulking episodes (SF 87). Representing the one whose soul is “set upon this life of death,” as Saint Augustine calls it (39), she is at least guilty of one cardinal sin, painted by Hieronymus Bosch in his picture The Seven Deadly Sins and the Four Last Things with death in the corner (Fraenger 256). This sin is acedia, i.e., sloth, which appears to be the main cause of her death in life. It is especially visible when she behaves apathetically and extremely unnaturally, reluctant to have the son in her lap (SF 77). That Mrs. Compson is figuratively dead is apparently sensed by Benjy in the scene that takes place in the mother’s bedroom on the day of the name alternation. Not only are her words empty, which Benjy is able to observe (Watkins 227). Her deadliness, suggested again through the smell of the sickness perceived on the cloth (SF 75), is also exemplified by the reflections in the mirror, a literary tool used quite frequently by Faulkner (Thompson 83). For the sake of comparison, when Benjy is near Caddy, the looking glass throws back the image of fire, a perpetual symbol of life, which illustrates a connection between Caddy, fire, and other illuminated objects that Benjy can see (Fant 105).105 However, when Benjy approaches his mother’s bed, the fire passes from sight, which seems to signify her figurative death in his life. As Thompson confirms, when “Ben turns from Caddy to his mother he suffers a sense of loss which may be symbolized by the disappearance of the reflected fire” (85). To add further evidence, the light the fire casts does not reach the mother’s heart or head, but just her hand, “where her rings were jumping,” whereas, at the end of the passage, those “rings jumped on Caddy’s back” (SF 75-76). Traditionally, a ring has always denoted a given promise (Ferber 170), so we may see this “jumping” as a shift of maternal responsibility to Caddy. This shift may also be read as the confirmation of Mrs. Compson’s figurative death in Benjy’s life on that particular day. All in all, this annihilation of the bond between mother and son is heralded in the earlier subscene of the name recollection. It is visible in the fragment in which Dilsey comments on the situation in the house with “him at one end of the house and her at the other” (SF 68). 105 Fant also states that the name “Candace,” derived from a Latin root “to shine,” denotes “the bright, shiny one” (106).

The Benjy and Jason Narratives and Scheler’s Phenomenon of Death 109 There also exists a testimony to the alternation of Benjy’s name as a prediction of death. In the story told to Benjy by Versh, we read: Versh said, Your name Benjamin now. You know how come your name Benjamin now. They making a bluegum out of you. Mammy say in old time your granpa changed nigger's name, and he turn preacher, and when they look at him, he bluegum too. Didn't use to be bluegum, neither. And when family woman look him in the eye in the full of the moon, chile born bluegum. And one evening, when they was about a dozen them bluegum chillen running round the place, he never come home. Possum hunters found him in the woods, et clean. And you know who et him. Them bluegum chillen did. (SF 84-85) First of all, it is visible in the fragment that the person who changed the name of the nigger was Benjy’s grandfather, so Caroline’s idea sets no precedent, reinforcing again the tragic flaw in the Compson family. Secondly, in the article “Faulkner’s Use of Folklore in The Sound and the Fury,” Peavy concludes that what results from the change of the name is both bad luck and death (445). Benjy’s mental retardation is obviously enough to speak of misfortune. As for death in a literal sense, Peavy cites Newbell Niles Puckett, who, in his work Folk Beliefs of the Southern Negro, explains the superstition, referring to an African-American with blue gums: “conjuration on the part of a blue-gummed Negro or a Negro with one eye black and the other blue is unduly effective and death usually results” (qtd. in Peavy 445). In The Sound and the Fury, what combines Benjy and the unfortunate blue- gum preacher is not their physical death, since Benjy does not die after the act of renaming. This is rather the power of conjuring, which, according to the popular belief depicted both by Puckett and by H.C. Davis, could culminate in bringing death to one’s door by a fatal blue-gum bite (qtd. in Peavy 445). The reference to Benjy as a bluegum does not highlight a fatal blue-gum bite itself, yet the fact that, for the representatives of the black society, Benjy’s new name will bring bad luck or death. The confirmation of their superstition is visible after Quentin’s suicide, when Roskus blames the two deaths in the Compsons’ house, i.e., Damuddy’s and Quentin’s, on the alteration of Benjy’s name: “They aint no luck on this place… I seen it at first but when they changed his name I knowed it” (SF 35). Moreover, when Quentin’s father passes away two years later, Frony, Roskus’s daughter this time, appears distinctly anxious when Benjy is to sleep with her son Luster: “You take Luster outen that bed, mammy… That boy conjure him” (SF 38). What the apprehensive Frony is clearly disturbed about is hard luck, i.e., the risk of transmitting an obviously non-transmissible disease of the brain from Benjy to her son Luster. How strongly the superstition is rooted in the blacks’ minds is conspicuous in Dilsey’s conduct, too. Although she

110 Chapter Two scorns the members of her family for such foolish reasoning, she puts a piece of wood between Benjy and Luster just in case. Apart from the superstition the black characters believe in, another prediction of finitude may be revealed in the recollection of the name alternation. In one of its subscenes, the first sound that Benjy catches is the tick- tocking of the clock, which is almost immediately followed by the tapping of the rain on the roof (Parker 12; SF 69). Bearing in mind Cowley’s observation about Faulkner’s attention paid to the weather (“Introduction” xxvi), and Kinney’s suggestion that Benjy interrelates the deaths in the novel (140), it is possible to stress one fact. Mr. Compson, Quentin and Roskus, who literally pass away in the book, are somehow associated with the rain, which “often stands as a synecdoche for all bad weather and thus a symbol of life’s unhappy moments” (Ferber 165). About the members of the family, Benjy voices his prophesy in the same way, as his father “smelled like rain” (SF 79), and “Quentin smelled like rain” (SF 81). In the fragment classified as a part of the name recollection (Stewart and Backus 443), Roskus is the one that notices “it going to rain all night” (SF 87). Interesting to spot is also the relation between Caddy, the clock, the roof, and the rain. Benjy observes: “I could hear the clock, and I could hear Caddy standing behind me, and I could hear the roof. It’s still raining, Caddy said” (SF 69). Seen as a self-fulfilling prophecy, it foreshadows Caddy’s departure from the family nest for good after her wedding. And what is more important, Caddy’s disappearance from Benjy’s life may bring about another exemplification of figurative death, but before we analyze the issue, we should elaborate on the Schelerian wave of becoming and unbecoming in Benjy’s universe. As in Scheler, who regards existence as permeated with the always fluctuating wave of becoming-unbecoming, in Faulkner the reader may experience a similar enantios, to recall Barthes again. In Van O’Connor’s opinion, “reading Faulkner one feels involved in a long history, of torment, suffering, and anguish but also of endurance, dedication, and love” (39). The unbecoming part of the wave has already been exemplified by the inanimate mother who brings death into Benjy’s life. The protagonists who balance the wave with the becoming are obviously Dilsey and Caddy. Due to the focus on Dilsey in the last chapter, let us concentrate on the figure of Caddy exclusively to illustrate the balance. Hailed by many scholars as Benjy’s real mother, Caddy is the one who “mothers motherless Benjy” (Spilka 460).106 For example, by contrast to Mrs. Compson, she carries Benjy regardless of her mother’s warnings against bad 106 Cynthia Dobbs also speaks of Caddy as “the substitute for their biological mother” (37).

The Benjy and Jason Narratives and Scheler’s Phenomenon of Death 111 posture. Not only does she like to look after Benjy, but she also knows perfectly well that, to calm down her whining brother, there has to be a cushion or fire. Furthermore, Caddy uses nicknames, usually recognized as amiability and cordiality toward other people, whereas Caroline is strongly opposed to calling him “Benjy,” as for her “nicknames are vulgar,” and “only common people use them” (SF 78). It is not surprising then that after Caddy’s wedding ceremony Benjy is seen crying at the gate, hoping that his sister will come back. However, the mother, even if given the cause of his pain by T.P., does not believe that Caddy is the reason for his sorrow, rejecting what her servants even know (SF 63). There are other heavy hints which illustrate how Caddy’s becoming counteracts Mrs. Compson’s unbecoming in Benjy’s existence. What proves that Caddy signifies life for her brother is her scent, because she smells, to him, of leaves (SF 5), and of trees (SF 88). Due to her natural fragrance, she probably reminds him of the pasture where he keeps himself amused. Additionally, what Caroline lacks is embodied in Caddy by the means of the previously mentioned symbol of fire. Instead of their mother’s illness, Benjy sees vivacity and animation in his sister, whose “hair was like fire, and little points of fire were in her eyes” (SF 88). Thus these two family members, mother and sister, typify the Schelerian wave of becoming-unbecoming in Benjy’s existence. The contrast between the women at the same time testifies to finitude’s presence in life, which constitutes, as we remember, the second assumption connected with the nature of dying. The flow of becoming and unbecoming is not only conspicuous in the above-mentioned differentiation between the dead in life and the truly alive. For Scheler it may be felt in a given person, as well (TM 141). Presented before as the one bringing life, Caddy is also recognized as a heroine who “living a fleshly existence… suffers a continual death through the flesh” (Gregory 101), which makes us look for the unbecoming in her personhood, too. When Caddy uses perfume for the first time, which for Volpe happens either in 1905 or 1906 (“Appendix” 104), Benjy tries to avoid her, owing to the scent she has sprayed herself with, which he recognizes as odor, not fragrance (SF 51). Not until Caddy washes herself does he stop escaping from his sister, who again smells like trees (SF 50). The history repeats itself in the following memories: first, when Caddy, after being in the swing with Charlie, washes her mouth to get rid of the repulsive odor (SF 58), and when the loss of her virginity makes the wailing Benjy push Caddy away (SF 85). All those moments in Benjy’s past horizon appear to anticipate Caddy’s figurative death at the wedding when she finally disappears from Benjy’s life, never coming back for good.

112 Chapter Two Caddy’s figurative death takes place at her wedding. First of all, this is clearly illustrated by the severing of the emotional relation between brother and sister (Branny 140). Next, the bride with “a long veil like shining wind” has the same attribute the mother possesses during the trip to the cemetery shortly after Mr. Compson’s death of 1912 (Volpe “Appendix” 104; SF 9, 47). We should also stress the fact that this attribute is characteristic of these two recollections. Furthermore, in the last subscene of the wedding recollection, when Caddy puts the veil around Benjy, he utters a very meaningful sentence that emphatically ends the memory. He notices: “and I couldn’t smell trees anymore and I began to cry” (SF 48), which additionally supports Branny’s suggestion about the broken bond. Moreover, while depicting his drinking experience, Benjy says that “it make me feel just like a squinch owl inside” (SF 46). This squinch owl is a screech-owl, whose hooting is first mentioned in the recollection of Quentin’s death (SF 34; RF 22), and the noise itself is deciphered by Ross and Polk as a sign of the death that will come next (RF 22). Drawing to the end of the interpretation of the Benjy section through Scheler’s phenomenology of death, what comes across the mind is a Latin dictum uttered by Mr. Compson: “Et ego in arcadia” (SF 53). In Faulkner the sentence is a misquote, because, cited appropriately, it should sound “Et in Arcadia ego” [“And I lived in Arcadia, too”] (Kopaliński 53). However, despite the mistake, the dictum summarizes the above efforts to show that Scheler’s thought can provide an illustration to the Benjy section, or in other words, that death is present in human existence from its very beginning. As Bätschmann states, this Latin motto is an inscription found in the 1621-23 painting of Giovanni Guercino, and in two versions painted later by Nicolas Poussin (1629- 30 and c. 1640), which, apart from the eponymous maxim, are all known under the title The Arcadian Shepherds (53-55). Guercino’s creation and Poussin’s first version belong to the tradition of memento mori, directed obviously to those that are still alive (Panofsky qtd. in Bätschmann 54). Those that read the Benjy section may discover the same message, because after turning the pages of the first narrative attentively, This Consciousness that is aware Of Neighbors and the Sun Will be the one aware of Death And that itself alone. (Dickinson 2526) When the reader enters Jason Compson’s world, presented in the third section of The Sound and the Fury, the situation is totally different. Due to his avoidance of death, Jason significantly embodies Scheler’s Western dweller, which is perceivable in the protagonist’s way of thinking and speaking. He talks for the

The Benjy and Jason Narratives and Scheler’s Phenomenon of Death 113 sake of talking (Blanchard 565), and his language is both “dead and deadening” (Bleikasten The Ink 118).107 Of great importance is the fact that Jason consciously refrains from making any references to finitude when he expresses his opinions. In the passage recounting the obsequies of his father, the terms suggestive of funeral rites (which would enable the reader to realize what situation is being related) are absent from Jason’s recollections. The words “funeral,” “undertaker,” “coffin,” and “grave” are shunned (Bockting “A Small” 154), and instead of the substantive “coffin” the character uses the neutral personal pronoun “it,” called by Bockting “the alienating it” (“A Small” 154). This shows Jason’s mental separation from death, but also his apprehensiveness of calling things by name, like in the following phrase: “making a hollow sound when it fell on it” (SF 249), where the first “it” refers to “mud,” which is clear as it is mentioned before in the passage, and the second one to “Mr. Compson’s coffin” (RF 161). The same may be stated about the word “grave,” which Jason evades: “When they begun to get it filled up toward the top Mother started crying” (SF 250), and in the sentence “I got to thinking about that and watching them throwing dirt into it” (SF 250). What permits the reader to identify the occurrence as a burial ceremony is the nouns “shovel” and “mud.” The words do not discommode Jason, who does not avoid employing them this time, because they both can appear in other contexts than the circumstances of death. The evasion of the subject of quietude is also perceivable in Jason’s conduct during the interment. We do not find him standing near his mother’s side, together with his uncle Maury, who tires to be a comfort to her in this distress. Preferring observation to active participation, Jason moves back, hiding behind the hack (SF 249). Unlike Maury, he does not conform to the accepted habit of throwing a lump of earth into the grave probably not to soil himself or his clothes. Besides, Jason’s “inertia vis à vis death,” as Scheler would call it (qtd. in TM 139), may be noticed in his process of thinking. During the funeral Jason hardly devotes any thoughts to his father and his decease. Instead, he concentrates on his uncle tippling behind one of the tombstones, and on his new suit stained with mud, for which he paradoxically seems to blame Maury. At the same time, Jason pities himself, because no one thought that he would get soaked (SF 249-250). The lack of courage to confront death leads to the inability to interpret the emotions that overcome him during the funeral, which at the very beginning he 107 Bleikasten calls Jason’s language in this way, because what it expresses is “the arrested image of a world” where he holds the same unchangeable opinions. It is also dead and deadening due to its harshness (The Ink 118).

114 Chapter Two depicts as “sort of funny” (SF 250). Later, he attempts to elucidate these feelings to himself as a kind of vexation, or even rage at his uncle (SF 252), which Ross and Polk regard as his incapacity to identify them with woe and bereavement at his father’s expiration: “Jason still cannot name grief or sorrow for what they are; he displaces his grief over his father’s death into anger at Uncle Maury” (RF 162). Nevertheless, the question remains whether Jason Compson feels any kind of misery or anguish over his father’s passing away. Bearing in mind his focus on his own persona, there is nothing between the lines that would have any signs of deep grief he would suffer. Quite the reverse, what one discovers is Jason’s disrespect for his dead father, whom he talks about acrimoniously (SF 225-26). Betraying his utter contempt for the parent (Aswell 208), the son even hints at his father’s madness: “we’d all been a damn sight better off if he’d sold that sideboard and bought himself a one-armed strait jacket with part of the money” (SF 245). Undoubtedly, death poses a problem for Jason. He does not think of it deeply, and he neglects the feeling of pain discerned by Scheler as its most perceptible herald, as “a death in miniature, a sign of death” (MS 89). Like Christ on the day of the Crucifixion, although not to such a great extent, Jason, on April 6, 1928, which falls on Good Friday, experiences an unbearable pain. He is racked with the growing ache which shoots through his head. Jason, nevertheless, does not slow down the pace of life in order to ease the pain and to simply accept it. Quite the opposite, he ignores the throbbing until it becomes so excruciating that he is forced to stop the car: “So I had to stop there at the forks… It felt like somebody was inside with a hammer, beating on it” (SF 297). Much as it hurts, he keeps driving and chasing his niece regardless of the more and more intensified pain, which does not make him rational enough to simply rest. Jason Compson ignores the soreness in his head in the same way as he takes no notice of death, whose consciousness has not been increased in his case by the feeling of suffering. Curiously enough, Scheler’s interdependency of pain and death is evident in the third section of the novel when the ache begins to be absolutely unbearable. Jason feels the strongest pain at twilight, which represents for Faulkner an unquestionable symbol of quietude: “it all would go into my head like it would explode any minute, and the sun getting down just to where it could shine straight into my eyes and my ears ringing so I couldn’t hear anything” (SF 300). Yet, the indicated interdependency, pointed out by Scheler and visible in Faulkner, surely escapes Jason. And here one can wonder whether it is possible to agree with Brooks that Jason is not an epicurean (William Faulkner: First 60), if the act of rejecting death and pain is taken into consideration. However, Jason does not devote his life to pleasure or sensuous living. Instead, he inflicts pain on the Other, so Brooks’s viewpoint is understandable.

The Benjy and Jason Narratives and Scheler’s Phenomenon of Death 115 When set beside his brothers who integrate expiration into their living, death dwells outside of Jason’s selfhood. In his case it is not the point of Scheler’s “metaphysical recklessness,” the natural and understandable muffling of finitude in the human mind that enables us to live normally (S 93). The fact is that this is Jason’s deliberate act of avoiding death. Since he does not regard the experiences he goes through as death-oriented, Jason Compson is the only narrator in The Sound and the Fury who does not accept finitude as an integral part of existence – the phenomenon innate in us during the act of procreation (MS 93). By the repudiation of dying as a process, he rather sees death as an event, as the last occurrence in life, which is caused by an external stimulus. Therefore his idea of demise comes down exclusively to Scheler’s understanding of finitude as a catastrophe. Obviously, Mr. Compson’s expiration, attributable partly to his alcohol abuse, and Quentin’s conscious suicide may be perceived as a catastrophe in Scheler’s terms. It is true especially when we take into account that Faulkner’s leading characters “wallow in the tale of their ancestors’ glories, spellbound with a strange hope in the midst of their despair, as they wait for the unpredictable and necessary catastrophe which is to seize them” (Magny 69). However, Jason’s treatment of death as Scheler’s catastrophe appears to extend beyond other cases of perishing. By way of illustration, while making a remark about Roskus’s passing away, Jason has not taken into account his age: “the only mistake he [Roskus] ever made was he got careless one day and died” (SF 312), whereas in the Benjy section there is no mention of an accident that might have occurred to Roskus. The overriding impression is that he dies due to his old age. With death seen as catastrophe, Jason does not consider it to be a real possibility that may come anytime. In regard to Metchnikoff quoted by Scheler, it is evident that this Faulknerian protagonist recognizes the instinct of life, but repudiates the harmless instinct of death. Rejecting the argument that one day the former should replace the latter, Jason does not think of dying as “orthobiosis,” as a natural need felt at the end of a purposeful life (Metchnikoff The Prolongation 320). When he depicts the hobbling Dilsey as “an old half dead nigger” (SF 230), he ostracizes her due to the infirmity of old age seen by him as her disadvantage. Also, by thinking of her as “half dead,” Jason reveals that from his viewpoint death connotes decrepitude, feebleness and worthlessness. This makes him representative of the depravation theory, which assumes that expiration is destructive, for it deprives people of their essential value. If this is so, then Jason’s attitude to death resembles more closely the perspective suggested by Thomas Nagel and Elias Canetti, who clearly treat perishing as evil. Entirely alien to Jason is the concept of finitude as the personal sacrifice made by the individual for the development of the human race. Regarding

116 Chapter Two Roskus’s demise as a catastrophe and the old Dilsey as already dead, he does not consider the death of the individual in terms of the whole population. And if he treats the end as a result of one’s carelessness, death does not amount for him to “the ‘sacrifice’ that surrenders one life for more and automatically higher life” (MS 89). In addition, he ignores the “ontological relationship” between every man and the world (MS 88), which is, first of all, necessary for sacrifice to take place, and secondly, reinforced at the moment of death. One of the reasons why the Jason section is viewed as a paranoid text is the character’s relationship with the Other (Bockting “A Small” 153-154). Unwilling to give, Jason brushes off the other person, opting consciously for self-imposed solitude. And if he is “incapable of a disinterested commitment to another human being” (Branny 162), it is not surprising that there can be no talk of sacrifice in Jason’s life. For instance, he does not feel obliged to serve well the customers in the shop, or he keeps complaining about his responsibility for maintaining “the flour barrel full” in the household (SF 243). Cultivating egoism eagerly, he leads a lonely life. He does not consider himself to be a member of the local community in Jefferson, to say nothing of shunning his family, or treating the house as a hotel. According to Beck, the Appendix proves Jason’s final liberation from his family, but this freedom is synonymous with “mediocre mercantile anonymity” (305), the one which replaces Scheler’s individuality and freedom as the consequence of uprooting the thought of death out of one’s consciousness. It is also possible to present Jason’s evasion of finitude through the issue of time. As observed before, the past, present, and future intertwine in the Benjy section, and the theme of death is one of the “nodal centres” that bind up Benjy’s thoughts (Absalom 143). With regard to Jason, even though in his section he mainly narrates the events of April 6, 1928, one cannot deduce that he is a person who lives in the present. Just the reverse, the reader has the impression that Jason exists either in the past or in the future. For example, on one hand, he blames his ordeal on his sister’s promiscuousness, which led to the separation with her husband, who was to arrange for Jason to work in a bank. On the other hand, Jason’s ceaseless speculation about market prices makes him live in the time ahead. As a result, when one tries to apply Scheler’s time structure to the Jason section, the ranges of the horizons are badly proportioned there. This Faulknerian protagonist would like to leave the present, to see the past as squeezed, and to extend the future with no limits, which is simply impossible. Moreover, his distorted temporal structure provides the reader with an additional argument why he has problems with the acceptance of death. With such a viewpoint on the aspects of time, Jason moves against the current of life, and does not notice the presence of demise. Any occurrences that happen to him, even his father’s funeral, are not regarded as death-oriented. He

The Benjy and Jason Narratives and Scheler’s Phenomenon of Death 117 is not able to see in life this balance between growth and decline, which Scheler calls the wave of becoming-unbecoming. By curious paradox, when he rejects decline and heads for growth, Jason’s existence is only characteristic of the former, because his life resembles neither Barthes’s enantios nor the two-faced Janus. If this is the case, then the totality achieved by Benjy is out of range for Jason, who instead worships “the mechanical conception of life” (S 99), the one that operates on pure calculation and repudiates any contemplation on the theme of death. As Aswell confirms, Jason does not consider life to be dependent on “absolute and eternal powers,” such as death, one could add, but on “the endless permutations of chance and change” (208), on constant machinations involving the profitable and the non-profitable. Scheler’s idea that the widespread evasion of death is caused by the gradual degeneration of morality may also be traced in Jason’s cold demeanor. With a name that paradoxically denotes “a healer” in Greek (Aschkenasy 103), but with no conscience “to nurse like a sick puppy,” as he says himself (SF 284), Jason Compson is obnoxious, not likable. In the whole section he narrates, one finds the irrefutable evidence that the ordo amoris has been infringed by him, and that love has been “alien to his thinking” (Watkins 228). Instead, Jason advocates Snopesism adopting the dehumanized attitude toward human mankind (Warren 112). “The black, the Jew, the foreigner, the intellectual: so many avatars of the despised and detested Other” are around him (Bleikasten The Ink 112). In fact, what determines Jason’s existence is the act of repudiating the unique value of the person, which Scheler undoubtedly considers to be one of the most significant factors that contribute to the ignorance of finitude. Without any pretense at politeness, Faulkner’s protagonist simply respects no one, no matter if he deals with a passer-by or his relative. While talking to Earl, his employer, Jason’s tone is definitely inappropriate, whereas Earl still shows his sympathy toward him, an unreliable worker, who has served their customers in a very rude manner (SF 242). Kinney finds Jason even “suicidal,” because by such conduct he deliberately weakens his already tentative position at work (152). As a family member, discourteous and insolent (SF 295-296), Jason holds a conversation with his mother when he intends to take advantage of her; he is ashamed of Benjy, whom he would place in the Jackson asylum instantly if he had the say in this matter (SF 276). A very illustrative example of his total moral depravity is the scene in which Luster asks Jason for the roadshow tickets received for free from Earl. With no intention of attending the show, Jason burns the tickets in the stove before Luster’s eyes (SF 318). Obviously, the tableau shows the worst conceivable act of savagery toward a child, and exemplifies nothing else but “Jason’s vindictive, resentful, all- devouring malice” (Matthews The Sound 63).

118 Chapter Two Jason’s maltreatment of Caddy’s daughter is particularly visible in the novel. He does not value Quentin as a person at all. He does not even consider her to be a human being, which is plain when he speaks to his mother of his baby niece as if she was an object: “it’s not that I have any objection to having it here; if it’s any satisfaction to you I’ll quit work and nurse it myself” (SF 243, emphasis added). The objectification is also explicit in another fragment when Jason belittles Quentin, and treats her as an equivalent of his lost bank post: “they brought my job home tonight” (SF 246). As an adolescent, Quentin experiences verbal tortures inflicted by her uncle, whose language cuts and wounds (Brooks William Faulkner: First 61). During the dinner he interrogates her with double meaning questions. For example, when he asks her about a piece of meat she has been eating, he alludes to a possible sexual intercourse with the boy Jason saw her with in town (SF 321).108 As for physical violence, Jason considers it to be an efficient way of bringing up children: he would intend to extort obedience from Quentin by imposing punishment with the lash (SF 225). However, he is frequently stopped either by the mother or Dilsey. On top of that, to separate the daughter from the mother, he hands over no letters addressed to Quentin, reading their private correspondence (SF 236). So disgraceful is Jason’s conduct toward his niece that she loses the will to live and develops, what Freud calls, the destructive/death instinct (“Beyond” 620; An Outline 5). During the dinner she says woefully: “I wish I was dead. I wish we were all dead” (SF 324). The problem of race, inextricably connected with Southern literature (Alexander 119), finds its exemplification in the figure of Jason, too.109 He is a racist who expresses such slogans as: “What this country needs is white labour” (SF 237). Although Jason makes the most of every opportunity to earn some money, he is not eager to bet on the New York Yankees, because their best player, the well-known Babe Ruth, has been rumored to be part black (RF 173; SF 314). Jason is proud that in the days of slavery the Compsons belonged to the class of planters: “my people owned slaves here when you all were running little 108 James G. Watson interprets the fragment as Jason’s invitation to become Quentin’s lover (115), which could be the continuation of the incest motif recurrent in Faulkner. 109 Margaret W. Alexander claims that Faulkner was a racist and knew about it, believing that the whole country behaved like that. According to the scholar, for Faulkner, being human meant being a racist, which was the view resulting from American culture (107). The question arises why, if a racist himself, Faulkner considered Jason to be the greatest villain in Yoknapatawpha County. The answer is unconsciously provided by Alexander, who claims that Faulkner realised it and attempted to do something about it as proved by “The Bear” (108), which strictly demarcates a line between the author and his character.

The Benjy and Jason Narratives and Scheler’s Phenomenon of Death 119 shirt tail country stores” (SF 298). In fact, he seems to regret that the times of slavery passed for good, as he is fond of divesting the African-Americans of their self-esteem: “That’s the trouble with nigger servants, when they’ve been with you for a long time they get so full of self importance that they’re not worth a damn” (SF 257-258). In addition, he ostentatiously manifests his deep prejudice against the Jewish nation: “I have nothing against jews as an individual… It’s just the race” (SF 237). His hatred toward the people roots out of the traditional belief that concerns their innate qualities of being money-wise, the feature that Jason lacks, but would like to have, which leads us to another point in our discussion. Apart from the fact that people do not rate highly on his list of priorities, Jason Compson exemplifies Scheler’s homo capitalisticus, who cherishes possession as a result of renouncing death.110 Anything that is of non-material value is not worth Jason’s attention, since it simply does not exist for him (Scott 16). For example, he does not see the above-mentioned roadshow as an event which might have some artistic merit, or at least be a form of entertainment, but as “something that brought nothing to the town and wouldn’t leave anything except what those grafters in the Mayor’s office will split among themselves” (SF 243). The thoughts that occupy his mind are pure calculation to that extent that his whole day revolves around the cotton market quotations which he checks as frequently as possible at the cost of his work time (SF 239). To earn more and more, he even sends $10 a month to a professional financial adviser in New York in order to receive reports analyzing fluctuations in share prices (SF 239). Despite the professional advice, Jason Compson represents an unsuccessful businessman, seen as a travesty of the mythical Jason who was to retrieve the “golden fleece” (Aschkenasy 97). What is also observed is the character’s irrationality and financial incompetence, when after receiving the adviser’s telegraph saying “sell,” Jason sends the answer ordering “buy” (Wallach 81; SF 304). While hearing his derogatory comments about the New York stockbrokers who send telegrams to inform him about closed accounts, one may have the impression that market losses are the rule in Compson’s life (RF 168; SF 282). Moreover, the financial transactions depicted in the novel reflect Jason’s destiny. According to Wallach, “the commodity markets are analogues, acting at times as projections, of his unconscious agony” (83). One of these analogues is evidently mirrored in the message dispatched by the advisor: “The market will 110 Comparing William Faulkner and Evelyn Scott, Peggy Bach states that the authors shared antipathy toward society, and spoke against industrialism in the South, as well (138).

120 Chapter Two be unstable, with a general downward tendency” (SF 304).111 The end of the agony mentioned by Wallach seems to happen on April 6, i.e., on that Good Friday. At the same time when Christ died on the Cross, Jason appears to be “sold out” by the same Jewish bankers, whom he defamed before in accordance to the medieval custom of denigration of the Jews on Good Friday (Collins “William” 226). Nevertheless, Collins’s view should be corrected. Jason is not sold out by the Jews, but he does sell his self due to his “obsessive and blundering transpositions of emotional values into financial terms” (Wallach 79). In other words, “he annihilates himself” by empty, nihilistic thinking when he discredits true and valuable feelings (Scott 17). With an insatiable appetite for financial benefits, Jason overlooks no possibility of generating profit, even illegally. Forging Mrs. Compson’s signature on Caddy’s checks that need his mother’s endorsement to be cashed, he regularly steals the money Caddy sends monthly for the upbringing of her daughter. In this way, similarly to his brother Quentin, he objectifies Caddy, treating her as a source of a small fortune (Minter Faulkner’s 44). As if that were not enough, Jason makes their mother believe that she burns Caddy’s checks that in fact have been falsified by him. Symbolically, Quentin also becomes his source of income, which is even visible graphically in the novel. Urged by Caddy, whose wish is to receive a letter from her offspring, Jason posts his sister a telegram with the following content: “Q writing today” (SF 239). With “Q” standing for Quentin obviously, this letter of the alphabet is also “one of the special telegraphic code letters assigned to each month’s cotton future” (Morrison qtd. in RF 157), which confirms that Quentin is synonymous with money in Jason’s mind, as well. With no scruples at all, Jason would like to use his siblings for his own ends. He comes up with the idea to send Benjy to a sideshow in order to use his retarded condition as a source of income (SF 243). Greedy as he is, Jason does not refrain from doing business even on the day of his father’s burial ceremony, when he makes money on no one else but his sister. Horrendous is his act, because for letting Caddy see her own daughter he demands one hundred dollars. What is even worse, he does not stop the car at the pre-arranged meeting point, but he enjoins Mink, who drives the vehicle, to pick up speed. As a result, 111 For Rick Wallach the quote is indicative of Jason’s unbalanced mental state (81). Interestingly enough, Ted Atkinson perceives it as Faulkner’s prophecy which anticipated the 1929 crash (16). Additionally, referring to Joseph Blotner, Atkinson draws a conclusion that the composition of As I Lay Dying was triggered off by the 1929 outburst of panic (15). Thus, Atkinson’s remark serves as additional evidence showing that in Faulkner one observes Scheler’s interdependence between the economic aspect and the theme of death.

The Benjy and Jason Narratives and Scheler’s Phenomenon of Death 121 they glide past Caddy and show her Quentin only through the car window (SF 254). In addition, Jason does not understand that a person may want to donate a certain sum of money to an institution – he is completely stunned that one man in Jefferson financially supported missionary work in China (SF 241; RF 157). Strictly connected with the attitude described by Scheler as homo capitalisticus is the transformation of the approach toward human corporality, which is also noticeable in Jason. His body ceased to be what Scheler defines as Leib, an animated and growing organism that lives and feels. His body became Körper, a biologically complex mechanism perceived as a physical object (S 94). To function normally, since the very morning, Jason has needed a Coca- cola, which appears in the 1956 Random House version of The Sound and the Fury (SF 237). In the 1990 Vintage International version of the novel Ross and Polk worked on, the same drink is hidden under the name “dope” (RF 155). To explain the usage of the word, the scholars claim that in this fragment “Faulkner is clearly drawing on the common belief that Coca-cola contained cocaine and was an addictive stimulant” (RF 155). By the 1890s the beverage had been purified of the touches of the narcotic. However, in Secret Formula, Frederick Allen states that the viewpoint on Coca-cola as a drug “quickly became an article of faith and part of the folklore, especially in the South” (qtd. in RF 156). Furthermore, as late as 1929, when The Sound and the Fury was published, a certain quantity of cocaine derivatives was still found in this beverage (Allan qtd. in RF 156). Thus, Faulkner must have been cognizant of the possible content of the drink, because, by alluding to it as “dope,” he apparently intended to highlight Jason’s hidden addiction to it. There remains one more point that concerns Jason’s stance on the body treated as a mechanism. The only relationship Jason seems to care a little about is the one with a prostitute, nevertheless, he visits Lorraine in order to satisfy his sexual needs. By the same token, he repudiates corporality as the foundation on which an intimate bond could be built, and treats the physical sphere of human nature as a commodity to buy. In fact, his desecration of physical love is very likely to be more relevant than it appears initially, for Jason’s first, well-known words, “once a bitch always a bitch,” echo in the last paragraph, constituting the brace of the section (SF 223, 329). However, it is true that Lorraine has been his constant partner, and he speaks favorably of his lady of the evening. For him, Lorraine is more decent than the one who is not of that femme fatale kind: “I’d like to see the good, church-going woman that’s half as square as Lorraine” (SF 307). Still, their relationship is far from being healthy if we take into account the fact that Jason forbade Lorraine to stay in touch with him by phone. Apart from this, he burns all her letters, from which we also find out that she calls him “daddy” (SF 240), which additionally testifies to the unhealthy relationship.

122 Chapter Two Jason does not act in accordance with the principles he claims he exemplifies. Caring about ranks in society (Watkins 228), he would like his family to be widely respected by the community he lives in. He asserts that he does his best “to make her [Quentin’s] name and my name and my Mother’s name a byword in the town” (SF 291). In reality, he is very sensitive about his own position in town and what the public think of him. He is especially interested to know if he is not considered to be crazy as his siblings – Benjy the idiot and Quentin the suicide (SF 290). Jason wants to be respected, but he has no respect for his niece. And although he once does declare that “money has no value” (SF 241), most of his actions certainly contradict that. Furthermore, Jason keeps talking about how hard he works (SF 292). However, when one follows his actions on April 6, not only does he get to work unpunctually (SF 235), but during his working hours he is occupied with self-interest rather than his duties. This discrepancy between the reality and Jason’s claim about his hard work, regarded as a feature denoting masculinity, is perceived by Harriet Hustis as a comic motif in The Sound and the Fury (109). The scholar also pays attention to the fact that the manhood exemplified by Jason, and Anse from As I Lay Dying, is just “a verbal enactment” (109). We should also mention the incongruity between Jason’s boast that he is an adept businessman and the shaky state of the Compsons’ finances he manages (Wallach 79), to say nothing of his car bought with his mother’s financial sources. Moreover, Jason’s statement that concerns his self-sufficiency must be discredited (SF 256), for he regularly cashes Caddy’s checks, blaming her for his lost job opportunity as a banker. Here, one should also point out that the erroneous attitude toward death adopted by Jason may ensue from another contributory factor, namely the influence of the preceding generation on the following one (Gold 24). In his book Joseph Gold brings to the reader’s attention the similarity of The Sound and the Fury to Faulkner’s 1935 short story “That Will Be Fine,” whose narrator is a small boy obsessed with money (23). As a matter of fact, it is hard not to think of Jason while reading about the lad’s fixation handed down to him by his Uncle Rodney, strikingly similar to Uncle Maury in his love affairs and his habit of borrowing coins and notes. What makes the reader wonder is also the very end of the story when the boy misinterprets shots as firecrackers and does not notice Uncle’s death. Believing that the corpse is “a side of meat,” a present from the husbands of Mottstown to Grandpa, the lad is still calculating how he could increase his capital. In addition to this, the boy’s ignorance is reinforced by the older generation when they send him away from home where the body is kept (287-288). Thus in the saga about Yoknapatawpha, Jason’s evasion of finitude may be justified to a certain extent, if we take into consideration the resemblance between him and the lad.

The Benjy and Jason Narratives and Scheler’s Phenomenon of Death 123 To reveal the wider picture of the problem presented in the Jason narrative, we ought to accentuate the mother’s conduct, as well. With her constant, many- year’s grumbling that she will depart from this world soon, Mrs. Compson continually makes the theme of dying tedious for all those around her. As a result, no one takes it seriously, and Jason, her favorite offspring, pays no heed to it at all, answering her cynically: “You’ve been saying that so long that I’m beginning to believe you” (SF 276). Besides, her hypochondria is an important point if Scheler’s differentiation between “natural age” and “actual age” is taken into account (S 83). Although she has not yet expired, the mother behaves as if she was already dead, which could also make Jason think of demise as something repulsive. Finally, it should be mentioned that by associating death with a feeling of disgrace Mrs. Compson grossly distorted the concept of finitude, and communicated it as such to her children. It is clearly visible when Jason recollects how his mother reacted when the fifteen-year-old Caddy had been caught red-handed, kissing a boy: “she went around the house in a black dress and a veil and even Father couldn’t get her to say a word except crying and saying her little daughter was dead” (SF 286). If we bear in mind the triviality of Caddy’s deed, the recollection, first of all, shows Mrs. Compson’s inclinations to dramatize a situation unnecessarily. Secondly, such theatrical behavior made her children create a mental picture of death as something inappropriate or shameful, which was the mistake made by her more than once. When Jason suggested that burning Caddy’s checks was not the wisest thing to do, the mother replied that she preferred seeing Jason in a coffin to accepting the money offered by Caddy, her allegedly fallen daughter (SF 274). In conclusion, in the first significant critical essay on The Sound and the Fury, Evelyn Scott speaks of Jason as being “in an agony of inexplicable anticipation of disaster for which his cruelties afford him no relief” (16). By curious paradox, the statement seems to be an apt summary of Jason’s attitude to dying, because, by avoiding the theme of finitude, he brings about death in his life, and acts similarly to his own mother. Although he is unwilling to use the words usually employed in the context of demise, he inflicts pain and wounds on the people he talks to. He forgets about the ordo amoris, represents the homo capitalisticus, and supports what Scheler calls the “mechanical conception of life.” And when he counts how much he possesses, he does not remember about the values that do count. In short, “Jason seems temperamentally, psychologically, and even biologically so constituted that he cannot respond with love or forgiveness or even a natural human kindness to others” (Hunt “The Locus” 89), which is nothing else but Scheler’s conclusion that results from existence without death.

Chapter Three Quentin’s Existence as Being-Towards-Death Evaluating Faulkner’s prose in a 1946 essay entitled “William Faulkner,” Robert Penn Warren singles out “philosophical weight” as one of his primary distinctive features (124). Jean-Jacques Mayoux also calls the father of Yoknapatawpha County “a philosopher, though perhaps without his knowing it” (172). As Kinney observes, there are two trends in Quentin’s line of deliberation: “a life philosophy” and “a death philosophy” (144). Obviously, these two philosophies must have looked different at various stages of Faulkner’s life, especially if we take into account his reaction to Hemingway’s suicide, the suicidal urge in Faulkner’s psyche, and the fact that he initially asked Joan Williams to post her correspondence to “Quentin Compson” (Hönnighausen 18, 24).112 Faulkner the philosopher created a character that could be described with the same epithet. Arthur Geffen observes in Quentin a “terrifying philosophical insight” (234), whereas for Eric J. Sundquist the Quentin section is characteristic of “a vapid philosophizing” (15). Perhaps what Sundquist perceives as colorless and flat is the outcome of Quentin’s “Don Quixote side” – which Jackson J. Benson touches upon, revealing the character’s personality traits (222). Far away from pragmatism, Quentin’s mental efforts to constantly nourish his hungry imagination make him fall into the recognizable picture of the thinker who is, for most of the time, found deep in contemplation, which permits one to inquire about his identity as Dasein. While trying to interpret “June Second 1910” through Heidegger’s philosophy of death, we should begin by asking if Quentin may be considered to be the Heideggerian Dasein as defined in the first chapter. William J. Sowder gives an affirmative reply. Noticing many characters in Yoknapatawpha County that could bear the name of “Dasein,” Sowder believes that Faulkner “attempts to treat each character as an authentic human being” (xvi). Quentin’s 112 Faulkner’s first reaction to Hemingway’s death was: “It wasn’t an accident. He killed himself.” Later he added, “I don’t like a man that takes the short way home” (qtd. in Hönnighausen 18). Joan Williams was a young woman the 52-year-old Faulkner tried to have a love affair with (Williamson 276).

126 Chapter Three authenticity in The Sound and the Fury in particular is mentioned by Lewis P. Simpson, too, although the critic does not refer to Heidegger’s philosophy to prove it (93). Therefore, it seems worthwhile to search for two features of Dasein, i.e., existence and mineness as reflected in Quentin’s world. Strictly connected with the notion of Being, both features appear to be applicable to Faulkner’s protagonist, because, as Heidegger’s Dasein, Quentin’s modus operandi is Being – he constantly thinks about his life. This is especially visible in the recollection in which Quentin describes his evening habit – back at home he would lie in his bed “thinking I was I was not who was not was not who” (SF 211, emphasis added). For Philip M. Weinstein, the quoted flow of words is the character’s “babble” (Faulkner’s 84). Nevertheless, despite this alleged gibberish at first glance, it escapes the critic that the first part of the quote is perfectly clear, as it presents Quentin in the process of careful deliberation over his own identity. Moreover, the critic notes that Quentin’s language “chokes on its quest for coherence,” and that “Quentin is the stream of consciousness technique itself” (Faulkner’s 84, emphasis added). If Quentin choked in his articulation, he would be speechless, and he is definitely far from being at a loss for words. Also, it is hard to disagree that his narrative exemplifies stream of consciousness, so the reader cannot expect grammaticality as if it were a for-and-against essay. Stream of consciousness does not discredit one’s quest for the answer to the question about Being. Even though Van O’Connor realizes that Quentin’s reasoning is usually presented “in a disordered, disturbed, even mad fashion” (11), the scholar believes that Quentin’s story is “the search of the modern protagonist, usually a sensitive aesthete, for a sense of radical significance” (14). Observable in the above quoted passage is Quentin’s quest for the meaning of existence, which similarly to many Faulkner’s protagonists, has not been forced on them by the surrounding world, but “born out of their very being” (Gresset 115). A similar opinion is held by Robert Penn Warren, who in his analysis of Faulkner’s primary techniques of narration speaks of “a dramatic method,” perfectly exemplified both in As I Lay Dying and The Sound and the Fury, which “each character unfolds in his own language or flow of being before us” (122-123). What simultaneously comes out both of Quentin’s deliberation over his own existence and of the critics’ lines of reasoning constitutes mineness as the second feature of Dasein. The feature is clearly illustrated by the pronoun “I” in Quentin’s statement, which signifies the scrutiny of his own Being, made by himself to himself. The case of employing the first person singular pronoun in the above quoted passage is not isolated one, since in Quentin’s section its usage is numerous (Bockting “The Impossible” on-line), which obviously stresses his focus on his Being.

Quentin’s Existence as Being-Towards-Death 127 On the first reading of The Sound and the Fury, one may get the impression that Quentin is more concentrated on what others say or do than on what he thinks, but a closer look at his deliberations helps to bring about another conclusion.113 First of all, when his section begins, Quentin puts the spotlight on himself by saying “I was in time again” (SF 93), and only then does he mention his relatives. Secondly, the people and events he probes into are insolubly connected with his own personage, and they truly constitute the material for Quentin’s meditation over existence. When we take into account the thoughts in which Caddy appears, it is true that a lot of space in the text has been devoted to his sister. However, if Kartiganer speaks about Quentin’s “fictionalization” of his sister (“‘Now’” 86), the protagonist rather creates the image of the person that does not exist. In the Appendix Faulkner explains that Quentin was the person that “loved not his sister’s body but some concept of Compson honor” (411), which provides tangible proof that he broods more over the abstraction than the entity. Obviously, it is not to say that Caddy is not needed by Quentin; it is rather not to overlap Caddy’s virginity with her brother’s personhood, since, similarly to Thomas Sutpen, Quentin cherishes “only the idea” of purity in the members of his household, not their selves (Bowling 112). Called by Gresset Faulkner’s “Ariadne’s clue” (115), with no section where she is a narrator, Caddy thus represents a thread given to readers to find their way out of the labyrinth of thought in The Sound and the Fury. The same is conspicuous with reference to Quentin’s father. For instance, the opening passages, with fragments in which Quentin relates the conversation with his father,114 are not exclusively an exemplification of the recollections that are to evoke his parent’s memory, or the feelings Quentin associates with him.
