Quentin recollects what his father told him while giving him his grandfather’s watch: “constant speculation regarding the position of mechanical hands on an 113 Obviously, we should dismiss the argument that one can entirely cut oneself off the external. As Mikhail Bakhtin asserts in “Discourse in the Novel,” “language is not a neutral medium that passes freely and easily into the private property of the speaker’s intentions; it is populated – overpopulated – with the intentions of others. Expropriating it, forcing it to submit to one’s own intentions and accents, is a difficult and complicated process” (qtd. in P. Weinstein Faulkner’s 113), which is visible in Quentin’s section. Here, I would like to stress that even though I partly disagree with Weinstein’s interpretation of Quentin’s search for his own existence, his analysis has been very stimulating to me. 114 There are critics who believe that Quentin’s conversations with his father may be imaginary. The thesis concerning incest with Caddy was, in fact, supported by Faulkner during one of the discussions at the University of Virginia, May 2, 1958 (Gwynn and Blotner 262). Nevertheless, Ross and Polk claim “there is no internal evidence in the novel to determine whether Quentin is remembering or imagining” (RF 149).

128 Chapter Three arbitrary dial which is a symptom of mind-function… And I saying All right. Wonder. Go on and wonder” (SF 94, emphasis added). Here, it is made plain that both father and son regard the mental sphere as relevant and both intend to stimulate it. However, the passage also reveals that Quentin disagrees with his parent’s opinion, being rather skeptical about its content. Thus, sharing the passion for cogitation on human’s existence, Quentin would like to maintain independence of the mind from his father’s rumination. As Marsha Warren confirms, even if the thoughts generated by his father circulate throughout the text, there is “no exchange, no agreement, only opposition, only conflict… which ultimately effect Quentin’s rejection of the Law/Truth of the Father” (qtd. in Foca 354). The additional evidence for the antagonism toward his parent may be Quentin’s comment on the observed argument of two boys, when he perceives in their conduct “that adult trait of being convinced of anything by an assumption of silent superiority” (SF 146). We may presume that he is talking here about conversations with his father, as in the next sentence he refers to those “using themselves and each other so much by words” (SF 146). That the act of cogitating in the manner of Heidegger is essential is even more visible in another fragment. It takes place when Quentin concludes that if the sky was overcast, it would be an ideal moment for him to stand at the window “thinking what he [father] said about idle habits” (SF 95). Here, as one of the unnecessary whims Quentin definitely considers the New London boat race between Harvard and Yale, because, instead of rowing, students ought to occupy themselves with thinking: “Thinking it would be nice for them down at New London” (SF 95). According to Merrill Horton, who draws a comparison between Balzac’s characters from The Human Comedy and Faulkner’s literary figures, Quentin Compson, like Athanase Granson from the story “The Old Maid,” shows an inclination to think all the time, which the scholar even regards as his problem (60). The undeniable level of difficulty in understanding the Quentin section also testifies to the importance of the mental sphere for the protagonist, because when “the mind of the character becomes more and more absorbed by the problem he is attempting to solve, Faulkner’s prose parallels the involvement” (Everett vii-viii). Moreover, Quentin’s wish to break free from others’ thinking is noticeable in his opinions that concern Gerald Bland. Quentin values in Bland the fact that at least once he showed determinism when he made up his mind not to give up the rowing he loves, which his mother would like him to leave behind (SF 112). The Heideggerian Being also conveys “the transcendens pure and simple” (BT 62), which Bogdan Baran has identified with “stepping forward” into the essence of Being (“Przedmowa” xix). No one can deny that the direction of Quentin’s thoughts is rather “backward,” for he does not live in the present, but

Quentin’s Existence as Being-Towards-Death 129 is exclusively immersed in the past. He is a figure of the past. “He talks like they do in minstrel shows” (SF 148).115 While traveling home from Harvard for Christmas, he puts his head out of the train window, “looking back” at an elderly black man with a mule (SF 107). Quentin plays with him a traditional verbal game that was popular between whites and blacks in the South,116 but by the same token he shows “his racialized Other” at the very beginning of the scene (Lester 137). What is more, the last day of his life is nothing else but the revision of what happened before – “a final examination of his life” (M. Brown 544). Nevertheless, in his essays on Faulkner’s art of writing, Warren Beck has remarked that there are moments when “a character’s awareness may move backward in associative recollection and forward in further realization” (323). While playing the game with the black man, Quentin “looks back” on the past (SF 107), but he has insight into himself, too. By reevaluating the traditional Southern game, Lester maintains that Quentin, after his sojourn in the North, gains “his anxious new awareness of its cultural constitution,” thereby realizing that black-white relationships are the result of culturally imposed racism (137, emphasis added).117 Apart from this, in The Sound and the Fury, there are scenes in which we observe that individualization attracts Quentin. His aspiration is to lead a life according to standards established by himself, rejecting, for instance, the community of the Harvard students (Gresset 119). On the day of his suicide, while observing his fellow students though the window swarming to the chapel for service, Quentin spots Spoade in the crowd. Compson’s perceivable sympathy toward him does not result only from the fact that Spoade is a Southerner. He likes him for his nonconformist behavior. Quentin accentuates that Spoade has never been punctual, but also that he has never missed a service without having his shirt or socks on regardless of the weather (SF 96). Spoade’s conduct unquestionably impresses Quentin. While looking at him through the window, Quentin compares his college mate to “a 115 In “Dialect and Modernist in The Sound and the Fury,” Matthews claims that through the mention of minstrel shows Faulkner wanted to signal his own estrangement from customs and traditions of the South (135). 116 The game was usually played between whites and black children. In the game the white person said “Christmas gift,” which meant that s/he was to get a gift first. In reality, instead of a gift, the white person expected a confirmation that the black child was “caught.” Then the child received some money (RF 58). 117 Cheryl Lester also mentions that Quentin suspects the consequences of the Great Migration of the black to the North in the second decade of the 20th century. Interestingly enough, African-American historians perceive the migration to be a more significant event in Southern history than WW1, whereas other historians stress the importance of WW1 in that region (128).

130 Chapter Three terrapin,” which needs water to live. However, Spoade is “like a terrapin in a street full of scuttering dead leaves,” which stand for the scurrying students (SF 96). While playing truant that morning, Quentin wants to stay out of the crowd, too, out of Heidegger’s “everydayness” understood as averageness preached by the “they.” He resists participating in the everyday ritual, so monotonous to him, of running among “the same ones [students] fighting the same heaving coat- sleeves, the same books and flapping collars flushing past like debris on a flood” (SF 96, emphasis added). Moreover, Quentin’s determination to remain a nonconformist, occupied with uncovering transcendental knowledge that concerns Being, is noticeable by those who count as his circle of friends. Aware that Quentin does not indulge in pastimes popular among the majority of students, Shreve, his roommate, knows better than others how Quentin spends his free time, when he says that “he’s got better sense than to chase after the little dirty sluts” (SF 96). Also, Herbert, Caddy’s husband, during one of the first conversations with his future brother- in-law, spots that Quentin represents a rara avis who has his own way of Being: “you dont look like these other hicks” (SF 134). Quentin himself appears to take pride in the fact that Bland’s mother favors him over the other Harvard students, which he explains by his Southern origin, and, connected with that, “a blundering sense of noblesse oblige” (SF 112). At some points in his life, Quentin Compson has to clash with the philosophy of the “they,” which in The Sound and the Fury has been spread to a great extent by his own parent.118 “The epicenter of the Compson family dynamics,” Mr. Compson exercises control over his family in order to be able to indulge in heavy drinking (Storhoff 8-9). Not only is his speech “disguised as philosophy,” but it serves to help him abuse alcohol openly (Storhoff 9). It is also his “idle talk,” as Heidegger would put it, by which the father tries to instill an inauthentic mode of Being in his son. First and foremost, Mr. Compson’s intention is to dissuade Quentin from any attempts to recognize his individuality through his nihilistic attitude toward life. In his statements, seen by Gresset as 118 Interesting is the fact that the roles ascribed to the parents in the Benjy section differ considerably in the narrative related by the student of Harvard. In the first story, the figure of the mother is emphasized more than the father, whereas in the Quentin section the situation is the other way round. In addition, in the first tale, Mr. Compson is presented rather as a victim of Mrs. Compson’s conduct. Despite his exposed drinking habit, and his great reluctance to explain to his offspring what death stands for, the reader has the impression that the children are under the watchful eye of the male parent. In the second section, Quentin’s attitude toward his hypochondriac and apathetic mother remains similar to Benjy’s, whereas the study of their father has been deepened much more explicitly.

Quentin’s Existence as Being-Towards-Death 131 flowery but full of “emptiness which is at the core of the being” (120), Quentin’s parent disseminates the averageness that Heidegger talks about, “teaching us that all men are just accumulations dolls stuffed with sawdust swept up from the trash heaps where all previous dolls had been thrown away” (SF 218). In other words, one resembles the other; all people digest the same pap; there is no room for creativity; the only mode of being should be passivity tinged with cynicism, as illustrated by the father’s behavior. With such a parental approach, Quentin’s personality along with that of the other siblings’ dissolve into anonymity, which results in “enfeebling the very idea of mine” (Wadlington 74). This is nothing else but the act of depriving Dasein of mineness, its individual feature that confirms its individualism. Secondly, there is an omnipresent purposelessness that accentuates the futility of human endeavors. No matter what one has gone through, “Father said a man is the sum of his misfortunes. One day you’d think misfortune would get tired, but then time is your misfortune” (SF 129). Thirdly, the father preaches to the son that there is no morality, either. This is visible when Mr. Compson generalizes about people’s memory, which is like a sieve, for they do not remember what dreadful acts they performed only yesterday (SF 98). In addition, he severely criticizes educational institutions, regarding Harvard as a place “where the best of thought… clings like dead ivy vines upon old dead brick” (SF 117-118). Quentin’s father also shares a feature typical of Faulkner’s male characters, namely “the complete denigration of women” (Mortimer qtd. in Johnson 76). 119 As a misogynist, he believes all females, with no exception to the rule, are perfect at “fertilising the mind” with whatever is evil (SF 119). He does not respect his wife, and blames her for everything (SF 125-126), although she is respected by other men in town, like Earl or the sheriff. This indirectly shows that Mrs. Compson may be a victim, not a perpetrator exclusively, and she should not thoroughly be blamed for their failed marriage (Williams 402-403). Further, in the conversation about the state of virginity, when Mr. Compson belittles its importance, Quentin objects to him, and states that we cannot simply reach a conclusion that it is not important. In the response, the father sustains his indifference, but once again expresses his nihilistic attitude about life, as well: “That’s what’s so sad about anything: not only virginity” (SF 96). The proclamation of the philosophy of the “they” preached by Mr. Compson touches upon the theme of finitude, too. Together with the atmosphere of 119 Faulkner’s “protagonists fluctuate between a nostalgic mythologizing of women such as Molly and the complete denigration of women and a denial that one needs them at all” (Mortimer qtd. in Johnson 76).

132 Chapter Three mortality, Kinney finds the Quentin section interwoven with “his father’s morbid vision and death” (148). In the views uttered by Mr. Compson, one can recognize the third component of Heidegger’s care. This component is falling, which, with its three features, demonstrates the inauthentic mode of Being- towards-death, i.e., the escape from death, or, to be more precise, avoidance of forming the positive attitude to dying. The first aspect of falling is temptation. Temptation is employed by Quentin’s father to talk into his son the belief that death, instead of being the possibility attributed exclusively to a given entity, should be regarded as “a mishap” that occurs only to others (BT 296). While divagating about virginity, Quentin’s father expresses the opinion that “it’s like death: only a state in which the others are left” (SF 96). Such an argument introduces an artificial, non-existing division between those who die and those who do not. Moreover, it rebukes Heidegger’s viewpoint, which assumes that when we are born, we are old enough to die. As a result, it may be deduced that Mr. Compson does not treat every human’s life as “Being-towards-death,” which for Heidegger appears to be a process. He rather sees it as existence with demise that is “Being-at-the-end,” which simultaneously constitutes the rejection of death both as my own, always likely to happen possibility, and as the non-yet phenomenon present in our life since the moment of birth. Tranquillization is the second aspect of falling. It denotes another way of escaping from death, instilled into Dasein by persuasion, which is partly illustrated in the novel. It is true that the father does not claim that Quentin will never pass away. Nevertheless, he aims at distorting its very well-known picture. With reference to Christ’s martyr-like death, Mr. Compson attempts to persuade his son that the main instrument of torture was not the Cross, but time: “Father said that. That Christ was not crucified: he was worn away by a minute clicking of little wheels” (SF 94). By curious paradox, according to Mr. Compson, time does kill, but it may be killed as well by nothing else but clocks. Thus “time is dead,” and it comes back to life only when the mechanism of the clocks halts (SF 105), which downplays the importance of death in favor of time. We should also add that while shifting the import from death to time, Mr. Compson’s tranquillization may be treated as a form of his own consolation, which Heidegger also mentions. The father knows that he is dying, and he wants to quiet down his own fear of death. He visualizes the event when he talks about a minister holding his hand, which makes his wife cry (SF 248). Eventually, by arousing indifference to death in Quentin, Mr. Compson tries to provoke a sense of alienation from death in his son, the third characteristic of falling, and at the same time the consequence of the first two. In the opening paragraph of his narrative, Quentin recalls how his father gave him his grandfather’s watch as a graduation gift, and described the present as “the

Quentin’s Existence as Being-Towards-Death 133 mausoleum of all hope and desire” (SF 93). The juxtaposition of time with a mausoleum would seem at first to be a peculiar expression of memento mori. It should help Quentin realize that death will never let us complete a project we are involved in while passing away. Therefore, he ought to use the time given to him reasonably, which echoes the point made by Heidegger. However, through this gift, Mr. Compson wishes Quentin “to gain the reducto absurdum of all human experience”120 (SF 93). For Ross and Polk this message says: “time reduces human experience to absurdity because all life concludes with death” (RF 44). In this context, according to Quentin’s father, death does not add any meaning to existence, but brings about hokum and preposterousness. As a result, there is nothing but alienation from finitude, which is the aspect of the philosophy proclaimed by the “they.” In this overwhelming atmosphere of ludicrousness, with his idle talk about death, Mr. Compson is one of “big talkers” in Faulkner (Hoffman 145). Due to his nihilistic attitude to life and death, he strives to instill in his son a conviction that the best he can do is to forget about death by ceasing to remember time. His wish is passed to Quentin with the words: “I give it [the watch] to you not that you may remember time, but that you might forget it now and then for a moment and not spend all your breath trying to conquer it” (SF 93). According to Ross and Polk, in the above declaration, Quentin’s father implies that inner serenity may be attained if one becomes oblivious of time, and simultaneously of death (RF 44). Nevertheless, by adding that “no battle is ever won,” and “victory is an illusion of philosophers and fools” (SF 93), Ross and Polk suggest Mr. Compson is aware that it is impossible to vanquish death (RF 44-45). When we listen to the scholars’ viewpoints, and try to figure out the meaning of Mr. Compson’s words, it appears that his stance on finitude is a contradiction in terms. Once he wishes Quentin to become unaware of time and death, but, on the other occasion, he hints that there is no way of escaping from the thought about the end. His schizophrenic attitude toward dying is the best revealed by the following quote: “any live man is better than any dead man but no live or dead man is very much better than any other live or dead man” (SF 125). Interpreting the words, Anna Foca claims that the statement does not help Quentin resolve his problem, “but rather reinscribes his intense fear that all grounds for judgment have been built on the fallacious yet effective objectification of other equally subjective human minds” (353). Thus lack of logic, evident in Mr. Compson’s opinion, certainly illuminates neither Quentin nor the reader. Together with the 120 This Latin phrase, as it is in the case of the one in Benjy’s section, was misspelled by Faulkner, and the correct one sounds as follows: “reductio ad absurdum” (Jędraszko 183).

134 Chapter Three son, we are in the maze of confusions that arises from the father’s idle talk replete with convoluted arguments and cryptic remarks. To all intents and purposes, there is no way of entirely avoiding the influence of the “they,” so it happens that Quentin fails on his path to discover his authentic Being. Definitely, he is infected with the philosophy of the “they,” spread around by his own parent. Impossible to omit is Quentin’s misogynistic attitude toward women, whom he considers to be of lower status: “Nothing but a girl,” he speaks repeatedly of a female child met on the day of his suicide (SF 171). As much as he declares that he loves Caddy, he does not respect his sibling. Due to the loss of her virginity, the brother shows his contempt for his sister, making a comparison between her sexual act and mating. Together with verbal abuse, Quentin happens to use physical violence, not to mention that he is usually the chief agent of ferocity (Bleikasten The Ink 81). For example, he slaps Caddy for kissing a town boy (SF 112). He wants her to accept his superiority when he forces her to utter “calf rope,” being a sign of surrendering (Calvin Brown qtd. in RF 44). At the same time he has no objections to touching Natalie, who he has been playing with in the barn (SF 167). In addition, he behaves gracefully toward Caddy’s seducer, treating him like a gentleman, whereas a few lines later, after showing his courteous manners, he calls his sister the worst names, such as “whore” (SF 197). He makes up her indifference toward the family, for when she asks whether he will take care of their father and Benjy while she is away, he asks her if she has ever thought of them, which we know is not true (SF 131). In fact, it is the egoistic Quentin who broods over such an abstract idea like the family’s honor (Collins “Miss” 82), simultaneously blaming Caddy for their ill-being (SF 138) in the same manner as his father did before with his wife. To defend Quentin, Anna Foca, who quotes Simone de Beauvoir, believes that the education his father conveys to him glorifies the past (348). In the past history was written by men, which resulted in the domination of patriarchy. If we broach the subject of time and clocks, the answer to the question of whether Quentin agrees with his father about the possibility of forgetting time appears to be negative. It is true that after waking up in the morning on June 2, Quentin rises from bed to silence the ticking watch by facing it down (SF 94), then by breaking its glass and destroying its hands (SF 98), which May C. Brown perceives as Quentin’s attempt to stop time (545). In fact, “time is his enemy, responsible for his loss of Caddy and hence for his suffering” (M. Brown 545). Nevertheless, Jean-Paul Sartre, who recognizes time as the main theme of the novel, expresses a different opinion: “To reach real time, we must abandon these devices, which measure nothing… Quentin’s breaking his watch has, therefore, a symbolic value; it forces us to see time without the aid of

Quentin’s Existence as Being-Towards-Death 135 clocks” (226). Initially, when the reader has leafed through the pages of the novel, there is no certainty whether Quentin destroys the watch to kill time, or if he ruins its mechanism to let time live, especially if one bears in mind Faulkner’s relativism, noted by Gail L. Mortimer: “the flux of experience” and “the illusion of stability implicit in asserting the finitude or boundedness of objects in this same reality” (45).121 More probable seems to be the latter, because Quentin opposes his father’s suggestion that it is possible to forget time; on the contrary, man is acutely aware of its flow. Much earlier in his life Quentin found out it was impossible to trick time and forget about its flow. In the past, at school, when he could hear that the clock announced three o’clock, and the lessons ended at a quarter past three, he tried to count the last fifteen minutes on his own, but he was never right, he was never able to win over time (SF 108-109). And the more attempts were made to shun time, the greater awareness of it Quentin gained (M. Brown 545-546). As a result, in the present of June 2, it is unnecessary for this protagonist to throw a glance at any kind of timing device to be cognizant of what time it is. “There was a clock, high up in the sun” (SF 102), which always says a given hour more or less accurately. Furthermore, the Harvard student has learned to tell time “almost to the minute” from the shadow of the sash appearing on the curtain in the dormitory room. He is even able to see it with his back turned, like animals that have eyes at the back of their heads (SF 93-94). Except for the sun and the shadow, the outside world communicates additional hints to Quentin, because the number of passengers in the car helps him to realize what time it is, as well (RF 84). His very body is also time-conscious due to the fact that it sends out unmistakable signals that announce appropriate meal times suggestive of a given hour: “Stomach saying noon brain saying eat oclock” (SF 129). The final confirmation that there is no possibility of living out of time Faulkner interweaves in the June Second narrative on its last pages. It is manifested by Quentin’s act of putting the watch face up, the same watch that in the morning he turned upside down (SF 213). If it is impossible to forget time, it is impossible to become oblivious of death. The combination of the two is proved by Bleikasten when he asserts that from the very beginning of his section “Quentin’s time is a time-for-death or even (insofar as his voice reaches us from beyond life) a time-in-death” (The Ink 91). With the option for the former rather than for the latter, as there seems to be 121 This scene may evoke one of Faulkner’s literary devices, namely the so-called “frozen moment.” According to John E. Bassett, it implies that “for Faulkner art depended paradoxically on being both something that stopped time and something that remained alive forever” (“Family” 417).

136 Chapter Three no evidence in favor of his being a ghost, Quentin’s awareness of time makes him brood about death even more deeply. Quentin Compson does not accept his father’s teaching about the inauthentic mode of Being-towards-death, and he repudiates the third feature of care, i.e., falling with its three aspects: temptation, tranquillization and alienation. In effect, the parent’s talk produces the adverse effect, for the Harvard student does not forget about death. However, Quentin is accused by his parent of not taking death for what it is. Instead, Mr. Compson claims that his son elevates it to the level of an apotheosis (SF 220). Imagining death as a divine state in which the mind hovers over the flesh, Quentin, according to his father, does not treat the human end as a physical annihilation, as completion, but as a transformation from one phase to another, still being alive. Whether Quentin believes in the afterlife or not may be a fairly problematic question for at least two reasons. Firstly, Faulkner paradoxically writes about both “assertion and denial of immortality” (Slatoff 196); and secondly, the author is often unwilling to explain everything clearly to the reader (Slatoff 178). At the beginning of the section, in one of the fragments classified in the hypertext edition as a part of the 1909 conversation with his father, which may also be Quentin’s comment given on June 2 if its content is taken into account, Benjy’s brother utters the words: “I will look down and see my murmuring bones and the deep water like wind, like a roof of wind, and after a long time they cannot distinguish even bones upon the lonely and inviolate sand. Until on the Day when He says Rise only the flat-iron would come floating up” (SF 98). At the beginning of the statement, the phrase “I will look down and see” exemplifies a prolepsis. It shows Quentin’s presumption that after his death he will possess a capability to observe his corpse floating in the river, which denotes his belief in the afterlife. What puzzles the reader is the epithet incorporated in this prolepsis, that is, “my murmuring bones,” as it is rather tentative if the phrase denotes just the sound of water. Next, there is a shift to physical annihilation, which may not signify the eradication of the soul yet, for the fragment about the bones in sand concerns only parts of the flesh. However, the denial of his possible resurrection may make the reader conclude that the statement, which started with the promise of a spiritual afterlife, ends with death, after which nothing happens. It is true though that in the next passage Quentin apparently mentions his belief in resurrection: “maybe when He says Rise the eyes will come floating up too, out of the deep quiet and the sleep, to look on glory” (SF 144, emphasis added). Yet again, regardless of the suggested drowsiness that implies an afterlife continuum, there is still this “maybe” that marks Quentin’s doubt.

Quentin’s Existence as Being-Towards-Death 137 Another fragment that refers to his suicide is also troublesome for the reader: “Niggers say a drowned man’s shadow was watching for him in the water all the time. It twinkled and glinted, like breathing, the float slow like breathing too, and debris half submerged, healing out to the sea and the caverns and the grottoes of the sea” (SF 111). Watching his mirror image in the surface of the water, Quentin again seems to prefer to believe that his shadow stays alive no matter whether before or after suicide, breathing now and watching afterward.122 Although the term “debris” plainly denotes the remains of dead tissue, the expression “healing out” signifies the opposite. This could suggest that Quentin regards death as a kind of therapy that will enable him to cure himself of his inner wounds. Clearly, the reader is certain about his preferable place of interment, which is a deep abyss of the sea. And this part of the quoted fragment is considered to be an allusion to “Kubla Khan” by Samuel Taylor Coleridge (RF 61), where the Alph, “the sacred river, ran / Through caverns measureless to man / Down to a sunless sea” (256). Surprisingly, there are a good many images in Coleridge that help us with a reading of The Sound and the Fury, and make the poem a summary of the novel in question. In the first stanza, the speaker describes the gardens that bear a strong resemblance to the place where Quentin was brought up, and to the events that he and his sister were entangled in. In the poem, there are “rills” (256), similar to the branch where all the Compsons’ offspring used to play; there is also “an incense-bearing tree” (Coleridge 256), which could be the one Caddy used to climb up and down, with an intense smell of honeysuckle in the air. In the verses “that deep romantic chasm which slanted / Down the green hill” (Coleridge 256), one may find the hill that is between the Compsons’ house and the branch. Nevertheless, the “romantic chasm” turns out to be “a savage place” in the second stanza of “Kubla Khan,” and the ambience that prevails there is compared to the situation in which a woman, by the light of the moon, cries over “her demon-lover” (256). This lover could represent Ames Dalton, for whom Caddy stealthily sneaked out of the house, but whom Quentin treated as an enemy, comparing him even to Pluto, the god of the underworld and the ruler of the dead (Watson 52). To return to the poem, in this savage place, the fountain that stood there is suddenly destroyed “with ceaseless turmoil” 122 It is interesting to notice that Quentin treats his own shadow as the Other, another human being. Significantly, it appears to have a body, as Quentin is talking about “my shadow’s bones” (SF 118), about “the belly of my shadow” (SF 119), or about “the middle of my shadow” (SF 138), which denotes a waist. His mirror image seems to lead its own separate life, too, which may be inferred from Quentin’s following statement: “I slowed still more, my shadow pacing me, dragging its head through the weeds that hid the fence” (SF 165, emphasis added).

138 Chapter Three (Coleridge 256), which in turn could resemble Quentin’s shattered dream to be with Caddy. The remains of the fountain are carried by the river, which finally “sank in tumult to a lifeless ocean,” where the caves are limitless, and where “the shadow of the dome of pleasure” is observable in the surface of water (Coleridge 256). If compared with the novel, these images reflect nothing else but Quentin’s intentions for how he would like to die, what his grave should look like, and where his body should rest. To this juxtaposition of the realistic images, we may add an interpretation that involves metaphors. In A Critical History of English Literature, David Daiches claims that the speaker in “Kubla Khan” tells the reader about “poetic creation,” and that the outside world can easily destroy this “palace of art” (898). Quoting R. H. Fogle, H. House, G. W. Knight, and D. Mercer, Duane B. Schneider considers Coleridge’s “Kubla Khan” to be a harmonious expression full of contrary phenomena, where one finds such pairs like “life-death, light- dark, and heat-cold” (68). Besides, the unity of clashing ideas is perceived to be a characteristic feature of a perfect work of art, created by joining the human and the supernatural (Hühn 236). In the opinion of Wanda Krajewska, “Kubla Khan” ends with the reader’s eyes turned toward the poet pictured “as a prophet, a magician (ll. 50-52) and one who has insight into eternal reality (ll. 53-54)” (74). When we relate the above to The Sound and the Fury, doubtless Quentin is a lyric poet (Benson 222). He employs the poetical language, and creates his own vision of the pleasure-dome with Caddy in its center. The vision, actually threatened in Quentin’s eyes by every man approaching his sister, has been carried to extremes by Quentin’s transformation of hell into paradise: “if it were just to hell;… Nobody else there but her and me” (SF 97). However, according to Stonum, death for Quentin appears to represent “the attainment of a region where things truly ‘finished themselves’” (84), which the scholar supports with the quote from the novel: “If things just finished themselves” (SF 97). Yet what seems to escape Stonum is the fact that the statement is actually expressed in the conditional – the same as the probable vision of paradise with Caddy in hell, and that results in a contradiction in terms. Be that as it may, the word “finished” retains the overtones of death in the opinion of Hönnighausen. If we bear in mind that it was the last word expressed by Christ on the Cross, Quentin’s final act may be ironically juxtaposed with Christ’s death. The Cross brought salvation, whereas in the novel, Hönnighausen suggests, one may experience the feeling of despondency characteristic of modernism (143). Comparing the earthly and the celestial, or perhaps the hellish, the juxtaposition of life and death is conspicuous in Quentin. Nevertheless, the harmonious reconciliation of the contradictory spheres observable in “Kubla

Quentin’s Existence as Being-Towards-Death 139 Khan” is almost entirely missing in Quentin’s deliberation. Instead, for the most part of the section, there is chaos, which makes the reader confused as to what sphere Faulkner’s protagonist believes in. There is mostly disorientation, since Quentin is usually indecisive about whether there is an afterlife or not, whether one can presuppose the existence of eternity in any form. Still, Stonum is not totally wrong when he claims that death for Quentin will be a territory “where things truly ‘finished themselves’” (84). The scholar only selected an inappropriate quote to prove it. At the very end of the narrative, there is Quentin’s final unequivocal declaration that death means the end: “A quarter hour yet. And then I’ll not be” (SF 216), which simultaneously denies the father’s accusation against the son that he treats demise as apotheosis. What additionally supports the conclusion is Quentin’s reply to his father after the parent’s criticism of his approach to finitude: “you will not even be dead and i [Quentin] temporary” (SF 220, emphasis added). This proves that even if there was a time when the accusation might have been Quentin’s line of reasoning, this is definitely denied before his felo de se. Intended to become Being-a-whole, Dasein is to reach its totality a priori by the constant interiorization of death in Dasein’s life. To achieve that one has to make death a part of life, which involves attention paid to our demise during earthly existence. It would be erroneous to claim that Quentin Compson gains the awareness of death exclusively on the day when he decides to take his life. On the contrary, in The Sound and the Fury, the reader has insight into “Quentin’s private eschatology” (P. Weinstein Faulkner’s 120). His narrative consists of a number of recollected episodes that explicitly exemplify the process of realizing the presence of finitude in his life, which is nothing else but Heidegger’s authentic mode of Being-towards-death. Of the various reminiscences rich in death-oriented thoughts, the most representative seems to be Quentin’s deliberation over the effect twilight makes on him, which takes place before going to bed in his parents’ house. In the passage, as it is in the Benjy section, the mention of twilight clearly merges with human death (Bleikasten The Ink 99), albeit Quentin muses upon the sense of a human’s existence in general. His reverie over the effect of the weakening light of the day resembles Hamlet’s well-known soliloquy. Quentin’s words are in fact a paraphrase of the Danish Prince’s famous expression on the grounds that the Faulknerian protagonist is occupied with “thinking I was I was not who was not was not who” (SF 211). In the reverie over being and non- being, in “this anguish scene,” not the will to live prevails, but the sense of tragedy that highlights “his sense that life has lost its value” (RF 138). Also, that the theme of transience occupies Quentin’s mind is visible when he thinks that “all stable things had become shadowy paradoxical all I had done shadows all I

140 Chapter Three had felt suffered taking visible form antic and perverse” (SF 211). Further, he finds himself in a state of lethargy, as if he was suspended in the vacuum, “lying neither asleep nor awake” (SF 211).123 Additionally, in the passage classified by the editors of the hypertext edition as the continuation of the same twilight theme, Quentin recollects the cedars having Caddy’s “vivid dead smell of perfume” (SF 219). At the same time, he makes a reference to the Gospels according to St. Matthew and St. Luke when he talks of “the swine untethered in pairs rushing coupled into the sea” (SF 219; RF 148-149), which relates to the demons who went into the pigs, and “perished in the waters” (Mt. 8.32). Worth mentioning here is a cluster of thanatological motifs present in the reverie, which recur in the Quentin narrative. First of all, the reason for his paying heed to twilight is that it is a part of the day when the smell of the honeysuckle, as “the saddest odour of all” (SF 210), irritates Quentin’s sense of smell. Moreover, for Faulkner’s protagonist, the odor intensifies when the plant is in bloom in spring, and with the falling rain, which shows that instead of considering spring as the rebirth of life, Quentin’s thought consciously keeps revolving about sadness, annihilation, and suffering. Apart from that, Quentin remembers that due to the rain “the draft in the door smelled of water, a damp steady breath” (SF 210-211), and water in The Sound and the Fury, and in other works by Faulkner like As I Lay Dying, or in the short story “Old Man,” serves as the space of death and destruction.124 Harold Bloom perceives the association of death with female sexuality as one of the relevant themes characteristic of Faulkner’s most valuable pieces of writing (1). The same opinion is expressed by Bleikasten, for whom Faulkner’s fiction exposes to view “the mute powers of sex and death” (The Ink 67). In The Sound and the Fury, long before his suicide, Quentin makes finitude present in his everyday life whenever he juxtaposes death with sexuality and corporeality of women (Branny 151). The way Quentin perceives demise through the prism of sex is pictured either by a medley of the two, or by a frequent transition from one subject to another. The shift is strikingly exemplified by the use of the expression “Little Sister Death” (SF 94), which is followed by “little dirty sluts” 123 In Faulkner’s poem having two titles, “A Dead Pilot” and “Boy and Eagle,” a young boy, “both dead and alive,” voices the emotions a soldier felt after imagining death (Samway 208-209). In the poem we read: “Here still the blue, the headlands; here still he / Who did not waken and was not awaked” (Faulkner qtd. in Samway 209). 124 Also see my article “The River as the Space of Death in William Faulkner.” Exploring Space: Spatial Notions in Cultural, Literary and Language Studies. Eds. Andrzej Ciuk and Katarzyna Molek-Kozakowska. Newcastle upon Tyne: Cambridge Scholars Publishing, 2010.

Quentin’s Existence as Being-Towards-Death 141 (SF 96), a similarly sounding phrase that might also be taken as a quasi- alliteration.125 It must be stressed that the motif of Little Sister Death did not originate during the composition of The Sound and the Fury. Indeed, it had appeared much earlier in narratives “The Kid Learns” (1925) and “Mayday” (1926). The first piece of writing tells a story of Johnny, taken by hand by “Little sister Death,” after he tried to protect a girl accosted by an old gangster (52). “Mayday,” Faulkner’s gift for Helen Baird after his failed courtship, is a fable about a young knight, Sir Galwyn of Arthgyl. In his quest for the face of the girl he saw in the waters of a dark stream, he seduces three princesses, who, however, leave him restless. The reflection haunting him appears to be “Little sister Death,” whose identity is revealed to the knight by the good Saint Francis (69). To join her, Sir Galwyn drowns himself, anticipating in great detail the fate of Faulkner’s better known character, Quentin Compson. In The Sound and the Fury, Caddy is obviously the figure who represents the coalescence of desire and death (Bleikasten The Ink 71). According to Wadlington, she is the embodiment of finitude, as she stands for both “the feminizing of death and the ‘dialogizing’ of death” (99). In Quentin’s discourse, this feminized death is clearly noticeable in the very phrase “Little Sister Death,” used for the first time when he alludes to “the good Saint Francis that said Little Sister Death, that never had a sister” (SF 94). One may ask: why is there the mention of the sister? In his book Saint Francis: Nature Mystic, Edward Armstrong claims that the saint referred to his sufferings as “sisters” (qtd. in RF 45). Consequently, when Quentin accentuates that neither Saint Francis nor Christ had a female sibling (SF 94), he stresses that those who have no sisters cannot exactly say what suffering, or death, signifies (RF 46). Thus the process of Being-towards-death in Quentin-“Thanatos” is insolubly linked with Caddy-“Eros” (Gresset 117), whose sexual side helps the Harvard student comport toward death. A relevant fragment that shows how sexuality interlaces with death is the scene at the branch when Quentin tries to persuade Caddy to commit suicide together. Through the words “I’ve already died for him [Ames]” (SF 188), Caddy declares her “sexual death,” which visualizes in Quentin’s mind “the threat of real death” (Irwin 41). Irwin also notes that when Quentin places his “phallic knife” at Caddy’s throat (46), and puts forward their ritual death together, his proposal suggests “a double killing that represents the equivalent, 125 Another, quite striking example of death juxtaposed with sex may be found in Sanctuary, when Temple, in the atmosphere of desire, lies in bed “like an effigy on an ancient tomb” (Novels 1930 228).

142 Chapter Three on the level of brother/sister incest, of the suicidal murder of the brother seducer by the brother avenger” (41). While lying close to Caddy, which looks like one of the phases of sexual intercourse indeed, Quentin also alludes to Damuddy’s finitude and Caddy’s muddy drawers (SF 188). In his discussion of this juxtaposition, Irwin sees the menace of sex that Quentin links in his consciousness with the picture of mud: “soft, dark, corrupt, enveloping – the image of being swallowed up by the earth” (45), which denotes nothing but extinction. Faulkner’s intention of starting the Quentin section with the scene confirms its primary importance (RF 128). The time of the day could not be different than twilight, defined in this fragment with the words “grey darkness” (SF 185). While the siblings are talking, “all smells and sounds of night” appear to be accumulating around them, which is suggestive of the coming end, too (SF 188). Further, the air appears “to drizzle with honeysuckle” whose smell implies the fusion of mortality with corporality (SF 186). Its fragrance brings back the memories of Caddy, but it also makes Quentin short of breath: “I had to pant to get any air at all out of that thick grey honeysuckle” (SF 188). In his discussion of the odor of the plant, Bleikasten speaks of the changeable meaning of honeysuckle from sexuality to the feeling of loss. Playing with the language, the scholar comments: “The sweet ‘honey’ of sisterhood, which Quentin so avidly ‘suckled’ in his childish greed, has thickened into a suffocating substance and now has the bitter taste of loss” (The Ink 54, emphasis added). The activity of the ever-moving world appears to have been suspended at least for a moment when Quentin, while approaching the branch, walks on the “island of silence,” and enters the “vacuum” created by crickets that fall soundless for a while (SF 186). Ross and Polk claim that the motif of crickets could come from Eliot’s The Waste Land (RF 129), where “the dead tree gives no shelter, the cricket no relief / And the dry stone no sound of water”126 (Eliot 1431). Later, in the middle of the branch scene, when the siblings keep going toward the forest, Quentin’s mind still records the signs of mortality. The ditch where the bones of their horse lie is metaphorically compared by him to “a black scar on the grey grass” (SF 190), which Hönnighausen interprets as “the theme of mutilation and death” wrought on the surrounding nature (142). Hönnighausen also notes the repetitive presence of the word “grey” in the Quentin section, which expressly stresses the symbolism of the hue in relation to the impending end of the speaker (142). 126 In the given quotation Eliot himself hints at a fragment from Ecclesiastes about old age before dying (1431).

Quentin’s Existence as Being-Towards-Death 143 In the scene at the branch Quentin gets closer to death in other ways. The description of Caddy’s state suggests at the very beginning that she is dead (SF 186). The brother finds his motionless sister in a lying position, partly immersed in the water, resembling a castaway on a bank. Her pale face, which merges with the sand she lies on, is visible only because of the hair contouring her head. Striking in the description of Caddy’s face is also Quentin’s simile, in which the odor of honeysuckle is juxtaposed with “a thin wash of lilac coloured paint” (SF 183), a coating of paint whose color is lilac. This dye is not evoked here by accident, as it denotes the color the writer associated with dying. When Faulkner aspired to be a poet, he composed a verse entitled “The Lilacs” (1920). Its subject matter deals with “death in life” (Blotner 78), and its lyrical character is an injured soldier in search of a woman who embodies death (Yonce qtd. in Blotner 78; Samway 210). Samway also mentions the similarity between Faulkner’s poem and Eliot’s “Portrait of a Lady,” in which, except for the motif of lilacs, a young man in love with an older lady of high society imagines her death at the end (209-210). The reader should also have in mind The Waste Land again, and especially its section “The Burial of the Dead,” where Eliot writes about “lilacs out of the dead land” (1430), the same mourning flowers that appeared earlier in Walt Whitman’s elegy on Lincoln “When Lilacs Last in the Dooryard Bloom’d.” What we may additionally regard as important in this recollection is the recurrence of references to Caddy’s wetness. A few times in this scene, Quentin relates that her skirt is integrated with water (SF 186), her knees are wet (SF 187), her blouse is found “damp” as well as her breast, against which he props his head (SF 189). Caddy herself pays heed to the fact that she is wet, for it is wetness that she communicates first to Ames when she meets him. The message is even repeated twice: “Im wet Im wet all over” (SF 192). In his discussion of female subjectivity and maternity in Faulkner, with a reference to Luce Irigaray’s remark about men’s aversion to fluidity, Philip M. Weinstein puts forward the distinction between “the dry drama” and “the wet drama” (Faulkner’s 37-38). The former, applicable to those near menopause or death, like Mrs. Compson or Addie Bundren, “denies desire and repudiates intercourse.” The latter, applicable to Caddy, Dewey Dell, Lena, Temple, “concedes desire and equates the fertile womb with rot and drowning,” which in fact provides us with another overlap of Eros and Thanatos.127 With reference to 127 Weinstein aptly notices that Faulkner’s male characters perceive the woman only as a sexual object; she is denied other spheres of life (Faulkner’s 117). Therefore Mrs. Compson’s conduct may be partly justified, because she is the product of Southern culture. She was only given a lesson about virginity by society (Faulkner’s 32), which

144 Chapter Three The Sound and the Fury, the very message about wetness, passed on to Ames, implies erotic overtones found in the watery imagery of the novel (Bleikasten The Ink 52). Nevertheless, water is also an element that bears “human finiteness” for Quentin (Bleikasten The Ink 102). In addition, in Faulkner: Myth and Motion, Richard Adams implies that Caddy’s state and the context she is presented in makes her Eliot’s Hyacinth Girl (qtd. in RF 131). As lilacs, hyacinth is in Faulkner the flower of death, since in “Mayday” Sir Galwyn associates “Little sister Death” with “young hyacinths in spring” (69), the thanatological image, which here is doubly reinforced by the season of the year. The picture of Caddy Quentin creates seems to stay rather in contrast to her true self as “an affirmative spirit” (Gregory 91), and her vivacity makes him distressed in Hunt’s opinion (“The Disappearance” 374). In fact, this is Quentin who cannot stand the smell of the honeysuckle, which makes him breathless (SF 127), whereas his sister’s heart pounds steadily whenever they talk about her lover (SF 188). Moreover, Caddy heads off into the forest, “toward the trees” (SF 191), which for her, as for Hester and Pearl in The Scarlet Letter (152-153), signifies freedom and the possibility of being one’s self. The cedar trees near the house are a setting where she dates, whereas her brother equates the trees with the place where finitude may be seen. He remembers that under the cedars his grandfather with a friend sat talking, and Quentin “thought of death as a man something like Grandfather,” that is, he associated another family member with finitude in his memories (SF 218-219). There are other points to show that Caddy chooses the path to life, whereas Quentin opts for the road to death. While she is heading for the forest to make love with Ames, Quentin bars her way so that they go and see the bones of their horse in the ditch. Although the bones are blanketed in darkness, they have been overgrown with vines, the symbol of life, but Quentin does not appear to accept this visible circle of life. Instead, he feels the drizzled honeysuckle, and sees Caddy’s and Ames’s bodies as one shadow (SF 190-192). Furthermore, relating the memory when Caddy made love with Ames, Quentin makes a reference to the myth about Persephone (SF 184). Due to the fact that he saw Caddy engaged in sexual intercourse, he compares himself to Euboeleus, a swineherd who witnessed how Hades abducted Demeter’s daughter to the world of the dead, and that is why he was engulfed by the earth with his herd (Piszczek 678; RF 125). Here, in Quentin’s eyes, Ames seen as Hades is the one that should be meant being a lady or not. As she is presented in the eyes of her children, we do not know her story; we can only ask why she repudiates the name “Compson,” and stresses that she is a Bascomb (Faulkner’s 38).

Quentin’s Existence as Being-Towards-Death 145 blamed for bringing death on them, for Caddy as Persephone has been taken symbolically to the kingdom of the dead. In the scene of the suicide attempt at the branch, the reader may notice other images that visualize the contrast between the siblings. While lying on the sand on her back, Caddy looks at the sky, which is pointed out a few times (SF 183, 188). Additionally, her shade, although “blurred,” does not blend with the surrounding darkness, but with Dalton Ames (SF 184), and, what is more, when she makes love, her head is also described as being “on the sky” (SF 192). Quentin, on the other hand, having watched Caddy with Ames in the forest, runs downhill and lies down at the branch with his face “close to the ground” (SF 193). There, “feeling the earth” that penetrates his clothes (SF 193-194), he lends an ear to the swoosh of water, and both water and earth are the symbols of the end (Bleikasten The Ink 102). What we can also add is that now the situation reverses: Quentin is the one that looks defunct, since he neither moves nor hears what Caddy is saying to him (SF 194). Moreover, with his face down, his lying position resembles the way in which people who committed suicide used to be buried in the past. If we refer to Arthur Brown’s division again, Caddy’s wedding, as in Benjy’s case, represents for Quentin her figurative death, which simultaneously exemplifies “the death of Others” from Heidegger’s perspective. Finding the wedding reception to be a central episode in the novel, Sundquist speaks of the event as “the death of Eden” for both Benjy and Quentin (11). According to the scholar, “the ‘loss’ of Caddy (wherever one pinpoints it) represents the crucial generative event in the book,” because this is “the moment of discovered grief that brings death, actual and metaphorical, into the psychological worlds of Benjy and Quentin; it is the moment of potential but elusive tragedy” (Sundquist 11). With certainty then, we may conclude that Caddy’s wedding is a traumatic experience and a real tragedy that took place in the lives of Benjy and of Quentin. Sundquist’s “death of Eden” refers to the words employed by Quentin. The words, in turn, come out to be the first line of John Keble’s poem “Holy Matrimony” (1822), which as a whole praises marriage as a union between man, woman, and God. Its first stanza reads as follows: The voice that breathed o’re Eden, That earliest wedding-day, The primal marriage blessing, It hath not passed away. (Keble 119) Bearing the poem in mind, Quentin finds himself in a diametrically different situation. First of all, he is in despair that the wedding is not his union with

146 Chapter Three Caddy. Instead, it is her union with Herbert, which for the brother denotes separation stressed symbolically when the sister “ran out of the mirror” (SF 100). Recognized in the Quentin section as a “refuge unfailing in which conflict tempered silenced reconciled” (SF 211), the mirror constitutes a requisite that appears at significant moments in The Sound and the Fury, especially with reference to Caddy’s matrimony, or her loss of chastity (M. Brown 547). This running out of the mirror is also perceived as Caddy’s meeting with reality and sexuality, as the moment at which she leaves Quentin’s imaginary world behind (M. Brown 547), which also means the parting of their ways. Additionally, Quentin recollects no vows at the wedding ceremony, usually regarded as the most memorable, but the wedding reception at the end of the day. He sees Caddy running “in the moonlight” (SF 100), and the image of the moon is treated by Faulkner as a meaningful thanatological symbol, sometimes juxtaposed with sexuality. As the imagery of finitude, Faulkner mentions the moon several times in his writings. In the epigraph of Mosquitoes (1927), the writer depicts the title mosquitoes, which allude to the characters of the novel, as creatures flying toward “the moon of decay and death” (8). In the play The Marionettes (1920), Faulkner creates the collage of the moon, sex and death, for Marietta’s breasts are “like twin moons that have been dead for a thousand years” (qtd. in Watson 14). In Light in August, the assemblage of the same themes is observed, when Joe, after hearing that the waitress has her period, escapes to the forest where “he seemed to see a diminishing row of suavely shaped urns in moonlight, blanched… Each one was cracked and from each crack there issued something liquid, deathcolored, and foul” (Novels 1930 538). If we return to the scene discussed above, Caddy’s figure also becomes blurred for Quentin. Hearing no clicking of her heels, he can see “the floating shadow of the veil running across the grass” (SF 100). Here, the moment of the loss is reinforced not only by describing Caddy through the image of the shadow, but what is distinct, by using the epithet “floating,” which has a clear connotation of water associated by the brother with death. Apart from this, the wedding memory evokes the smell of roses. When we reach for Faulkner’s widely anthologized short story “A Rose for Emily,” the flower symbolizes the defunct Homer, whose skeleton is found after Emily’s funeral (129-130).128 Thus, in stark contrast to Keble’s poem, Caddy “passes away” from Quentin’s life on the day of her wedding, and her departure represents for the brother the experience of the loss, felt by those who stay alive, to recall Edwards and Macquarrie interpreting Heidegger. 128 For M. C. Brown the mention of the roses symbolizes sexuality (547).

Quentin’s Existence as Being-Towards-Death 147 There are other important episodes supporting the interpretation of Caddy’s wedding as her figurative death. Just after the wedding recollection, the action shifts to a present-time conversation with Shreve. Apparently, with the allusion to Quentin’s Sunday clothes, Shreve asks: “Is it a wedding or a wake?” (SF 100), which Kinney regards as the exemplification of “synonymity of copulation and death” (143). If we bear in mind how the action shifts, Caddy’s marriage reception obviously reminds us of a watch over the body of a dead person, or an occasion when a family and friends get together after or before a funeral. Unhappy about the wedding, Benjy, who senses Caddy’s loss, cannot stop himself from bellowing (SF 100). For Quentin, the memory is painful, and the invitation to Caddy’s wedding occupies a special place in his dormitory room. In fact, the invitation resembles an offering on an altar, or a coffin in a church indeed, for “it lay on the table a candle burning at each corner upon the envelope tied in a soiled pink garter two artificial flowers” (SF 115). The events before the wedding ceremony are of no less importance and prepare the reader for Caddy’s figurative death. When the parents discover Caddy’s pregnancy, Mr. Compson proposes that his wife and daughter would go to French Lick, a holiday spot in Indiana (RF 71), where Caddy is expected to find a husband, at least by her mother (SF 126). With the day drawing to a close, the atmosphere when they prepare for their departure is fairly depressing, because in the background the mother’s constant crying may be heard, and in the air the smells of camphor and honeysuckle waft in and around the house. The most remarkable aspect is Quentin’s mention of the trunks taken down from the attic and dragged on the stairs, which he compares to nothing else but coffins (SF 117). Nevertheless, in the French Lick fragment, the phrase “found not death at the salt lick” initially seems to be enigmatic (SF 117). First of all, there is a word game in the phrase “French Lick,” and secondly, a salt lick is a sort of supplementary medication given to animals, or a kind of bait used by hunters to attract animals; while licking a stick, creatures do not move and become easy prey for those whose intention is to kill them (RF 71). French Lick surely constitutes a hunting place for the Compson family, for Herbert takes the bait and falls into a trap by marrying Caddy, who gives birth to a child that is not his. However, if we juxtapose “French Lick” with “French kiss,” it is conspicuous that the death-oriented hunting is eclipsed by sexuality again, because, instead of death, Caddy has a rendezvous with Herbert, which hurts Quentin very much, as the phrase reverberates a few times in his section (SF 117, 126). The leitmotif of death also recurs in the recollection that depicts the events on the eve of Caddy’s marriage ceremony. The first line of Keble’s poem “Holy Matrimony” is again interwoven in the picture of Caddy lying on the bed (SF

148 Chapter Three 130). And again, Quentin is far away from finding any associations between physical love and life, for he presents the situation in gloomy colors. With twilight, the smell that lingers in the air is not of the honeysuckle this time, but the odor, not the fragrance, of the apple tree. This carries connotations of the biblical “tree of knowledge of good and evil” (Gen. 2.9), whose fruit eaten by Eve brought the original sin to the Earth, and with the sin death. In another fragment, during the siblings’ conversation, the subject of demise is touched upon explicitly, when Caddy utters the following words: “I died last year I told you I had but I didnt know then what I meant” (SF 153). In the opinion of Ross and Polk, the statement may be the product of Quentin’s imagination (RF 109). He prefers to think of Caddy as dead, because in a while he will be dead himself. Yet if the words are uttered by Caddy, they may denote her despair due to the marriage imposed on her (RF 109). What is more probable is that she may equate her imaginary death with orgasm, especially if in the earlier memory at the branch, to Quentin’s query whether she loved her lovers, she replies: “When they touched me I died” (SF 185). Wadlington interprets the fragment as Caddy’s capability “to enact voluptuous martyrdom” (82), which weds Thanatos and Eros again. However, the sexual act presented as death, or a burden, was committed by her with pleasure, as she does not seem to regret it in any way. And the interesting thing is also that, straight after the passage in which Caddy alludes to her hypothetical death before the wedding ceremony, there is a time shift to the very day of Quentin’s suicide. We find there his remark: “Some days in late August at home are like this, the air thin and eager like this, with something in it sad and nostalgic and familiar” (SF 153, emphasis added). If we remember that the date of Caddy’s wedding is ascribed to 24 April in 1910 (Volpe “Appendix” 106), it is clear that for Quentin his suicide parallels Caddy’s wedding. Therefore Quentin felt the loss before June 2, before he made up his decision to take his own life. Moreover, the fact that Faulkner juxtaposed in his imagination April, marriage and death is also visible in another piece of writing. In “Mountain Victory,” “the dying April afternoon” heralds Major Weddel’s death in ambush, which partly results from his unwillingness to wed a nameless mountain girl (746).129 Welcoming Thanatos through the figure of Eros, which is noticeable in many fragments of his stream of consciousness, Quentin, as the Heideggerian Dasein, comes closer and closer to the thought of departure from this world. 129 There seems to exist a high correlation between The Sound and the Fury and “Mountain Victory.” Except for death, we observe a decaying, patriarchal family, who does not tolerate the girl’s unconventional behavior, the girl’s desire to escape, her brother’s violence toward her. For the analysis of the story see Johnson.

Quentin’s Existence as Being-Towards-Death 149 This “preliminary understanding” of demise (Macquarrie An Existentialist 112), which originated on Damuddy’s funeral, is reinforced emphatically by the Faulknerian character over and over again when he associates situations in life with finitude. Thus it may be concluded that Quentin is cognizant of the presence of death in his existence not only through the notion of time, but also when he incorporates the phenomenon of death into his thinking through the sphere of sexuality. Nevertheless, the question arises if this interiorization of the thought of death in his consciousness leads to the authentic or inauthentic Being- towards-death. As stated before, the inauthentic approach in Heidegger’s view stands for the treatment of death as “a mishap” (BT 296). According to this approach, demise is regarded as a slight incident that sooner or later will take place in our life, yet in the meantime there is no cause for concern, since it has nothing to do with us. The authentic approach assumes that death is “the end of Dasein” (BT 303), grasped in Schrag’s words, as an idea that is to be “interiorized” in our thinking process (95). Quentin Compson seems to be one of the few protagonists to whom death is not only a subject-matter that frequently occupies one’s mind. For him it becomes a part of life, or to express it with more emphasis, a way of life, because, in Faulkner’s words, Quentin is a literary figure who “loved death above all” (A 411). In addition, when he is resurrected by Faulkner in Absalom, Absalom!, he continues to shroud himself in morbidity, since, as David Minter has noted in A Cultural History of the American Novel, Quentin’s field of study is also graveyards (225). The reader of The Sound and the Fury may easily see with what seriousness Quentin treats the subject of finitude, interiorizing it completely in his life. In accordance with Heidegger’s thought, he does not recognize death as an unpredictable incident that occurs by mischance, “as a well-known event occurring within-the-world” (BT 297). From the very beginning of his narrative, one may notice that for Faulkner’s hero demise is rather an event that happens within-the-mind, due to the fact that Quentin’s mind is “death-ridden” (Bleikasten The Ink 68). He is a protagonist who personifies death, thinking of it as “a friend,” “a man something like Grandfather” (SF 218). As Taylor confirms, in the character’s vision, death takes shape of a Confederate officer, an interlocutor with whom his grandfather talked about Colonel Sartoris (39). As a result, using Schrag’s other words (100), we may deduce that Quentin’s outlook on finitude stands in opposition to the “external” Epicurean perspective on the phenomenon in question, which differentiates his reasoning from the philosophy of death proclaimed by the “they.” And if Quentin rejects their predominant thinking, we may describe his attitude as the authentic Being- towards-death. Yet, there is one significant fact: the act of accepting finitude in

150 Chapter Three one’s consciousness, supported strongly by Heidegger, leads Quentin to a desire for death, first to kill his sister Caddy, and then himself. The questions that arise, then, are how it is possible that despite the interiorization of demise Quentin commits felo de se, and whether suicide should be treated as a negation of the authentic Being. Despite the considerable evidence that demonstrates how Quentin realizes the philosophy of Being-towards-death, it is plain that on June 2 the Faulknerian protagonist partly fails to be an authentic Dasein as defined by Heidegger. Regardless of the previously gained awareness of the presence of death in his existence, Quentin’s behavior on the day of his suicide may exemplify the inauthentic Being to some extent. “Brooding over death,” as the philosopher would say (BT 305), Quentin “actualizes” his end, in Heidegger’s words, when he considers what time and how he will pass away. First of all, he knows an exact time when he is going to die: “A quarter hour yet. And then I’ll not be” (SF 216). Secondly, it is not difficult for the reader to foreshadow the place of his felo de se if we take into account his allusions to watery imagery, or even his walks back and forth from the river to other sites numerous times. Furthermore, the narrator of “June Second 1910” intends to take his life professionally. In the hardware store, he carefully decides on two flat irons that will be heavy enough to pull his body down to the bottom. He even opts for small irons, which parceled up look like a pair of shoes for those who will see him walking around with the pack (SF 105).130 On top of that, while deliberating over the act of self-destruction, Quentin experiences a moment of doubt that maybe he does not know enough to commit suicide. As Ross and Polk claim, “Quentin wonders whether he is smart or knowledgeable enough to commit suicide ‘properly,’ or whether he will bungle it and reduce it to absurdity” (RF 56). On the one hand, one may infer that what Heidegger and Faulkner’s protagonist seem to have in common is a particular emphasis put on knowledge, which for both appears to be necessary to approach death appropriately. On the other hand, the reader can sense a touch of irony, because the information gained at Harvard does not serve as the foundations of Quentin’s future life, but of his death (SF 105). In another fragment, the formal system of education seems to be ridiculed, too, as studies at Harvard are compared to “a fine dead sound” (SF 217), purchased for Benjy’s pasture, which could again imply Quentin’s suicide, or the knowledge gained at university. The Harvard freshman makes additional meticulous preparations for the journey to the other side of the Styx. He wants to leave all his belongings in 130 In The Marionettes, one of the characters says: “All things must die, and dead things are very heavy” (Faulkner qtd. in Samway 216).

Quentin’s Existence as Being-Towards-Death 151 perfect order, so that after his death no one has to deal with anything: he packs his trunk and addresses it to have it sent home; he piles neatly the books from the library; he inscribes an envelope with a trunk key to his father, he writes two notes (SF 99), both to Shreve, as Ross and Polk suggest (RF 52). With the traces of pedantry, Quentin pays assiduous attention to his outward appearance, as well. By curious paradox, he starts the day with his “funeral toilet” (Bleikasten The Ink 79): he takes a bath and shaves before he drowns himself (SF 99). It is interesting to note that while washing himself he starts bleeding, and this is the “water [that] made my finger smart a little,” which in a way heralds the form of his suicide (SF 99). Besides, before he leaves his room in the evening, he brushes his hair for half an hour (SF 214). And when his vest gets marked with blood after the fight with Bland, Benjy’s brother is more interested in removing it rather than taking care of his black eye (SF 204). After his return to the dormitory, he tries to clean the stubborn stain with gasoline, although he later changes clothes and chooses to die in his old suit. With his elegiac language, Quentin Compson visualizes beforehand the act of self-destruction. He anticipates his actions and the impressions that he believes will take place shortly before and at the moment of his demise. When he brushes his hair, his mind does not wonder to the past, as it has been before, but to the future, in which he imagines his journey to the bridge: how his car will pass the car going to Boston in which Shreve will sit, how they will throw a glance at each other without saying goodbye (SF 214). His vision ends with the quote: “the road empty in darkness in silence the bridge arching into silence darkness sleep the water peaceful and swift not good-bye” (SF 214). Short as the fragment is, it constitutes a lyrical depiction of his suicide. There is an accumulation of the words traditionally linked with dying, together with Quentin’s associations of death with sleep and of water with the “promise of oblivion” (Bleikasten The Ink 90, 369).131 While drinking water in the dormitory bathroom, Quentin also appears to anticipate his drowning sensations. He describes how his “cooling fingers” help him to cool down his throat with the water that has “the taste of dampened sleep in the long silence of the throat” (SF 216), the feeling he wishes to experience during submergence in the river. Over and above all of that, during the course of June 2, Quentin holds at least a few rehearsals of his suicide. His death wish is so strong that he would even like to watch his own demise, destroying his own shadow. Despite the futility of his efforts, Benjy’s brother intends to “trick” his own reflection, as he calls it, by “blot[ting] it into the water, holding it until it was drowned” (SF 131 In Light in August McEachern’s death is linked with sleep (Novels 1930 550); in Requiem for a Nun, drowning is linked with the act of forgetting (65).

152 Chapter Three 111). He has in view the annihilation of his shadow when he moves into the shadow of the quay, which is much bigger than his own (SF 114), or later, when he walks on purpose on the shaded side of the road to have his shadow engulfed by the wall of the building (SF 166). He also tries to trick it by heading east so that his shadow is behind him on the ground (SF 114). What is more, near the river, he reminds himself that he has to be careful in order not to look where it is (SF 118). Other attempts to kill his own shadow are the acts of treading it “into the concrete” (SF 118), “into [the] pavement” (SF 124), “into the dust” (SF 138), or “into the dappled shade of the trees” (SF 149). So numerous are his attempts, that the repetition of the act leaves no doubt about his willful “self destruction” (Brylowski 54). Of importance is also the fact that Quentin’s obsessive stepping on his shadow is accompanied by the ringing of bells (SF 118, 124), which may be read as the confirmation of his death rehearsed in this manner. A few theories could be quoted to explain these rehearsals of self- destruction. From the angle of anthropology, in James Frazer’s The Golden Bough, a book that Faulkner had been familiar with before writing The Sound and the Fury (Collins “William” 227),132 there is a mention of the shadow, which is treated by the savage as the reflection of the soul (189). The act of stepping on the shadow is recognized as perilous: “if it is trampled upon, struck, or stabbed, he will feel the injury as if it were done to his person; and if it is detached from him entirely (as he believes that it may be) he will die” (Frazer 189). With the mention of The Golden Bough, Brylowski analyzes Quentin’s act of self-destruction, and refers to Ernst Cassirer’s thought echoing Frazer’s discovery. Cassirer claims: “A man’s shadow plays the same role as his image or picture. It is a real part of him and subject to injury; every injury to the shadow affects the man himself” (qtd. in Brylowski 53). Quentin’s behavior casts no doubt on his intention to hurt himself once and for all, which Brylowski interprets as Quentin’s denial to agree to exist in a world visualized by his own father (54). From the viewpoint of the analytical psychology, Quentin’s case may be studied on the basis of Carl Gustav Jung’s theory of the shadow. Denoted as “the ‘negative’ side of the personality, the sum of all those unpleasant qualities we like to hide” (Jung 87), for Quentin the shadow represents the layer of his psyche he intends to suppress irrevocably. In the article “Quentin and the Walking Shadow,” Louise Dauner considers Quentin’s silhouette to be “the Double, the alter ego, the ‘dark brother’,” whose repression may signify Quentin’s wish to punish himself for his sexual desire for his sister (77). It may 132 Collins claims that in 1925 Faulkner read Sherwood Anderson’s copy of the book.

Quentin’s Existence as Being-Towards-Death 153 also imply his rejection of “his instinctual nature,” which Caddy, in contrast to her brother, chooses to follow all the time (78). Dauner’s interpretation overlaps with the arguments presented by Ross and Polk. If Quentin regards his own shadow as “an objective correlative for the self, especially the unacceptable ‘the dark side’ of the self,” this means that he treats his body reflection as a separate entity, as “an Other” (RF 64-65). Such a psychological approach to his own shadow symbolizes Quentin’s unwillingness to satisfy this Other’s desires, needs, and yearnings. When the shadow is to Quentin “an image of the loathed body” (Bleikasten The Ink 92), his attempts to annihilate it may be interpreted as his rejection of the bodily sphere. In the conscious act of repudiating his own corporality, Quentin disconnects his body from his personhood as if it were a foreign object, and he focuses only on the mental sphere of the self.133 As Matthews confirms, “Quentin constantly tramples on his shadow, as if in furious denial of his bodiedness” (The Sound 54). Moreover, the attempts to destroy his shadow are regarded as a conflict between the “feeling self” and the “rational self,” the split that even proves Quentin’s schizophrenic personality (Bockting “The Impossible” on-line). Obviously the death wish of the Harvard student is an outcome of his reasoning (Jenkins qtd. in Bockting “The Impossible” on-line), but, interestingly enough, Quentin’s body “fights his death-wish” (Aschkenasy 100). It is noticeable at the very beginning of the section when Quentin wonders: “when you dont want to do a thing, your body will try to trick you into doing it, sort of unawares” (Aschkenasy 100; SF 102). Quentin’s rejection of physicality simultaneously denotes the denial of his own sexuality. The repudiation is seen in Quentin’s comment on Versh’s story, about a man who castrated himself in the woods, when the Harvard student expresses his wish to be devoid of sexual organs: “It’s not not having them. It’s never to have had them then I could say O That That’s Chinese I dont know Chinese” (SF 143). His college friend Shreve also reveals that Quentin is not the kind of person who would spend time with prostitutes (SF 96). His only object of desire seems to be his sister Caddy, whose body he surprisingly appears to be unconcerned about (Kartiganer “Quentin” 393). Still, Quentin is envious of Caddy’s sexual experiences, asking himself “why couldn’t it have been me and not her who is unvigin” (SF 96). Irwin regards this worry as “a displaced 133 Jean-Jacques Mayoux regards the tension between the mental and physical spheres as characteristic of Faulkner’s writing in general (161). For example, the disorder perceivable in Quentin is illustrated in The Hamlet, where one reads about Eula Varner: “It was as if only half of her had been born, that mentality and body had somehow become either completely separated or hopelessly involved” (Novels 1936 818).

154 Chapter Three concern with his own inability to lose his virginity, for… Quentin’s virginity is psychological impotence” (38). When asked by his sister about his intimate experience, he confabulates about the number of sexual intercourses (SF 188), or fantasizes about acts of love with Caddy. On the whole, Quentin mainly takes his steps in the sphere of the mind, and creates his world with words.
