In Blanchard’s opinion, he “escapes into words which signify no reality” (565), for “language is the only tool he has to effect the shape he wants” (Polk “Trying” 150).134 Quentin’s inclination to create his world only verbally makes him conjure up disturbing visions that are pure abstractions. As mentioned before, he fantasizes about committing incest, yet, according to Kartiganer, this “incest he seeks is the purely poetic one he tries to impose on Caddy through verbal pressure alone – an engagement not of flesh but of metaphor” (“Quentin” 392). Louis D. Rubin holds a very similar opinion when he suggests that the incest is purely Quentin’s idée fixe, not a literal act (50-51). However, the character’s way of thinking does not disturb Rubin as much as Kartiganer, because for the former scholar Quentin is a sexually inexperienced adolescent who fears the loss of virginity, therefore his reaction to his sister’s sexuality is normal and understandable. Another queer vision Quentin creates purely in his mind is the transformation of his own sex. In the world of imagination, he wishes he could change his gender, becoming Mrs. Ames, the mother of Dalton, who is Caddy’s lover, and everything in order to control his conception and not to let Mr. Ames father Dalton: “If I could have been his mother lying with open body lifted laughing, holding his father with my hand refraining, seeing, watching him die before he lived” (SF 98). In addition to this, Quentin envisages what also seems to be at the border of the normal. He would like to beget his own father, altering into his ancestor, as it is conspicuous in the following fragment: “I will am my fathers Progenitive I invented him created I him Say it to him it will not be for he will say I was not and then you and I since philoprogenitive” (SF 152).135 As a matter of fact, there are not many critics who have decided to make an attempt 134 Jackson J. Benson draws the conclusion that to a certain extent Quentin is Faulkner’s reflection. Not only did the author behave similarly to his character, being perceived by those who knew him as immersed in thought (215), but also, in contrast to Cornell Franklin, with whom Faulkner lost his first battle about Estelle Oldham, his future wife, he was not a thriving businessman. Instead, he was an aspiring writer who could relieve his emotions in the field of writing by means of language (225). 135 As for the meaning of the word “philoprogenitive,” the entry of The Oxford English Dictionary suggests two meanings: first, “inclined to production of offspring,” second, “loving one’s offspring” (779).

Quentin’s Existence as Being-Towards-Death 155 at deciphering the phrase, but Ross and Polk may help. The scholars recognize the quote to be Faulkner’s reference to Eliot’s poem “Mr. Eliot’s Sunday Morning Service,” which they perceive as the author’s hint at “trafficking too heavily in words, at the expense of physical reality” (RF 107-108). This additionally backs up the above-mentioned opinions of Blanchard, Kartiganer, or Polk. Finally, what is left to add is that the philoprogenitive deliberations are not limited to The Sound and the Fury. They seem to reach the apogee of complexity in Absalom, Absalom!, where Quentin thinks of Shreve: “Yes, we are both Father. Or maybe Father and I are both Shreve, maybe it took Father and me both to make Shreve or Shreve and me both to make Father or maybe Thomas Sutpen to make all of us” (Novels 1936 216). To sum up, by actualizing the act of taking his own life, Quentin does not follow the authentic mode of Being-towards-death, or Being-towards-the-end, from Heidegger’s perspective. Both the envisaging of death as an event and the endless attempts to destroy his own shadow make his life an exemplification of Being-at-the-end. In fact, this conclusion is inscribed in the text of The Sound and the Fury, for the reason that in one of his last reveries before the self- destruction, there is a clash of the phrases “the end. I am. Drink. I was not” (SF 216). Despite a close reference to his father’s drinking habit, the juxtaposition of the words could signify “a play on Quentin’s death: he is at ‘the end’” (RF 145). Recalling Schrag’s words about death “existentially pre-enacted” (113), what we may observe here is the Heideggerian actualization of death by drowning, which is Quentin’s pre-enacting of his own finitude in a realistic way, not in an existential manner. Heidegger’s authenticity, understood as the “disclosure of Dasein… as a clearing-away of concealments and obscurities” (BT 167), is possible to achieve through the inauthenticity. David Minter in turn draws the conclusion that what we come across in The Sound and the Fury is both “an art of concealment as well as disclosure” (Faulkner’s 51). The planned suicide and its rehearsals appear to be the chain of concealments in Quentin’s existence from Heidegger’s point of view. However, encouraged by Minter, one ought to deliberate on the exemplification of disclosure. In relation to Quentin’s status as Dasein, with existence and mineness in mind, it seems risky to totally disqualify his authentic Being just on the grounds of the actualization and the mode of Being-at-the-end, especially if on June 2 Quentin’s thoughts typify Heidegger’s phenomenon of Being-towards-the-end. Heidegger speaks of the authentic Being-towards-death as “the possibility of the impossibility of any existence at all” (307). While listening to the boys who boast that they will catch a trout nobody has fished out yet, Quentin concludes that “they all talked at once, their voices insistent and contradictory and

156 Chapter Three impatient, making of unreality a possibility, then a probability, then an inconvertible fact, as people will when their desires become words” (SF 145, emphasis added). Again, this is an example of Quentin’s statement the reader may not be certain about, for even if on the surface his opinion concerns the boys’ conduct, below the obvious layer the juxtaposition with the people creating the world verbally appears to be equivocal. On the one hand, it could refer to Quentin’s desire to persuade his father of the fantasized act of incest with Caddy, but on the other hand, it could be read as Quentin’s criticism of his parent, who advised him to become unaware of death by forgetting time, namely “making of unreality a possibility.” As it has been mentioned in the chapter on philosophy, the possibility of the impossibility is additionally treated by Heidegger as “Nichtigkeit,” rendered by Macquarrie and Robinson as “nullity” (BT 329), or preferably by Edwards as “nothingness” (Heidegger 49). The thinking of death as nothingness also finds its reflection in Faulkner’s writing. In the statement given at the University of Virginia, denying the author’s interest in ameliorating the human predicament, the creator of Yoknapatawpha County declared his curiosity about human conduct, understood by him as follows: “it’s motion, it’s life, the only alternative is nothingness, death” (Gwynn and Blotner 267). In scene V in Macbeth, the source of the novel’s title, one also reads about life as “a tale / Told by an idiot, full of sound and fury, / Signifying nothing” (34). The word “nothing” is emphatically the last one in Macbeth’s speech, given when he finds out about the queen’s death. The second section of The Sound and the Fury provides irrefutable proof for Faulkner’s thinking of demise as nullity, too. On the day of Quentin’s suicide, during the last meeting with his college mate, Shreve puts a question to him: “What are you up to?,” and Caddy’s brother ripostes: “Nothing” (SF 208), which is exactly the meaning of death in Heidegger’s philosophy. Additional evidence for such interpretation is also demonstrated in another fragment. The bridge where the Faulknerian protagonist commits suicide is described as suspended between “silence and nothingness” (SF 212). That Faulkner links death and nothingness in his literary imagination is also noticeable in his other novels. If we recall Quentin’s anticipatory sensations while drinking water in the dormitory bathroom before his suicide, we may note that Darl in As I Lay Dying (1930) has similar connotations. The water in the bucket Darl likes drinking from is perceived by him as “a round orifice in nothingness” (Novels 1930 8). In Light in August (1932) McEachern, who dies struck with a piece of furniture by his foster child, is depicted as the one walking “into the descending chair which Joe swung at his head, and into nothingness. Perhaps the nothingness astonished him a little, but not much, and not for long”

Quentin’s Existence as Being-Towards-Death 157 (Novels 1930 549-550). And in Requiem for a Nun (1951), coupling death as nothingness with drowning, Gavin Stevens, who tries to inquire about the past, utters such words to Gowan, Temple’s husband: “blow your own brains out: stop having to remember, stop having to be forever unable to forget: nothing; to plunge into nothing and sink and drown forever and forever” (65). To return to The Sound and the Fury, this reasoning of death as nothing is not conjured up on the day of his felo de se, because such an approach is adopted by Quentin much earlier. In one of the scenes where Thanatos realizes itself through Eros, that is, on the eve of the wedding, Caddy asks in private what Quentin is plotting this time, and he replies: “Nothing” (SF 137). The reading of this nothing as death is reinforced when from the conversation between sister and brother the reader immediately moves to the present, to the description of the river, where Quentin commits suicide. This proves once again that the thought of death in Quentin’s case does not appear on June 2, or just before. Quite the contrary, demise, with sadness and misery, has been rooted in Quentin’s line of thinking since remotest memory. Warren Beck believes that in Faulkner’s literary world, where his protagonists carry out their inner battles, their existence is perceived as one in process, always in motion (283), which Heidegger insists on, as well. It is unnecessary here to repeat Quentin’s death-oriented reminiscences to spot a mental process of coming gradually to death as a phenomenon in the chain of the past episodes. It is sufficient to stress that the on-going process of becoming receptive to finitude is only emphasized, or even exaggerated, on the last day of his life. When on this red-letter day, at the bridge, one of the boys asks where Quentin intends to go, he answers: “Nowhere. Just walking” (SF 147). It is the walk along the river – the nowhere, with death – the nothing in his head, which was bred there a long time ago, so what we observe on June 2 is just the final phase of this continuum of nothingness in his life. Thus, the last day of Quentin’s existence illustrates the last point of Dasein’s totality reached by grasping the end as a phenomenon of life during life, which is definitely the authentic approach to finitude in Quentin’s case. The circumstance of Being-a-whole, or in other words, reaching totality before an actual physical expiration, also takes place on condition that Dasein understands and accepts the existential-ontological definition of death. What is conspicuous is that on June 2 Quentin realizes the majority of the points interwoven in Heidegger’s phenomenological explanation of quietude. To start with, the author of Being and Time speaks of death as Dasein’s ownmost possibility. In The Sound and the Fury there is irrefutable proof that Quentin has grasped this point. Similarly to Glen Gray, who explains “ownmost” as the “most private” (qtd. in Edwards Heidegger 10), when Quentin is asked by the

158 Chapter Three jeweler about the reason for his formal outfit, he answers that he is holding “just a private celebration” (SF 104). As a result, on the day of his suicide, Quentin comprehends perfectly well that death is his own possibility, that no one will die instead of him, and there is no possibility of representability to die instead of Others. Moreover, this Faulknerian protagonist undoubtedly regards finitude as non-relational, preferring seclusion on June 2. On the day of his suicide, Quentin avoids people: he leaves the town, choosing a walk in the deserted places, he is unwilling to join his friends, he makes an unsuccessful attempt to escape even from the “sister,” as he calls the girl accompanying him (SF 158), and what is significant, the last minutes of his life he spends alone in the empty dormitory, which is his conscious choice, for he knows that his friends will not return soon (SF 213). If we take into account other points in Heidegger’s definition, death for Quentin is certain, as he needs no empirical proof to be aware of it. His preparation for departure from this world paradoxically proves that death is realistic for Quentin, too. The outcome of such deliberation is also his perception of finitude as a phenomenon impossible to be outstripped, that is, to be won over, or left behind, which is testified by the very words uttered by Quentin: “A quarter hour yet. And then I’ll not be” (SF 216). That the presence of death is grasped mentally is unquestionably visible in Quentin’s discourse. As an audible sign of the deliberating mind, his language on June 2 clearly abounds in words and phrases tinged with death. Immersed in the observation of people and objects around, Quentin compares a crowd of students to “scuttering dead leaves” (SF 96), and their coat collars to “debris on a flood” (SF 96); he mentions bells “ringing in the long dying light-rays” (SF 97). What does not escape his notice is an African-American on the tram with “a dead cigar stub” (SF 105), together with a shop assistant carrying a parcel as if it was “a dead pet rat” (SF 158).136 After the fight with Gerald Bland, not surprisingly around the twilight reflected in the basin of water, Quentin pictures his face as “cold and sort of dead” (SF 203). Even the word “Harvard” produces for him “a fine dead sound” mentioned before (SF 217). In the description of noise, Quentin persists in using the verb “to die away:” “the chimes ceased and died away” (SF 101), the noise made by the car “began to die away” (SF 209), he heard his “watch and the train dying away” (SF 149), and Mrs. Bland’s voice “sort of died away,” too (SF 181). 136 Bleikasten claims that rats in Faulkner’s fiction appear in the sexual context, which proves the merging of death with sex once again. The critic notes that this rodent is mentioned in the fragment after Caddy’s loss of virginity as well as in Mosquitoes, Sanctuary, and Elmer, the novel Faulkner never finished (The Ink 371).

Quentin’s Existence as Being-Towards-Death 159 Although predominating on June 2, such a thanatological discourse is not a revelation of Quentin’s last day of life. In the past events, he mentions his uncle “Louis’ voice dying way,” “as though his voice were a part of darkness and silence” (SF 142). In another fragment, which, according to the editors of the hypertext edition of the novel, describes the impact of twilight on Quentin, he recollects “that vivid dead smell of perfume” belonging to Caddy (SF 219). What is more, on his way home from Harvard for Christmas in 1909, behind the window Quentin sees fences stretched “like part of the skeleton of a horn” (SF 106). Summarizing the presence of death in Quentin’s discourse, we should add that such a manner of speech is observable in his father’s talk, as well, for he utters such statements as: “clocks slay time,” “time is dead” (SF 105), or “the best of thought… clings like dead ivy vines upon old dead brick,” when he refers to Harvard (SF 117-118), or “the talk will die away,” when he hints at Caddy’s pregnancy (SF 126). The quoted examples may imply that the father could have taught the son such a rhetorical style. Nevertheless, there are a few exemplifications like these above, and they are definitely outnumbered by Quentin’s ones. Similarly to the former personification of finitude as a Confederate officer, as a friend, a little girl who Quentin meets at a bakery on June 2 appears to be another embodiment of death due to her appearance and conduct. Seen as “a symbol of Fate” (Bleikasten The Ink 78), the girl may personify the phenomenon of nothingness that “presences” (Heidegger “Time” 2), and she may be “something like an empirical anchor” of death (Macquarrie qtd. in Edwards Heidegger 50). Addressed by the word “sister,” and referred to as “the little girl” (SF 162-163), she looms out as this “Litter Sister Death” Quentin mentions at the beginning of the section (SF 94). In her appearance, black and its various shades largely dominate: she is dirty (SF 155), “her face looked like it had been streaked with coal-dust” (SF 182), which sends us below the surface of the earth; she has “two patent-leather pigtails,” (SF 155), which Ross and Polk read as black (RF 111); her eyes are also “black,” but they are “friendly,” too (SF 162), like the previous embodiment of finitude being a boon companion. Additionally, depicted as “unwinking” (SF 162), the eyes are compared to “two currants floating motionless in a cup of weak coffee” (SF 155, emphasis added), which implies the arrest of movement associated with dying. When she stares at Quentin intently, Little Sister bears a certain resemblance to the “motionless” girl from “Mountain Victory,” whose “eyes wide and still and empty” constantly gaze at Weddel, dead at the end (748). Peculiar about her sight is the fact that when Quentin offers her an ice cream, she gives him “a black still look” (SF 159), and when he asks some men for help to find the place where she lives, the girl “looked at them blackly,” too (SF 161). This “black” look may denote

160 Chapter Three gloominess in both examples, but it can also be an intended pun on Faulkner’s side, for the unique usage of the word “black” is observable in the discourse of the first narrator, as well. Benjy mentions the color where we would not expect to find it, for instance, in the following sentences: “Roskus sitting black against it [the fire]” (SF 36), or “he [father] stood black in the door” (SF 92), which in both cases, as a matter of fact, refers to the people that die in the narrative. The girl, like Quentin’s shadow he cannot get rid of, keeps walking persistently behind him. Even though he has made an attempt to escape from her, she reappears again and again, always carefully watching what he is doing (SF 165-166), similarly to the reaper in Bosch’s painting Death and the Miser (c. 1485/1490), in the collection of the National Gallery of Art in Washington (Fraenger 67). Like the finitude nobody knows, the little girl represents an enigma, for she is described as “secretive, contemplative” (SF 157); she says “nothing,” she remains mute and answers no questions (SF 156). What is also very suggestive of death in the description of the sister is the fact that her face arouses in Quentin the association with “emptiness” (SF 155), and that “she didnt even seem to breathe” (SF 158). Additionally, Benjy’s brother makes a supposition that the girl lives in one of the houses by the river (SF 163). The buildings appear to be empty and characteristic of “breathlessness” (SF 164), which also emphasizes her connections with water as the future place of Quentin’s felo de se. Moreover, in the proximity of the same river Quentin finds a coin he hands to the girl, which can symbolically be read as an obol paid to Charon for crossing the Styx (SF 165). Their walk in search for the girl’s home figuratively resembles death row. While strolling together up the street to a town marshal, they are “on the shady side” (SF 161). There is also one passage in which they amble “in the thin dust,” moving silently (SF 167), which resembles Macbeth’s “way to dusty death” (Shakespeare 34), mentioned by the king in the fragment containing the novel’s title. Also, the road Quentin takes with the little Italian girl later becomes “still and empty” with “the sun slanting more and more” (SF 168). What additionally implies that Quentin’s walk with the girl seems to be a progression to the world of the dead is his comment on the singing of a bird. When they stroll along this lifeless road, Quentin, feeling water, observes that a bird, heard somewhere in the forest, stops singing “as though cut off with the blow of a knife” (SF 169).137 137 What is worth noticing is the fact that after the quoted fragment, Quentin begins his statement with the words “oh, hell, sister” (SF 169), which reminds us of his imagery of the afterlife with Caddy in the inferno. It is interesting that the relationship of brother and sister in hell also indirectly concerns the little girl and her brother Julio, who intends to “beat hell outa” her for walking with strangers (SF 176).

Quentin’s Existence as Being-Towards-Death 161 The imagery of the moon also suggests that the meeting with the little girl is for Quentin the meeting with death personified. As presented before, Heidegger incorporates the illustration of the moon into his philosophy of Being-towards- death to explain the concept of the not-yet in his analysis of Dasein’s totality. Interestingly enough, the reader may attribute the image of the moon to the little girl, for the bread she nibbles is in the shape of the half moon (SF 163), which in Heidegger’s philosophy symbolically signifies the presence of death in human life before one’s actual expiry. The literary collage of death and the moon in Faulkner has already been mentioned, but we may additionally support the link of the loaf with death, quoting Collins. Collins pays attention to June 2, 1910, as a Thursday in the Octave of Corpus Christi, and perceives the bread as the Eucharist (“William” 225), clearly the symbol of Christ’s sacrifice remembered during every mass. With reference to Quentin, Shreve pays heed to his roommate’s faultlessly elegant outfit, not understanding why he is “dressed up and mooning around like the prologue to a suttee” (SF 125). “To moon around” means “to move around languidly,” and the word “suttee” denotes an ancient custom in Hinduism, which forced a wife to be cremated with her husband (Longman 1065, 1676).138 As a consequence, Quentin’s mooning on June 2, that is, his walking slowly around with “Little Sister Death,” seems to be the confirmation of Heidegger’s thought. If we treat the girl as the personification of finitude, the presence of death may be observed, or in other words, nothing “presences,” being Macquarrie’s “empirical anchor,” as nothingness “belongs to being present… Being ‘is’ just as little as nothingness, but both are” (Heidegger The Question 97). Quentin’s thought on June 2 also reflects the reaching of totality by Dasein, which negates the inauthentic Being. With thanatological associations, from the very morning, Faulkner’s protagonist thinks of death in the same manner as he did before in his previous episodes. When he wakes up, he thinks of his dead father and recollects how his parent compared the watch to “the mausoleum of all hopes and desires” (SF 93). The narrow road Quentin walks during the day is depicted by him as the one that “became defunctive in grass,” which literally implies its disappearance (SF 165). Still, Ross and Polk suggest that the word “defunctive” does not barely denote something that has stopped living. For Faulkner it has a wider sense for the reason that it signifies the 138 Faulkner also employs the motif of a suttee in his story “Red Leaves,” where he relates the drama of a Negro servant forced by a tribe to pass away with his Indian master, Issetibbeha, in order to serve him in the world of the dead, together with the master’s hound and mare (340-341). In Faulkner’s letter to Cowley, dated 7 November 1945, while explaining Issetibbeha’s story, the author mentioned the servant’s “suttee,” too (Selected 207).

162 Chapter Three “funereal,” as well (RF 117). The scholars claim that Faulkner found such a meaning in one of his favorite Shakespeare’s poems “The Phoenix and the Turtle,” in which we read: Let the priest in surplice white That defunctive music can Be the death-divining swan, Lest the Requiem lack his right. (RF 117) Moreover, some buildings Quentin passes by are in a deplorable state: unpainted, their gates destroyed, “a barn broken-backed, decaying quietly among rank orchard trees” (SF 165). Inside the houses there is no sign of movement, either (SF 163). And if one recalls how Benjy, aware of the presence of death, describes the surrounding world, it is very easy to notice here a correlation between the brothers’ perspectives. The people Quentin meets on this day are also seen as those in whom death abides. In the description of the shop assistant in the bakery, where Quentin comes across the little girl, the dominant shade is gray. Her face, her hair, and her glasses are all of this tint, being “all iron-grey” (SF 157), which reminds the reader about the last words in “A Rose for Emily:” “a long strand of iron-gray hair” found by Homer’s side after Emily’s funeral (130). Apart from this, the shop assistant is likened to a librarian who becomes lifeless step by step “among dusty shelves of ordered certitudes long divorced from reality, desiccating peacefully” (SF 155). The rims of her glasses are also compared to “something on a wire,” which makes a cross-reference to the image of the gull (RF 112), seen in turn by Bleikasten as the suspension of dynamism (The Ink 101). Furthermore, what stresses inanimateness is the fact that her hair is thinning out, and when the woman’s hairdo is depicted, instead of the word “head,” Quentin uses “skull” to highlight her deadliness (SF 155). The next figure who is almost covered by the shroud of death is the squire who handles a case against Quentin for allegedly kidnapping the little Italian girl. In fact, he bears certain similarities to the shop assistant, for in the description of his appearance the same epithet is used for his hair, and he also wears “steel spectacles” (SF 177). His deadliness is stressed by his “cold, pale eyes” and “his stiff crest” (SF 178-179), which highlights his posture restricted in movement. He does nothing but sits, asks questions, and carefully watches all those around. As in the case of the old shop assistant, the environment he works in is suggestive of decomposition, because the judge is seated behind the old “scarred” table in the “bare room smelling of stale tobacco,” where in the corners the specks of dust are found (SF 177-180). Furthermore, the man writes some information in “a huge dusty book” with a scraping noise made by “a foul

Quentin’s Existence as Being-Towards-Death 163 pen,” dipped into an inkwell, which in turn is filled up with something similar to “coal dust” (SF 177). Let us finally answer if Quentin’s single act of suicide nullifies the whole process of achieving the authentic Being-towards-death. Heidegger negates suicide, which to him cannot lead to freedom resulting from the acceptance of the fact of death. This freedom, in the opinion of Heidegger, may be reached by the authentic Being-towards-death conditioned previously by anticipation that helps Dasein to uncover the thinking of the “they” (BT 311). It is true that Quentin commits suicide, but that fact does not actually negate his anticipation of finitude. The evidence to support the claim is provided by the very author of The Sound and the Fury in the Appendix, where Faulkner states that Quentin “loved and lived in a deliberate and almost perverted anticipation of death” (A 411, emphasis added). Although his death has been defined as his definite possibility, not indefinite as Heidegger would wish, it has also been interpreted as his ownmost, non-relational, certain and outstripped possibility. His act of self-destruction is Being-at-the end, but it is also characteristic of the authentic Being-towards-the-end not only because death, as the Heideggerian nothingness, “presences” on June 2, but this day is just another day of his existence when Faulkner’s protagonist ponders deeply over the subject of death, as Heidegger would wish. When we bear in mind the events before June 2, the authentic Being-towards-death is conspicuous long before the day of his suicide, because Quentin Compson has lived on death, i.e., he has been able to perceive death almost every time and everywhere, imagining people in the context of finitude. Moreover, he has accepted the fact that he is dying, prepared to face demise (Taylor 40), which is another condition stipulated in Heidegger’s philosophy of the authentic Being-towards-death. According to Heidegger, this anticipation of the end conditions the Being- towards-death resulting in freedom. For Faulkner freedom is a key term, too. He believes that what is indestructible in man is “his simple will to freedom” (LG 241), which may be understood as his free choice to decide what to do with his own life. In the words of David Minter, Faulkner “remained convinced that freedom suffices only when people are spiritually sure enough of themselves to know what they truly want” (A Cultural 228). Turning our thoughts to The Sound and the Fury, Quentin is more than certain that he wishes to commit suicide, which is a liberating idea to him. According to Sowder, on the day of his suicide freedom finds its place in life (94), and Quentin’s “possibilities for living” are, “in anguish, correlated with his possibilities of dying” (99). Additionally, in her discussion of the reasons for Quentin’s suicide in the light of Simone de Beauvoir’s theory on patriarchy, Anna Foca concludes: “Having exhausted several attempts at reconciling what he has learned and what he has

164 Chapter Three lived, including trying to expunge his idealism and to adapt to, rather than radically dismantle, the given societal framework, Quentin resigns himself and opts for complete liberation,” being “able to resolve his conflicting desires, experiences, only in death” (356, emphasis added). The proof of Quentin’s choice for death instead of for life is found in the fragment in which he wonders about his non-existence. He says: “Again. Sadder than was. Again saddest of all. Again” (SF 118). First of all, Ross and Polk suggest that the words appear at the end of the conversation with his father about incest and death (RF 71).139 Secondly, if “again” is read as Quentin’s suffering, and “was” as his non- existence, we may infer that he prefers death to going through his painful experiences one more time (RF 71), so suicide is his conscious choice, which liberates him. As the illustration of the authentic Being-towards-death, the day when freedom finds its place is also the day of transformation. For Godden, June 2 is a moment when Quentin discovers new concepts; therefore he has to reshape his previous perspective on his own culture (111), which, to a certain extent, makes him a new human being. There are even extreme voices, like Donald Kartiganer’s, according to which Quentin’s felo de se constitutes the only truly meaningful act (“‘Now’” 84). The scholar further claims that the act itself “is not a means of ending a life still cluttered with reality, but of replacing it: of epitomizing a condition of being in which form will not falter” (“‘Now’” 84). In addition, Mark Spilka observes “a richness of comprehension” during the last hours of his existence (456). Consequently, it may be concluded that the day of his suicide is a moment at which Heidegger’s Being realizes itself, as well. It is possible to read the day this way, especially if behind Quentin’s decision we observe his final confirmation of the transformation from unsteadiness in purpose to his deliberate choice, “his supreme creation, his tour de force” (Kartiganer “‘Now’” 87). The same as previously, on the day of his suicide Quentin is very sensitive to the presence of death, but one has an impression that June 2 differs from any other days. While reading his memories, we can often observe the character’s motionlessness, whereas, on this red-letter day, Quentin is extremely active. He decides to eat out in the morning, he walks a lot alone or with the Italian girl, he observes the boys fishing, he does the shopping, he travels by tram and by car, he gets into a scuffle with Bland, and he keeps returning to his room in the dormitory. As Geffen states, his fatal decision “animates many of the minutest 139 Scholars differ in their opinions what the fragment concerns. The editors of the 2003 hypertext of The Sound and the Fury classify this passage as part of Quentin’s meeting with Natalie in the barn, which, however, is hard to support.

Quentin’s Existence as Being-Towards-Death 165 of his activities on his last day” (247). Therefore Quentin no longer belongs to the group of characters in Faulkner’s literary world where one “paralyzes itself at the level of action,” as Kartiganer would wish (“Quentin” 392). In a word, Quentin paradoxically appears to be more alive on the day of his suicide than in the episodes of the past, and his burst of activity gives proof that he puts a stop to an existence led only verbally.140 When the jeweler, paying attention to Quentin’s formal clothes, asks him about the reason for his celebrating, the Harvard freshman replies that this is his private celebration, namely his birthday (SF 104). This birthday may be interpreted as his final revelation, his act of distinguishing the real from the made up, if Quentin’s whole section, in the eyes of many critics, Zender asserts, is perceived as “the slow uncovering of a denied self-understanding, in which meanings for Quentin’s experiences contrary to the ones he consciously intends gradually emerge from beneath his evasions and rationalizations” (747). Quentin’s previous confabulations about the issue of incest, seen indeed as non-sexual and defying change, serve as “a way of not experiencing life” (Zender 747). This implies sheer stagnancy in terms of real life experiences, and activity only in the mental sphere, the situation that does not arise on June 2. Galvanized into action, Quentin, however, does not neglect his mental sphere. This is clearly illustrated in the recurrent image of the gull, which makes Quentin see himself from a different angle. Just after he mentions the static position of the gull, which Bleikasten perceives, among other things, as the picture of “hampered flight” (The Ink 101),141 Quentin speaks to himself about how in the past he clung to ideas such as honor or virginity: “Holding all I used to be sorry about like the new moon holding water” (SF 105). With reference to the old superstition of the black people, for whom it forecast a dry spell (RF 56), Quentin expresses criticism toward his own self of the past, i.e., he was static in a way as he kept believing in “values long dead” (Bleikasten The Ink 84). Finally, he understands he formalized tradition too much, which was accompanied by lack of liveliness (O’Donnell 85). As a result, what he believed 140 This theme appears to have been born in Faulkner’s mind before the publication of The Sound and the Fury. According to Van O’Connor, in Mosquitoes, which came out in 1927, Faulkner reveals that “actions are more important than words and doers more important than talkers” (7). 141 Bleikasten interprets the gull as a “model of delicate poise and dynamic immobility.” Moreover, the fact that the gull is often described as motionless may also imply that it is above the flow of time. Furthermore, the critic notes that the birds in the novel are found on “invisible wires” twice, which additionally poses a question about their alleged freedom in the air (The Ink 101).

166 Chapter Three in turned in “pseudo-tradition,” the tradition that was dead (85).142 In a way, by comparison to the moon, which for Heidegger stands for the presence of death in Dasein’s existence, Quentin held inside him the “values long dead,” being at the same time “dry,” because his fight for Caddy’s chastity and the family’s honor turned out to be a pointless battle. There is additional evidence to support Quentin’s mental transformation liberating him from the self of the past. In “The Language of Chaos,” May C. Brown notes that his suicide may be treated as a ritual, as the act of purification (549). Previously, the critic maintains, the watery imagery was associated with sex, and together with it, with Caddy, one may add, but now on June 2 there seems to be no link with sexuality. More truly, according to Brown, what Quentin concentrates on is in effect his own personhood, both in the past and in the present (549). If that is the case, the suicide represents the act of purifying himself out of his obsession connected with the figure of Caddy, or rather with the very ideas of virginity, sexuality, and family honor that stand behind her apparition in his memory. Later during the day, he deliberates: I thought about how I’d thought about I could not be a virgin, with so many of them walking along in the shadows and whispering with their soft girlvoices lingering in the shadowy places and the words coming out and perfume and eyes you could feel not see, but if it was that simple to do it wouldnt be anything and if it wasnt anything, what was I. (SF 183) In her discussion about how sexuality in Southern culture was presented in literature in Faulkner’s days, Anne Goodwyn Jones touches upon the public perception of sexual behavior displayed by particular members of society: black women were perceived as sexual, socially favored white women as non-sexual, black men as excessively sexual, and white men were to protect white ladies (56). In The Sound and the Fury, Caddy is not a sexless woman, whose hymen has to be shielded from sexual advances, so Quentin cannot play the traditional role of the protector. As the fragment quoted above illustrates, he finally realizes that he has paid too much heed to the notion of virginity, lifting it up to the level of apotheosis (Deshaye on-line). Simultaneously, he has forgotten that losing virginity is also a part of pure biology.143 The rhetorical question “what was I” 142 O’Donnell speaks of “pseudo-tradition” both with reference to a short story “There Was a Queen” and to The Sound and the Fury. While referring to Narcissa’s deed, O’Donnell claims: “For the moment a tradition begins to be formalized into a code, it commences to lose vitality; when it is entirely formalized, it is dead – it becomes pseudo-tradition” (84-85). 143 Contrary to Quentin, Caddy seems to have always valued experience more than theory. Her inquisitiveness is plainly conspicuous on the day of Damuddy’s death. What also impresses her is that Dalton Ames has “crossed all the oceans all around the world” (SF 187).

Quentin’s Existence as Being-Towards-Death 167 seems to be the confirmation of his realization of “perverted manhood,” which Mark Spilka notes while discussing Quentin’s attempt to protect Caddy from her alleged promiscuity, when he himself was not prepared to cross the threshold of sexuality (464). And the boundary was, in fact, fairly easy to cross with so many women around, which Quentin admits on the day when he welcomes freedom in life through death. Quentin’s idiolect may be treated as more proof showing that he has achieved a sort of emotional stability thanks to his final decision. Scrutinizing the language and style in The Sound and the Fury, Richard Gunter observes that the parts in which the protagonist narrates his actions on June 2 are characteristic of simplicity (149). For instance, the depictions of his preparations for his suicide are one of the easiest to follow for the reader indeed. This absence of complication, together with Quentin’s firm intentions and purposefulness perceivable on that particular day, signifies the clarity of thought difficult to see if the whole section is read for the first or even the second time.144 Similarly, at the end of his story when the last moments are narrated, Quentin’s tone becomes balanced (Godden 127), which suggests a certain level of stability after living on the intellectual and emotional seesaw observable before. Godden also remarks that the smell of honeysuckle has stopped being so intense (127), which overlaps with the above-mentioned opinion of May C. Brown, which concerns the watery imagery and sexuality on June 2. Finally, drawing a comparison between Quentin and Willa Cather’s Latour in Death Comes for the Archbishop, Merrill M. Skaggs concludes that “in their last days, both sit in the centers of their consciousness where all former states of mind are within reach of a hand” (94, emphasis added). This conclusion openly exposes the control of the flow of thoughts, and it also implies the character’s careful deliberation before his act. On his final day, too, once and for all, Quentin Compson sets himself free from the phantom of his father and his theories. If we bear in mind how galvanized into action Quentin is, his energetic conduct appears to be the repudiation of his father’s behavior. In the analysis of fatherhood in Faulkner and 144 A detailed study of sentence structures in the first, second and third sections is presented by Irena Kałuża in The Functioning of Sentence Structure in the Stream-of- Consciousness Technique of William Faulkner’s “The Sound and the Fury.” Far from denying that Quentin’s section is sometimes confusing to the reader, the scholar remarks that Quentin speaks “a language of formal ingenuity” (89). The troublesome fragmentation observable in the Quentin section is also unique. Quentin’s sentence structure, identified with Faulkner’s, reflects the mental process as it works in a natural way, whereas a standard sentence structure readers experience is usually ordered by grammatical rules (80).

168 Chapter Three Morrison, Philip Weinstein considers Mr. Compson’s “incapacity” to be his personality trait: “he is the one who can make nothing happen” (What 106), and he lives in “an impotent world of books” after 1865, which replaced the Southern legend of noblesse oblige with economic transactions (What 108). For Benson Quentin’s choice of death is even read as his disagreement with a life that would become the repetition of his father’s existence connected with “an anti-idealistic, anti-heroic, and detached cynicism” (227). In his reverie within the last minutes of his life, while pondering over the meaning of his existence, Quentin expresses such Latin words: “Non fui. Sum. Fui. Non sum” (SF 216), which mean “I was not. I am. I was. I am not” (RF 145). In the opinion of Godden, the obviously chaotic statement exemplifying “a dead language” may be, in fact, the parody of the father’s vision of the world (111-112). As the statement is a contradiction in terms, one may also add that it constitutes the travesty of Mr. Compson’s introductory remark on the first page of the Quentin section, i.e., time leads to “the reducto absurdum of all human experience” (SF 93). Interestingly enough, the answer Quentin utters almost straight away is unequivocal; with neither repetition nor lack of logic he just says, “I was. I am not” (SF 216). Together with the audible sound of the bells that announce his death, the statement shows that a natural course of events has been restored in his life after the pandemonium resulting from the philosophy of the “they,” propagated by the father. And this tragedy has to take place in order to refuse to obey the father’s supremacy, “to become ‘the arbiter of his own virtues,’ through suicide itself,” Spilka comments, playing on the opinion expressed by Mr. Compson (465; SF 219). This way Quentin’s finally comes through the door of maturity, which Caddy passed through a long time ago when she left the Compsons’ roof (M. Brown 547-548). Commenting upon parental relations in Absalom, Absalom!, Carolyn Porter maintains that Charles’s maneuvers to make Sutpen persuade Henry into killing his illegitimate son lead to the “unmaking” of the father (194). However, by destroying Sutpen’s design, Charles Bon, at the same time, is dead himself: “Without a father, no son, but without a son, no father” (Porter 194). To paraphrase Heidegger, Quentin has comported himself understandingly toward the thought of death, and June 2 of 1910 exemplifies the moment of gaining freedom. Nevertheless, when we treat Quentin’s suicide as his final stance on his father’s ideas, Quentin also “unmakes” Mr. Compson, but, by the same token, he “unmakes” himself as a human being, too. At the end of the day, Quentin Compson is dead. Far from idealizing his final choice, which for Quentin signifies liberation, but for those alive the renunciation of life, Quentin Compson should not be blamed for it. Those who triggered the whole mechanism of self-destruction are the people from his household, namely his father and his mother.

Quentin’s Existence as Being-Towards-Death 169 As Arthur Geffen notes, with his destructive perspective on temporality, Mr. Compson’s thinking and actions “help to destroy his son” (233). For Philip Weinstein the father is the one who is not able to deter Quentin from taking his own life (What 107). In truth, the parent’s advice is useless to all the children, because what he has tried to impress on them is nihilism to a great extent. Assessing the lack of his contribution to the development of the Compson offspring, Weinstein regards Mr. Compson’s “reducto absurdum” as uprooting his own personhood out of the present, and he compares the father to a shadow or even to death: “Ungrounded, he imagines himself as not there – like a shadow or like death itself” (What 108). Additionally, Faulkner himself suggests that the flow of tragedy in their family was handed down to Quentin by his own parent, when the author comments upon “the basic failure Quentin inherited through his father, or beyond his father,” in the first session at the University of Virginia (Gwynn and Blotner 3). Talking about Mrs. Compson, Joseph Gold, as Geffen about the father, believes that the mother, although unconsciously, was of service to her son in taking his life (29).145 Watkins also perceives her as a source of Quentin’s trouble, which he would not have suffered from, if she had done her best as a parent: “if I’d just had a mother so I could say Mother Mother” (Watkins 225; SF 213).146 And when Bleikasten inquires about the beginning of “this lethal course,” as Quentin’s trajectory of thinking is called, the scholar also points to Mrs. Compson (The Ink 75), who in Quentin’s memory is associated with the dungeon in a book illustration remembered from his childhood: When I was little there was a picture in one of our books, a dark place into which a single weak ray of light came slanting upon two faces lifted out of the shadow… It was torn out, jagged out. I was glad. I’d have to turn back to it until the dungeon was Mother herself she and Father upward into weak light holding hands and us lost somewhere below even them without even a ray of light. (SF 215, emphasis added) It is a fact that Quentin does not commence thinking of death in general, and then of his own, on the last day of his existence. The thought has been growing in him since he started to be fed with the ideas of his father and the emotions of his mother. In the words of Mark Spilka, it may be inferred then: 145 In the Dilsey section, Mrs. Compson asks: “What reason did Quentin have? Under God’s heaven what reason did he have? It cant be simply to flout and hurt me” (SF 374), which shows she focuses on herself, not on her child. 146 Watkins observes that the same opinion is expressed by Darl in As I Lay Dying, when he is asked by Vardaman about his mother’s whereabouts. “I haven’t got ere one” is his reply (Watkins 225; Novels 1930 65).

170 Chapter Three Quentin is the family’s ‘bitter prophet,’ its tragic historian; like Stephen Dedalus, he is acutely aware that family history has become a nightmare. To awaken from it he must wrestle, like Stephen, with the protean nature of reality, the changing shapes of time, place, and value. But unlike Stephen he has no resourceful father, compassionate and wise, to guide him; nor any fertile, faithful mother, waiting to show him what a woman is. Instead his father and mother are his misfortune, his heritage of crippling pessimism and self-pity. (456) Thus, according to Faulkner, “the premier American novelist of family” (Kartiganer “Quentin” 381), Quentin’s narrative makes its contribution to The Sound and the Fury as “a story of blood [that] gone bad” (LG 222). The protagonist does not commit suicide because of Caddy or incest, but due to the deprivation of positive social patterns that would have enabled him to take a healthy view of the institution of marriage, desire, and suffering (Guetti 57). In plain terms, the blood has gone bad, for the family of the Compsons have gradually disintegrated, and the causes of this dissolution should be traced to a profound lack of love, which was never handed down from the parents to the children. As one reads in the Appendix, Quentin was “incapable of love” (412), a feeling that Faulkner thought a great deal of while writing about the fall of the Compsons’ house, and also of the Sartorises, the McCaslins, the Sutpens, and the Snopeses (Bowling 111).147 Owing to the severe lack of love at home, there is the philosophy of the “they,” whose rejection causes Quentin to immerse himself in the world of his own mind, which is in fact Heidegger’s plan for Dasein. With the act of thinking as his main activity, Quentin looms out to be Alexander’s “civilized white man,” who “has tasted the fruit of the tree of knowledge, of good and evil, and he is guilty of the sin of disobedience and is doomed to death” (110).148 Although Quentin has not sinned against the Native American, or against the land by appropriating it, and his guilt about the African-American is not so dreadful, he has sinned against his own nature, the self.149 By curious paradox, plunging into 147 If we look at the Compson family from a wider angle, it is clear that in Southern society “something” went bad, too. The preserved sexlessness of the white lady and the chagrin of the outgoing plantation proprietor, which resulted from economic changes after the Civil War, obviously had an impact on the institution of the family, hence it would be unjust to see Quentin’s parents as the only root of all evil (Hönnighausen 143). 148 In the case of Faulkner’s characters, Margaret W. Alexander speaks of a threefold sin: against nature, the Indians, and the black (110). 149 Bleikasten, who criticizes Quentin’s suicide as an act of surrender, regards his death as “a final purgation, washing him of the sin of existence, effacing the very trace of his having been alive” (The Ink 89, emphasis added). In another fragment, the critic notes that “the ceaseless movement of becoming,” observable constantly in the world, is for Quentin nothing but “a hemorrhage of being” (The Ink 100).

Quentin’s Existence as Being-Towards-Death 171 the thicket of thoughts, for the most part of his existence, Quentin has neglected the real world surrounding him. To speak the words of Bockting, “his inner world overpowers the outer world” (“The Impossible” on-line), which leads to the conclusion drawn by Benson: “Quentin’s world is simply overdone. It is far too ingenious and melodramatic” (222). Embodying “consciousness” (Benson 214), Quentin chooses from the outside only what stimulates the inside, and he lives in a world created with subjectively biased, nonobjective, innermost thoughts, recollections, and images (Kinney 149). “This activity of perception and conception,” Kinney claims, “leads to suicide” (149).150 Finally, Quentin’s decision about felo de se exemplifies what James Guetti calls Faulkner’s interest in “imaginative failure” (58): he commits suicide, because he has been incapable of refraining from thinking (Horton 65), and what he has thought about night and day is obviously death. The act of killing himself is then a result of Quentin’s thanatomania, that is, the total subordination of life to death, which once again constitutes Heidegger’s idea, and which has been stimulated by Quentin’s own parents. For Sartre, on the day of his suicide, “Quentin cannot, for one second, conceive of the possibility of not killing himself” (230), i.e., he cannot imagine his life as the possibility of any existence, but as “the possibility of the impossibility of any existence at all” (BT 307), which again amounts to death as defined by Heidegger. Sartre even draws the conclusion that “Quentin’s soliloquy and his last walk are already his suicide” – “he is already dead,” when we read his observations in his narrative (230). All things considered, it is possible to interpret William Faulkner’s The Sound and the Fury through Martin Heidegger’s philosophy that concerns the phenomenology of death. As Heidegger’s Dasein, Quentin finds himself mentally on the path of Being-towards-death both inauthentically and authentically. He falls prey to the “they,” but on the other hand, he manages to preserve his individualization. Heidegger’s actualization is also his mode of Being to a certain extent, although his felo de se, as his conscious choice, becomes the act of liberation from existence now and here. However, no matter if he sets himself free, it is a great tragedy that the thought of death is necessary for him to act and to shift his perspective, or to cite Matthews, “to affirm his identity by dissolving it” (The Sound 52). 150 The obsessive acts of deliberating over every possible subject matter is ridiculed by Jason. Although he refers to Benjy, he states as follows: “I dont reckon he even knew what he had been trying to do, or why Mr Burgess knocked him out with the fence picket. And if they’d just sent him on to Jackson while he was under the ether, he’d never have known the difference. But that would have been too simple for a Compson to think of. Not half complex enough” (SF 328-329, emphasis added).

Chapter Four Faulkner’s Final Answer to Death: Dilsey’s Responsibility and Caddy’s Fecundity In the 1948 essay “Reality and Its Shadow,” disregarding the world of literature, Emmanuel Levinas expresses his view about fictitious protagonists: they are “prisoners” in an enclosed space of a novel (10). Moreover, writers move in “a world of shadows,” i.e., they create stories with a shroud of mystery and use stylistic devices such as allusions (Levinas “Reality” 13). To treat the statement as his final stance on fiction would be, however, a great misunderstanding since, in his later works, the philosopher changed his perspective and admitted the importance of literature (C. Davis 91). In reference to L’Au-delà du verset by Levinas (1982), Colin Davis presents the literary hierarchy compiled by the thinker: in the first place there are sacred writings, in the second national literatures, and in the third all other texts (94-95). The hierarchy is based on texts’ “capacity to articulate the call of the Other,” nevertheless, Levinas offers no justifications as to why a given book is more powerful than other works (C. Davis 94-95). Shifting our attention to William Faulkner, Eric J. Sundquist has no doubts that this author, together with Cooper and Hawthorne, belongs to the canon of American literature (6). Also, if we remember Tambling’s difference between philosophy and literature, that the former names and the latter evokes,151 the Dilsey section may serve as an illustrative explanation of the teachings presented by the French philosopher. Thus bearing in mind what Levinas says in Time and the Other, namely that it sometimes appears to him that “the whole of philosophy is only a meditation of Shakespeare” (72), the following analysis constitutes an attempt to discuss Faulkner’s story about Dilsey through Levinas. The aim is not to provide the justifications that Levinas lacks, according to Davis, but to better understand the Other and the self. 151 In his article “Levinas and Macbeth’s ‘Strange Images of Death’” Jeremy Tambling claims: “In this difference between defining a term, and the point that a literary text does not name or state, but evokes and performs, lies a difference between philosophy and literature” (369).

174 Chapter Four The space of the house that belongs to the Compson family may exemplify Levinas’s area of the il y a. Paradoxically, as the absence that is present, the void that may be felt, or the silence that is possible to hear, the phenomenon of the il y a is drawn in the reader’s imagination when one enters the house with Dilsey at dawn on 8 April of the 1928. From the words uttered by the irritable Mrs. Compson, who has been waiting for her servant for at least an hour, we find out about the previous lack of any sounds (SF 333), which can be “the murmur of silence” Levinas talks about in Time and the Other (46). Before the conversation develops, or even with the first words exchanged between Dilsey and her landlady, one is aware of this neutrality that is possible to sense, this indistinguishability of the there is in the Compsons’ house with Dilsey, who appears inside when the whole place, quiet, empty, and impersonal, is overtaken by sleep (SF 332). There is no movement anywhere yet, which may give the reader the impression of anonymity mentioned in the definition of the il y a (EE 52), the anonymity found in Miss Quentin’s room (SF 352), and the anonymity felt while imagining “the quiet stairwell” or the shadow of “a grey window” when “the day dawned bleak and chill” (SF 330, 333). There are other characteristic features of the il y a felt in the house. The lack of personality expressed in French by a verb form of the il y a is to a certain extent noticeable in a neutral genre ascribed to things in English. Furthermore, while taking shape at night, the il y a, floating about the Compsons’ house, is preserved in the visual image of the staircase, which early in the morning “descended into complete darkness” (SF 333). The void linked with the il y a can, nevertheless, be sensed much later during the day in the household. Luster, Dilsey’s grandson, is usually a live wire, but once, when he feeds Benjy, he falls into a reverie and starts pondering over an unclear issue. At the same moment, “his other hand lay on the back of the chair and upon that dead surface it moved tentatively, delicately, as if he were picking an inaudible tune out of the dead void” (SF 345, emphasis added). It is a fact that the phenomenon of the il y a appears in The Sound and the Fury before the beginning of the fourth section. When we look at Benjy’s childhood memories, the there is has already been present in the first section of the novel, nota bene on the day of Damuddy’s funeral. Like in Levinas, for one thing, the il y a comes into being in the middle of the night, when Benjy, even if not alone, lies in bed, and for another thing, what Benjy perceives is the sound of silence after he shushes himself: “I stayed hushed. We could hear us” (SF 92). The striking similarity between Levinas and Faulkner is also the fact that when he hears this “murmur of silence” (TO 46), Benjy is also a child, for the quoted fragments are derived from the recollection when he is a three-year-old boy. Yet the particular paradox of the audible quiescence has been doubled somewhat in

Faulkner’s Final Answer to Death: Dilsey’s Responsibility and Caddy’s Fecundity 175 Faulkner through a stylistic device of synesthesia. Benjy hears the lack of light in the room they occupy: “We could hear the dark” (SF 92), being a case that is definitely not isolated, as Benjy repeats it a few times. In effect, Sundquist speaks of the novel’s “own self-enclosing darkness” (9), which makes blackness, the feature of the il y a, definitely emanate from more than two scenes of the work. The darkness, impersonality, and anonymity equated with the il y a in the house of the Compson family are dispersed by the event of hypostasis carried out by Dilsey. Although she is regarded by Alexander as “a flat, mindless stereotype” (113), her actions speak louder than the words of the critic. Every single day, by walking over the threshold of the Compson residence, Dilsey finds herself in “a situation where an existent is put in touch with its existing” (TO 51). There she holds the position of a cook, child minder, caregiver and guardian, which clearly exemplifies the act of hypostasis. The act is plainly performed by her in full consciousness: “I does de bes I kin,” she declares while stroking Benjy’s head to quiet him down (SF 396). This appears to be “a contract with oneself” (Manning 45), a contract deliberately imposed by Dilsey on herself, for she knows perfectly well that she is the only person left in the house to pacify Benjy. And in her case this is not a one-time effort. There are actually innumerable acts of hypostasis carried out by her throughout many years. On April 8, 1928, even an Easter Sunday looks mundane as any other day, because she is in the kitchen on her own with no one else. This is a convention in the Compson house, so it may be added that the individualization of the previously nameless existence constitutes her own personal achievement. Levinas’s dialectic that concerns hypostasis may also reveal itself in the existence Dilsey opts for. In the historical context, with the Emancipation Proclamation of 1863, she gained freedom, but immediately lost it, remaining at a post reserved for a slave. In the words of Warren Beck, “she becomes the epitome, as of Faulkner’s own period, of the emancipated but not yet free and still direly circumstanced ones” (300). For Branny, on the other hand, the performance of duties helps the Gibsons set themselves free, although they stay the Compsons’ “shadows” (155). In the role of a servant, Dilsey feels obliged to get up very early, which by virtue of her age may constitute a considerable difficulty, but that, as a matter of fact, curves her personal identity to an individual shape. No matter if it is Monday, Sunday or Easter, she literary builds up a fire in the kitchen stove she has been chained to almost throughout her whole life. Figuratively, this is the act through which she unweariedly brings about a radical transformation from the seemingly impervious impersonality of the Compson house to the highly desirable subjectivity achieved by her own efforts, which in fact create her entire existence (Taylor 47). Owing to the years

176 Chapter Four of her toil, of her constant and sustained efforts, Quentin from “That Evening Sun,” while spotting Nancy before a cold stove, juxtaposes this picture with “a kitchen being warm and busy and cheerful”(293), which is the image of the kitchen as the heart of the house engraved in his mind by nobody else but Dilsey.152 The impossibility of fleeing from the burden of the paradoxically liberating existence, which for Levinas manifests itself in suffering, is also the attitude that Dilsey adopts. One obtains an irresistible impression that she gradually debilitates with every section of the novel so as to find her almost totally enervated in the last narrative: “She toiled painfully up the steps, shapeless, breathing heavily” (SF 333). With the plain difficulty in moving, short of breath, she takes every step in pain. And what is interesting is that, when asked about her state of health, Dilsey feels like talking only to those who understand her predicament, for if interlocutors are not elderly enough she lets her daughter speak instead of responding herself (SF 364). Yet, however sick and tired she gets, she keeps moving around the house, “hobbling along” (SF 228), and even though she can hardly walk, she climbs up and down the stairs, for example, to fetch a water bottle for Mrs. Compson lying in bed (SF 333). In the discussion of irreducible pain that limits movement, Levinas speaks of the state of total passivity that enables one to sense the proximity of death.153 This kind of experience may be applicable to Dilsey, as well. For example, while carrying out her duties, she utters the words: “It caught me in the hip so bad now I cant scarcely move” (SF 87). Additionally, in the Appendix, which for some could serve as a concluding chapter of the novel, when Melissa Meek pays her a visit, the apathetic Dilsey is found motionless in a rocker, waiting peacefully for the end with her “almost sightless” eyes (A 418). Obviously, this disposition to remain inert in pain, this familiarity with inactivity comes to Dilsey by virtue of her age, which is perhaps an aspect more emphatically accentuated by Scheler rather than Levinas, yet definitely noticed by Faulkner, who comments on it through Jason: “She was so old she couldn’t do any more than move hardly” (SF 229). Apropos of Jason, he appears to be a compelling exemplification of Levinas’s philosophy of pain as equated with passivity. When he was afflicted 152 With reference to Trudier Harris’s words in From Mammies to Militants, Philip Weinstein speaks of the kitchen as a place reserved for the black woman: “the one room in the house where the white woman can give up spatial ownership without compromising herself” (What 6-7). However, it seems to be the perspective of the white, not the black, as Dilsey criticizes Mrs. Compson for her incapability to cook. 153 In “Mayday” that preceded The Sound and the Fury, Pain and Hunger are the allegorical companions of Sir Galwyn before he faces “Little sister Death.”

Faulkner’s Final Answer to Death: Dilsey’s Responsibility and Caddy’s Fecundity 177 by a throbbing headache, caused in fact regularly by the odor of gasoline, “it seemed that he could feel the prolonged blow of it [the wind] sinking through his skull, and suddenly with an old premonition he clapped the brakes on and stopped and sat perfectly still. Then he lifted his hand to his neck and began to curse,” for there was no camphor to ease the unbearable pain (SF 382-383). Here, together with Jason’s inertia, what comes to the reader’s notice is that this irreducible pain escapes any rational thinking at the moment of sensing it (TO 69). In Jason’s case, instead of reasoning, there is anger that certainly confirms the strength of the soreness. It also makes him come closer to finitude, or at least to the moment that some people imagine to be comparable to it. To minimize the headache, he even attempts to reduce a basic physiological need, “trying to breathe shallowly, so that the blood would not beat so in his skull” (SF 384). For Levinas death comes as menace, violence, or a struggle in which an opponent is impossible to hold in a clinch. This argument is profoundly illustrated in the Dilsey section by a scuffle that ensues between Jason and a member of the show troupe. After the skirmish in the car, Jason manages, albeit for a short time, to fell the adversary to the ground, whose description as “the fatal, furious little old man” is sufficient to make Jason’s opponent the literary incarnation of demise (SF 387, emphasis added). Moreover, like the thought of death that visualizes itself in Levinas as violence “against me” (TI 234), the assailant threatens Jason’s existence with “a rusty hatchet high in his hand” (SF 387). For one thing, it perfectly matches the Levinasian picture of death as menace and violence, whose tools are graspable, and for another, it represents the image of death for Jason, who “grasped at the hatchet, feeling no shock but knowing that he was falling, thinking So this is how it’ll end, and he believed that he was about to die” (SF 387). In his comment on Jason’s threat of risking his life, Michael Zeitlin writes that “on April 8, 1928, Jason barely escapes an amputation, or worse, at the hands of the old man” (69). What additionally is noticeable by the scholar, who recalls André Malraux’s comparison of Faulkner’s literary world to Poe’s with reference to the theme of death,154 is both the element of unpredictable surprise and a Poe-like, murky setting, for “Jason did not expect to find him there when he entered ‘the dark place’” (68-69).155 Thus, in the last section of The Sound and the Fury one may find the reflection of Levinas’s thought that concerns death as a premature and 154 In “A Preface for Faulkner’s Sanctuary,” while comparing Faulkner and Poe, André Malraux speaks of “the same psychological material, the same hatreds, horses, coffins, and obsessions” (273). 155 Also see the fragment of The Sound and the Fury: “The galley was dark, rank with stale food” (SF 385).

178 Chapter Four unpredictable phenomenon, as a grave threat or jeopardy lying in wait. The “instinctive knowledge of death” mentioned by Levinas is also detectable (TI 233), because when Jason considers his demise, he is actually more concerned about his life, inquiring a couple of times if he is bleeding or not (SF 388). And what is interesting to notice is that in the face of death Jason behaves in the same way as Macbeth, whose conduct demonstrates a most common reaction to the incoming end: the attempt to repulse it by taking action and not abandoning all hope (TO 72). In the fight with the assailant, Jason is thinking: “Get it over with, and then a furious desire not to die seized him and he struggled, hearing the old man wailing and cursing in his cracked voice” (SF 387-388), which visibly follows the maxim Levinas believes, namely dum spiro, spero. If Jason exemplifies Levinas’s approach to death as menace and violence, Dilsey’s attitude toward quietude reveals what the French philosopher perceives as the unknowledgeable. First and foremost, she is unwilling to fuel any speculation over the subject in question. After Quentin’s suicide, on Roskus’s irrational superstition about two demises that must be followed by one more corpse, Dilsey gives a blunt and logical answer: “Going to be more than one more… Show me the man what aint going to die” (SF 35). The similar attitude is observable after Mr. Compson passes away. When Roskus’s comments on Benjy’s inherent capability to feel one’s death frighten Frony, who consequently does not want her son to sleep with Benjy, Dilsey, more interested in putting the two to bed, harshly cuts off the whole conversation: “Hush your mouth… Aint you got no better sense than that. What you want to listen to Roskus for, anyway” (SF 38). And what is more, exactly the same curt reply is heard after her husband’s allusions to the demise of Quentin and of Mr. Compson as misfortune ensuing from the alternation of Benjy’s name (SF 35, 37). The above illustrations exemplify Thadious M. Davis’s observation that in Faulkner’s characterization “black figures are rooted in a traditional folk culture that defies time while accepting mortality” (82). Dilsey’s children are informed of finitude, whereas the whites are not, yet what else is perceivable in The Sound and the Fury is that Dilsey is unwilling to deliberate over the subject in question. “Capable of intuition and decisive acceptance of realities” (Beck 314), Dilsey realistically approaches the notion of finitude, as one of those Faulknerian protagonists who do not need to discuss extensively important issues to understand them (Watkins 216). What Dilsey fully accepts is this indisputable fact that everyone will die sooner or later, therefore there is no reason for creating more or less incredible stories about dying. By contrast to Quentin, whose almost every association is with demise, Dilsey, in the above quotations, presents herself as a person unwilling to hypothesize over finitude. By excluding rumination over it, her life appears to reflect Levinas’s thought

Faulkner’s Final Answer to Death: Dilsey’s Responsibility and Caddy’s Fecundity 179 about mortality exposed in God, Death, and Time, namely “death is the end of what makes the thinkable thinkable” (90). There is another illustration that shows that for Dilsey, much the same way as for Levinas, death may be interpreted as an enigma. On the day when Damuddy’s funeral takes place, when asked by Caddy why they have to remain silent, Dilsey answers: “You’ll know in the Lawd’s own time” (SF 29). In view of Scheler’s philosophy, it has been treated as the exemplification of the death evasion; however, if we bear in mind the above quoted scenes and look upon Dilsey’s answer from Levinas’s perspective, something else may be perceived. With the emphasis on the word “own,” the phrase quite explicitly implies finitude graspable only by God. Ergo, this “Lawd’s own time” in Faulkner parallels Levinas’s initial “nothingness of knowledge” (“The Philosopher” 153), the issue the least unknown, beyond human comprehension. Also, what should not escape one’s notice is the fact that the above citation supports Levinas’s point of view classifying death as an event that will come from the future: “You’ll know in the Lawd’s own time,” that is, you will know when you die on a day you know nothing about. Accordingly, completely unexpected and accidental, incomprehensible a priori, death in the eyes of Dilsey contradicts Scheler’s and Heidegger’s perspectives on quietude, which, according to the philosophers, may be approached phenomenologically. The next point to consider in regard to the question of death is the notion of time, which in Levinas is inseparably bound up with infinity. It must be mentioned that time is first of all an aspect through which Faulkner makes Dilsey distinguishable from the Compson brothers. Each of the three siblings, together with other family members, appears to have a certain difficulty with temporality (Edel qtd. in Aschkenasy 102). It happens that Benjy cannot measure clock time; Quentin checks if it is likely to kill it; Jason, permanently late, is unable to keep up with the clock, whereas Dilsey “never seems lost in space or time as the contrasting characters do” (Skaggs 96). Not only does she feel comfortable about it, but she also knows what time it is, even though the clock with only one hand does not tell the time correctly (SF 341). For this reason, she “can read through the defacement” (RF 178). With reference to Mircea Eliade’s concept of profane and sacred time, Geffen believes in Dilsey’s capability to go beyond time: she is aware that the profane time one must bear is not tantamount with “the be-all and end-all of existence” (241). Due to her faith, she is cognizant of the sacred time being “far above and beyond superficial clock time” (Geffen 241), which apparently overlaps the notion of infinity. It is also interesting to observe the correspondence between Levinas’s comparison of time to spring and Faulkner’s emphasis in setting three out of four narratives in this season. The time ascribed by Faulkner to Dilsey’s story

180 Chapter Four entitled “April Eighth 1928” is obviously the time of a spring day. Additionally, compared to spring, which creates something new, but in a way is burdened with the past, time brings alterity. Having heard the Easter sermon preached by Reverend Shegog, Dilsey utters: “I’ve seed de first en de last… I seed de beginnin, en now I sees de endin” (SF 371). What the passage reveals is, on the one hand, the events that have already occurred in the Compson family, if we refer to the beginning. On the other hand, there is the ultimate breakdown of the household Dilsey foresees, which provides the interpretation for the end. According to Aschkenasy, in the quoted passage, Dilsey “eulogizes the Compson family and pronounces its death” (103), and for Skaggs, she also “sees the first and the last, the beginning and the ending, with human wholeness that includes inevitable loss and death, bringing tears to her eyes” (96). Levinas’s entity grasps time through the encounter with the Other rather than death. If we transfer the idea to the stage of The Sound and the Fury, it may be inferred that Dilsey has no problems building human relationships with the Other, so neither does she have great difficulty in reading time. She is not like Joe Christmas, who feels “the urgency of the need to keep these Others [women, blacks, Yankees] separate from the self,” and that is why his identity is unspecified (Mortimer 13). Quite the reverse, Dilsey does not separate herself from the Other, and her identity, her understanding of time, and her perception of death are strongly determined by the people near her. For most of her life, Dilsey’s individual time and the time of her family have intermingled with the time of the Compson family. However, there is a telling difference in alterity time brings to these families. Bearing in mind the meaning of alterity, understood as an issue revealed in the encounter with death, as well as with the Other, we may observe that what is given to the Compsons is exclusively the alterity conveyed by death. In their lives most of the Compson family members prefer to meet death literally as well as metaphysically, rather than another human being. As Bleikasten states, neither Quentin nor Jason is courageous enough to move forward “from self to other” (The Ink 123). And even though Quentin does see himself in a mirror as the Other, this Other is “unreal, imaginary, dead” (Bleikasten The Ink 98). Certainly, Caddy and Benjy are in the minority here. They long for the Other, but they are doomed to experience mainly the alterity of finitude in such a family house. Using Levinas’s words employed in his criticism of Heidegger, we may thus conclude that, with no male descendant to continue the line, “the essence of time” that happens to the Compsons is constituted by “the finitude of being,” not by infinity (TI 284). In the case of Dilsey’s time, the situation is dissimilar. Alterity brought with time is the otherness experienced both in death and in the relationship with the

Faulkner’s Final Answer to Death: Dilsey’s Responsibility and Caddy’s Fecundity 181 Other: she is “other and interrelated at the same time” (Weinstein Faulkner’s 16). Additionally, Skaggs notices that “Faulkner’s Compsons seem only to lose; yet Dilsey… finds as useful a life, by losing it in service to others” (93-94). First of all, Dilsey treats death as the unknowledgeable, as mystery, not fighting with it. Instead, she lets death impose its foreign will on her (TI 234). Although she is in mourning and full of grief over her husband’s death (SF 39), she is not presented in The Sound and the Fury as Mrs. Compson, who has kept moaning about the disappearance of her spouse for many years. Dilsey simply accepts the fact that her husband died. Secondly, she allows other people to force upon herself their own whims, but she does not react to them aggressively, as Jason does in such situations. Those whims of the enemies, who do not wish her well or take advantage of her, are transformed by Dilsey into “the desire that is for the Other” (TI 236). For instance, we can observe it when the slowly limping Dilsey clumps upstairs in order to fetch a hot bottle for Mrs. Compson. Thirdly, by contrast to those she serves everyday, Dilsey does not depart from this world without issue, therefore, one may say, paraphrasing Levinas, that she gives birth to an infinite being. In Dilsey’s position then, “the essence of time” is not established on the right understanding of death (TI 284), but it is constituted by infinity reinforced by positive interhuman relations and fecundity. And this is precisely what differentiates the Compsons from the Gibsons, for love and the preservation of life are the characteristics the former lack and the latter possess (T. Davis qtd. in Branny 155).
