The infinity stemming from our acts toward the Other is sealed by Faulkner in his Nobel Prize address, which in truth echoes the rendering of the Dilsey section (Slatoff 188). In the speech, the father of Yoknapatawpha County claims that man’s immortality is not guaranteed by his “inexhaustible voice, but because he has a soul, a spirit capable of compassion and sacrifice and endurance” (ESPL 120). As Scott notes in her essay, “Dilsey isn’t searching for a soul. She is the soul” (16), and the heart for Faulkner is “an organ of feeling… antithetic to the head” (Slatoff 194). In opposition to Quentin, she does not attempt to play with time, making the significance of existence conditioned on death. Rather, while observing the clock in the kitchen, she has a capability to understand its “enigmatic profundity” (SF 341), thanks to which the Gibsons “endured” (A 427), as the last and the only comment in the Appendix under Dilsey’s name confirms. On these grounds, it is possible to conclude that Dilsey advances the alterity of the Other rather than the alterity of death. Understanding that finitude is our final possibility, she could have chosen the Heideggerian way of thinking. Instead of this, cognizant of the unknowable that comes as an enigma, she opts for the alterity of the Other. After suffering severely, feeling physical pain

182 Chapter Four through which the proximity of death comes into view, she does not focus on her own dying. She rather prefers to look carefully at the faces of the Compson family to be able to help if it is necessary. Analyzing The Sound and the Fury, Matthews observes that in the Dilsey section the imagery of the face is explicitly visible (The Sound 79). When we pay attention to particular depictions, it is noticeable that death reveals itself in the faces of the protagonists. One need only think of Jason’s “hazel eyes with black-ringed irises like marbles” (SF 348, emphasis added). Apart from the associations with Jason’s unpleasant character, the description highlights the hue and temperature traditionally associated with death. Further, during the quarrel with his mother, his eyes are characterized to be “empty of anything. It was as though his eyes were holding their breath” (SF 349), which again stresses lifelessness plainly attributable to dying. Besides, Mrs. Compson’s appearance suggests the proximity of death. “Her face [is] flaccid” (SF 349), hair is white, eyes are pouched and “so dark as to appear to be all pupil or all iris” (SF 348), which may signify possible symptoms of a debilitating illness. The signs of mortality are also noticeable in Benjy’s “bloated, decaying” body (Sundquist 13). Able to feel finitude, Benjy, in the final part of The Sound and the Fury, is additionally pictured as a carrier of death. Not only is his skin “dead-looking,” but his figure is also “dropsical” (SF 342). First of all, the word “dropsical” may be treated as a synonym for “unhealthy,” as in Faulkner’s story “Red Leaves,” where Moketubbe is “diseased with flesh, with a pale, broad, inert face and dropsical hands and feet” (321). But then again, when the word is referred to dropsy, or edema, as it is known nowadays, it may denote one of the causes of death, if not treated. Furthermore, while talking about Benjy’s face, we should point out that “his thick mouth hung open, drooling a little” (SF 342), which may be the image of the defunct. Also, his distinctive pace of walking ought to be mentioned, since he moves through the house “with a shambling gait” like a person losing one’s strength (SF 342). And in another passage we read: “Ben sat, tranquil and empty” (SF 354), which highlights his lack of liveliness, as well. Obviously, the space of death has not been confined exclusively to the bodies of the protagonists who appear in the Dilsey section. Through “the shabby garden” and “the broken fence” (SF 360), the reader one more time enters the household, whose derelict state metaphorically adds to the picture of the family on the verge of collapse. In front of the reader’s eyes, the “paintless house with its rotting portico” disintegrates and falls apart (SF 372). The clock ticking in the kitchen is compared to “the dry pulse of the decaying house” (SF 355), and a gray light is noticeable in the corridors (SF 333). There are objects in the house that are depicted as “dead,” for example, the surface of the chair

Faulkner’s Final Answer to Death: Dilsey’s Responsibility and Caddy’s Fecundity 183 Luster lies his hand on is described as “dead” (SF 345), and the bottle with hot water is compared to “a dead hen” (SF 337). And this fatality and mortality that abide within the walls appear to be limited only to the Compsons’ estate. With his capability to detect death, Benjy, who has been whimpering since the morning, stops crying as soon as they wander off from the place, which in fact occurs as if by magic: “They reached the gate. Dilsey opened it... They passed out the gate… Ben ceased” (SF 361). Only when they walk back through the gate does Benjy start to moan again. “They reached the gate and entered. Immediately Ben began to whimper again” (SF 372). In the last part of The Sound and the Fury the room occupied by Quentin, Caddy’s daughter, especially gives the impression of lifelessness. Inside, what one can feel is “that dead and stereotyped transience of rooms in assignation houses” (SF 352). Straightaway, the relation of death and sex, so often evoked by Faulkner, is unconcealed. Furthermore, apart from the implied relentless passage of time, the evanescent atmosphere of the place is highlighted with grief or even loneliness brought into the room with “the forlorn scent of the blossoms” (SF 352). In a way, this odor of sadness foreshadows the subject of the conversation carried on when Dilsey, Mrs. Compson, and her son enter Quentin’s bedroom. The topic of the conversation is a suicide note possibly left by Quentin, which in turn is an allusion to her uncle’s felo de se. The emptiness found in the room on that Easter Sunday is contrasted by Brooks with Christ’s abandoned tomb, which again shows the inverted correlation with Christ’s Passion (William Faulkner: First 69). Instead of victory over death, there is another defeat in the family’s history, since with specific reference to Good Friday, one can attend Miss Quentin’s crucifixion this time, according to the scholar (William Faulkner: First 70). Dilsey’s body also carries in itself the signs of mortality (Sundquist 13). When readers enter the last section of The Sound and the Fury the sight that meets their eyes is an elderly woman “with an expression at once fatalistic” (SF 331), who bears “a resemblance to death” (Kinney 155) waiting for her just around the corner. She had been a big woman once but now her skeleton rose, draped loosely in unpadded skin that tightened again upon a paunch almost dropsical, as though muscle and tissue had been courage or fortitude which the days or the years had consumed until only the indomitable skeleton was left rising like a ruin or a landmark above the somnolent and impervious guts. (SF 331) What we can see here is Dilsey in the final phase of existence. Her skin is not well-toned, but falling in folds; her belly is dropsical, unhealthy; the insides are depicted with the adjectives “somnolent” and “impervious,” which used figuratively can refer to the inadequate functioning of her body. The very word

184 Chapter Four “skeleton” makes us think of death rather than life, and its comparison to “a ruin” carries connotations of bones in a grave after the process of decomposition. On top of that, with “her fallen breasts” (SF 330), with her face described as “collapsed” (SF 331), i.e., sunken, lacking strength or healthiness, Dilsey metaphorically appears to wear death on herself: she is “a grim memento mori,” as Bleikasten states (The Ink 133). Dressed in shabby clothes, Dilsey even wears garments “moribund” in color (SF 331), which additionally stresses how close to death she is. Admittedly, in the above cited fragment there are thanatological overtones, but they are certainly balanced with the undercurrents of the opposite meaning. Apart from the comparison to a ruin, Dilsey’s skeleton is also treated as “a landmark above the somnolent and impervious guts,” which makes Dilsey a protagonist subjected to putrescence and durability at the same time (Dobbs 41). Interestingly enough, for Philip Weinstein, what makes the black maid this landmark is her “otherness,” understood as a prominent feature undiscovered in other white protagonists of the novel (What 13). Compared to “a landmark,” a distinct place on the horizon which helps not to get off a track, Dilsey sticks out of the crowd of the grayish Compsons who lack her fortitude, willpower, and determination. In the words of Dobbs, Dilsey “becomes a monument, a myth, a lieu de mémoire not only for the characters within the novel who are stabilized by her presence, but also for Faulkner and his generations of readers” (41).156 Dilsey’s body as a lieu de mémoire is plainly perceived by Dobbs in the historical context to be a sign of the past times. However, with “the indomitable skeleton,” which highlights how strong her character is, and which strangely enough is more visible than her decaying flesh (Dobbs 42), Dilsey is like a rock that remains unyielding to various pressures of life in the past, in the present and in the future, both for Faulkner’s generations and for those who still come, and will come next, as she is a monument of humanity, and with it, a mark of perseverance. And, undoubtedly, she knows a lot about life. During the Easter sermon the tears that fall down her cheeks are described as coming “in and out of the myriad coruscations of immolation and abnegation and time” (SF 368), so the wrinkles observable in Dilsey’s face are not only the outcome of passing days 156 In “‘Ruin or Landmark’? Black Bodies as Lieux de Mémoire in The Sound and the Fury,” Cynthia Dobbs derives the term “lieu de mémoire” from Pierre Nora’s “Between Memory and History: Les Lieux de Mémoire,” whose statement she quotes at the beginning of her article, in which we can read: “the most fundamental purpose of lieux de mémoire is to stop time, to block the work of forgetting, to establish a state of things, to immortalize death, to materialize the immaterial” (Nora qtd. in Dobbs 35). Thus we can infer that through her own demeanor Dilsey immortalizes death.

Faulkner’s Final Answer to Death: Dilsey’s Responsibility and Caddy’s Fecundity 185 and years. These noticeable crinkles have been formed on her face because of “sacrifice and self-denial for others, i.e., for the Compsons” (RF 182). Accordingly, this sacrifice is nothing else but the reflection of Levinas’s responsibility for the Other, so we may say that this indomitable skeleton of hers represents “a challenge to death” (Bleikasten The Ink 133). As a result, sacrifice as evidence of responsibility is a common thread spun by the French philosopher and the father of Yoknapatawpha County. It is additionally confirmed by Faulkner in his Nobel Prize address, in which he states that the writer should fully concentrate on “the old verities and truths of the heart,” i.e., “love and honor and pity and pride and compassion and sacrifice” (ESPL 120). Seeing Levinas’s question of death in the faces of the Compson family members, Dilsey answers the query by the assumption of the responsibility for another mortal being, the responsibility evaded not only by Quentin (Taylor 41), but, first of all, by his father and mother. Like Caroline Barr, a model for the protagonist,157 of whom Faulkner said quintessentially in “Funeral Sermon:” “She was born and lived and served, and died” (ESPL 118), Dilsey lives for the Others. Although conscious of her own mortality, she forgets about her own self and her own dying, and helps “the tortured white family” (Blake 98). In Levinas’s spirit, running the whole house for the Compsons, she remembers about their first body, giving them her own body, for, as Dobbs notes, her body belongs to them (40). The moment of taking responsibility takes place every single day when early in the morning she builds a fire under the roof that does not belong to her, and bakes the bread for those who dwell there (SF 332). Advanced in years, she is the one that puts on the apron and starts serving the Others. She bustles about the kitchen; she prepares breakfast, when almost everyone else is still in bed (SF 336). Also, facing her grumpy landlady, she advises Miss Cahline to return to bed in order not to get cold (SF 338). And even though the devilment of the ungrateful Jason has not escaped her, Dilsey does not leave him to his own fate and looks after her former charge, urging him to sit and eat breakfast before he goes out (SF 355). What is more, Dilsey feels responsible for those who are in the springtime of life, whose bodies have not demonstrated mortality yet. Taking upon herself the task of upbringing the young, she also epitomizes Levinas’s level of fecundity in terms of a teacher-and-student relation. For example, she works on forming the character of her mischievous grandson, and she does not let Quentin indulge in a 157 Robert Cantwell, who during his visit to the Faulkners had talked to Caroline Barr, mentioned in his account that there was a marked difference in appearance between the character and the model: Dilsey was described as obese, whereas Caroline Barr had in fact a “trim figure” (61).

186 Chapter Four coffee-drinking habit. Additionally, she instructs other people in the duty of responsibility: she wants Luster, her spiteful, self-centered grandson, to go upstairs and help Benjy get dressed (SF 335), or to watch over him so that Benjy will not burn his hand, sitting near the stove, or to feed Benjy (SF 344).158 And even if today’s educationalists might object strongly to the way Dilsey verbalizes her teaching, in contrast to Jason, her brusqueness to Luster never deters her from taking care of her grandson (Matthews The Sound 65). Her responsibility also means the protection of the Other from the Other. When Jason tussles with his mother about the key to open Quentin’s room, Dilsey, her servant, protects her from her own son (SF 351). In the commotion at Miss Quentin’s door, convinced that Caddy’s daughter is inside, Dilsey does not want the adolescent she feels responsible for to be afraid of Jason, so she tries to reassure the girl: “dont you be skeered, honey, I’se right here” (SF 352). And when Mrs. Compson is devastated by her son’s behavior, Dilsey is also near the Other, leading her landlady to her bedroom, although she is likely to possess less physical strength than Mrs. Compson (SF 354). Hence, by contrast to Jason, who appears to be the main source of evil in the house, Dilsey’s aim is not to heighten tension in the place where anything hardly makes sense, but quite the opposite, “to offset the destructive effect of the Compsons’ overwhelming emotional failure” (Collins “William” 227). Full of understanding, she comes with the intention of releasing the pressure that cumulates in the air in every situation when madness, chaos, and mischief overwhelm the place. Above all this, Dilsey is prepared to shoulder ultimate responsibility for Benjy, who nobody worries about. Touching his hands, she checks if Benjy is not cold (SF 342), or if her grandson does not take advantage of him (SF 398). Despite the fact that Benjy “the idiot” is welcomed neither in the church of the white nor of the black, she takes him with her to an Easter service. She has enough courage to take upon herself the task that other church-goers abandon. Certainly, the people can perceive in Benjy’s face this demand or the prayer Levinas mentions. However, the feeling they experience is just uneasiness, not the Levinasian disquietude that forces them to act like Dilsey does. The church- goers only look “with the covertness of nocturnal animals” (SF 363), which reminds us of the il y a that brings back darkness, inhuman neutrality, 158 The relationship between Dilsey and Luster is a good example of Ralph Ellison’s stance on Faulkner’s way of presenting the African-American. According to the author of Invisible Man, Faulkner shows both heroes and villains (329-330), which is visible in another fragment of the novel in the context of the body: Dilsey’s skin is characteristic of “a rich, lustrous quality,” which is distinctly contrasted with Luster’s one layered with “a faint dusting of wood ashes” (SF 341).

Faulkner’s Final Answer to Death: Dilsey’s Responsibility and Caddy’s Fecundity 187 depersonalization. Unwilling to encounter the Other face-to-face, they are unable to carry out the act of hypostasis that could individualize their existence. Another clear contrast between Dilsey and other church-goers is the attitude of the latter toward Reverend Shegog. At first, they are very enthusiastic about the visit of the new preacher, but when he appears, they look at him with consternation, in a very similar way as they look at Benjy. They are disturbed and alarmed on the grounds that his appearance does not match the picture of a minister they have drawn in their minds. Instead of a sturdy posture comparable to their minister, they are confronted with “the insignificant looking man sitting dwarfed and countrified” (SF 366), “a meagre figure” (SF 367), with “a wizened black face” (SF 365). To a certain extent, the Reverend may even be contrasted with Benjy, as he is “undersized,” when Benjy is the opposite; he is also compared to an “aged monkey,” whereas Benjy is recognized to be a bear (SF 365). Thus, judging Shegog’s physical appearance, the whole congregation is unable to leave behind their stereotyped thinking and approach the Other with affection, which does not escape Dilsey again. Among the comments of disapprobation, she is certain that the Reverend is a charismatic figure: “I’ve knowed de Lawd to use cuiser tools dan dat” (SF 366). Long before Shegog’s sermon wins over the community, Dilsey is able to read the face of the Reverend as the embodiment of Levinas’s à-Dieu, showing her affection toward the stranger, not only toward those living by her side. In conclusion, Dilsey is able to build the relation with the infinite, because she answers the question symbolizing death in Levinas when she replies with the responsibility for the Other. Conscious of the fact that she is mortal, she kindles within herself this “rational hope” (GDT 63) that it is possible to discover “infinity in the finite” (GDT 110), that is, to give meaning to finitude instead of considering it as nothingness, which is confirmed in the scene where Caddy discusses the alternation of Benjy’s name with her nanny: My name been Dilsey since fore I could remember and it be Dilsey when they's long forgot me. How will they know it's Dilsey, when it's long forgot, Dilsey, Caddy said. It'll be in the Book, honey, Dilsey said. Writ out. (SF 71) According to Ross and Polk, the “Book” brought up here is “God’s Book of Life” (RF 34), which one reads about in Revelation, where in turn it is written: “And I saw the dead, small and great, stand before God; and the books were open: and another book was open, which is the book of life: and the dead were judged out of those things which were written in the books, according to their works” (Rev. 20.12). Juxtaposing these two quotations, it is noticeable that with no illusions about fatality, Dilsey hopefully trusts that her deeds toward the

188 Chapter Four Other will be at least remembered by God, that her award will be conferred upon her in the afterlife (Geffen 235). Accordingly, with her care and readiness to help and serve the people who exist near her here and now, Dilsey realizes the Levinasian philosophy of “infinity in the finite.” The evidence of its realization is additionally given “in the book” that we may hold in our hands. When we bear in mind that Caroline Barr was a model for Dilsey, and, at the same time, open Go Down, Moses (1942), we discover Faulkner’s tribute to his Mammy for “a fidelity without stint or calculation of recompense,” for “an immeasurable devotion and love” (Novels 1942 2).159 Dilsey does not have to wait very long to hear how the Other calls her, which makes her feel obligated to take responsibility. As soon as Mrs. Compson realizes that her housewife is in the kitchen, she begins “calling ‘Dilsey’ at steady and inflectionless intervals” (SF 333). Her call does not seem to be explicitly expressed though, since Mrs. Compson utters it “without inflection or emphasis or haste, as though she were not listening for a reply at all” (SF 333). Nevertheless, Dilsey has no difficulty in recognizing the character of the call. With a skill of clairvoyance, she “did penetrate the walls and ceiling and saw the old woman…, calling her name with machinelike regularity” (SF 336-337, emphasis added). Dilsey can also hear Mrs. Compson’s cry for help when Jason, her own son, uses force to get hold of a key to Quentin’s room. Even if well aware of her landlady’s inborn laziness and clumsiness in looking after children, Dilsey, when summoned, immediately answers the call without thinking twice. When Miss Cahline laments for the treatment received from her own son, Dilsey reassures her that nothing will happen to the Other in need (SF 351). Dilsey notices death in the form of the query emanating from Mrs. Compson’s face. The black servant answers the question with “here I is” (SF 333), which, even if ungrammatical, is exactly the same reply Levinas gives in Otherwise than Being to express the existent’s answerability for the Other (114). And such an unequivocal response has not been given only once. With the words “I right here,” Dilsey confirms her readiness to answer the Other’s cry for help when another conflict in the family arises (SF 351). What should also come to the fore is that Dilsey’s state of health is fairly poor, even worse than Mrs. Compson’s, and climbing and descending the stairs cause pain. However, Dilsey is far from disclaiming the responsibility despite the fact that it is not hers, that there are no external factors imposing it on her: “‘You’re not the one who has to bear it,’ Mrs Compson said. ‘It’s not your responsibility. You can go away. You dont have to bear the brunt of it day in and day out’” (SF 339). Yet, in terms of 159 “Her white children bless her” is the statement engraved by Faulkner on Barr’s tombstone (P. Weinstein What 12).

Faulkner’s Final Answer to Death: Dilsey’s Responsibility and Caddy’s Fecundity 189 responsibility Dilsey realizes perfectly well that there is no possibility of substitution, that no one else, except for her, can carry out the duties she takes toward the Other: “Ef I dont worry bout y’all, I dont know who is,” she declares (SF 361). Obviously the person who does not hear the call from the Other is Jason. This is not surprising, nevertheless, as he is the kind of person that “goes through the motions of listening in order to deceive himself as to what he already hears” (SF 350). He does not listen to the call coming from his mother: “‘Jason,’ she called through the door. There was no answer” (SF 353). Neither does he reply to Dilsey when she tries to persuade him not to wake up Quentin, Caddy’s daughter, without particular purpose (SF 346). Neither does he see the ban on negligence Levinas talks about in Dilsey’s face, when he gives her an order to climb the stairs and wake his niece up, even though this is a very strenuous task for the person who used to be his child minder: “They heard her a long while on the stairs” (SF 347). However, it does not interest Jason, who even hurries her up. In fact, Jason never answers the Other’s cry for help, and instead he makes use of defenselessness emanating from the countenance, ready to murder. Sharing with his mother his comments on the argument with Dilsey, he reveals this wish: “Did you ever have one [servant] that was worth killing?” (SF 347, emphasis added). In other words, he breaks the ban on killing which is carved on the face, i.e., “Thou Shalt not Kill” (Levinas Entre 104), which according to Llewelyn should be read as “Peace be with you” or “Shalom” (102). Even more, in the words of Jill Robbins, analyzing Levinas’s language of the face, we can say that Jason Compson is a “murderer who takes violent aim at the face of the other” (67). By his endless verbal assaults on Dilsey, Caddy and her daughter, his own mother, a sheriff, and his boss, so in one word, on everybody, he does not encounter the human being. He is Levinas’s murderer who “loses not only the face of the other but also his own face, that is, he is ashamed, and, as it were, forfeits his own alterity” (Robbins 67-68). Like Cain’s face Robbins refers to, Jason’s face “falls” (68), or speaking the words of the author of The Sound and the Fury, his face is “in shadow,” when he approaches Dilsey (SF 349). Through the whole course of the story, Jason wishes to take over the Other, including not only his relatives and workers, but also official upholders of public order whom he commands what to do (SF 354). In “Ethics as First Philosophy,” Levinas talks about the subject who creates one’s own identity by affirming one’s presence in the world as “hateful” (82). With full concentration on the self, affirming just the I, Jason Compson leads a life that is a chain of “acts of repulsing, excluding, exiling, stripping, killing” (Levinas “Ethics” 82). He is repulsive toward his own mother when he calls her “old fool” (SF 351), or when he says that they would live in “a fine pigsty” if

190 Chapter Four she really did household chores (SF 347). He excludes his mother from dealing with matters in her own house when he pushes her away from the door to Quentin’s room (SF 351). He strips his own mother of her dignity when he frisks the pockets of her black gown in search of the key to unlock the room (SF 350). He kills, defying the ban “Thou Shalt not Kill” in Dilsey’s face, whenever he orders her to perform a task beyond her power. Finally, one can conclude that the non-ethical Jason only usurps the space that should have been devoted to the Other. In “Ethics as First Philosophy” we read: “My being-in-the-world or my ‘place in the sun’, my being at home, 160 have these not also been the usurpation of spaces belonging to the other man whom I have already oppressed or starved, or driven out into a third world” (Levinas 82). Jason Compson clearly draws the boundaries around the self. No matter if he is in or out of the house, his room remains locked up. He does not let his mother in when she knocks and calls for him, and he even changes the lock in order to make sure he is the only one who has a key to it (SF 346). As a consequence, unless he lets the Other enter his space, it is not surprising that when he would like to enter their space, Quentin’s room to be exact, he is left with a knob in his hands (SF 349). Whenever Dilsey reacts to the Other’s cry for help, she obviously shows her goodness, and for Levinas goodness, which realizes itself in love, comes before Being. In “William Faulkner: The Importance of Love,” Bowling speaks about love as Faulkner’s primary theme in his most significant works, mentioning Dilsey as one of the author’s “great lovers,” those ordinary, common people leading a prosaic life, who exceed the alleged grayness of existence by their dedication and allegiance (110). Far away from the idealistic vision of love, Bowling, first of all, claims that in Faulkner love is understood as “the spiritual affinity between man and nature, between man and his fellow man, and among the members of a family;” secondly, the necessity of love in Faulkner’s world evinces itself either through its lack or aberration (110). In his deliberations over the presence of love, Bowling finally concludes that what is written between the lines in Faulkner is his belief that “without love, no one can ever be a human being... With Faulkner, the opposite of love is not hate: it is doom” (116). Accordingly, Dilsey, with her love to the Other, goes beyond the doom perceivable in the Compsons’ faces, and gives the answer to the initially unanswerable question posed by death. Simultaneously, she is able to notice that the countenance of the Other denotes the Levinasian à-Dieu, this being-toward- God instead of the Heideggerian Being-towards-death. As Geffen notes, the 160 The phrase “my place in the sun” is a quotation from Pascal’s Thoughts, whereas “my being at home” is an allusion to Heidegger’s existence for itself (Levinas “Ethics” 87).

Faulkner’s Final Answer to Death: Dilsey’s Responsibility and Caddy’s Fecundity 191 apocalyptic vision expressed in the fragment “I’ve seed de first en de last… I seed de beginnin, en now I sees de endin” (SF 371) may also be interpreted as Dilsey’s encounter with Divinity, showing “that she, like Shegog, has seen God face to face” (240), and “there is none good but one, that is God” (Mt. 19.17).161 In the final section of The Sound and the Fury, there is a confirmation that, despite the presence of death, the existence of being-toward-God may be realized. Following Levinas’s Beyond the Verse, where the philosopher recognizes the reading of the Torah and its exegesis as his “movement-towards- God” (qtd. in Keenan 94), Keenan believes that for Levinas a ritual of reading the Law is “arguably read alongside the aporia of death” (94). In Dilsey’s section there is a similar situation when the reader peruses the sermon preached by Reverend Shegog. In the homily, the subject of death continuously recurs, for the preacher mentions: the Jewish generations who died under the yoke of bondage in Egypt, the parable about Lazarus (SF 368; RF 182), Herod’s order to kill all children under two years old, the lamentation of their mothers in deep mourning (SF 369; RF 183), Jesus’s death on Calvary (SF 370), and finally, one’s own death when the Reverend utters: “Let me lay down wid de Lawd” (SF 369). Yet, despite the fact that death seems to dominate in the sermon, it is not the main message revealed there. John T. Matthews claims that while listening to the preacher the whole congregation participates in a traditional Christian ritual of regeneration: “For Baptists like the Gibsons, every believer appropriates Christ’s death as his or her own…, and then partakes of Christ’s triumph over death figured in his resurrection” (The Sound 81-82). Thus, with all those who listen to the sermon, Dilsey is reassured that her efforts have not been in vain, and whatever she has done for the Compsons, it is the sacrifice for the worthwhile cause, her step toward God himself. And what is also worth mentioning here is that the homily is the confirmation that the à-Dieu may also tighten the bonds of society (Keenan 104). As Matthews remarks, the sermon “binds together the congregation as a black community” (The Sound 83). Additionally, Dobbs observes that the Easter mass “provides a welcome moment of community and peace” (43), proving that there exists a communion among the blacks, which is something that the whites actually lack (Branny 166). We may conclude the deliberation over Dilsey’s final answer given to death by mentioning a Polish reference Faulkner was aware of. In “Foreword to The Faulkner Reader” (1954), Faulkner deduces that, irrespective of the purpose of writing, the artist’s aim is “to uplift man’s heart” (ESPL 181), which is a very 161 In his diaries Jan Lechoń writes about his impressions after reading Faulkner. What the Polish writer observes is that Faulkner’s mind is very religious (Maszewski “William” 483-484).

192 Chapter Four close repetition of the statement expressed in his speech in Stockholm (ESPL 120).162 What Faulkner does not reveal in his Noble Prize address is that the quote turns out to be Sienkiewicz’s formula (Najder 59). As Faulkner testifies, the formula was derived from one of the Polish author’s books kept in his grandparents’ library (ESPL 179, 180).163 Appreciating the Polish mark in the literary output of the American writer, we should mention that Faulkner elaborates upon Sienkiewicz’s belief, adding the following: this hope and desire to uplift man’s heart is completely selfish, completely personal. He [the writer] would lift up man’s heart for his own benefit because in that way he can say No to death… Some day he will be no more, which will not matter then, because isolated and itself invulnerable in the cold print remains that which is capable of engendering still the old deathless excitement. (ESPL 181-182, emphasis added) This No to death, understood by Wadlington as “the confrontation with mortality which tests as it enacts the power to exist” (16), may also be read as Dilsey’s answer to death reflected in her attitude to the Other. If we look at her, this black servant appears to express this No to death in her behavior. Weaker and weaker, she confronts her mortality, but despite her feebleness, she does her best to make her and Others’ lives meaningful. Owing to her efforts, Dilsey “uplifts” the Compsons’ hearts. Thus she arouses this “deathless excitement” Faulkner talks about, showing that existence may be the perception of God in the Other’s face, this being-toward-God beyond Being-towards-death. In A Cultural History of the American Novel, David Minter claims that Faulkner preferred to guarantee Caddy’s right to privacy without putting her in the spotlight (219), which is conspicuous in the whole book, in which we gradually hear less and less about Faulkner’s “heart’s darling” (qtd. in Gwynn and Blotner 6). Nevertheless, as Stonum notes, “her decreasing centrality does not necessarily compromise the centrality of the ideal” (77). By curious paradox, with no voice of her own in the four sections, what a great number of scholars perceive as central in their analysis of Caddy is her promiscuity, instead of the ideal. For Alexander, the name Caddy, or Candace, is “sweet and sexually seductive” (108- 109); for Warren she is “the promiscuous Caddy” (119), and Charles Anderson considers her to be a “promiscuous nymphomaniac” (qtd. in Storhoff 16). While Samuel C. Powell points at “the darkness of her soul” (qtd. in Baum 188), Mayoux simply sees her as “a bitch” (167), and Joseph Gold as “a whore” (28). 162 “Foreword to The Faulkner Reader” of 1954 appears to be a largely extended version of Faulkner’s Nobel Prize address, delivered on December 10, 1950, in Stockholm. 163 Najder claims that Faulkner was familiar with Sienkiewicz’s Trylogia, but remembered and cited just Pan Wołodyjowski, translated by Jeremiah Curtin (59). Faulkner himself calls Sienkiewicz “that old half-forgotten Pole” (ESPL 181).

Faulkner’s Final Answer to Death: Dilsey’s Responsibility and Caddy’s Fecundity 193 Beginning the article on Faulkner’s “Mountain Victory,” whose protagonist bears a certain resemblance to Caddy, Bradley Johnson states that in the vast majority of cases Faulkner creates complex female characters (65). In effect, Caddy’s promiscuity should be viewed with suspicion, if, according to Joy Farmer, she is judged by Quentin, who builds up his misogynic opinions on “his myopic Southern society, which permits just one interpretation of Caddy’s behavior” (321). Therefore all readers should take into account social standards of female conduct accepted by society in the second decade of the twentieth century before passing their judgments (Storhoff 16).164 The truth is that, similarly to Frances Newman’s heroine in The Hard-Boiled Virgin (1926), Caddy does not seem to regard her virginity as relatively important and its loss as the act of deflowering her womanhood. Instead, she appears to care about her lover Dalton. First she refuses to converse with him, thinking that he did harm to her brother Quentin, however, when she realizes that such an occurrence has never taken place, she naturally wants to see Dalton to apologize to him (Watkins 218). Her overquoted promiscuity seems to result from “despair over the loss of Ames,” which she experiences on her return from French Lick (Collins “Miss” 82), where she is forced to participate in the masquerade of chasing after the husband and father of her child. We do not have to believe Faulkner’s comments found in the Appendix that allude to Caddy’s alleged promiscuity. In the Appendix Faulkner makes Caddy a lover of a German staffgeneral, whereas in the sections “Caddy alone has broken out of the vortex of Compson history” (Burton 617). According to Zender, not only does she dream of fleeing from “Southern insularity,” but she ties the knot with the man of the North to stay there after their divorce, too (748). One of Branny’s observations also shows that we cannot say with any certainty whether in the photo the woman next to the German general is really Caddy, because her age could actually indicate Quentin, her daughter (141). And even when Caddy’s entry in the Appendix is scrutinized, the information about her alleged sexual escapades is extremely limited in contrast to the material about Melissa Meek, to whom, surprisingly, its considerable part is devoted. Melissa Meek, a librarian whose aim is to save Caddy, who does not wish to be saved (A 420), primarily comes into existence to highlight the Compson family and Caddy’s figure in the novel, serving as her antithesis (Beck 306). When one thinks of 164 A good example which illustrates American public feelings in the late 1920s is a great commotion after the publication of Frances Newman’s novels The Hard-Boiled Virgin (1926), where the loss of virginity is of little importance, and Dead Lovers Are Faithful Lovers (1928), where the reader sees a wife and her spouse’s lover in a favourable light (Jones 60-61).

194 Chapter Four Melissa, a “mouse-sized and –colored” spinster (A 413), whose description makes her similar to the lifeless shop assistant from Quentin’s narrative, compared to a librarian “among dusty shelves” (SF 155), one certainly kindles an affinity for Caddy, a person of flesh and blood. In addition, similarly to Burton, Beck remarks that the story about Caddy constitutes “an open-ended biography” (303), whereas the short episode about Melissa ends with “the death of a long-sustained retrospective dream” putting a stop to her crusade to save Caddy (309).165 What one of the chapters in Caddy’s biography could be focused on is certainly fecundity as defined by Levinas. Bearing in mind Florence Leaver’s observation on the idea of fecundity in Faulkner (204-205),166 and the traces of Caddy’s actions, we may exemplify Levinas’s otherness seen in the feminine with the story about Faulkner’s “heart’s darling.” First and foremost, the smell of trees makes Caddy embody fecundity (Bleikasten The Ink 51).167 Furthermore, involved in an intimate relationship with Dalton Ames, Caddy discovers the Other as well as sexuality, fighting back the violence of death in the way Levinas discusses it. Without any verbalization, her womanhood is revealed by voluptuousness, or “love of love” (TI 265), which definitely is not a pure satisfaction of sexual desire. It rather stands for the communication of love (Baum 191) manifesting itself through caress visible in the description of her feelings for Dalton: “I would die for him I’ve already died for him I die for him over and over again every time this goes” (SF 188). As Baum states, Caddy’s attention to the opposite sex is the next step on the path to full development (191), so her fondness for Dalton, expressed in the form of a touch, is simply one of the modes of being in Levinas’s terms. And the caress readable in the phrase “I die for him” is nothing else but Caddy’s act of losing herself in the territory “between being and not-yet-being” (TI 259), the territory where the 165 A separate story entitled “Candace” was, in fact, created by Alan Cheuse, who places emphasis on her wish to gain experience (340). The writer, however, touches upon her promiscuity (349). Interestingly enough, to flee from her fate, Cheuse’s Caddy makes an unsuccessful suicidal attempt by stepping into a lake, but she does not manage to carry it out till the end (350). 166 Florence Leaver regards the word “fecund” as one of Faulkner’s favorites. The critic highlights the motif of “the fecund earth” in Yoknapatawpha County, connecting with it the fecundity of the woman and the presence of the moon (205-206). Additionally, for Benjamin S. Lawson, in Go Down Moses “the fecund wilderness world of the deer and bear nonetheless dwindles,” not to mention the childlessness of Ike and Sam Fathers (181). 167 To be exact, Bleikasten perceives Caddy as the embodiment of fecundity as well as of dirtiness (The Ink 51). The scholar also notices that the tree/girl metaphor is a recurrent motif, which appeared earlier in The Marionettes, The Marble Faun, Soldiers’ Pay and Mosquitoes (368).

Faulkner’s Final Answer to Death: Dilsey’s Responsibility and Caddy’s Fecundity 195 sense of touch speaks instead of the sense of speech. We should also mention that Caddy attempts to demonstrate love through caress to the overintellectualized Quentin, who creates the world verbally. When Quentin asks his sister if she hates Dalton, she tries to make her brother understand what has been going on between them: “she held my hand against her chest her heart thudding I turned and caught her arm / Caddy you hate him dont you / she moved my hand up against her throat her heart was hammering there” (SF 187). Obviously, in Caddy’s unplanned game with Dalton, to which Levinas compares caress, there is no talk about physical love aiming at the inception of pregnancy. However, when Quentin is conceived, Caddy enters another stage of her life, namely the plane of fecundity. At the moment when her daughter is born into the world, Caddy also finds herself at the plane of infinity, which apparently distinguishes the sister from the brothers. In the words of Gene Fant, she becomes “the queen of the Compson eunuchs,” which is also a reference to the Acts of the Apostles (Fant 106; Acts 8:27). With the gelded Benjy, with Jason, “the childless bachelor” (A 415), whose “mental and emotional sterility” contributes toward the biological death of the household (Branny 162), with Quentin, for whom “love is just a word” (Baum 191), Caddy is the only Compson who marks her presence by “an act of creation,” giving birth to a child (Bassett “Family” 411). It is thanks to her that the line of the family will not end. Her daughter then is Caddy’s tertium datur, which stands for the reply given to the question of death, because, by giving birth to Quentin, Caddy is the only person in the Compson household who, among the whites, achieves Levinas’s “victory over death” (TO 90).168 Nevertheless, it is in a way only a partial victory on Caddy’s side. First and foremost, Caddy’s intimate relationship with Dalton remains only temporary, so even if her fecundity opens the gates to infinity, Caddy, Dalton, and Quentin the girl do not constitute a family. And when we take into account the fact that Caddy lets Quentin be raised under the Compsons’ roof, which some critics read as the act of abandonment, her victory over finitude may not appear to be complete, either. Certainly, we should evoke Caddy’s unsuccessful attempt to see her daughter through the car window, for which Jason charges her a steep price (SF 254), together with a few other occurrences when she breaks the ban on entering the house. That the episodes illustrating her maternal instinct are not isolated is also visible in Caddy’s long lasting correspondence with Jason. In one of the letters to Jason we read: “I had no answer to my letter about Quentin’s easter 168 Also see Gail L. Mortimer’s conclusion referring to The Hamlet by Faulkner: “Man is helpless in the face of the eternal, fecund, impervious Other, whether field or wilderness or woman” (110).

196 Chapter Four dress. Did it arrive all right? I’ve had no answer to the last two letters I wrote her… You promised you would let me know when she needed things… You are opening my letters to her” (SF 236). In other words, Caddy misses her child dreadfully, which is also accentuated intertextually by Alan Cheuse in his sequel to Caddy’s saga. In Cheuse’s story Caddy states: “Separated from her, I feel like part of my body itself has been taken from me” (349).169 On the other hand, with all due respect to Caddy’s efforts, money, dresses, and regularly sent letters are not able to be a maternal substitute for Quentin. The reiteration of a parent in a child discussed by Levinas (TI 268) is reflected in Quentin’s feelings about the house where she grows up. As it was with her mother, the lack of love, acceptance and guidance makes Quentin feel awkward and uncomfortable in the place where she should receive protection and support. The atmosphere in the decaying family makes her escape from the Compson house in the same way as her mother did in the past, climbing down the same tree (SF 357). Additionally, what Quentin shares with Caddy is curiosity about the world, together with an unwillingness to strictly observe the proprieties, as she seems to be a lone wolf going her own way. Nevertheless, in spite of repeating her mother’s patterns of behavior, Quentin preserves her own “ipseity” mentioned by Levinas (TI 268). What drastically differentiates her selfhood from Caddy’s is her attitude toward Benjy, whom she treats with overwhelming aversion and easily perceivable disrespect. By contrast with her mother, she does not want to have a meal at the same table with Benjy sitting nearby: “Why dont you feed him in the kitchen? It’s like eating with a pig” (SF 86), to say nothing of nourishing Benjy herself, as Caddy was in the habit of doing. In his analysis of Levinas’s writing, Colin Davis touches upon “the reader- Other,” in front of whom “the text is opened out” presenting its own ethical value (99). According to Sundquist, what is open to us in the last section of the novel is the completion of “the crucifixion of the Compsons” (14). Nevertheless, the crucifixion the scholar mentions is not the last word that should conclude the work of Faulkner. As the reader-Other who searches for the answer to the question of death in the Compsons’ faces and in their space, one should respond with Dilsey’s responsibility, which reaches the level of infinity and fights back against death. The second answer is obviously Caddy’s path of fecundity, which, although partially trodden, also reaches the same level of infinity. That is why the last sound perceived by the reader-Other in the Faulknerian novel should be Dilsey’s and Caddy’s “No” to death. 169 According to Minter, men in Yoknapatawpha are more destructive than women, and if the female suffer, they have usually gone through calamitous experiences because of men (A Cultural 221).

Epilogue Treating the theme of death in a light-hearted manner, Faulkner once told a friend: “You know, after all, they put you in a pine box and in a few days the worms have you. Someone might cry for a day or two and after that they’ve forgotten all about you” (qtd. in Minter Faulkner’s 39). More seriously, one year before his death in a 1961 essay, with reference to Albert Camus, Faulkner wrote that “if the only solution to the human dilemma is death, then we are on the wrong road” (ESPL 113, emphasis added). The same essay concluded with a deliberation over the artist’s purpose in writing, in which he mentioned the “same foreknowledge and hatred of death” accompanying writers for all their years (114). Reading these quotes, one may ask why Faulkner wrote The Sound and the Fury, where death leaks out almost on every page, and one may also wonder why, in one of the versions of the introduction to the novel, he claimed that by writing it he had intended the creation of “a beautiful and tragic little girl” (Southern 220). It seems that it was this foreknowledge that forced him to write the first three sections of the novel, whereas this hatred, which is puzzling to some extent, found reflection in the Dilsey section, in which he said “No” to death with a view to standing on the right road again. Faulkner constantly jumped off this right road both before and after the publication of the novel in question, which shows that the subject of death frequently circulated in the author’s mind. One of the themes in Faulkner’s early poetic output was the acceptance of death, together with the loss or the search for a lady (Samway 243). His next novel after the Compsons’ saga, As I Lay Dying (1930), through its very title, revealed the main point touched upon in the work. The ending of Sanctuary (1931), with Temple Drake in the Luxembourg Gardens, was the repetition of the image of “the Luxembourg gardens and death,” which Faulkner had actually conceived in a 1925 prose poem mentioned in a letter to his mother (Selected 17-18). The collection of short stories entitled These 13, published in September 1931, was dedicated to his wife Estelle and to his daughter Alabama, who, born on 11 January of the same year, lived only nine days (Blotner Faulkner 749; Watson 107). His own child’s death must have affected the writer deeply, which, together with other harrowing experiences, made Faulkner return to the theme of mortality again and again, for example, in Absalom, Absalom! (1936), The Wild Palms (1939), and Requiem for a Nun (1951).

198 Epilogue Through his returns to the motif of death, Faulkner paradoxically achieved immortality. It is true that, in the early years of his literary career, he endeavored to win acclaim among an audience of readers. Later, however, he even regretted having signed his books, which were to be the only proof of his existence, as he wrote to Cowley in 1949 (Selected 285). In 1953, Faulkner repeated his conviction that what was important after a writer’s death was “the old deathless excitement” his works should engender (ESPL 182). Nowadays, nobody doubts that, by creating The Sound and the Fury, which the author considered to be “a Tyrrhenian vase,” initially lying near his bed to touch and kiss (Mississippi 224), Faulkner managed to achieve the immortality he envisaged. As he wished, his immortality came with “literary self-dismemberment,” with the transformation of the author into his novels, short stories, and poems (Irwin 159), fortunately representing the whole gallery of vases of different kinds to interpret, even if, in Faulkner’s life, they served as an outlet for personal problems. Having drawn the conclusions in the preceding chapters, what is left to add is that in this work I have proposed one of the paths of thinking that the reader of Faulkner could follow, and certainly there are many other possible interpretations, because one Faulkner does not exist. As Joel Williamson argues in William Faulkner and Southern History, referring to the “placeness” of Southern culture, “there is a place for everything and every person, and everyone and everything ought to be in its place” (403). After placing Freud or Lacan in Yoknapatawpha County, it was time to place Scheler, Heidegger, and Levinas there as well, since, using the last words in the novel, Faulkner in The Sound and the Fury puts death “in its ordered place” (SF 401).
